1

What is React &
the Declarative Model

Interview Question   CORE

What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built a page header that shows the reader's name in a greeting and in a badge.
  • 2 The reader changes the name, your script updates the greeting, and the badge keeps the old name.
  • 3 How do we make every place on the page show the new name?

Plain JavaScript is imperative, React is declarative

Every website shows values that change: the reader's name after they edit their profile, the number of items in a shopping cart, the temperature in a city. When a value changes, the page must show the new value everywhere it appears. So every web developer meets the same question: when a value changes, how does the page change with it?

The browser does not show your HTML file directly. It reads the file, builds an object in memory for every tag, and draws the screen from those objects. Together they are called the DOM (Document Object Model). HTML is the text you write; the DOM is what the browser builds from it and keeps while the page is open. So changing the page always means updating the DOM.

There are two ways to update the DOM when a value changes.

The first way is imperative programming, which you know from plain JavaScript: you give the browser commands. You find the element, then you set its text:

Imperative: find the element, set its text
1const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
Find it
2greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, Elena Ruiz';
Set its text

The first line asks the browser for the element whose id is greeting. The second line replaces the text inside that element. The browser does exactly what each line says and nothing more, so every other element on the page stays as it was. That is why it is called imperative programming: you give the browser every command yourself. The word comes from the Latin imperare, "to command", the same root as emperor. Like an emperor, your code orders every step: find this element, set that text. It fits well when one element changes in one place, like a clock in a corner of the page. It fits badly when the same value appears in many places. If the name also appears in a badge, the badge needs its own two lines, and if you forget them, the badge keeps the old name.

The second way is declarative programming, which this chapter teaches: instead of commands, you declare what the element should show:

Declarative: what the greeting shows
1<p>Welcome back, {readerName}</p>

This looks like HTML, but one part is new: {readerName}. The curly braces mark a place in the markup where a JavaScript value goes, and here that place holds the variable readerName (Lecture 4 shows everything such a place can hold). Notice what is missing: there is no line that finds the <p>, and no line that sets its text. React reads the description, builds the <p> on the page, and puts the current value of readerName inside it. When readerName holds "Elena Ruiz", the page shows "Welcome back, Elena Ruiz". That is why it is called declarative programming: you declare the result, and React updates the DOM to match it. The word comes from the Latin declarare, "to make clear, to announce": you announce what the page should show, and React works out the steps.

The badge works the same way:

Declarative: what the badge shows
1<span>Subscriber: {readerName}</span>

The greeting and the badge read the same readerName. There is no second command to forget, so the two places cannot show different names.

Two ways to update the DOM when a value changes

(1) Update the DOM with imperative programming (plain JavaScript): you give the browser every command yourself, finding each element and setting its text.

(2) Update the DOM with declarative programming (this chapter): you declare what each element should show, and React updates the DOM to match.

React still lets you reach one element directly for the few jobs declarative code cannot do, such as moving the cursor into a search box. Lecture 30 covers that.

React is a JavaScript library for building pages out of components. In this chapter, we write our first component, SiteHeader, which describes the whole header from one value, readerName. We will see why imperative code misses an element, why a value must live in one variable, and what React changes on the page when the value changes. At the end, we compare the two ways again.

In this lesson the name stays fixed in the code. Lecture 14 shows how a value changes while the page is open, and Lecture 15 follows, step by step, how React then updates the page. Other lessons grow this one component: Lecture 5 splits a page into many components, Lecture 6 passes values from one component to another, and Lecture 12 explains why a component must only describe the page and never change it.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • In plain JavaScript I find each element and change its text. What do I write instead in React?
  • The name shows in two places. Do I write it twice?
  • When the name changes, does React rebuild the whole header and wipe what the reader typed?

You need only HTML and plain JavaScript:

  • HTML: Tags such as <p> and <span> describe the page, and an id such as id="greeting" gives one tag a name.
  • Plain JavaScript: const and let store a value in a variable, and + joins two strings into one.

The browser keeps the page as a tree of objects

The DOM from the opening is a tree: its objects nest the same way the tags nest in the HTML file. Each object in it is called a DOM node. What you see on the screen is drawn from the DOM, so changing a node changes the page.

Plain JavaScript changes the page through these nodes. Here are the three tools the questions use:

Three plain JavaScript tools
1const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
Find one node
2greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, Elena';
Replace its text
3const header = document.getElementById('header');
4header.innerHTML = '<p>Welcome back, Elena</p>';
Replace all inside

document.getElementById searches the DOM for the node with that id and gives it back. textContent replaces the text inside one node. innerHTML is bigger: it takes a string of HTML, throws away every node inside the element, and builds new nodes from the string. The browser does each of these at the moment the line runs.

A component is a function that returns a description

In React, the description of the page lives in a component: a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns markup. Lecture 2 gives the full rules. Here is the header as a component:

SiteHeader returns a description
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena';
The name, stored once
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p>Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span>Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 </header>
8 );
9}

SiteHeader is an ordinary function. The two words in front of it, export default, let another file use it (Lecture 8). Inside it, readerName holds the name. The function returns markup that looks like HTML: a <header> with a greeting and a badge, and {readerName} in both. This markup is called JSX. It is JavaScript, not HTML, so a few names differ: the HTML attribute class is written className. Lecture 3 shows what JSX becomes and why.

Our code never calls SiteHeader and never touches the DOM. React calls the function, reads the description it returns, and builds the DOM nodes from it: a <header>, a <p> with "Welcome back, Elena", and a <span> with "Subscriber: Elena". React builds them inside one element of the HTML page that we hand to it, and Lecture 9 shows how. A component returns what the page should show, and React builds the page from it.

Principles of React: Declarative Synchronization

QUESTION 1

Finding elements by identifier misses unqueried widgets

The site header displays a personalized greeting and a subscriber status badge. In plain JavaScript, an update script searches for elements by string identifier and updates their text content directly:

updateHeaderUser (Naive Script)
1function updateHeaderUser(name) {
2 const greeting = document.getElementById('greeting');
3 if (greeting) {
4 greeting.textContent = 'Welcome back, ' + name;
Updates greeting
5 }
6}
The badge query was omitted from the script

When we run updateHeaderUser('Elena Ruiz') the greeting updates to "Welcome back, Elena Ruiz", while the badge remains stuck on "Subscriber: Elena".

Why does updating the name update the greeting while leaving the badge on the old text?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The imperative script updated one queried element and skipped the badge.

In plain JavaScript, our code must query every matching DOM node by hand. If a script searches for greeting but forgets badge, the browser leaves the unqueried element unchanged. The greeting displays the new name while the badge displays the old name, creating immediate state drift between memory and the screen.

In React, we do not query elements by identifier. Instead, we write SiteHeader, a component function that returns markup describing the entire header for the current data:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Authoritative value in memory
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 </header>
8 );
9}

React calls SiteHeader, reads the returned description, and builds the real DOM elements on the page. Both the greeting and the badge display "Elena Ruiz". Because our code never queries the DOM, no element can be skipped or left behind.

Imperative hunting compared to declarative description
Imperative DOM Scripting:
App Code  --- document.getElementById('greeting') ---> [ DOM: Greeting ] updated
App Code  - - - (forgot badge query) - - - - - - - - > [ DOM: Badge ]    STALE

Declarative React Component:
Data ('Elena Ruiz') ---> SiteHeader() ---> [ Description Tree ] ---> DOM updated
PRINCIPLE 1

Describe what the page shows for the data instead of changing elements by hand

In plain JavaScript, code searches the document for each element and changes its text directly. If an update misses one element, the screen shows old data. In React, a component function returns a description of the markup for the current data, and React builds the page from that description. We describe what the interface shows instead of writing commands to find and change elements.

We should do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'Elena';
return <h1>Welcome, {name}</h1>;
React builds element
}
We should not do this:
function updateHeader(name) {
const el = document.getElementById('name');
if (el) el.textContent = name;
misses unqueried elements
}

In our SiteHeader component, writing plain JavaScript required updateHeaderUser to search for greeting and badge by their string identifiers. Forgetting badge left the screen showing "Elena" in the badge alongside "Elena Ruiz" in the greeting. In React, we write SiteHeader as a function that returns the complete header markup. React calls SiteHeader, reads the returned description, and constructs the DOM elements on the screen. Because our code never queries the DOM, no element can be skipped or left behind.

QUESTION 2

The name shows in two places across the header

The reader's name appears inside both the greeting paragraph and the subscriber badge. A developer pastes static markup into the component and hardcodes the initial name into the badge:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Updated local variable
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: Elena</span>
Hardcoded text
7 </header>
8 );
9}

When React renders this component, the greeting paragraph displays "Welcome back, Elena Ruiz", but the badge displays "Subscriber: Elena".

Why does the badge still display Elena after the variable was changed to Elena Ruiz?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The badge markup contains a hardcoded string instead of reading the variable.

Typing static text into markup duplicates data. The greeting paragraph reads the variable readerName, so it displays "Elena Ruiz". But the badge contains the literal text "Subscriber: Elena", completely detached from the variable. When the variable updates, the hardcoded string remains frozen.

The fix is to store the name in one local variable and read that variable in every place that displays it using curly braces {readerName}:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Single source of truth
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 </header>
8 );
9}

The variable readerName serves as a single source of truth. Both the greeting and the badge derive their text from that single variable. When readerName changes to "Elena Ruiz", both elements update together because both are built from the same value.

Single variable read in multiple elements
Duplicate static text:
Variable ('Elena Ruiz') ---> [ Greeting: Elena Ruiz ]
Hardcoded String        ---> [ Badge: Elena ] (state drift)

Single source of truth:
Variable ('Elena Ruiz') ----+---> [ Greeting: {readerName} ] (Elena Ruiz)
                            |
                            +---> [ Badge: {readerName} ]    (Elena Ruiz)
PRINCIPLE 2

Keep each value in one variable and read it everywhere it appears

When a value appears in more than one place on the screen, do not type it into the markup more than once. Store the value in a single local variable and read that variable in every place that shows it using curly braces. Because every part of the markup reads from this single source of truth, all parts update together and can never disagree.

We should do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'Elena';
single source of truth
return (
<div>
<h1>Welcome, {name}</h1>
<span>Subscriber: {name}</span>
</div>
);
}
We should not do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'Elena';
return (
<div>
<h1>Welcome, {name}</h1>
<span>Subscriber: Elena</span>
fixed text drifts
</div>
);
}

In SiteHeader, pasting the static text "Subscriber: Elena" directly into the badge markup caused state drift the moment readerName changed to "Elena Ruiz". The greeting read the updated variable, while the badge stayed frozen on the old literal string. Replacing the fixed text with {readerName} ensures that both elements read the exact same variable. When readerName is updated in our code, both the greeting and the badge reflect the new name simultaneously.

QUESTION 3

Rebuilding the header wipes the search box

The site header contains a search input alongside the user greeting. The user types "elections" into the search box. To update the user name, an imperative script replaces the container HTML with a template string:

updateHeaderWithInput (Naive Script)
1function updateHeaderWithInput(name) {
2 const header = document.getElementById('header');
Finds container node
3 const html = '<p>Welcome, ' + name + '</p><input placeholder="Search..." />';
4 header.innerHTML = html;
Wipes living input element
5}

The script runs, and the name updates to "Elena Ruiz". But the text "elections" disappears from the search box, and keyboard focus drops back to the document body.

Why does updating the name wipe out the search text and lose keyboard cursor focus?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Assigning to innerHTML destroyed the input element and created a brand-new one.

When JavaScript assigns a new string to innerHTML, the browser engine throws away all existing DOM nodes inside that container. Even though the new HTML string includes an <input> tag, the browser constructs a brand-new DOM element from scratch. The typed text belonged to the destroyed element, and the active cursor belonged to that destroyed node. As a result, the search query is lost and keyboard focus is reset to the page body.

In React, we describe the entire header from data, including the input element:

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Authoritative value in memory
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 <input placeholder="Search..." />
Node identity preserved
8 </header>
9 );
10}

When data changes, React does not rebuild the container with innerHTML. Instead, React compares the new description with the previous one. React sees that the <input> element has not changed. It applies the minimal necessary operations: it updates only the text nodes containing the reader name. The <input> element remains the exact same DOM node on the page, so the typed query and active cursor focus stay completely intact.

innerHTML compared to React update
Destructive innerHTML:
Old: [ <p>Elena</p> ] [ <input> "elections" (focused) ]
      | container.innerHTML replaces nodes
New: [ <p>Elena Ruiz</p> ] [ <input> "" (focus lost) ] (new DOM nodes)

React surgical update:
Old: [ <p>Elena</p> ] [ <input> "elections" (focused) ]
      | React diffs descriptions and patches text node only
New: [ <p>Elena Ruiz</p> ] [ <input> "elections" (focused) ] (same input node)
PRINCIPLE 3

When data changes, React updates only the text that differs

When data updates, React does not destroy and recreate elements on the page. Replacing containers with innerHTML destroys living elements, wiping typed input text and losing cursor focus. Instead, React compares the new description with the previous one and applies the minimal changes needed. Unchanged elements remain in place, so an input field keeps what the user typed and keeps its focus.

We should do this:
function Header() {
const name = 'Elena';
return (
<div>
<h1>Welcome, {name}</h1>
updates text
<input placeholder="Search..." />
keeps focus
</div>
);
}
We should not do this:
function updateHeader(name) {
const container = document.getElementById('header');
const html = '<h1>Welcome, ' + name + '</h1><input>';
container.innerHTML = html;
wipes input text and focus
}

In plain JavaScript, assigning a new string to header.innerHTML tore down the existing search box. The user's typed search query "elections" vanished, and the active cursor was thrown out of the input. In React, changing readerName from "Elena" to "Elena Ruiz" causes React to compare the new description with the old one. React observes that the <input> element and the layout container are unchanged. It mutates only the text nodes containing the name. The search box keeps its text, its event listeners, and its active cursor focus.

Step 1
First, we declare the site header component
<SiteHeader.jsx>

We construct SiteHeader.jsx to establish the declarative foundation for our header. Instead of writing separate HTML tags and later writing scripts to query them, we define a component function that returns our layout description.

We store the reader's name in a single local variable, readerName, and project it into both the greeting paragraph and the subscriber badge using curly braces. Notice that our code contains zero calls to document.getElementById and zero calls to textContent.

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Authoritative value in memory
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 </header>
8 );
9}

Because SiteHeader describes its output directly from readerName, state drift is eliminated at the architectural level. If a developer changes readerName in memory, both widgets update simultaneously during the next render.

Step 2
Next, we add the interactive search input
<SiteHeader.jsx>

We enhance SiteHeader.jsx by adding a search input <input placeholder="Search articles..." /> alongside our greeting and badge. In naive JavaScript updates using innerHTML, appending or modifying text inside the header destroys all living input elements, clearing whatever the reader typed and resetting cursor focus.

In React, the input is declared directly as part of the component description. When reader data updates, React keeps the exact same <input> DOM node on the screen, preserving user text and keyboard focus without manual intervention.

SiteHeader.jsx
1export default function SiteHeader() {
2 const readerName = 'Elena Ruiz';
Authoritative value in memory
3 return (
4 <header className="site-header">
5 <p id="greeting">Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span id="badge">Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 <input placeholder="Search..." />
Focus preserved
8 </header>
9 );
10}

Notice that static elements, dynamic text, and interactive inputs coexist cleanly within a single component. React manages the boundary between unchanging nodes and dynamic text nodes automatically.

Step 3
Finally, we mount the site header inside
<App.jsx>

To complete our application, we mount SiteHeader inside the root component App.jsx. In standard JavaScript applications, assembling a page often required separate initialization scripts to locate root containers and inject HTML strings.

In React, the entire user interface organizes into a unified component hierarchy. App.jsx acts as the primary root container, embedding SiteHeader into the application layout. When React renders App, it evaluates the component tree in memory and constructs the resulting DOM elements in a single, predictable operation.

App.jsx
1import SiteHeader from './components/SiteHeader.jsx';
Header component
2
3export default function App() {
Renders application root
4 return (
5 <main className="app-container">
6 <SiteHeader />
Mounts declarative header at root
7 </main>
8 );
9}

The application now runs as a cohesive declarative tree. React mounts the component into the browser document and manages all future updates through description diffing rather than manual DOM manipulation.

Component Summary

App

The application root mounts the top-level layout. It embeds the site header into the primary page document, anchoring the component hierarchy without directly querying or mutating browser DOM nodes.

SiteHeader

The header component holds reader identity in memory as a single source of truth. It projects that value into both the greeting and subscriber badge via JSX curly braces, ensuring all widgets update together while preserving input focus.

In plain JavaScript DOM scripting, keeping multiple header widgets synchronized required writing fragile element queries and manual string setters that broke whenever markup identifiers changed. In React, the entire header derives from a clean, declarative component function. Because SiteHeader maintains reader identity in a single variable and reads it everywhere, the greeting and badge remain in permanent synchronization. Changing the reader's name updates every element across the screen simultaneously with zero risk of state drift.

Where you will meet this

  1. Multi-Widget Navigation Bars: When a user logs in, their display name, notification count, and account status must appear synchronously across desktop navigation bars, sidebar drawers, and profile banners. Declarative components ensure that every element reflects the exact same data without manual element queries.
  2. E-Commerce Shopping Carts: The number of items in a user's cart appears in the header cart pill, the checkout button badge, and the order summary sidebar. Reading cart count from a single variable guarantees that item totals match across the entire screen.
  3. Search Filters and Form Headers: Live search bars, active filter pills, and result counters all display aspects of the current query. Declarative rendering ensures that updating the filter count never wipes the user's active search input or interrupts cursor focus.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is React, and how does its declarative, component-based model differ from plain JavaScript DOM scripting?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not merely testing whether you know how to write a component function. They are probing whether you understand the fundamental architectural shift from imperative DOM mutation to declarative state synchronization. A junior developer talks about convenience or shorter syntax. A senior engineer explains that imperative DOM scripting couples application logic directly to fragile document queries, creating inevitable state drift when data appears in multiple widgets. They articulate that React models the user interface as a pure projection of data, computing minimal necessary DOM mutations in memory to preserve element identity and input focus.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is claiming that "React is faster than the real DOM because the Virtual DOM has zero performance cost." That claim fails the interview. A well-written, hand-optimized DOM script targeting a single node can execute faster than React's component evaluation and diffing passes. React's true value is predictable synchronization, not raw micro-benchmark speed. Another dangerous trap is telling the interviewer that React throws away and rebuilds the DOM on every render. If React rebuilt the DOM tree, every active text input would lose focus and unsubmitted form state would vanish. React diffs descriptions in memory and surgically mutates only changed text nodes.

3. What is Actually Going On

In plain JavaScript, we write imperative commands that find specific elements by identifier and mutate them step by step. If our code misses one element, the screen shows stale data.

In React, we write component functions that return JSX describing what the screen should look like for the current data. React calls our component, evaluates the returned description, and constructs the real DOM elements.

When a value like readerName updates, React calls the component again, compares the new description with the previous one, and applies the minimal necessary operations. It changes only the specific text that differs, leaving living DOM nodes and active keyboard focus completely intact.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this model gets tricky in production is when developers carry old imperative habits into React applications. Attempting to query DOM nodes directly with document.getElementById inside a React component bypasses React's synchronization pipeline, creating severe conflicts between React's in-memory model and physical browser pixels. Similarly, using innerHTML or destructive container updates inside a component destroys living DOM node identity, wiping input selections and breaking accessibility focus rings. Embracing React means fully trusting declarative data projection and delegating physical DOM mutations entirely to the library.

Glossary

  • DOM (Document Object Model): The objects the browser builds in memory from the HTML, one for every tag, arranged as a tree. The screen is drawn from the DOM, so changing the page means updating the DOM.
  • Imperative programming: Code that gives the browser every command itself, such as finding an element and setting its text. From the Latin imperare, "to command".
  • Declarative programming: Code that declares what the page should show for the current data, while React updates the DOM to match. From the Latin declarare, "to make clear, to announce".
  • State Drift: A defect where two or more elements on the screen show conflicting or out-of-date information because manual updates failed to synchronize every matching node.
  • Component: A JavaScript function whose name starts with an uppercase letter that returns a description of user interface markup in JSX.
  • Single Source of Truth: The architectural practice of storing a piece of data in one place and reading that exact value everywhere it is displayed to prevent disagreement.
  • Minimal Necessary Operations: React's strategy of comparing new interface descriptions with previous ones and updating only the specific text nodes or attributes that changed.

Beyond the basics

  • Describing user interfaces with components: A comprehensive introduction to defining reusable component functions and organizing modular interface files (see react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui).
  • Thinking about UI declaratively: Contrast imperative step-by-step programming with declarative state-driven interface design using concrete browser scenarios (see react.dev/learn/reacting-to-input-with-state).
  • Render and commit mechanics: Detailed breakdown of how React evaluates component descriptions in memory and commits minimal operations to the physical DOM (see react.dev/learn/render-and-commit).
  • Rules of components and pure rendering: Core constraints governing component functions, ensuring predictable execution and zero side effects during rendering (see react.dev/reference/rules/react-calls-components-and-hooks).
  • Your first React component: Practical guide to component capitalization rules, JSX return contracts, and hierarchical composition (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Declarative Interface Projection

➔ ALWAYS describe what the page shows for the current data instead of writing imperative commands to find and mutate elements.

➔ IF data updates across the screen THEN let React compute the minimal necessary operations instead of replacing containers with innerHTML.

❒ Multi-Widget Data Consistency

➔ ALWAYS store shared values in a single local variable and read that variable in every place that displays it.

➔ IF multiple elements display the same reader identity THEN read the value via JSX curly braces so that widgets can never drift out of sync.

❒ DOM Node Identity and Input Focus

➔ ALWAYS delegate DOM mutation to React's diffing engine to preserve living node identity, active text selections, and keyboard focus.

➔ NEVER use innerHTML to rebuild containers holding input fields because destroying living DOM elements wipes typed text and resets focus to the document body.

DO THIS: derive all interface markup from a single variable in memory

5 <p>Welcome back, {readerName}</p>
6 <span>Subscriber: {readerName}</span>
7 <input placeholder="Search articles..." />
8 </header>
9 );
10}

DO NOT DO THIS: query elements by identifier to mutate them by hand

Component Anatomy &
the Capitalization Rule

Interview Question   CORE

What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built an article card component to display a headline and summary.
  • 2 You mount it with <articleCard />, but the page stays blank and the function never runs.
  • 3 What rules govern how we write and name a component?

Calling a function yourself or letting React run it

Every website breaks its interface into reusable pieces: a card for an article, a button for an action, a row for a comment. In JavaScript, we write functions to build these pieces. So every web developer meets the same question: when we write a function that describes a piece of the user interface, how do we run it and put it on the page?

There are two ways to run a function that describes UI.

The first way is a function call, which you know from plain JavaScript: you call the function with parentheses yourself:

Function call: you run the function yourself
1const card = articleCard();
Runs immediately

Inside articleCard(), the code runs right away. Your code calls the function, waits for it to finish, and takes the returned value. The browser evaluates each line synchronously at that exact moment. That is why it is called a function call: our code issues the call and controls when it happens. It fits well for helper functions that compute values, such as calculating a shopping cart total or formatting a date. It fits badly for building a React interface: if you call component functions directly, React cannot track when they run or coordinate updates to the page.

The second way is a component tag, which React uses and this chapter teaches: instead of calling the function with parentheses, you write its name as a capitalized tag in markup:

Component tag: React runs the function
1<ArticleCard />

Notice what is missing: there are no parentheses () after ArticleCard. You do not call the function. Writing <ArticleCard /> hands React a reference to the function itself. React takes custody of that function, decides when the page needs it, and calls ArticleCard() during its render phase. That is why it is called a component tag: you declare where the component belongs in the markup, and React handles the execution.

A second component works the same way:

Component tag: author badge
1<AuthorBadge />

Our code never calls AuthorBadge(). React calls AuthorBadge() when rendering the layout, reads the markup it returns, and builds the HTML elements on the screen.

Two ways to run a function that describes UI

(1) Run a function with a function call (plain JavaScript): you call the function with parentheses yourself, evaluating its lines immediately.

(2) Run a function with a component tag (this chapter): you write its name as a capitalized tag in markup, and React calls the function during render.

Calling a component function directly also bypasses element tracking and breaks the order of Hooks when components hold state. Lecture 37 covers that rule.

In this chapter, we write our first reusable component, ArticleCard. We will see who calls it and when, why component names must start with a capital letter, why long markup after return needs parentheses, and why components must be defined at the top level of the file. At the end, we compare the naive JavaScript reflex against React's component rules.

In this lesson the card displays fixed text. Later lessons grow this component: Lecture 3 explains the JSX syntax it returns, Lecture 4 puts values inside it with curly braces, and Lecture 5 nests cards inside a larger page. Lecture 6 passes different stories into the card with props, and Lecture 12 explains why a component must always return the same markup for the same data.

This lesson answers four questions:

  • Who calls my component function, and when does it run?
  • Does capitalizing a component name change how React runs it?
  • Why does placing markup on a new line after return produce a blank card?
  • Can I declare a component inside another component function?

The questions stand on what Lecture 1 established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A React component is a function that returns a description of the UI in JSX, and React builds the DOM elements from that description.
  • Plain JavaScript & HTML: Functions take parameters and return values with return. HTML tags describe elements on the page.

Passing a component tag hands React a function reference

A React component is a regular JavaScript function that returns JSX markup describing a slice of the user interface. We use export default to mark the main component function of a file so that other files can import and reuse it. Unlike monolithic HTML files where markup and behavior live in separate documents, a component packages structure and presentation into a single cohesive unit.

In standard JavaScript, when we want a function to run immediately, we write parentheses after its name, such as ArticleCard(). Calling a function evaluates its lines right away and produces its return value synchronously. In React, our code does not call component functions directly. When we write <ArticleCard /> in markup, we do not call ArticleCard(). Instead, JSX passes the function itself, known as a function reference, to React.

React takes custody of the function reference and enters its render phase. React decides when to call the component function based on what is happening in the application. When React renders the parent layout, it calls ArticleCard, inspects the JSX markup it returns, and builds the corresponding DOM elements on the screen. Because React orchestrates rendering, it can optimize screen updates, coordinate child lifecycles, and skip unnecessary work.

Capital letters tell the compiler to build a component

Browsers natively recognize a fixed catalog of HTML tags, such as <article>, <h2>, <p>, and <button>. A web application combines these native building blocks with custom components created by developers. When a compiler parses markup containing both native tags and custom components, it must determine whether each tag represents a built-in browser element or a JavaScript function.

React resolves this distinction using a strict casing rule: PascalCase. Under PascalCase, the first letter of each compound word is capitalized, such as ArticleCard. When the JSX compiler converts markup into JavaScript code, it checks the casing of the tag name. If the tag begins with a lowercase letter, the compiler emits a string literal: _jsx("article"). If the tag begins with an uppercase letter, the compiler emits an unquoted variable identifier: _jsx(ArticleCard).

If a developer accidentally names a component with a lowercase letter and mounts <articleCard />, the compiler treats it as a native HTML tag. React instructs the browser to create an element named articlecard, which the browser appends as an empty, unstyled DOM node. Because this is a frequent developer mistake, React prints two clear warning messages in the browser development console: one warning that the tag uses incorrect casing and should use PascalCase, and a second warning that the tag is unrecognized in the browser.

JavaScript inserts semicolons after isolated return keywords

JavaScript includes a language mechanism called automatic semicolon insertion, or ASI. When the JavaScript parser reaches the end of a line, it checks whether the statement is complete. If the keyword return stands completely alone on its line, the parser treats the return statement as finished and automatically inserts an invisible semicolon immediately after it: return;.

If a developer writes return on one line and places multi-line JSX markup on the next line, the function immediately terminates and returns undefined. The JSX markup below the return statement is unreachable and never executes. React receives undefined for the component, paints nothing on the screen, and reports no error in the browser window. Bundlers such as esbuild emit a build warning alerting the developer that an expression is unreachable due to an automatically inserted semicolon.

To prevent automatic semicolon insertion when returning multi-line markup, developers open a parenthesis ( on the exact same line as the return keyword. The opening parenthesis signals to the ECMAScript parser that the return expression is incomplete and continues across multiple lines. The parser waits until it encounters the matching closing parenthesis ); before ending the statement, allowing the complete JSX tree to evaluate reliably.

Defining a function inside another creates a new function on every run

In JavaScript, developers frequently declare helper functions inside other functions. A function declared inside the body of an outer function is called a nested function. Every time the outer function executes, JavaScript creates and allocates a brand-new inner function in memory with a distinct object reference.

When a developer defines a React component inside the body of another component, this allocation becomes an architectural bug. Every time the outer component renders, it defines a completely new component function. When React compares the new render with the previous one, it sees a different function reference at that position in the tree. React concludes that the old component was removed and an entirely new component was mounted in its place.

Because React treats different component functions as completely different elements, it destroys the existing DOM subtree and constructs new DOM nodes from scratch. If the component contains an interactive <input>, any text the user typed is immediately destroyed, and keyboard cursor focus is lost. To preserve component identity across renders, developers define every component at the top level of the file, outside and alongside other components.

Principles of React: Component Anatomy

QUESTION 1

Writing a component does not run it until markup uses it

A developer creates a new article card component and adds a logging statement to track when the function executes:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 console.log('ArticleCard runs');
Logs each component execution
3 return <article className="card">Morning Dispatch</article>;
4}

In App.jsx, the developer defines the layout container without mounting the card. The browser renders the shell, and the console displays nothing. Next, the developer adds <ArticleCard /> twice inside App.jsx. The browser displays two article cards, and the console logs "ArticleCard runs" twice.

Who calls ArticleCard, and when does it run?

ANSWER

The code works as React intended. React calls the function when another component renders markup that names it.

Declaring a component function does not execute it. In plain JavaScript, declaring function ArticleCard() allocates the function in memory, but nothing runs until code invokes it. In React, our application code never writes ArticleCard(). Instead, App returns markup containing <ArticleCard />. Writing the tag hands React a function reference.

While React renders App, it encounters the tag, invokes ArticleCard(), and takes custody of the returned <article> description. If <ArticleCard /> is written twice, React calls the function twice, producing two separate <article> elements. If no markup references the component, React never executes the function. When inspecting the browser DOM in Developer Tools, the elements panel shows <main> and two <article> tags; the custom tag <ArticleCard> never exists in the DOM.

Function reference passed in markup compared to execution during render
Markup in App:  <ArticleCard />  ---> Passes function reference to React
Render Phase:   React runs App   ---> React calls ArticleCard()
                                 ---> Receives <article> description
Browser DOM:    <main> contains <article>, never <ArticleCard>
PRINCIPLE 1

React calls a component when markup names its tag

When we write a component, our code does not call its function. We write its name as a tag, such as <Card />, inside another component's markup. The tag hands React a reference to the function. While React renders the parent, it calls the component function and places the returned HTML elements into the DOM. The browser DOM shows the HTML tags the function returned, never the component tag.

We should do this:
function App() {
return <Card />;
React calls Card when rendering App
}

In our ArticleCard component, adding console.log('ArticleCard runs') proves who controls execution. When App returns an empty <main> container without <ArticleCard />, the function never runs, and the console stays silent. When App mounts <ArticleCard /> twice, React evaluates ArticleCard twice, printing two log messages and placing two separate <article> elements into the DOM. In browser Developer Tools, the living tree displays two <article> nodes; the custom tag <ArticleCard> never exists in the browser DOM.

QUESTION 2

A lowercase component tag leaves an empty element in the DOM

A developer writes an article card using standard JavaScript camelCase conventions, naming the function articleCard and mounting it as <articleCard />:

articleCard (Naive Lowercase Declaration)
1function articleCard() {
2 return (
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
Headline never renders
5 </article>
6 );
7}
8export default function App() {
9 return <articleCard />;
Compiles to native HTML string literal
10}

The build compiles cleanly, but the browser displays an empty space. When the developer inspects the DOM in Developer Tools, the elements panel shows <articlecard></articlecard>, and the development console displays two warnings about incorrect casing and an unrecognized tag.

Why does articleCard compile cleanly while displaying nothing on the screen?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Lowercase tags instruct React to create native HTML elements rather than calling component functions.

When the JSX compiler parses <articleCard />, it inspects the first character of the tag name. Because a is lowercase, the compiler assumes it is a built-in browser element, compiling it to _jsx("articlecard", {}). At runtime, React passes that string to document.createElement("articlecard") Because HTML allows custom elements, the browser instantiates an empty HTMLUnknownElement with no styles and no children. The JavaScript function articleCard() is never executed. React detects the mismatched casing and logs two warning messages to the development console.

The fix is capitalizing the first letter of the component name in both the function declaration and the JSX tag:

ArticleCard (PascalCase Correction)
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
Headline displays reliably
5 </article>
6 );
7}
8export default function App() {
9 return <ArticleCard />;
Emits unquoted function identifier
10}

The uppercase initial letter tells the JSX compiler to emit an unquoted function identifier _jsx(ArticleCard, {}). React receives the function reference from memory, executes ArticleCard(), and paints the headline and summary to the screen.

Compiler AST branch on tag casing
Lowercase 'a':
  <articleCard /> ---> _jsx("articlecard")
                  ---> document.createElement("articlecard")
                  ---> empty unknown DOM element

Uppercase 'A':
  <ArticleCard /> ---> _jsx(ArticleCard)
                  ---> React calls ArticleCard()
                  ---> living article DOM element
PRINCIPLE 2

Start every component name with a capital letter

PascalCase a naming convention where the first letter of each word is capitalized

In JSX, the first letter of a tag tells the compiler what to create. A lowercase tag tells the compiler to request a native HTML element from the browser, so the function never runs and the browser creates an empty unknown element. A capitalized name in PascalCase tells the compiler to reference our function, allowing React to run it and put its markup on the screen.

We should do this:
function Card() {
return <article>Content</article>;
}
<Card />;
React runs capitalized component function
We should not do this:
function card() {
return <article>Content</article>;
}
<card />;
lowercase tag creates empty HTML element

In ArticleCard, writing function articleCard() and rendering <articleCard /> produced a silent failure on screen. The terminal reported no build errors, but the browser DOM contained an empty <articlecard> node with zero styles and zero child elements. Inspecting the browser console revealed two diagnostic warnings: one explaining that <articleCard /> uses incorrect casing and should use PascalCase, and another noting that <articleCard> is unrecognized. Changing the name to ArticleCard in both the function declaration and the JSX tag allowed React to execute the function and display the headline and summary.

QUESTION 3

Starting markup on the line after return returns nothing

A developer formats ArticleCard by placing the <article> tag on a new line below return for visual clarity:

ArticleCard (Naked Multi-Line Return)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return
Automatic semicolon inserted here
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
Unreachable markup
5 </article>;
6}

In the browser, the article card is completely missing, with zero errors on the page or in the console. In the terminal build output, the bundler emits a warning that the following expression is not returned because of an automatically inserted semicolon.

Why does placing markup on the line below return leave the card blank?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Automatic semicolon insertion causes the function to return undefined before reaching the markup.

JavaScript features automatic semicolon insertion. When the engine encounters a line break directly after return without an expression on that same line, it inserts a semicolon. The function evaluates return;, immediately terminating and returning undefined. The multi-line JSX expression below it is never evaluated. React receives undefined for ArticleCard and renders an empty slot, displaying nothing on the screen without throwing an error in the browser.

The fix is opening a parenthesis ( on the exact same line as the return keyword:

ArticleCard (Parenthesized Return Fix)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Opening parenthesis connects expression across lines
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
Evaluates reliably
5 </article>
6 );
7}

The opening parenthesis signals to the JavaScript engine that the return statement continues across multiple lines until the closing parenthesis );. Automatic semicolon insertion is prevented, and the component function evaluates the entire JSX tree.

Automatic semicolon insertion on isolated return
return             ---> JavaScript inserts semicolon: return;
                        (terminates early and evaluates to undefined)
  <article> ...    ---> Unreachable code never evaluated

return (           ---> Parenthesis signals expression continuation
  <article> ...    ---> Evaluates complete JSX tree reliably
PRINCIPLE 3

Open parentheses on the same line as return for multi-line markup

automatic semicolon insertion JavaScript inserting a semicolon after an isolated return keyword

When the return keyword stands alone on its line, JavaScript automatically inserts a semicolon after it. The function returns undefined, ignoring any markup written on following lines and leaving the screen completely blank. To return multi-line markup, open a parenthesis on the same line as return so JavaScript knows the expression continues.

We should do this:
return (
<article>Content</article>
evaluated as return expression
);
We should not do this:
return
semicolon inserted here, returns undefined
<article>Content</article>;
unreachable code never evaluated

In ArticleCard, formatting the component with return on line 2 and <article> on line 3 triggered automatic semicolon insertion. The JavaScript runtime inserted a semicolon after return;, causing ArticleCard to return undefined immediately. In the browser, the article card disappeared with zero console errors, while the terminal build warned that the following expression was unreachable. Adding opening and closing parentheses around the markup connected the return statement across lines, restoring the article card to the browser view.

QUESTION 4

Defining a component inside another component recreates it on every render

A developer notices that ArticleCard is only used inside App.jsx, so they define function ArticleCard() inside the body of function App()

App.jsx (Nested Component Anti-Pattern)
1export default function App() {
2 function ArticleCard() {
Reallocated on every render of App
3 return (
4 <article className="article-card">
5 <input placeholder="Feedback..." />
Input text wiped on render
6 </article>
7 );
8 }
9 return <ArticleCard />;
React destroys and rebuilds DOM subtree
10}

On initial page load, the article card renders normally. But when App re-renders, any text typed into the <input> field vanishes, and keyboard cursor focus resets.

Why does defining ArticleCard inside App cause its DOM elements to reset on subsequent renders?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Defining a component inside another creates a brand-new function identity on every parent render.

In JavaScript, declaring a function inside another creates a new function object in memory every time the outer function runs. When App renders again, it executes from the first line, allocating a fresh ArticleCard function with a different memory reference. React compares the previous element descriptor with the new element descriptor. Because the component function references differ, React concludes that an entirely different component type has replaced the old one.

React destroys the existing DOM subtree and constructs brand-new elements from scratch. Any internal DOM state, such as text typed into an <input> or active cursor focus, is immediately wiped out. In addition, rebuilding DOM nodes on every render is substantially slower than surgical property patching.

The fix is moving function ArticleCard() to the top level of the module file, outside and alongside function App()

Top-Level Component Declaration
1function ArticleCard() {
Single stable function identity
2 return (
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <input placeholder="Feedback..." />
Input text retained
5 </article>
6 );
7}
8export default function App() {
9 return <ArticleCard />;
Preserves living DOM elements
10}

When declared at the top level, ArticleCard retains a stable function reference across every render of App. React recognizes that the component type is identical, updates only what changed, and preserves existing DOM elements, user input text, and cursor focus.

Nested component definition compared to top-level declaration
Nested:
  App() render 1 ---> creates ArticleCard_A
  App() render 2 ---> creates ArticleCard_B (new identity -> destroys DOM)

Top-level:
  Module loads   ---> creates ArticleCard once
  App() render 1 ---> uses ArticleCard
  App() render 2 ---> uses ArticleCard (stable identity -> preserves DOM)
PRINCIPLE 4

Define every component at the top level of the file

nested function a function defined inside the body of another function

Defining a component inside another component creates a new function object every time the outer component runs. Because React sees a different component type on every render, it destroys the existing DOM elements and builds new ones from scratch, wiping out typed input text and resetting focus. Always declare components at the top level of the file so their identity remains stable.

We should do this:
function Child() {
return <p>Content</p>;
stable function identity
}
function Parent() {
return <Child />;
reuses existing DOM across renders
}
We should not do this:
function Parent() {
function Child() { return <p>Content</p>; }
recreated every run
return <Child />;
React destroys and rebuilds DOM
}

When ArticleCard was defined inside App, the initial mount looked identical to a top-level component. But when App rendered a second time, React evaluated App from the top, allocating a fresh ArticleCard function in memory. React compared the previous element descriptor with the new one and observed two different function references. React concluded that a different component type had replaced the old one, destroying the existing <article> node and constructing a new one. Moving ArticleCard to the top level gave the component a permanent function identity, allowing React to update the DOM surgically without rebuilding elements.

Step 1
First, we construct the article card component
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We construct the standalone article card component ArticleCard.jsx to encapsulate headline and summary copy into an isolated, reusable function. Notice that the function name begins with an uppercase letter: ArticleCard. This PascalCase naming guarantees that the JSX compiler treats <ArticleCard /> as a custom component rather than an unknown HTML tag. The component function contains no hardcoded DOM queries, mutates no external variables, and returns semantic HTML elements wrapped in a single root <article> tag.

When returning multi-line JSX markup from a component function, you encounter a foundational JavaScript syntax crossroad:

  • Option 1 (The Foundational Way): Write a naked multi-line return without wrapping parentheses, exposing the code to automatic semicolon insertion.
  • Option 2 (The Modern Idiomatic Way): Wrap the multi-line JSX expression in parentheses, signaling to the parser that the return expression continues across lines.

First, examine Option 1 with a naked multi-line return:

Option 1: The Foundational Way (Naked Multi-Line Return)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return
Parser automatically inserts semicolon here
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
Unreachable code never evaluated
5 </article>;
6}

In Option 1, the JavaScript engine encounters a newline immediately after the return keyword. Under the rules of automatic semicolon insertion, the parser inserts a semicolon after return;. The function immediately terminates and returns undefined. The JSX markup on the following line is never evaluated, and the browser displays a blank card with zero errors.

Now, examine Option 2 with defensive parenthesized return wrapping:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Parentheses prevent automatic semicolon insertion
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2 className="headline">Morning Dispatch</h2>
Story headline text
5 <p className="summary">Civic updates.</p>
Story summary
6 </article>
7 );
8}

In Option 2, the opening parenthesis ( tells the ECMAScript parser that the return expression continues across multiple lines. Semicolon insertion is prevented, and the component function reliably evaluates the entire JSX tree. Notice how ArticleCard.jsx functions as a pure presentation component: it owns zero state, requires no external DOM lookups, and cleanly packages the news card into a predictable, reusable unit.

Notice how ArticleCard.jsx satisfies the core architectural rules of component anatomy:

  1. It uses PascalCase naming (ArticleCard) so the compiler treats it as a custom component.
  2. It returns a single root container element (<article>) satisfying JavaScript expression return grammar.
  3. It encloses its multi-line return inside parentheses to neutralize automatic semicolon insertion traps.
  4. It is declared at the top level of the file so its component identity remains stable across renders.
Step 2
Finally, we mount the card declaratively inside
<App.jsx>

To complete our application layout, we mount ArticleCard.jsx inside the root container App.jsx. In standard JavaScript development, inserting a new widget required querying an existing container with document.querySelector and appending elements imperatively. In React, the entire document organizes into a declarative hierarchy. Notice that App.jsx imports ArticleCard as an unquoted JavaScript identifier and mounts it using the self-closing tag <ArticleCard />. We do not call ArticleCard() directly with parentheses; writing <ArticleCard /> tells React's mounting engine to register an independent element in the render tree and execute the component during the render pass.

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Imports component
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <main className="app-shell">
6 <ArticleCard />
Mounts component declaratively as tag
7 </main>
8 );
9}

When React evaluates App, the JSX compiler transforms <ArticleCard /> into _jsx(ArticleCard, {}). React attaches the component to its virtual tree, executes ArticleCard() in memory, and paints the returned <article> node inside <main> in a single atomic operation. Because the component follows PascalCase naming and declarative invocation, the browser receives living, semantic DOM elements without manual query scripts or silent lowercase failures.

Notice how App.jsx establishes clean declarative boundaries:

  1. It imports ArticleCard as a first-class function identifier from its module path.
  2. It mounts <ArticleCard /> as a declarative JSX element, registering an independent component boundary.
  3. It performs zero manual DOM querying or element manipulation, delegating page mounting to React.

Component Summary

App

The application root mounts the top-level layout. It embeds the article card into the primary page document, anchoring the component in React's virtual DOM tree without directly querying or mutating browser DOM nodes.

ArticleCard

The news dispatch card encapsulates headline and summary markup into an isolated, reusable function. By using PascalCase capitalization and parenthesized return expressions, it satisfies compiler invariants and renders predictable, pure UI.

In plain JavaScript development, assembling an article card required writing imperative element creation scripts or template strings that leaked variables and lacked structure. In React, the entire card encapsulates inside a standalone component function. Because ArticleCard uses PascalCase capitalization and parenthesized return statements, the compiler treats it as a first-class component, emitting unquoted function references that React reconciles and mounts safely into the page.

Where you will meet this

  1. Design System Component Libraries: When authoring buttons, modals, input cards, and layout grids in a shared component library, every component must enforce PascalCase naming to ensure downstream consuming applications can mount them as standard JSX tags without compiler confusion.
  2. Micro-Frontend Layout Shells: In large enterprise web applications where independent teams ship isolated widgets into a unified page, mounting widgets declaratively as <ArticleCard /> allows the parent shell to manage lifecycles and error boundaries without executing arbitrary synchronous function calls.
  3. Static Site and Editorial Publishing: In modern content management pipelines, editorial layout templates are composed of reusable story cards, author profiles, and breaking news banners, providing predictable, type-safe rendering without fragile HTML string concatenation.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is a React component, and what rules govern how you write and name one?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not merely testing whether you know how to write a function keyword. They are probing whether you understand how JSX transpiles into function calls and why React insists on orchestrating execution. A junior candidate answers that capitalization is just an aesthetic style convention. A senior engineer explains that the JSX compiler branches on Unicode casing: lowercase tags compile to string literals for native elements, while uppercase tags compile to unquoted function references that React invokes during render.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is claiming that you can call component functions directly inside curly braces {ArticleCard()} to save typing. While executing the function returns markup in simple examples, calling a component directly strips its component boundary, inlining child markup into the parent and breaking React's ability to isolate updates or manage Hooks. Another frequent trap is defining helper components inside parent render functions, which causes React to destroy and rebuild DOM trees on every render pass.

3. What is Actually Going On

A React component is a standard JavaScript function that returns JSX markup. We never invoke it directly; we write it as a tag, like <ArticleCard />, inside another component. That tag passes a function reference to React. When React renders the parent, it executes the function and commits the resulting elements to the DOM. Four concrete rules govern component authoring: (1) start names with a capital letter in PascalCase so the compiler emits function references, (2) open parentheses on the same line as return so automatic semicolon insertion does not return undefined, (3) declare components at module top level so function identity remains stable across renders, and (4) return a valid single root element or Fragment.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this gets tricky in production is diagnosing subtle silent bugs. A lowercase tag compiles cleanly without terminal syntax errors; the only clues are an empty custom tag in DevTools and two development console warnings. Similarly, an unparenthesized multi-line return renders a blank component without throwing a browser runtime error, though modern bundlers emit build warnings. Finally, defining components inside parent render functions works deceptively on initial mount, only to destroy user input text and reset focus rings the moment parent state triggers a second render.

Glossary

  • Component: A self-contained JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and returns a description of user interface markup in JSX.
  • PascalCase: A naming convention where the first letter of each compound word is capitalized, used by the JSX compiler to distinguish custom component functions from native HTML elements.
  • Function Reference: An unquoted reference to a JavaScript function in memory, passed to React so the runtime can execute the function during render.
  • Automatic Semicolon Insertion: A JavaScript language feature that inserts an invisible semicolon after an isolated return keyword, causing functions to return undefined if markup starts on the next line.
  • Nested Component: A component function defined inside the body of another component, causing React to treat it as a brand-new component type and rebuild its DOM on every render.

Beyond the basics

  • Authoring your very first React component: Learn how to declare component functions, manage module exports, and compose user interfaces (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component).
  • Rules of component rendering: Understand why React must orchestrate component and Hook execution and why calling components directly is forbidden (see react.dev/reference/rules/react-calls-components-and-hooks).
  • Describing user interfaces with components: Deepen your mental model of declarative component trees and UI projections (see react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui).
  • Importing and exporting components: Structure modular applications using standard default and named ES module exports (see react.dev/learn/importing-and-exporting-components).
  • Passing data with props: Pass data cleanly down the component tree without nesting function declarations (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Component Naming and Compiler Casing

➔ ALWAYS name custom components in PascalCase so the JSX compiler emits an unquoted function identifier rather than an HTML string literal.

➔ NEVER define component functions in lowercase or camelCase because the browser treats lowercase tags as native elements and fails silently.

❒ Return Statement Layout

➔ ALWAYS wrap multi-line JSX return statements in parentheses with the opening parenthesis on the same line as the return keyword.

➔ NEVER place multi-line JSX markup on the line after return without an opening parenthesis because automatic semicolon insertion will return undefined.

❒ Component Declaration Scope

➔ ALWAYS declare component functions at the top level of the file so their function identity remains stable across renders.

➔ NEVER define component functions inside the body of another component because React will destroy and reconstruct its DOM elements on every render.

DO THIS: name custom components in PascalCase, open parentheses on the return line, and declare at module top level

code.txt
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>
5 </article>
6 );
7}
8export default function App() {
9 return <ArticleCard />;
10}

DO NOT DO THIS: name components in lowercase, place markup below bare return, or nest component definitions

2 function articleCard() {

5 <h2>Morning Dispatch</h2>

7 }

9}
