JSX Syntax &
the Single-Root Rule

Interview Question   CORE

What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built an article card component and pasted HTML markup for a headline and image.
  • 2 The build halts immediately with syntax errors about adjacent elements and unclosed tags.
  • 3 What rules must markup follow when written inside a React component?

Raw HTML is markup, JSX is JavaScript

Every website is built out of markup: headings, paragraphs, images, and lists. In traditional web development, you write HTML directly in markup files. In React, you write markup inside JavaScript functions. So every web developer meets the same question: when we write markup inside a component, how does that markup differ from plain HTML?

You know markup from raw HTML, the plain text of a standard web page: you write the tags as text, and the browser parses them:

Raw HTML: browser parses text markup
1<h2 class="title">Night Trains Return</h2>
2<img src="/img/train.jpg">
Unclosed void tag
3<p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>

The browser reads the HTML file as a string of text. Its parser is forgiving: it accepts multiple tags side by side at the document level, allows void tags like <img> without a closing slash, and copies attributes like class directly to the element. That is why it is called raw HTML: the browser receives markup text directly. Inside a component, the markup no longer sits in an HTML file for the browser to parse: it sits inside a JavaScript function, and the JavaScript engine cannot run markup text.

React components write markup in JSX instead: you write the tags inside JavaScript, and the build compiles every tag into a function call:

JSX: markup compiled to JavaScript expressions
1<article className="card">
2 <h2 className="title">Night Trains Return</h2>
3 <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="A night train" />
Self-closing slash
4 <p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
5</article>

Notice the differences from raw HTML. All three tags sit inside one enclosing <article> container, the <img> tag closes itself with a trailing slash />, and the styling attribute is written className instead of class. The build compiles each tag into a _jsx function call that evaluates to a plain JavaScript object. Because a JavaScript function returns only one value, all tags must sit inside a single root element (or a Fragment, <>...</>). Because JavaScript enforces strict grammar, every tag must be closed, and attributes use JavaScript DOM property names. That is why it is called JSX: it is a JavaScript XML syntax extension that describes elements.

A second component shows the same rules at work:

JSX: top stories list item
1<li className="story-item">
2 <span className="bullet" />
Self-closing span
3 Morning Dispatch
4</li>

The <span /> tag closes itself with a trailing slash, and className sets its CSS class without colliding with JavaScript's reserved class keyword.

JSX can also evaluate JavaScript expressions and variables directly inside the markup using curly braces. Lecture 4 covers that syntax.

In this chapter, we learn the grammar of JSX on our ArticleCard and TopStories components. We will see why JSX compiles to element descriptor objects, why a component must return a single root element, how Fragments group tags without adding DOM wrapper nodes, why every tag must close, and why attributes use DOM property names. At the end, we compare raw HTML against JSX.

In this lesson the markup displays fixed text. Later lessons build on what we establish today: Lecture 4 puts variables inside JSX with curly braces, Lecture 5 nests components in a tree, and Lecture 6 passes data with props. Lecture 10 conditionally renders markup, and Lecture 11 renders lists of elements.

This lesson answers five questions:

  • Is the markup returned by our components genuine HTML?
  • Why must every component return a single root element?
  • How can we group sibling tags without adding unnecessary wrapper divs?
  • Why does JSX reject unclosed image and break tags?
  • Why does React warn against writing standard class and for attributes?

The questions stand on what earlier lessons established:

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): A component describes what should appear on the screen in JSX, and React builds the real DOM elements from that description.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): A component is a capitalized function in PascalCase that returns JSX, and opening parentheses on the return line guard against automatic semicolon insertion.
  • Plain JavaScript & HTML: Functions return a single expression with return. HTML tags describe page elements.

The compiler transforms JSX tags into function calls and element objects

JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It is a syntax extension that allows developers to write HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript files. While JSX looks like HTML, the browser engine never executes JSX directly. Before code reaches the browser, a build compiler parses the markup and transforms every tag into a JavaScript function call named _jsx().

When the compiler processes <h2 className="headline">Night Trains Return</h2> it transforms that tag into _jsx("h2", { className: "headline", children: "Night Trains Return" }) At runtime, calling _jsx() produces a lightweight JavaScript object called a React element. A React element is an in-memory descriptor with properties such as type: 'h2' and props. React reads these descriptor objects during render and calls document.createElement() to create the real browser DOM nodes.

Because JSX tags compile into standard JavaScript function calls, JSX expressions are first-class JavaScript values. You can assign a JSX tag to a local variable, pass it as an argument, or return it from a function. Furthermore, any attributes written on a JSX tag become key-value pairs on the second argument of _jsx(). Understanding that JSX is JavaScript provides the foundation for all syntax rules that follow.

JavaScript functions return one expression unless wrapped in a root or a Fragment

In JavaScript, a return statement can only return a single value or expression. When you write return 42; the engine returns that single number. If you attempt to write two expressions side by side without an operator, such as return a b; the JavaScript parser halts with a fatal syntax error. Even if you separate them with the comma operator, as in return (a, b); the comma operator evaluates both but returns only the second expression b, discarding a.

Because every JSX tag compiles into a distinct _jsx() function call, writing two adjacent tags side by side after return is equivalent to writing two function calls without an operator: return _jsx("h2", ...) _jsx("p", ...); This syntax is invalid JavaScript. To return multiple elements from a component, you must wrap them inside a single enclosing root element, such as an <article> container or a <main> shell.

Wrapping adjacent elements in an extra <div> satisfies the compiler, but it inserts a real DOM element into the page. Intermediate <div> nodes pollute the DOM tree and break CSS rules that rely on direct parent-child relationships, such as child selectors (.stories > li) or flexbox and grid layouts. To group siblings without adding an extra DOM node, React provides a virtual container called a Fragment, written <>...</>. React unpacks Fragments in memory and mounts child elements directly into the parent container.

JSX requires closed tags and JavaScript property names

In native HTML, elements fall into two distinct categories: container elements that enclose content, and void elements that cannot contain children. The HTML specification defines a fixed dictionary of void elements, including <img>, <input>, <br>, and <hr>. In HTML, these tags never require closing tags. In contrast, JSX enforces strict XML grammar where every opening tag must be explicitly terminated, either with a matching closing tag or with a trailing self-closing slash (<img /> or <br />).

In raw HTML markup, developers write class="headline" and <label for="email">. However, in JavaScript, class and for are reserved keywords used for declaring ES6 classes and writing loops. Decades ago, the browser DOM specification resolved this collision by naming element object properties element.className and element.htmlFor. Because JSX attributes become keys on a JavaScript props object, React aligns with these DOM property names, using className and htmlFor to prevent reserved keyword collisions.

Beyond className and htmlFor, React writes multi-word HTML attributes in camelCase, such as tabIndex instead of tabindex and strokeWidth instead of stroke-width. If a developer writes raw HTML attribute names, React still sets the property on the element but prints clear warning messages in the browser development console. As an explicit exception to the camelCase rule, accessibility attributes (aria-*) and custom data attributes (data-*) keep their hyphens to match standard HTML specifications.

Principles of React: JSX Syntax and the Single-Root Rule

QUESTION 1

A component returns descriptor objects rather than HTML strings

A developer creates an article headline and assigns the JSX markup to a local variable before returning it from ArticleCard:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const headline = <h2 className="headline">Night Trains</h2>;
In memory
3 console.log(headline);
Prints JavaScript object, not HTML string
4 return headline;
5}

The developer inspects the browser console expecting to see a rendered HTML string such as <h2 class="headline">Night Trains</h2> Instead, the console prints a plain JavaScript object with properties type: "h2" and props: { className: "headline", children: "Night Trains" }

Is the markup returned by a component genuine HTML?

ANSWER

The code works as React intended. JSX is a syntax extension that produces plain JavaScript objects.

At build time, the compiler translates <h2 className="headline">Night Trains</h2> into _jsx("h2", { className: "headline", children: "Night Trains" }) At runtime, calling _jsx() evaluates to a plain JavaScript object called a React element. React evaluates these in-memory descriptors during render and calls document.createElement("h2") to paint real DOM nodes on the page. The browser engine never encounters JSX directly.

How JSX transforms into DOM elements
JSX Source:     <h2 className="headline">Night Trains</h2>
                      |
                      v  (Compiler Transform)
Function Call:  _jsx("h2", { className: "headline", children: "Night Trains" })
                      |
                      v  (Runtime Evaluation)
React Element:  { type: "h2", props: { className: "headline", ... } }
                      |
                      v  (Commit)
Browser DOM:    <h2 class="headline">Night Trains</h2>
PRINCIPLE 1

JSX is JavaScript that describes elements

Markup inside a component is not an HTML template string. The build compiles each tag into a _jsx function call that evaluates to a plain JavaScript object called a React element. React reads these descriptor objects during render and constructs the corresponding browser DOM nodes. Because JSX is JavaScript, you can place element expressions anywhere a JavaScript value is valid, such as inside variables or return statements.

We should do this:
const element = <h2 className="title">Night Trains</h2>;
compiles to _jsx("h2", { className: "title", children: "..." })

In our ArticleCard component, logging a JSX tag proves what exists in JavaScript memory. When you declare const headline = <h2 className="headline">Night Trains</h2>; and pass it to console.log(headline), the console does not display a string of angle brackets. Instead, it displays a plain JavaScript object with properties type: "h2" and props: { className: "headline", children: "Night Trains" } The browser DOM is never touched during this assignment; React evaluates these descriptor objects during its render pass and coordinates the creation of physical DOM elements.

QUESTION 2

A component must return a single root element

A developer attempts to return a story headline and a summary paragraph side by side from ArticleCard:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
Adjacent tags violate return grammar
2 return (
3 <h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
4 <p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
5 );
6}

When the developer executes the build command, compilation halts instantly with a fatal syntax error. The Babel compiler reports: SyntaxError: Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped in an enclosing tag. Did you want a JSX fragment <>...</>? The esbuild bundler emits an unexpected token error, and zero code executes in the browser.

Why does placing two sibling tags after return cause the compiler to fail?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A JavaScript function can only return a single value.

Each JSX tag compiles into an independent _jsx() function call expression. In JavaScript, a return statement can only return a single value. Placing two function calls side by side after return is invalid language grammar. Even if wrapped in parentheses with the comma operator, JavaScript evaluates both expressions but returns only the second value, discarding the first. To satisfy ECMAScript function return grammar, all sibling elements must be enclosed inside a single root container element, such as an <article className="card">.

To fix this failure, enclose the adjacent sibling tags inside a single root container:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Single root container satisfies return grammar
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
5 <p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}
JavaScript function return grammar with JSX
Adjacent Sibling Tags (Syntax Error):
  return _jsx("h2", ...) _jsx("p", ...);  <-- Multiple return values forbidden!

Single Root Container (Valid JavaScript):
  return _jsx("article", {
    className: "card",
    children: [ _jsx("h2", ...), _jsx("p", ...) ]  <-- Single return value!
  });
PRINCIPLE 2

A component returns one root because a function returns one value

Every JSX tag compiles into an independent _jsx function call expression. In JavaScript, a return statement can only return a single value. Placing two adjacent tags side by side without an enclosing container attempts to return two separate expressions, which violates JavaScript language grammar and halts compilation. To return multiple elements, enclose them inside a single root container.

We should do this:
return (
<article className="card">
single root container
<h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
<p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
</article>
);
We should not do this:
return (
<h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
adjacent floating tag
<p>Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
cannot return two values
);

In our ArticleCard component, returning <h2> and <p> side by side demonstrates the physical return limit of JavaScript. The compiler attempts to transpile the code into return _jsx("h2", ...), _jsx("p", ...); In JavaScript, returning multiple bare expressions is a fatal grammar error. Even with parentheses, the comma operator would discard the heading and return only the paragraph. Wrapping both tags in an <article className="card"> container produces a single outer _jsx("article", ...) call with the heading and paragraph packaged as an array inside its children prop, satisfying ECMAScript return grammar.

QUESTION 3

Grouping siblings with a div can break list and layout styling

A developer creates a component named TopStories that returns two story items. To satisfy the single-root rule, the developer wraps both list items in a <div>:

TopStories.jsx
1export default function TopStories() {
2 return (
Wrapper div creates unnecessary intermediate DOM node
3 <div>
4 <li>Night trains return</li>
5 <li>High-speed rail opens</li>
6 </div>
7 );
8}

In App.jsx, the developer mounts TopStories inside a styled unordered list: <ul className="stories"><TopStories /></ul> The stylesheet defines .stories > li { color: #0f766e; } When the page renders, the list items appear with standard black text, completely unstyled.

Why should you group siblings with a Fragment when no wrapper element is needed?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. An intermediate div creates a real DOM element that interrupts direct parent-child relationships.

A <div> tag compiles to _jsx("div", ...) and creates a real DOM node in the browser. In HTML5, the only permitted direct children of a <ul> element are <li> elements. When TopStories wraps items in a <div>, the living DOM structure becomes <ul><div><li></li><li></li></div></ul> CSS child combinators (.stories > li) require direct parent-child relationships, so the selector matches zero items. Furthermore, intermediate divs break CSS flexbox and grid alignments that format direct child tags.

The fix is using a React Fragment, written <>...</>. A Fragment satisfies JavaScript's single return requirement in memory without emitting any DOM element:

TopStories.jsx
1export default function TopStories() {
2 return (
Fragment groups siblings without creating a DOM node
3 <>
4 <li>Night trains return</li>
5 <li>High-speed rail opens</li>
6 </>
7 );
8}

With a Fragment, the DOM becomes <ul><li>...</li><li>...</li></ul> and document.querySelectorAll('.stories > li').length evaluates to 2.

DOM structure with wrapper div versus React Fragment
With Intermediate <div>:            With React Fragment <>...</>:
  <ul>                                 <ul>
    <div>  <-- Interrupts styling!       <li>Night trains return</li>
      <li>Night trains return</li>       <li>High-speed rail opens</li>
      <li>High-speed rail opens</li>   </ul>  (Direct child elements)
    </div>
  </ul>
PRINCIPLE 3

Group with a Fragment when the page needs no extra element

Fragment a virtual JSX container that groups children without rendering a DOM node

Wrapping elements in a <div> creates a real DOM element that can disrupt CSS child selectors, flexbox hierarchies, and grid layouts. When elements must be grouped solely to satisfy the single-root rule, wrap them in a Fragment, written <>...</>. A Fragment satisfies the single-return requirement in JavaScript without adding any node to the browser DOM. Use an element like <article> only when the page requires a semantic container or styling box.

We should do this:
<ul className="stories">
<>
<li>Night trains return</li>
mounts directly in ul
<li>High-speed rail opens</li>
</>
</ul>
We should not do this:
<ul className="stories">
<div>
extra div breaks child selectors and list semantics
<li>Night trains return</li>
<li>High-speed rail opens</li>
</div>
</ul>

In our TopStories component, returning list items wrapped in a <div> reveals the architectural cost of unneeded DOM nodes. The HTML specification dictates that the only permitted direct children of a <ul> element are <li> elements. When TopStories wraps items in a <div>, the living DOM structure becomes <ul><div><li></li></div></ul> Styles defined for .stories > li fail to match because div is not an li. Replacing <div> with <>...</> produces a clean flat hierarchy where the list items mount directly inside <ul>, allowing child selectors and CSS grid alignments to apply cleanly.

QUESTION 4

Every tag in JSX must be explicitly closed

A developer pastes an image element into ArticleCard following standard HTML void element syntax:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
Unclosed void tag breaks parser
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Night train">
5 <h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The terminal compiler halts immediately with a fatal syntax error. The esbuild bundler reports: SyntaxError: Unexpected closing "article" tag does not match opening "img" tag

Why does JSX reject unclosed HTML void tags like img and br?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The JSX parser requires explicit closing boundaries for every tag.

In native HTML, the browser parser maintains a hardcoded dictionary of void elements (<img>, <input>, <br>, <hr>) that cannot contain child content and never require closing tags. In contrast, JSX enforces strict XML grammar with zero tag dictionaries. When the parser encounters <img, it expects either a matching closing tag </img> or an explicit self-closing slash />. Without a closing slash, the parser assumes that downstream tags (<h2>, </article>) are inner children of the image. When it encounters </article>, the open tag stack mismatches and compilation fails.

The fix is adding an explicit self-closing trailing slash to the image tag:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Trailing slash closes void tag explicitly
3 <article className="card">
4 <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Night train" />
5 <h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}
AST parser tag stack for unclosed versus closed tags
Unclosed HTML Void Tag:              Explicitly Terminated JSX Tag:
  <article>                            <article>
    <img src="...">  (stays open!)       <img src="..." />  (closed!)
      <h2>...</h2>   (child error)       <h2>...</h2>
  </article>         (stack mismatch!) </article>  (tree matches!)
PRINCIPLE 4

Close every tag, including <img /> and

void elements HTML tags that cannot contain children and have no closing tags in HTML

While standard HTML allows void elements like <img> and <br> to remain open, JSX enforces strict XML syntax where every tag must be explicitly terminated. Without a closing tag or a trailing self-closing slash, the compiler treats all subsequent markup as child content of that tag. Always terminate self-contained tags with a trailing slash, such as <img /> or <br />, so the parser can resolve the element boundary.

We should do this:
<article className="card">
<img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Train" />
closed slash
<h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
</article>
We should not do this:
<article className="card">
<img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Train">
unclosed tag
<h2>Night Trains Return</h2>
</article>

In our ArticleCard component, pasting raw <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Night train"> breaks the compiler because the JSX lexer cannot infer where the image element ends. Because the tag lacks a self-closing slash, the parser treats the subsequent <h2> tag as an inner child of the image. When the parser eventually encounters </article>, it finds an open <img node on its parsing stack that was never closed. Adding the trailing slash <img ... /> informs the parser that the element terminates immediately and possesses zero children, emitting a clean _jsx("img", { ... }) call.

QUESTION 5

JSX attributes map to JavaScript property names

A developer adds a newsletter subscription form to ArticleCard using standard HTML attribute names:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
Raw HTML attributes trigger warnings
2 return (
3 <form className="newsletter-form">
4 <label class="label" for="email">Newsletter</label>
5 <input id="email" />
6 </form>
7 );
8}

The application compiles and renders the form controls on screen. However, when the developer opens the browser development console, two red warnings appear: Warning: Invalid DOM property 'class'. Did you mean 'className'? and Warning: Invalid DOM property 'for'. Did you mean 'htmlFor'?

Why does React warn against writing class and for attributes?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Raw HTML attribute names trigger development console warnings and collide with JavaScript reserved keywords.

JSX attributes become keys of a JavaScript object passed to _jsx(). In JavaScript, class and for are reserved language keywords used for class definitions and loops. Decades ago, the W3C DOM Level 1 specification resolved this collision by naming element object properties element.className and element.htmlFor. React aligns with these DOM properties so attributes map directly to JavaScript object keys. Multi-word attributes use camelCase (tabIndex, strokeWidth). Hyphenated accessibility attributes (aria-*) and custom data attributes (data-*) keep their hyphens to match HTML standards.

The fix is renaming class to className and for to htmlFor:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
DOM property names className and htmlFor silence warnings
3 <form className="newsletter-form">
4 <label className="label" htmlFor="email">Newsletter</label>
5 <input id="email" />
6 </form>
7 );
8}
Mapping JSX attributes to JavaScript DOM properties
JSX Attribute:        Props Object:            DOM Property / Method:
  className="title"    --> { className: "title" }    --> element.className
  htmlFor="email"      --> { htmlFor: "email" }      --> element.htmlFor
  aria-label="Close"   --> { "aria-label": "Close" } --> element.setAttribute
PRINCIPLE 5

Write attributes as JavaScript names

Attributes in JSX become keys of a JavaScript props object. Because class and for are reserved keywords in JavaScript, React uses the corresponding browser DOM property names className and htmlFor. Multi-word attributes use camelCase, such as tabIndex and strokeWidth. As an exception, accessibility attributes starting with aria- and custom attributes starting with data- keep their hyphens to match HTML standards.

We should do this:
<label className="label" htmlFor="email">Email</label>
maps cleanly to DOM properties and silences console warnings
We should not do this:
<label class="label" for="email">Email</label>
prints console warnings for invalid properties class and for

In our ArticleCard component, adding a newsletter signup form with <label class="label" for="email"> demonstrates how React enforces DOM property naming. While modern bundlers allow reserved words as object keys, React inspects incoming props during render. When it detects class or for, it logs prominent warnings in the development console because the underlying DOM nodes expect className and htmlFor. Renaming attributes to className and htmlFor aligns directly with element.className and element.htmlFor, leaving the console clean while preserving accessibility and CSS styling.

Step 1
First, we construct the article card component
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We construct the standalone article card component ArticleCard.jsx to encapsulate headline, thumbnail, and summary copy into an isolated, reusable function. Notice that the component encloses its markup inside a single root <article> tag, satisfying JavaScript's single expression return grammar. The thumbnail image uses an explicit self-closing slash <img ... /> to satisfy JSX tag closure rules, and the styling attributes use className instead of class.

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
Single semantic root encapsulates card copy
3 <article className="card">
4 <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Night train" className="thumbnail" />
5 <h2 className="headline">Night Trains Return</h2>
6 <p className="summary">Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Notice how ArticleCard.jsx functions as a pure presentation component. It owns zero internal state, requires no imperative DOM query scripts, and packages the news story into a predictable, reusable unit. By using a semantic <article> element as its root, the component provides accessible meaning to screen readers and a natural styling boundary for layout CSS.

Notice how ArticleCard.jsx satisfies the core architectural rules of component anatomy:

  1. It uses PascalCase naming (ArticleCard) so the compiler treats it as a custom component.
  2. It returns a single root container element (<article>) satisfying JavaScript expression return grammar.
  3. It encloses its multi-line return inside parentheses to neutralize automatic semicolon insertion traps.
  4. It uses self-closing syntax on <img /> to satisfy XML tag closure invariants.
Step 2
Next, we group list items with a Fragment
<TopStories.jsx>

When returning multiple sibling elements that belong inside an external container like a <ul>, you encounter a foundational architectural crossroads:

  • Option 1 (The Bloated DOM Way): Wrap the sibling list items in an intermediate <div>, polluting the DOM tree and breaking CSS child selectors.
  • Option 2 (The Modern Idiomatic Way): Group the sibling list items with a React Fragment <>...</>, preserving direct parent-child relationships with zero DOM overhead.

First, examine Option 1 with an intermediate <div> wrapper:

Option 1: The Bloated DOM Way (Intermediate Div Wrapper)
1export default function TopStories() {
2 return (
Intermediate div creates extra node inside ul
3 <div>
4 <li className="story-item">High-speed alpine rail opens</li>
5 <li className="story-item">Sleeper booking platform launches</li>
6 </div>
7 );
8}

In Option 1, the intermediate <div> satisfies JavaScript's single return requirement. However, when mounted inside a parent <ul className="stories">, the living DOM structure becomes <ul><div><li></li><li></li></div></ul> This structure violates HTML5 list specifications, increases browser node count, and breaks CSS rules like .stories > li because the list items are no longer direct children of the list container.

Now, examine Option 2 using a clean React Fragment:

TopStories.jsx
1export default function TopStories() {
2 return (
Fragment mounts items directly into host ul
3 <>
4 <li className="story-item">High-speed alpine rail opens</li>
5 <li className="story-item">Sleeper booking platform launches</li>
6 </>
7 );
8}

In Option 2, the compiler wraps the siblings inside _jsx(Fragment, { children: [...] }) This satisfies JavaScript's single return value requirement at compile time. At runtime, React unpacks the Fragment and appends both <li> nodes directly into the host <ul> container. The living DOM tree remains clean and flat, allowing CSS child selectors and list styling rules to apply without obstruction.

Notice how TopStories.jsx establishes clean grouping:

  1. It returns multiple sibling <li> tags without introducing extra DOM nodes.
  2. It satisfies JavaScript return grammar by enclosing siblings in a virtual Fragment container.
  3. It preserves parent CSS child selectors like .stories > li.
Step 3
Finally, we assemble the layout shell inside
<App.jsx>

To complete our application layout, we import and compose ArticleCard.jsx and TopStories.jsx inside the primary page shell App.jsx. In standard JavaScript, assembling this layout required querying container elements and appending nodes imperatively. In React, the entire document organizes into a declarative hierarchy. Notice that App.jsx wraps TopStories inside a semantic <ul className="stories"> list, providing the proper host container for the Fragment's child items.

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
2import TopStories from './components/TopStories.jsx';
3export default function App() {
4 return (
Primary shell mounts card and stories list
5 <main className="app-shell">
6 <ArticleCard />
7 <ul className="stories"><TopStories /></ul>
8 </main>
9 );
10}

When React evaluates App, the JSX compiler transforms <ArticleCard /> and <TopStories /> into function calls. React reconciles the tree in memory and paints the returned <main>, <article>, and <ul className="stories"> nodes in a single atomic pass. Because TopStories returns a Fragment, the browser DOM receives <ul><li>...</li><li>...</li></ul> without any intermediate wrapper node. CSS rules such as .stories > li match both items directly, producing an accessible layout.

Notice how App.jsx establishes clean declarative boundaries:

  1. It imports child components as first-class function identifiers.
  2. It embeds TopStories inside an authentic semantic <ul> element.
  3. It performs zero manual DOM querying or element manipulation, delegating page mounting to React.

Component Summary

App

The application shell orchestrates the page layout. It embeds the article card and hosts the top stories list container, anchoring components in React's render tree without imperatively querying or mutating DOM nodes.

ArticleCard

The article card encapsulates story markup into a single semantic article element. By using self-closing tags and className property alignment, it satisfies compiler invariants and renders predictable UI.

TopStories

The story list returns sibling list items grouped inside a React Fragment. It satisfies single-expression return grammar in JavaScript memory while emitting a flat, wrapper-free DOM tree.

In plain JavaScript development, assembling an article page required writing imperative element creation scripts or concatenating HTML strings that easily broke with unclosed tags or keyword collisions. In React, markup and rendering logic unify inside components governed by JSX rules. Because components return single root containers or Fragments, the compiler can optimize element descriptors in memory and mount them cleanly into the living DOM.

Where you will meet this

  1. Editorial and Content Management Feeds: In content publishing platforms, article cards, breaking news tickers, and author bios are assembled from modular JSX components where strict tag closure and semantic root containers prevent layout breakage.
  2. Design System Component Libraries: When authoring navigation menus, dropdown lists, and data grids, components frequently return multiple list items or table cells wrapped in Fragments so parent layout containers format them without intermediate wrapper interference.
  3. Accessible Web Forms: When authoring registration and checkout forms, form inputs and descriptive labels must strictly map attributes to htmlFor and className while preserving aria-* tags to ensure assistive screen readers interpret form controls accurately.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What is JSX, what syntax rules must every snippet follow, and how do Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not merely testing whether you know how to write angle brackets inside a JavaScript file. They are probing whether you understand how JSX transpiles into function calls and why React enforces strict XML-like grammar. A junior candidate answers that JSX is simply "HTML in React." A senior engineer steps to the whiteboard and explains that JSX is syntactic sugar for _jsx() function calls that return plain JavaScript element descriptors. They explain that the single-root rule is an inescapable consequence of JavaScript function return grammar, not an arbitrary framework preference.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is claiming that you can wrap adjacent siblings in a <div> anywhere without architectural consequences. Candidates often say "just put a div around it" whenever the single-root error appears. While adding a <div> silences the compiler, it pollutes the DOM tree with redundant nodes, breaks HTML5 list semantics (<ul><div><li>), and destroys CSS flexbox and grid layouts that depend on direct parent-child relationships. Another fatal trap is assuming that JSX attributes are identical to HTML attributes, forgetting that class and for collide with JavaScript reserved keywords and trigger console warnings.

3. What is Actually Going On

Under the hood, the build compiler transforms each JSX tag into a _jsx(type, props) function call. In JavaScript, a function can only return a single expression value. When you return two adjacent tags without an enclosing root, the compiler attempts to emit two separate function calls in a single return slot, which violates language grammar. Every component must therefore return a single root element or a Fragment. Furthermore, while browser HTML parsers have a hardcoded whitelist of void elements that never require closing tags, the JSX parser enforces strict XML grammar where every tag must be explicitly terminated with a closing tag or a self-closing slash (<img />). Finally, JSX attributes become keys on a JavaScript props object, so React uses DOM property names like className and htmlFor to prevent keyword collisions.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this gets tricky in production is understanding how React Fragments work in memory. When you write <>...</>, the compiler emits _jsx(Fragment, { children: [...] }) React detects the internal Fragment symbol during reconciliation and treats it as a virtual container. When committing to the DOM, React completely skips creating a wrapper DOM node; it unpacks the child array and appends the child elements directly into the parent container. However, the shorthand <>...</> cannot accept attributes or keys. When rendering collections of grouped elements inside a loop, you must explicitly import Fragment from 'react' and write <Fragment key={item.id}>...</Fragment> as explored in Lecture 11.

Glossary

  • JSX: A syntax extension for JavaScript that allows developers to write declarative, HTML-like markup inside JavaScript files, compiling into nested _jsx() function calls.
  • React Element: A lightweight, plain JavaScript object created by _jsx() that describes a DOM element's tag name, attributes, and children in memory.
  • Fragment: A virtual JSX container, written <>...</>, that groups multiple sibling elements to satisfy the single-root rule without rendering any node in the browser DOM.
  • Void Element: An HTML element that cannot contain child nodes or text content (such as <img>, <input>, or <br>) and must be self-closed in JSX.
  • className and htmlFor: JavaScript DOM property names used in JSX instead of HTML's class and for attributes to avoid colliding with ECMAScript reserved keywords.

Beyond the basics

  • Writing markup with JSX: Master the foundational syntax rules and compiler requirements of JSX in React components (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • React Fragment reference: Explore how Fragments group elements without wrapper nodes and when to use keyed Fragments (see react.dev/reference/react/Fragment).
  • JavaScript in JSX with curly braces: Learn how to evaluate dynamic variables and expressions inside markup (see react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces).
  • Common DOM components and attribute props: Review the complete reference of HTML attributes and their JSX property equivalents (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • React 19 upgrade guide on JSX transforms: Understand why modern React requires the new JSX transform without manual React imports (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ The Single-Root Return Invariant

➔ ALWAYS return a single root element or Fragment from every component function because JavaScript functions can only return a single expression value.

➔ NEVER return adjacent sibling tags without an enclosing container because two floating expressions violate ECMAScript function return grammar.

❒ Sibling Grouping and DOM Fidelity

➔ ALWAYS use a React Fragment (<>...</>) when grouping sibling elements solely to satisfy the single-root rule without adding DOM overhead.

➔ NEVER wrap sibling elements in an unnecessary <div> when an extra container breaks CSS child selectors, flexbox hierarchies, or list semantics.

❒ Tag Closure and XML Strictness

➔ ALWAYS explicitly terminate every JSX tag with a closing tag or a self-closing trailing slash (<img />, <br />).

➔ NEVER leave HTML void elements unclosed because the JSX parser enforces strict XML grammar and halts compilation.

❒ Attribute Mapping and Reserved Keywords

➔ ALWAYS write JSX attributes using DOM property names like className and htmlFor to prevent collisions with JavaScript reserved keywords.

➔ NEVER write raw HTML class and for attributes in JSX because they trigger browser development console warnings.

DO THIS: return a single root or Fragment, close every tag, and use JavaScript DOM property names

3 <article className="card">
4 <img src="/img/train.jpg" alt="Train" className="thumb" />
5 <h2 className="title">Night Trains Return</h2>
6 <p className="summary">Sleeper routes reopen.</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

DO NOT DO THIS: return adjacent floating tags, leave void elements unclosed, or use raw class attributes

JavaScript Expressions in JSX with Curly Braces

Interview Question   CORE

How do you use JavaScript expressions inside JSX with curly braces?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You store an article's headline and image path in JavaScript variables for your card component.
  • 2 Typing the variable names directly between tags and inside attribute quotes renders the word "headline" and breaks the image.
  • 3 How do you bring live JavaScript values into JSX markup?

Literal text is fixed, curly braces run JavaScript

Every web application displays data: article headlines, author photos, reading times, and publication dates. In Lecture 3, our markup displayed fixed text written directly between tags. In real applications, that data lives in JavaScript variables. The question every developer meets: when we build an interface from data, how do we insert values from JavaScript variables into markup?

Until now, every character you wrote between tags or inside quotes was literal text. Writing a variable's name there does not bring in its value:

Literal text: characters parsed as static markup
1<article className="card">
2 <h2>headline</h2>
Renders literal text headline
3 <img src="avatarUrl" alt="Author" />
Requests /avatarUrl
4</article>

The compiler treats everything outside curly braces as static character text: <h2>headline</h2> renders the word "headline", and src="avatarUrl" instructs the browser to request the literal URL /avatarUrl. That is why it is called literal text: the compiler reads each character literally. Literal text stays right for values that never change, such as alt="Author" or className="card", but it can never show what a variable holds.

To show what a variable holds, JSX uses curly brace expressions: wrap an expression in curly braces to open a window into JavaScript.

Curly brace expressions: dynamic values evaluated during render
1<article className="card">
2 <h2>{headline}</h2>
Evaluates headline variable
3 <img src={avatarUrl} alt="Author" />
Evaluates avatarUrl path
4</article>

The variable headline sits inside curly braces {headline}, and the image path sits directly after = in braces {avatarUrl} without quotes. When React renders ArticleCard, the compiler switches into JavaScript mode for each pair of braces, evaluates the expression, and places the resulting value into the element descriptor. That is why they are called curly brace expressions: curly braces that evaluate JavaScript expressions inside JSX.

Curly brace expressions: reading time calculation
1<p className="read-time">
2 {readTime * 60} seconds
Evaluates arithmetic expression
3</p>

A second element shows the same rule at work: inside curly braces, {readTime * 60} runs standard JavaScript arithmetic and prints the computed number directly into the paragraph.

Later, we will see that values passed into other components through props also use curly braces (Lecture 6).

In this chapter, we learn how curly braces evaluate JavaScript on our ArticleCard component: where braces can be placed, why attributes take unquoted braces, why braces accept expressions but reject statements, when the expressions run, how React handles booleans, null, and numbers, why objects stop the render, what double curlies mean, and how line breaks affect spacing. At the end, we compare static markup against curly brace expressions.

In this lesson, our expressions use local variables and arithmetic. Later lessons build on what we establish today: Lecture 5 composes components into trees, Lecture 6 passes values through props, Lecture 10 conditionally renders markup with ternaries and boolean operators, Lecture 11 renders lists of items, Lecture 12 explores pure rendering, Lecture 14 introduces reactive state, Lecture 48 examines XSS safety, and Lecture 83 covers inline style objects.

This lesson answers eight questions:

  • How do we show what a variable holds instead of its literal name?
  • Why does quoting an attribute break variable lookup?
  • Why do curly braces accept expressions like ternaries but reject statements like if or for?
  • When does the code inside curly braces actually run?
  • Why does a boolean or undefined variable leave an empty spot on screen without an error?
  • Why does passing a Date or an object into content stop the render?
  • What does double curly brace syntax mean in attributes like style?
  • Why does a line break between text and braces drop the space?
  • Lecture 1 (Declarative components and DOM construction): In Lecture 1, we learned that a component describes what should appear on the screen in JSX, and React builds the real DOM elements from that description.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy and PascalCase naming): In Lecture 2, we learned that a component is a capitalized function in PascalCase that returns JSX, and opening parentheses on the return line guards against automatic semicolon insertion.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX Syntax and the single-root rule): In Lecture 3, we learned that JSX is JavaScript syntax compiling tags into _jsx() calls, returning a single root element or Fragment, closing all tags, and aligning attribute names with DOM properties.
  • Native browser foundations: We build on standard HTML markup, browser image loading, JavaScript variable declarations with const and let, expression evaluation, and the browser development console.

Curly braces step out of static markup into JavaScript

Curly braces ({}) open an inline window from static JSX markup into live JavaScript execution. This evaluation window works in exactly two places: between tag content (such as <h2>{headline}</h2>), and directly after the equals sign in an attribute (such as src={avatarUrl}). Outside these two positions, curly braces cannot be used to name tags (writing <{tag}> halts compilation). Any text outside curly braces remains static literal characters.

When constructing attribute strings from multiple dynamic pieces, developers cannot mix quotes and braces like src="/img/{photoId}.jpg". In JSX, quotes treat everything inside as static text. To combine dynamic variables with static text, developers use a template literal enclosed in backticks inside a single pair of braces, such as ` src={/img/${photoId}-${size}.jpg} , or JavaScript string concatenation with the plus operator +`. Inside the braces, standard JavaScript string rules apply.

In standard JavaScript files, developers write single-line comments with double slashes //. However, between JSX tags, characters outside curly braces are treated as literal text nodes. If a developer writes // note between tags, the browser renders the characters "// note" directly onto the page. To write a comment between JSX tags, the comment must be enclosed inside curly braces as {/* note */}, instructing the compiler to evaluate a JavaScript comment that emits zero output.

Expressions produce values while statements perform actions

In JavaScript grammar, code divides into expressions and statements. An expression is any piece of code that resolves to a single discrete value in memory. Numbers (4 + 2), variables (headline), template literals, ternary conditions, and function calls are all expressions. In contrast, a statement performs an action or controls execution flow without producing a value. Language statements include if, for, while, switch, and variable declarations (const x = 1).

Because every JSX tag compiles into a _jsx(type, props) function call, any children or attributes written in curly braces become arguments passed into that function call. In JavaScript, function call arguments can only accept expressions. Attempting to pass a control-flow statement like if into a function argument, as in _jsx("p", { children: if (admin) ... }) is a fatal syntax error. To choose between values inside JSX braces, developers use the ternary conditional operator (condition ? a : b). When statements like if or for are necessary, they must be executed above the return statement, storing their result in a local variable that is passed into JSX.

React converts types to text nodes or invisible slots

When React renders JSX expressions to the DOM, it evaluates the runtime type of each expression to determine its screen representation. Strings and numbers evaluate directly into browser DOM text nodes ({readTime} prints "4", and {0} prints "0"). In contrast, the primitive values true, false, null, and undefined are treated as empty slots. React renders nothing to the DOM for these values. This design allows conditional rendering expressions without printing unwanted words like "false" or "undefined" onto the page.

Numbers always print on screen, including zero (0). If an arithmetic operation produces NaN, React prints the characters "NaN" into the DOM and emits a console warning when NaN is a sole child. When an array of strings or numbers is passed as content, such as {['Rail', 'Travel']}, React flattens the array and renders the items concatenated side by side into the DOM without automatic spacing.

Objects and functions require explicit conversion for content

In JavaScript, plain objects and Date instances are non-primitive data structures. If a developer attempts to place a raw object or Date instance directly into JSX content, such as <p>{publishedAt}</p> React throws a fatal runtime exception: "Objects are not valid as a React child (found: [object Date])". React does not guess how an object should be formatted. To display data from an object or date, the developer must explicitly read a primitive property (person.name), call a formatting method (publishedAt.toLocaleDateString('en-GB')), or invoke a helper function.

A function reference represents the function definition itself, while a function call invokes the code and returns its resulting value. If a developer places a bare function reference into JSX content, such as <p>{formatReadTime}</p> React renders an empty paragraph and logs a console error: "Functions are not valid as a React child". To render the output of a function, the developer must call the function with parentheses, as in <p>{formatReadTime(readTime)}</p> passing its return value to the JSX window.

In attributes like style, developers frequently encounter double curly braces: <div style={{ color: 'pink', fontSize: 20 }}> The double curlies are not a special React operator. The outer pair of braces is the standard JSX evaluation window, stepping out of markup into JavaScript. The inner pair of braces is a standard JavaScript object literal { color: 'pink', fontSize: 20 } Writing style={theme} with an object variable const theme = { color: 'pink' } produces the exact same DOM styles. Lecture 83 explores HTML components and inline style object properties in full detail. In content, double curlies like <h2>{{headline}}</h2> create an object literal { headline }, which stops the render with an invalid child error.

The JSX compiler trims whitespace that includes line breaks at the start and end of text lines. If an expression and following text are split across separate lines, such as placing {readTime} on one line and min read on the next, the compiler strips the leading space, rendering 4min read with words joined together. To preserve a space across line breaks, developers keep text and expressions on a single line or insert an explicit string space expression {' '}.

Principles of React: JavaScript Expressions in JSX with Curly Braces

QUESTION 1

Curly braces evaluate variables while static tags print text

A developer creates an article card component and declares a local variable for the headline, then writes the tag name directly in markup:

ArticleCard (Unbracketed Identifier)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const headline = "Night Trains Return to Europe";
Local variable
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h2>headline</h2>
Renders literal string
6 </article>
Check the read time later
7 );
8}

The developer inspects the browser expecting to see the story title. Instead, the screen displays the word "headline", and beneath it the raw characters "// check the read time later" appear directly on the page.

How do you display the value of a variable inside JSX markup instead of its literal name?

ANSWER

The code does not work. The compiler treats unbracketed text between tags as static character content.

At build time, the JSX compiler translates <h2>headline</h2> into _jsx("h2", { children: "headline" }) passing the literal string "headline" into the element descriptor. The compiler does not inspect the identifier against variables in scope. Likewise, the characters // check the read time later sit outside curly braces, so the compiler treats the slashes as plain text and paints them onto the screen.

To evaluate JavaScript variables and expressions, you must enclose them in curly braces: <h2>{headline}</h2> When the compiler encounters an opening curly brace {, it steps into JavaScript evaluation mode, translating the tag into _jsx("h2", { children: headline }) During render, React reads the variable from memory and paints "Night Trains Return to Europe" into the DOM text node. To write a comment between tags that does not emit visible text, wrap the comment in curly braces as {/* check the read time later */}

Static markup text mode versus evaluated JavaScript window
Static markup:   <h2>headline</h2>      --> _jsx("h2", { children: "headline" })
Evaluated JSX:   <h2>{headline}</h2>    --> _jsx("h2", { children: headline })
PRINCIPLE 1

Curly braces open JavaScript in two places, and everything else is text

Text outside curly braces is treated as static character content. The compiler translates unbracketed words directly into string literals, rendering the literal identifier name to the screen. To evaluate a JavaScript variable or expression, wrap the code in curly braces. Curly braces open an evaluation window in exactly two places: between tag content and immediately after an attribute equals sign.

We should do this:
const title = "Night Trains";
<h2>{title}</h2>
renders variable value
We should not do this:
const title = "Night Trains";
<h2>title</h2>
renders literal text "title"
QUESTION 2

Attributes take unquoted expressions or static string literals

The developer declares an author avatar image path in a variable and passes the identifier inside attribute quotes:

ArticleCard (Quoted Attribute)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const avatarUrl = "/img/anna.jpg";
Local image path
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <img src="avatarUrl" alt="Author" />
Quoted attribute
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The developer saves the file and opens the browser. Instead of the author's photo, the card shows a broken-image icon, and the network console reports GET http://localhost:5173/avatarUrl 404 (Not Found)

Why does quoting a variable name in an attribute break resource loading?

ANSWER

The code does not work. Quoting an attribute forces the compiler to treat the value as a static string literal.

In JSX, attribute values enclosed in double quotes are emitted directly as static string values. Writing src="avatarUrl" causes the compiler to generate _jsx("img", { src: "avatarUrl" }) When the browser parses the resulting DOM element <img src="avatarUrl">, its network engine resolves avatarUrl as a relative path against the current origin, dispatching a request to http://localhost:5173/avatarUrl which fails with a 404 error. Placing curly braces inside quotes, as in src="{avatarUrl}", also fails because the braces remain literal string characters. Lecture 48 explores how React blocks dangerous javascript URLs in href and src attributes.

To pass a dynamic variable into an attribute, remove the quotes and enclose the expression in curly braces immediately after the equals sign: src={avatarUrl}. The compiler compiles this to _jsx("img", { src: avatarUrl }) resolving the variable to /img/anna.jpg in memory. If you need to construct a dynamic path from several variables, use a template literal inside a single pair of braces: ` src={/img/${photoId}-${size}.jpg} `.

Attribute string literal versus unquoted expression binding
Quoted attribute:    src="avatarUrl"    --> requests /avatarUrl (404 Not Found)
Unquoted expression: src={avatarUrl}    --> resolves /img/anna.jpg (200 OK)
PRINCIPLE 2

An attribute takes a quoted string or one braced expression

In JSX, double quotes instruct the compiler to create a static string literal. Writing quotes around an attribute name passes that exact text to the DOM, causing the browser to request non-existent paths. To bind an attribute to a dynamic variable or expression, omit the quotes and wrap the expression in a single pair of curly braces directly after the equals sign.

We should do this:
const avatar = "/img/anna.jpg";
<img src={avatar} alt="Author" />
loads image
We should not do this:
const avatar = "/img/anna.jpg";
<img src="avatar" alt="Author" />
requests 404 URL
QUESTION 3

Braces evaluate expressions while statements belong above return

The developer wants to display a label indicating whether an article requires a long read, and writes an if statement inside the paragraph:

ArticleCard (Statement in Braces)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const readTime = 4;
Reading duration in minutes
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <p>{if (readTime > 10) 'Long read'}</p>
Control statement
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The developer saves the file and the development server halts. The terminal reports a fatal build error: SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'if'

Why does embedding a JavaScript control statement inside JSX fail the build?

ANSWER

The code does not work. Function call argument slots in JavaScript cannot accept control-flow statements.

Every JSX tag compiles into a _jsx() function call where child content becomes argument expressions: _jsx("p", { children: ... }) In ECMAScript grammar, an argument passed into a function call must be an expression, a unit of code that evaluates to a value. A control-flow statement like if, for, while, or const controls program flow or performs actions, but it produces no value. Placing an if statement into a function argument slot violates language grammar, halting the compiler.

To evaluate conditional choices inside JSX curly braces, use a ternary conditional expression (condition ? a : b), which evaluates to a single value. Writing <p>{readTime > 10 ? 'Long read' : 'Quick read'}</p> compiles into valid JavaScript and evaluates to "Quick read" when readTime is 4. When complex branching requires multiple statements, execute the if statement above the return statement and store the resulting string in a local variable before passing it into JSX.

Function argument slots accept expressions and reject statements
Statement in args:  _jsx("p", { children: if (...) }) --> SyntaxError
Expression in args: _jsx("p", { children: test ? a : b }) --> Valid value
PRINCIPLE 3

Braces hold one expression, and statements go above the return

JSX tags compile directly into JavaScript function calls where children become argument values. In ECMAScript grammar, function call argument slots accept only expressions that produce a value. Control-flow statements like if, for, or while produce no value and halt compilation. Use an inline ternary expression inside braces, or compute the value using statements above the return.

We should do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>{minutes > 10 ? "Long" : "Quick"}</p>
ternary
We should not do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>{if (minutes > 10) "Long"}</p>
syntax error
QUESTION 4

Embedded expressions run each time React renders the component

The developer creates an article element and reassigns the local variable on the following line to see if the element updates:

ArticleCard (Render Timing Log)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 let headline = "Night Trains Return to Europe";
3 const card = <h2>{headline}</h2>;
Creates element descriptor
4 headline = "Alps Sleeper Routes Reopen";
5 return card;
6}

The developer expects the heading on screen to display "Alps Sleeper Routes Reopen". Instead, the screen continues to show "Night Trains Return to Europe".

When does code inside JSX curly braces execute, and does reassigning a variable update the screen?

ANSWER

The code works. Expressions inside curly braces evaluate synchronously at the moment the JSX line runs, producing an immutable element descriptor.

When React renders ArticleCard, it invokes the function from top to bottom. When execution reaches const card = <h2>{headline}</h2> the JavaScript engine evaluates the expression {headline} using the value in scope at that instant ("Night Trains Return to Europe"). The compiler creates a plain JavaScript object { type: 'h2', props: { children: 'Night Trains Return to Europe' } } This object holds the evaluated string value, not a live reference to the headline variable. Reassigning headline on the subsequent line changes the local variable, but it does not alter the already-created element descriptor.

Calling a helper function such as {formatReadTime(readTime)} demonstrates the exact execution timing. Each time React calls ArticleCard, the function call in curly braces executes, logging its output to the console during render. In development with StrictMode enabled, React invokes the component twice to check for side effects, logging twice. Because expressions execute on each render, values must be computed before the JSX line that consumes them. Dynamic values that change over time in response to user interaction require React state hooks, introduced in Lecture 14.

Synchronous expression evaluation into immutable element descriptors
1. let headline = "Night Trains";
2. const card = <h2>{headline}</h2>; --> descriptor captures "Night Trains"
3. headline = "Alps Reopen";         --> variable changes; descriptor unchanged
PRINCIPLE 4

The code in braces runs each time React renders the component

When React renders a component, it invokes the function from top to bottom. Each expression inside curly braces executes synchronously during that run, computing its value and storing it directly into the in-memory element descriptor. The rendered descriptor captures the value at that moment in time. Reassigning a local variable after creating an element does not update the screen.

We should do this:
const title = "Night Trains";
const card = <h2>{title}</h2>;
evaluates "Night Trains"
return card;
descriptor holds frozen value
QUESTION 5

Content holes render invisible while strings and numbers paint text

The developer places a boolean variable in the markup to show whether an article is featured on the homepage:

ArticleCard (Boolean Value)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const isFeatured = true;
Boolean flag
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <p>Featured: {isFeatured}</p>
Boolean expression in content
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The developer opens the browser expecting to see the text "Featured: true". Instead, the browser displays "Featured: " followed by an empty space, with zero errors in the console.

Why does rendering a boolean variable produce an empty slot instead of visible text?

ANSWER

The code does not work. React's primitive render matrix treats booleans as invisible empty slots that emit zero DOM nodes.

When React reconciles JSX child expressions, it routes values according to their runtime data types. Strings and numbers evaluate directly into visible DOM text nodes ({readTime} prints "4", and {0} prints "0"). In contrast, the primitive values true, false, null, and undefined are classified as empty slots. React skips these values entirely, appending nothing to the DOM tree. This behavior enables conditional rendering shortcuts, such as rendering a badge only when a condition is met, without printing unwanted words like "false" or "null" onto the screen.

Because undefined renders as an empty slot, typographical errors in property names fail silently. If a developer writes {article.titel} instead of {article.title}, JavaScript evaluates the missing property to undefined, and React renders an empty heading without throwing an error. When a boolean flag must appear as literal text on screen, convert it explicitly using a ternary expression ({isFeatured ? 'Featured' : 'Regular'}) or the String() function.

React primitive render matrix type routing
Expression Type:     Evaluated Value:     DOM Output:
String / Number  --> "Night Trains" / 4   --> Paints visible text node
Boolean          --> true / false         --> Empty slot (zero DOM nodes)
Null / Undefined --> null / undefined     --> Empty slot (zero DOM nodes)
PRINCIPLE 5

Predict what content braces print from the value's type

React evaluates the data type of content expressions to determine what appears in the DOM. Strings and numbers render directly as visible text nodes. In contrast, booleans, null, and undefined are treated as empty slots and render nothing. To display the text of a boolean on screen, convert it explicitly to a string or use a ternary expression.

We should do this:
const isFeatured = true;
<p>{isFeatured ? "Featured" : "Standard"}</p>
text
We should not do this:
const isFeatured = true;
<p>Status: {isFeatured}</p>
renders empty slot
QUESTION 6

Content requires primitive text values rather than raw objects

The developer creates a Date instance for the article publication date and passes it directly into a paragraph:

ArticleCard (Date Object Child)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const publishedAt = new Date(2026, 9, 6);
Date instance
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <p>Published: {publishedAt}</p>
Raw date object in content
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The browser screen goes completely blank. The browser development console reports a fatal runtime error: Uncaught Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: [object Date])

Why does placing an unformatted object or date directly in content crash the render?

ANSWER

The code does not work. React forbids non-primitive objects and date instances as direct child content.

In JavaScript, plain objects and Date instances are complex reference data structures. React requires child content to be primitive values (strings, numbers) or valid element descriptors that can be mapped directly into DOM nodes. Because objects can represent countless structures, React refuses to guess how an object should be formatted or serialized. Passing a plain object or a Date instance directly into content causes React's reconciliation engine to halt immediately and throw a fatal "Objects are not valid as a React child" exception.

Likewise, passing a bare function reference without parentheses, such as <p>{formatReadTime}</p> fails to print text. React skips functions as children and logs a console error: "Functions are not valid as a React child". To render content from objects, dates, or functions, you must explicitly provide primitive strings or numbers. Call formatting methods on dates ({publishedAt.toLocaleDateString('en-GB')}), read primitive object properties, and invoke functions with parentheses ({formatReadTime(readTime)}).

Direct object child rejection versus formatted primitive conversion
Raw Date child:       <p>{publishedAt}</p>       --> Objects are not valid
Formatted Date child: <p>{publishedAt.format()}</p> --> Paints date text node
PRINCIPLE 6

Content needs a string or a number, so read the field, call the function, or format the date

React child content requires primitive values that can be rendered as text nodes. Passing a plain object or a Date instance directly into content stops rendering with a runtime error because React does not guess object formatting. Passing a bare function reference renders nothing and logs an error. Always extract primitive properties, invoke functions, or format dates explicitly.

We should do this:
const date = new Date(2026, 9, 6);
<p>{date.toLocaleDateString("en-GB")}</p>
text
We should not do this:
const date = new Date(2026, 9, 6);
<p>{date}</p>
throws Objects are not valid as child
QUESTION 7

Double curly braces pass object literals into the evaluation window

A developer encounters double curly braces in an inline style attribute and wonders if it represents a dedicated templating operator:

ArticleCard (Double Curly Braces)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const headline = "Night Trains Return to Europe";
Headline text
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h2 style={{ color: 'pink', fontSize: 20 }}>{headline}</h2>
6 <h2>{{headline}}</h2>
Double curlies in content
7 </article>
8 );
9}

The developer saves the file and the render crashes immediately with the error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {headline})

Does React provide a dedicated double curly brace syntax for dynamic styles and attributes?

ANSWER

The code does not work. Double curly braces are simply a standard JavaScript object literal enclosed inside the JSX evaluation window.

In JSX, double curly braces {{ }} do not represent special framework syntax or interpolation tags. The outer pair of curly braces opens the standard JSX evaluation window, stepping out of static markup and into JavaScript mode. The inner pair of curly braces defines an ordinary JavaScript object literal { color: 'pink', fontSize: 20 } Because the style prop accepts a JavaScript object mapping CSS properties in camelCase to values, passing an inline object literal is standard practice. Declaring const theme = { color: 'pink', fontSize: 20 }; and writing style={theme} produces the exact same DOM styles.

However, writing <h2>{{headline}}</h2> in content creates a JavaScript object literal { headline: "Night Trains..." } inside the JSX window. Under the child validation rules explored in Question 6, React rejects plain objects in content, halting rendering with an invalid child exception. Double curlies belong exclusively in attributes that expect JavaScript objects, while text content requires a single pair of braces around the variable.

Deconstruction of double curly brace syntax
Attribute: <div style={ { color: 'pink' } }>
                       ^   inner object  ^
                       outer JSX window
PRINCIPLE 7

Double curlies are an object inside the braces

The double curly brace syntax is not a special React operator. The outer pair of braces opens the standard JSX evaluation window, while the inner pair defines a standard JavaScript object literal. Attributes like style accept an object, making inline object literals convenient. Using double curlies in content creates an object in memory, triggering a fatal invalid child error.

We should do this:
const title = "Night Trains";
<h2>{title}</h2>
one pair prints variable value
We should not do this:
const title = "Night Trains";
<h2>{{title}}</h2>
passes object, stops render
QUESTION 8

Whitespace with line breaks trims unless protected by space expressions

To keep code within an eighty-character line budget, a developer formats a duration badge by splitting the expression and text across two lines:

ArticleCard (Whitespace Across Lines)
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const readTime = 4;
Reading duration in minutes
3 return (
4 <p>
5 {readTime}
6 min read
Split across line break
7 </p>
8 );
9}

The developer inspects the browser layout expecting to see "4 min read". Instead, the screen displays 4min read, with the number and word joined together without a space.

Why does splitting an expression and adjacent text across separate lines delete the separating space?

ANSWER

The code does not work. The JSX compiler strips whitespace that contains line breaks at the boundaries of text lines.

In native HTML, browsers collapse whitespace containing newlines into a single horizontal space. In contrast, the JSX compiler optimizes string output by trimming leading and trailing whitespace that includes a line break. When {readTime} sits at the end of one line and min read begins on the next, the compiler strips the newline and the indentation spaces preceding min read. The text node renders directly adjacent to the evaluated number, producing the joined string 4min read.

Spaces that sit entirely within a single line are preserved by the compiler. To guarantee that a space survives formatting, keep the expression and following text on a single line: <p>{readTime} min read</p> If code formatting tools or line budgets require breaking across lines, insert an explicit string space expression {' '} immediately following the dynamic expression: {readTime}{' '}min read. Because {' '} is a distinct JavaScript string expression, React renders a space text node that survives compiler trimming.

Whitespace trimming across line breaks versus preserved space tokens
Split lines:      {readTime}\nmin read     --> "4min read" (space stripped)
Space expression: {readTime}{' '}\nmin read --> "4 min read" (preserved)
PRINCIPLE 8

A line break between text and braces removes the space

The JSX compiler strips whitespace that contains line breaks at the beginning and end of text lines. When an expression and following text are placed on separate lines, the separating space is removed, joining the text directly against the evaluated value. To preserve a space across line breaks, keep the text on a single line or insert an explicit string space expression.

We should do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>{minutes} min read</p>
one line keeps space
We should not do this:
const minutes = 4;
<p>
{minutes}
min read
line break removes space: 4min read
</p>
