Step 1
First, we construct the article card with evaluated expressions
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We construct ArticleCard.jsx by declaring local data variables for the headline, author avatar URL, reading duration, publication date, and featured status. Inside the JSX markup, we use curly braces to project variables into text content, bind unquoted attributes, evaluate a ternary badge, format the date, and apply an inline style object.

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard() {
2 const headline = "Night Trains Return to Europe";
Story headline
3 const avatarUrl = "/img/anna.jpg";
4 const readTime = 4;
Reading duration in minutes
5 const isFeatured = true;
6 const publishedAt = new Date(2026, 9, 6);
Publication date

In the first snippet, ArticleCard.jsx declares local scope variables for story copy, reading metrics, and publication metadata. These variables reside purely in JavaScript function memory.

7 return (
Returns markup with evaluated expressions
8 <article className="card" style={{ borderColor: "#0e7490" }}>
9 <img src={avatarUrl} alt="Author" className="avatar" />
10 <h2>{headline}</h2>
11 <p>{readTime} min read • {publishedAt.toLocaleDateString("en-GB")}</p>
12 <span>{isFeatured ? "Featured Story" : "Standard Story"}</span>
13 </article>
14 );
15}

Notice how ArticleCard.jsx satisfies the compiler invariants established across our question cycles:

  1. It binds src={avatarUrl} without quotes, ensuring the browser resolves the true image path without dispatching a 404 network request.
  2. It projects {headline} directly into heading text content through the curly brace evaluation window.
  3. It evaluates {isFeatured ? "Featured Story" : "Standard Story"} via an inline ternary expression, avoiding invisible boolean slots and satisfying function argument grammar.
  4. It formats the Date instance using toLocaleDateString("en-GB"), ensuring a valid primitive text string is passed into child content.
  5. It applies an inline style object using double curlies style={{ borderColor: "#0e7490" }} passing a clean mapping without crashing the render.
Step 2
Finally, we mount the article card into the application container
<App.jsx>

We create App.jsx to serve as the root application container. The root shell imports ArticleCard and mounts it declaratively inside a semantic main element, providing a clean container without polluting the component with unnecessary DOM wrappers.

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from "./ArticleCard.jsx";
Imports child card
2export default function App() {
3 return (
4 <main className="container">
5 <h1>Morning Dispatch</h1>
6 <ArticleCard />
7 </main>
8 );
9}

Reviewing App.jsx reveals three architectural strengths:

  1. It imports child components as first-class function identifiers without manual DOM querying.
  2. It hosts ArticleCard inside a clean layout hierarchy without intermediate wrapper interference.
  3. It keeps the root container focused entirely on structure, allowing the child card to manage its own local data evaluation.

Component Summary

App

The application shell hosts the page layout and mounts the article card container without imperatively manipulating DOM nodes.

ArticleCard

The article card encapsulates story markup, declaring local variables and evaluating them inside content and attributes using curly braces.

In plain JavaScript development, updating an article card required querying elements by class name and imperatively setting element.textContent and element.src. In React, curly braces provide a declarative evaluation window directly inside the markup, ensuring that element descriptors always reflect evaluated memory values cleanly.

Where you will meet this

  1. Content and Media Platforms: When building article feeds, blog cards, and video galleries, metadata such as headlines, author avatars, view counts, and publication timestamps are bound to markup using curly brace expressions.
  2. Dashboard Widgets and Metrics Cards: Financial and analytics dashboards project dynamic numerical calculations, formatted currencies, and percentage changes into table cells and metric badges using inline expressions.
  3. Dynamic User Profiles and Avatars: User account headers bind dynamic profile photo URLs, display names, verification badges, and localized join dates using unquoted attributes and ternary operators.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you use JavaScript expressions inside JSX with curly braces?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not merely checking if you know where to type curly braces. They are probing your understanding of ECMAScript compiler grammar, the difference between expressions and statements, and how React processes different data types during render. A junior developer says curly braces are "for inserting variables into HTML." A senior engineer explains that curly braces establish an evaluation window in content and attributes where expressions become arguments to _jsx() function calls, evaluating synchronously during render.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is attempting to write control-flow statements like if or for inside curly braces ({if (active) ...}). Candidates often forget that JSX compiles into JavaScript function arguments, which grammatically reject control statements. Another frequent trap is quoting dynamic attributes (src="{avatarUrl}"), which emits literal strings and triggers network 404 errors, or passing raw objects and Date instances into content, causing fatal runtime crashes.

3. What is Actually Going On

Under the hood, the JSX compiler treats everything outside curly braces as static text. When it encounters {, it steps into JavaScript evaluation mode. The expression inside is evaluated once when the component function executes, and its result is placed into the React element descriptor. React's primitive render matrix translates strings and numbers into DOM text nodes, while treating booleans, null, and undefined as empty slots that emit zero DOM nodes. Non-primitive objects and Date instances stop the render with an error, requiring explicit formatting. Double curlies (style={{}}) are simply an outer JSX evaluation window enclosing an inner JavaScript object literal.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this gets tricky in production is whitespace handling and boolean zeros. In JSX, line breaks strip surrounding whitespace, causing {readTime} and min read on separate lines to render as 4min read unless an explicit {' '} token is added. Additionally, while false renders nothing, the number 0 renders visibly, meaning {count && <Badge />} displays a visible "0" when count is zero, a common defect explored further in Lecture 10.

Glossary

  • JSX Evaluation Window: The syntactic zone opened by curly braces ({}) in content or attributes that switches the compiler from static markup to live JavaScript execution.
  • Expression: An ECMAScript code unit that evaluates to a discrete value in memory (such as variables, math operations, ternaries, and function calls) and can be passed into JSX braces.
  • Statement: An ECMAScript code unit that controls execution flow or performs actions without producing a value (such as if, for, while, or const) and is forbidden inside JSX braces.
  • Primitive Render Matrix: React's internal type-routing rules that paint strings and numbers as DOM text nodes while rendering booleans, null, and undefined as empty slots.
  • Empty Slot: An invisible DOM placeholder emitted when React encounters booleans, null, or undefined in child content, emitting zero DOM nodes.
  • Double Curlies: A syntactic combination where an outer pair of JSX curly braces encloses an inner JavaScript object literal, commonly used in inline style props.

Beyond the basics

  • JavaScript in JSX with curly braces: Master the official syntax reference and rules for evaluating expressions in markup (see react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces).
  • Writing markup with JSX: Review how JSX compiles to JavaScript function calls and element descriptors (see react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx).
  • Conditional rendering in React: Explore how ternaries and boolean operators drive conditional UI rendering (see react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering).
  • Common DOM components and attribute props: Examine how React DOM handles properties, styles, and children (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • Keeping components pure: Understand why expressions evaluated during render must remain pure calculations (see react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ The JSX Evaluation Window Invariant

➔ IF projecting dynamic values into content or attribute positions, THEN wrap variables and expressions in curly braces ({}) to open the evaluation window.

➔ IF authoring text outside curly braces, THEN treat it as static character content because the compiler does not evaluate unbracketed identifiers.

❒ Dynamic Attribute Binding

➔ IF binding an attribute to a dynamic JavaScript value, THEN use unquoted curly braces (src={avatarUrl}).

➔ IF passing a static, unchanging string literal, THEN use quotes (alt="Author"), avoiding curly braces inside quotes which remain literal characters.

❒ Expressions Versus Statements

➔ IF evaluating logic inside JSX curly braces, THEN use value-producing expressions (variables, math, ternaries, function calls).

➔ IF control flow requires statements (if, for, while), THEN execute them above the return statement and pass the resulting value into JSX.

❒ Primitive Render Matrix and Object Content

➔ IF displaying dates or objects in JSX child content, THEN format them into primitive strings or numbers before placing them inside curly braces.

➔ IF passing an object to an element, THEN do so only for attributes that accept objects (such as style), avoiding objects in content which crash the render.

DO THIS: evaluate variables in curly braces, use unquoted attributes, and format objects into strings

9 <p>{readTime} min read</p>

12}

5

UI as a Tree &
Component Hierarchy

Interview Question   CORE

How does React organize nested components into a tree, and why does hierarchy dictate data flow?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build a news page with a header, an article feed, story cards, and author bylines.
  • 2 Declaring all sections in one giant function sprawls, while sharing variables between separate functions fails.
  • 3 How does React organize nested components into a tree, and how does data travel between them?

A component tree divides the page into focused jobs

Every web application contains multiple visual sections: headers, article feeds, story cards, and bylines. In earlier lessons, our components were single functions that returned markup for one piece of the interface. When building a full page, every developer meets the same question: how do we organize the markup and functions that create the page?

A first full page often keeps every region inside one large component function, a monolithic layout:

Monolithic layout: all page regions inside one function
1export default function PageLayout() {
2 return (
3 <div className="content-app">
4 <header>Daily Articles</header>
Inlines site header in monolith
5 <main>
6 <article>Night Trains</article>
Hardcodes article markup in root
7 </main>
8 </div>
9 );
10}

All regions of the page sit inside one function: the <header>, <main>, and <article> tags are returned in a single return statement. The browser renders the markup without errors. That is why it is called a monolithic layout: one single function contains the entire structure. As the page grows, that function grows to hundreds of lines, and every new card repeats the same markup.

React's answer is a component tree: split the page into nested components that each manage one focused responsibility.

Component tree: nested components with divided responsibilities
1export default function App() {
2 return (
3 <div className="content-app">
4 <NewsHeader />
Header component manages banner
5 <EditorialFeed />
Feed component manages article list
6 </div>
7 );
8}

Instead of dumping every element into App, the top-level component returns <NewsHeader /> and <EditorialFeed />. Inside EditorialFeed, the feed returns two <ArticleCard /> components, and each card returns an <EditorialByline />. When React mounts App, it walks from App down through each child, assembling an in-memory hierarchy called a component tree. The browser DOM receives the exact same HTML elements, but the code divides into modular parts with clear names and focused jobs. That is why it is called a component tree: a top-down hierarchy of components.

Component tree: feed nesting article cards
1function EditorialFeed() {
2 return (
3 <main className="feed">
4 <ArticleCard />
First article node
5 <ArticleCard />
Second article node
6 </main>
7 );
8}

A second component shows the hierarchy at work: EditorialFeed renders two <ArticleCard /> tags, so ArticleCard appears twice in the tree while its function is written once.

Later, we will see how parent components pass values down to their children through props (Lecture 6).

In this chapter, we learn how React organizes components into a tree on our news page: why returned JSX builds the tree rather than function order in the file, why splitting monolithic components into root, branch, and leaf nodes improves maintainability, and why unidirectional hierarchy dictates that shared data must live in the closest common parent. At the end, we compare monolithic layouts against component trees.

In this lesson, all components sit in one file and pass data directly. Later lessons build on what we establish today: Lecture 6 explores passing values down the tree through props, Lecture 7 covers nesting content through the children prop, Lecture 8 explores the module dependency tree across separate files, Lecture 10 examines conditional rendering branches, Lecture 12 explores pure component rendering, and Lecture 15 traces how React walks the tree during render before committing changes to the DOM.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • How does React know which component goes where when several functions are declared in the same file?
  • Why should we split a working monolithic component into smaller functions?
  • Why can't sibling components talk directly to each other, and how does data travel between them?
  • Lecture 1 (Declarative components and DOM construction): In Lecture 1, we learned that React describes interfaces from data rather than manual DOM manipulation with document.getElementById and textContent, keeping multiple UI regions in sync without state drift.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy and PascalCase naming): In Lecture 2, we learned that a component is a capitalized function defined at the top level of a file, and React invokes that function declaratively when its custom tag is used.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX Syntax and the single-root rule): In Lecture 3, we learned that JSX compiles tags into element descriptors, requiring a single root element where a React Fragment (<>...</>) groups siblings without adding wrapper elements to the browser DOM.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript Expressions in JSX with curly braces): In Lecture 4, we learned that curly braces ({}) open an evaluation window in content and attributes, projecting JavaScript variables into markup while null and undefined render as empty slots.
  • Native browser foundations: We build on standard HTML semantic tags (<header>, <main>, <article>), JavaScript function scope with const and let, reference errors, and the browser development console.

The component tree models your interface from root to leaves

In computer science and web development, user interfaces are universally modeled as trees. A tree is a hierarchical data structure composed of connected nodes, starting at a single root node that branches downward into child nodes. Web browsers use tree structures to model HTML documents through the Document Object Model (the DOM) and style hierarchies through the CSS Object Model (the CSSOM). Mobile platforms like iOS and Android represent their view hierarchies as trees. React embraces this exact same model: it organizes your user interface as a component tree composed of your custom component functions.

To discuss component architecture with senior engineers, we use standard genealogical tree terminology:

  • The root component is the top-level node where the tree begins (App), and it is the very first component React renders.
  • A branch component is an intermediate container that groups related sections and renders child components (such as Header or ArticleList).
  • A leaf component is a terminal node at the bottom of the tree that renders native HTML elements directly without nesting further custom components (such as AuthorBadge).
  • Within the tree, a component that returns another component is its parent, the nested component is its child, components sharing the same parent are siblings, and components higher up the chain are ancestors.

It is crucial to distinguish between the React component tree and the browser DOM tree. As Lecture 1 demonstrated, custom component tags vanish into plain HTML when rendered to the screen. If you inspect the browser's native Elements tab, you see only native HTML tags like <header>, <main>, and <article>. The browser DOM has zero knowledge of App, Header, or ArticleCard. The React component tree, by contrast, lives in JavaScript memory and consists exclusively of React components. Developers inspect this living component tree using the React DevTools Components tab, which reveals the true architectural hierarchy that drives the application.

How does React build this tree? React does not inspect your file directory or the order in which functions are declared. Instead, React evaluates the JSX returned by each component function. When App returns <Header /> and <ArticleList />, the JSX compiler converts those tags into React element descriptors: _jsx(Header, {}) and _jsx(ArticleList, {}). These descriptors form parent-child branches in memory. Because each component function returns element descriptors describing what should appear next, React traverses these descriptors from the root downward, creating the nested component tree for that render pass.

Separation of concerns divides a layout by responsibility

When building web applications, developers face an architectural decision: should a layout live in one large function, or should it be divided across smaller components? In software engineering, separation of concerns means assigning each piece of code a single focused responsibility. In a React application, App orchestrates high-level page regions, branch components group semantic features, and leaf components manage specific presentation controls.

In the browser DOM, a decomposed component tree produces the exact same HTML elements as a monolithic single-function component. Component tags leave zero extra wrapper elements in the browser DOM. The benefits of splitting are architectural: code becomes readable, reusable, and testable. In code reviews, senior engineers flag 500-line monolithic functions because untangling layout bugs in a giant file is painful. However, engineers also avoid the opposite extreme: fragmenting every individual HTML tag into a separate trivial component.

As official React documentation teaches in Thinking in React, keep a small piece of markup inline inside its parent until it grows distinct data, styling, or logic of its own. When a section of markup develops an independent concern or needs to be rendered multiple times, extract it into a dedicated component.

Function scope isolates variables between sibling components

In JavaScript, variables declared with const or let inside a function body belong strictly to that function scope. Code executing outside that function cannot access those variables. If a component function attempts to read a variable declared inside another component, JavaScript halts execution and throws a fatal ReferenceError. Because sibling components never call each other, no direct horizontal pathway connects them in memory.

When developers hit scope boundaries, some attempt to read values from the browser DOM using document.getElementById('feed-reader').textContent In React, this imperative lookup fails with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'textContent') As Lecture 15 will explore, React executes all component functions during render to compute the UI description before committing any changes to the browser DOM. At the moment a header component renders, the DOM nodes for sibling components do not exist yet.

Because data cannot flow horizontally between siblings or upward from children, React enforces unidirectional top-down data flow. When two sibling components need the same piece of information, that value must live in their closest common parent. The parent holds the value and passes it downward to each child by writing it as an attribute on the child tag, such as <Header readerName={readerName} /> The child receives this value through its props, a mechanism Lecture 6 explores in full detail.

Principles of React: UI as a Tree and Component Hierarchy

QUESTION 1

The order of functions in a file does not decide the tree

A developer writes five components in a single file to build a content page: App, Header, ArticleList, ArticleCard, and AuthorBadge. In the JavaScript file, the developer declares AuthorBadge first, followed by App, ArticleList, Header, and ArticleCard. To verify how React executes the code, the developer adds a console.log statement to each component function:

Component Execution Order (Shuffled Root)
1function AuthorBadge() {
2 console.log("AuthorBadge runs");
Leaf component
3 return <span>By Clara</span>;
4}
5function App() {
6 console.log("App runs");
Root component
7 return <><Header /><ArticleList /></>;
8}
Component Execution Order (Branch Containers)
1function ArticleList() {
2 console.log("ArticleList runs");
Branch container
3 return <main><ArticleCard /><ArticleCard /></main>;
4}
5function Header() {
6 console.log("Header runs");
Branch header
7 return <header>Articles</header>;
8}
Component Execution Order (Card Leaf)
1function ArticleCard() {
2 console.log("ArticleCard runs");
Child card
3 return <article><AuthorBadge /></article>;
4}

When the application mounts, the developer inspects the browser console expecting the functions to run in the order they were defined in the file. Instead, the console prints App, Header, ArticleList, ArticleCard, AuthorBadge, ArticleCard, and AuthorBadge.

How does React know which component goes where when several functions are declared in the same file?

ANSWER

The code works. React builds the component tree from what each component returns in JSX, not from the order of functions in the file.

When the application loads, root.render(<App />) explicitly designates App as the root of the tree. React invokes App(). When App() returns <Header /> and <ArticleList />, React discovers its two immediate children. React then evaluates Header(), which logs its name and returns a semantic <header> tag. Next, React evaluates ArticleList(), which logs its name and returns two separate <ArticleCard /> tags.

React then visits the first <ArticleCard />, logging its name. That card returns <AuthorBadge />, prompting React to evaluate AuthorBadge(). React then visits the second <ArticleCard />, logging its name, and evaluates its <AuthorBadge />. Notice that ArticleCard and AuthorBadge both run twice because their tags appear twice in returned JSX. The order of function definitions in the file plays no part in execution. To change where a component appears in the hierarchy, you move its tag inside returned JSX, not its function definition.

File definition order versus top-down render execution sequence
File Declaration Order:           Top-Down Render Walk:
1. function AuthorBadge()         1. App()
2. function App()                 2. Header()
3. function ArticleList()    -->  3. ArticleList()
4. function Header()              4. ArticleCard()  -> AuthorBadge()
5. function ArticleCard()         5. ArticleCard()  -> AuthorBadge()
PRINCIPLE 1

The JSX each component returns builds the tree

component tree the hierarchy of components created by what each function returns in JSX

React builds the component tree from what each component returns in JSX, not from where functions sit in a file. React starts by calling the root component. When that component returns child tags, React calls those child components next, and continues down until only HTML tags remain. Moving a function up or down in your file changes nothing on screen. To change where a component appears in the hierarchy, move its tag inside the parent component's returned JSX.

We should do this:
function Card() {
return (
<article>
<Badge />
returned JSX makes Badge a child
</article>
);
}
QUESTION 2

Splitting a monolith keeps the HTML while dividing responsibilities

A developer builds the content page by inlining all header, article list, story cards, and author details into a single App component function:

Monolithic Single-Function Layout
1export default function App() {
Monolithic root
2 return (
3 <div className="content-app">
4 <header><h1>Daily Articles</h1></header>
5 <main>
6 <article><h3>Night Trains</h3><span>By Clara</span></article>
7 </main>
8 </div>
9 );
10}

The page renders properly in the browser and displays all articles. However, senior engineers flag the pull request during code review, asking for the layout to be decomposed into modular components. The developer wonders why they should break apart a component that already works.

Why should you split a page into smaller components when a single function already renders the required markup?

ANSWER

The code works. A monolithic component renders the exact same DOM elements as a decomposed tree, but it creates unmaintainable code sprawl.

In the browser DOM, custom component tags vanish into plain HTML elements, as Lecture 1 explained. Whether you write all markup inside App or split it across five components, the final DOM tree rendered to the screen is identical. Component tags introduce zero DOM wrappers and zero rendering performance penalties.

The difference lies entirely in code organization and separation of concerns. In a 500-line monolith, no developer can locate or update specific UI elements without scanning the entire file. The article card markup is copied and pasted for every story, meaning any layout change must be repeated across multiple blocks. Furthermore, testing or reusing individual parts of the interface is impossible.

When you decompose App into Header, ArticleList, ArticleCard, and AuthorBadge, each component receives exactly one job:

  • App acts as the root coordinator, managing high-level page regions.
  • ArticleList acts as a branch container, grouping the feed of stories.
  • ArticleCard encapsulates card layout, written once and reused for multiple stories.
  • AuthorBadge serves as a leaf component, displaying author details directly.

The boundary of this rule is important: keep a small piece of markup inline inside its parent until it grows distinct data or logic of its own, as official documentation does in Thinking in React.

Monolithic inlined layout versus decomposed component tree
Monolithic Layout:                Decomposed Component Tree:
App (500 lines)                   App (root coordinator)
  - inlined header markup           ├── Header (site branding)
  - inlined story card 1     -->    └── ArticleList (feed container)
  - inlined story card 2                  ├── ArticleCard (reusable card)
  - inlined footer markup                 │     └── AuthorBadge (leaf)
                                          └── ArticleCard (reusable card)
PRINCIPLE 2

Split the page into components with one job each

separation of concerns giving each component one focused responsibility in the interface

Writing an entire page in one large component produces the same HTML in the browser DOM, but makes code difficult to read, test, and reuse. Split the page by separation of concerns into components that each handle one clear responsibility. The root coordinates high-level regions, intermediate components group related sections, and terminal components render specific content. Keep a small piece of markup inside its parent until it grows distinct data or logic of its own.

We should do this:
function App() {
return (
<div>
<Header />
manages top header region
<ArticleList />
manages article feed
</div>
);
}
QUESTION 3

Sibling components cannot read each other's local variables

A developer wants to personalize the content page by displaying the reader's name ("Elena") in both the header greeting ("Welcome back, Elena") and the article feed ("Picked for Elena"). The developer declares const readerName = "Elena"; inside ArticleList. Then, inside Header, the developer attempts to display {readerName}:

Sibling Scope Communication Failure
1function Header() {
2 return <header>Welcome back, {readerName}</header>;
3}
4function ArticleList() {
5 const readerName = "Elena";
Declared locally in sibling
6 return <main><h2>Picked for {readerName}</h2></main>;
7}

When the developer refreshes the browser, the page does not render. The screen goes completely blank, and the browser console throws a fatal runtime error: ReferenceError: readerName is not defined The developer tries to fix this by querying the DOM element using document.getElementById('feed-reader').textContent but the call throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'textContent')

Why can't a header component read a variable declared inside an article list component?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Sibling components have isolated JavaScript function scopes and share no direct horizontal connections.

In JavaScript, variables declared with const or let inside a function exist strictly within that function scope. When Header executes, JavaScript looks for readerName in Header's local scope and the global scope. Because readerName is trapped inside ArticleList, the runtime halts immediately with a fatal ReferenceError.

Attempting to reach across through the browser DOM with document.getElementById('feed-reader') also fails with a null reference error. As Lecture 15 will explore, React executes all component functions during render to calculate the UI tree before committing any changes to the browser DOM. At the moment Header runs, the DOM elements for ArticleList do not exist yet.

Because siblings never call each other, data in React travels strictly downward along parent-child branches. To share a value between two siblings, place that value in their closest common parent (App). App declares const readerName = "Elena"; and passes it downward to each child component by writing it as an attribute on their tags: <Header readerName={readerName} /> and <ArticleList readerName={readerName} /> Each child component then accesses that value through its props (which Lecture 6 explores in full detail).

Common Parent Data Placement
1function App() {
2 const readerName = "Elena";
Shared in closest common parent
3 return (
4 <div>
5 <Header readerName={readerName} />
6 <ArticleList readerName={readerName} />
7 </div>
8 );
9}

Now both lines render cleanly: "Welcome back, Elena" in the header and "Picked for Elena" in the feed.

Horizontal sibling scope crash versus top-down flow from common parent
Broken Horizontal Access:         Top-Down Common Parent Routing:
Header <-------- ArticleList      App (declares readerName = "Elena")
(ReferenceError: not in scope)     ├── Header (receives readerName)
                                   └── ArticleList (receives readerName)
PRINCIPLE 3

Data travels down the tree so a shared value lives in their common parent

closest common parent the lowest shared component in the tree that sits above all components needing a value

In JavaScript, variables declared inside one function are invisible to other functions. Sibling components never call each other, so no direct communication path connects them. To share a value between siblings, place that value in their closest common parent. The parent passes the value downward to each child component by writing it as an attribute on the child tag.

We should do this:
function App() {
const user = "Elena";
declared in common parent
return (
<div>
<Header user={user} />
<Feed user={user} />
</div>
);
}
We should not do this:
function Header() {
return <header>{user}</header>;
ReferenceError: not defined
}
function Feed() {
const user = "Elena";
isolated in sibling scope
return <main>Feed</main>;
}
Case Study
Let's Design a Practical Example

To synthesize our three principles into production code, we build a multi-section article feed application. We decompose a monolithic layout into an application shell App.jsx, a site banner Header.jsx, a story feed container ArticleList.jsx, and modular leaf components ArticleCard.jsx and AuthorBadge.jsx. We assemble this implementation across four sequential steps, routing shared user data downward from the root container.

Step 1
First, we decompose the application shell
<App.jsx>

We construct App.jsx as the root coordinator of our component tree. In a monolithic approach, an engineer might dump all header, feed, and card markup directly into this single file. In React, we separate concerns: App declares the shared reader name and mounts Header and ArticleList as direct children in the component tree, passing the shared value downward along both branches.

App.jsx
1import Header from "./components/Header.jsx";
2import ArticleList from "./components/ArticleList.jsx";
3export default function App() {
4 const readerName = "Elena";
Shared value in common parent
5 return (<div className="content-app">
6 <Header readerName={readerName} />
7 <ArticleList readerName={readerName} />
8 </div>);
9}

Reviewing App.jsx reveals three architectural strengths:

  1. It establishes the root boundary of the component tree without inlining presentation details.
  2. It holds the shared reader name in the closest common parent, preventing scope crashes across sibling branches.
  3. It composes major page regions through clean JSX nesting, allowing child subtrees to be developed independently.
Step 2
Next, we assemble the site header banner
<Header.jsx>

We construct Header.jsx to manage publication identity and reader greetings. Notice how Header encapsulates its markup inside semantic <header> tags. By receiving readerName as an attribute from App, Header displays the personalized greeting without needing to query DOM nodes or access sibling memory. If the site branding changes, developers update Header.jsx without touching the article feed.

Header.jsx
1export default function Header(props) {
Branch banner
2 return (
3 <header className="site-header">
4 <h1 className="site-title">Daily Articles</h1>
5 <p className="greeting">Welcome back, {props.readerName}</p>
6 </header>
7 );
8}

Reviewing Header.jsx highlights two key design invariants:

  1. It isolates header markup within a semantic container that can be styled and tested in isolation.
  2. It consumes props.readerName directly, demonstrating how shared values arrive from parent containers.
Step 3
Then, we construct the article feed container
<ArticleList.jsx>

We construct ArticleList.jsx as a branch component coordinating the article feed. Notice how ArticleList renders a semantic <main> tag, projects props.readerName into the section heading, and mounts two <ArticleCard /> tags. ArticleList does not need to know how an article card is styled; it simply defines where cards sit within the feed layout.

ArticleList.jsx
1import ArticleCard from "./ArticleCard.jsx";
2export default function ArticleList(props) {
Branch feed
3 return (
4 <main className="feed-section">
5 <h2 className="feed-title">Picked for {props.readerName}</h2>
6 <ArticleCard />
7 <ArticleCard />
8 </main>
9 );
10}

Notice the structural role of ArticleList: it serves as an intermediate branch in the render tree. It is a child of App, and simultaneously the parent of two ArticleCard nodes. Mounting <ArticleCard /> twice demonstrates that each JSX tag creates an independent node in the component tree.

Step 4
Finally, we build the article card and author badge
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We construct ArticleCard.jsx and its nested child AuthorBadge.jsx to seal the bottom of our tree. ArticleCard encapsulates the headline and story summary inside a semantic <article> element, mounting <AuthorBadge /> to display author details. AuthorBadge represents a pure leaf component, rendering native HTML <span> elements directly without nesting further custom components.

First, examine the terminal leaf component AuthorBadge.jsx:

AuthorBadge.jsx
1export default function AuthorBadge() {
Terminal leaf
2 return (
3 <div className="author-badge">
4 <span className="author-name">By Clara Foster</span>
5 <span className="publish-date">September 27</span>
6 </div>
7 );
8}

Now, examine ArticleCard.jsx which encapsulates card layout and nests the leaf badge:

ArticleCard.jsx
1import AuthorBadge from "./AuthorBadge.jsx";
2export default function ArticleCard() {
Presentation card
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h3 className="story-title">Night Trains Return</h3>
6 <p className="story-summary">Sleeper routes connect Europe.</p>
7 <AuthorBadge />
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Reviewing ArticleCard.jsx reveals three architectural lessons:

  1. It demonstrates multi-level tree depth: App nests ArticleList, which nests ArticleCard, which nests AuthorBadge.
  2. It encapsulates story presentation into a reusable card that can appear multiple times across the feed.
  3. AuthorBadge terminates the tree cleanly, returning native HTML elements directly to the browser DOM.

Component Summary

App

The root application shell coordinates top-level page regions. It initializes the shared reader name and mounts the site header and article feed branches. What is its structural role? It provides a stable layout boundary and acts as the closest common parent for the entire component tree.

Header

This branch container groups site branding and personalized reader greetings. It encapsulates top-level presentation for the header region, keeping header markup completely separate from the article feed.

ArticleList

This branch container organizes the central story feed. It renders the personalized section title and mounts nested article cards, defining the structural subtree for the feed body.

ArticleCard

This presentation component frames the headline and summary for an individual story. It encapsulates card markup and nests the author badge leaf component.

AuthorBadge

This leaf component renders author attribution and publication dates directly into native span elements, terminating the bottom of the component tree.

In legacy web applications, developers built pages by pasting raw HTML markup into monolithic files or manipulating arbitrary DOM nodes across scripts. In React, interfaces are organized as a clean, hierarchical component tree. App sits at the root, branching downward into Header and ArticleList, which terminate in leaf components like ArticleCard and AuthorBadge. This hierarchy provides immense clarity: each component owns a single responsibility, React walks the tree predictably from the root downward, and data flows reliably along parent-child branches.

Where you will meet this

  1. Content and Media Publications: Large publishing platforms decompose complex front pages into navigation headers, featured story grids, and article card leaves, allowing teams to rearrange sections without rewriting card code.
  2. E-Commerce Product Catalogs: E-commerce platforms organize product listing pages into category filter branches, product grid containers, and individual product card leaves that can be tested and reused across the site.
  3. Application Shells and Dashboards: Enterprise SaaS dashboards use root shell components to compose consistent navigation headers, sidebars, and main content feeds out of isolated branch components.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How does React organize nested components into a tree, and why does hierarchy dictate data flow?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not merely checking if you know what a component is. They are probing your understanding of React's execution model, tree data structures, lexical scope isolation, and why React enforces unidirectional data flow. A junior developer says React "builds a tree from HTML tags." A senior engineer explains that React evaluates JSX element descriptors returned by component functions from the root downward to construct an in-memory component tree, and that hierarchy dictates data flow because functions maintain isolated scopes while React provides zero horizontal communication pathways between siblings.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is assuming that function declaration order in a file determines runtime hierarchy, or attempting to share variables horizontally between adjacent sibling components. Candidates often forget that JavaScript lexical scope isolates variables within function bodies, leading to fatal ReferenceError crashes when trying to read values across siblings. Another frequent trap is attempting imperative DOM queries like document.getElementById during render, which returns null because React executes component calculations before committing elements to the DOM.

3. What is Actually Going On

Under the hood, React starts execution at the root component designated by root.render(). When a parent component returns JSX, the compiler translates custom tags into element descriptors (_jsx(Child, {})). React traverses these descriptors top-down, calling each child component in turn until only native DOM tags remain. Because components are independent functions that never invoke each other directly, no horizontal connections exist between siblings. Data can only flow downward along parent-child branches. When siblings need to coordinate around a shared value, that value must be lifted to their closest common parent, which passes it down to each child via props.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this gets tricky in production is understanding that while a parent always executes before its children, React does not guarantee a strict execution order between siblings. Relying on one sibling running before another to set global variables or trigger side effects violates React's pure rendering model, a critical invariant explored in Lecture 12. Furthermore, in deep hierarchies, passing shared values down through multiple intermediate containers creates prop drilling, which motivates architectural patterns like children composition in Lecture 7 and React Context in Lecture 27.

Glossary

  • Component Tree: The hierarchical data structure of React element descriptors formed by what components return in JSX, representing the component structure for a single render pass.
  • Root Component: The top-level component where a React application begins (App), acting as the first component React renders and the ancestor of all other components.
  • Branch Component: An intermediate container in the component tree that groups related UI sections and renders child components.
  • Leaf Component: A terminal component at the edge of the component tree that has no custom child components and renders native HTML elements directly.
  • Closest Common Parent: The lowest shared parent component in the hierarchy that sits above two or more components that require the same data.
  • Separation of Concerns: The software design principle of dividing an application into distinct components, where each component addresses a single, well-defined responsibility.
  • Function Scope: The JavaScript language boundary where variables declared inside a function body are private to that function and invisible to outside code.
  • ReferenceError: The JavaScript runtime exception thrown when code attempts to access a variable identifier that does not exist within the current lexical scope.
  • React DevTools: A browser extension that inspects the living React component tree in memory, contrasting with the browser Elements tab which displays the HTML DOM.
  • Unidirectional Data Flow: The architectural invariant where data travels strictly downward along parent-child branches from ancestors to descendants.

Beyond the basics

  • Understanding your UI as a tree: Master the official guide to render trees and module dependency trees in React (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Thinking in React: Step 1 Component Hierarchy: Explore how to break a design mockup into a structured component hierarchy (see react.dev/learn/thinking-in-react#step-1-break-the-ui-into-a-component-hierarchy).
  • Your first component: nesting and organizing: Review official guidelines on nesting components and defining them at the top level (see react.dev/learn/your-first-component#nesting-and-organizing-components).
  • Passing props to a component: Examine how values travel down parent-child branches in the component tree (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).
  • Keeping components pure: Understand why components must not depend on sibling rendering order or shared mutable variables (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Tree Structure and JSX Nesting

➔ IF determining component hierarchy, THEN read the nesting of tags inside returned JSX rather than the order of function declarations in a file.

➔ IF moving a component in the UI hierarchy, THEN move its tag within returned JSX, because moving a function definition in a file changes nothing on screen.

❒ Component Decomposition and Separation of Concerns

➔ IF structuring a multi-section layout, THEN decompose it into root, branch, and leaf components with one focused responsibility each.

➔ IF evaluating whether to extract a component, THEN keep small pieces of markup inline until they grow distinct data, styling, or logic of their own.

❒ Execution Order and Unidirectional Data Flow

➔ IF tracing component execution, THEN trace top-down from parent to child, remembering that unmounted child subtrees never execute.

➔ IF sharing a value between sibling components, THEN place that value in their closest common parent and pass it downward, because siblings cannot read each other's local variables.

DO THIS: Decompose layouts into parent-child trees and route shared data through common parents

code.txt
1function App() {
2 const user = "Elena";
3 return (
4 <div className="app">
5 <Header user={user} />
6 <ArticleList user={user} />
7 </div>
8 );
9}

DO NOT DO THIS: Dump entire layouts into 500-line monoliths or attempt horizontal sibling variable access

code.txt
1function Header() {
2 return <header>{user}</header>;
3}
4function ArticleList() {
5 const user = "Elena";
6 return <main><article><h3>Night Trains</h3></article></main>;
7}

Lecture
6

Passing Data with Props &
the Read-Only Contract

Interview Question   CORE

How do you pass data into a component, and why can a component never change its own props?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You render three article cards in a feed to display morning news stories.
  • 2 Without inputs, every card displays identical text, while mutating incoming data crashes in development.
  • 3 How do you pass data into a component, and why are props read-only?

Props let one component show different content

Every web application displays repeated visual structures: news feeds, product listings, and user comments. In earlier lessons, our components returned fixed markup or read local variables declared inside their own function bodies. When multiple cards share the same frame but display different data, every developer meets the same question: how does each component display its own unique content?

A component that writes its text inside its own function body is a hardcoded component:

Hardcoded component: fixed text inside component body
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>Transit Accord Reached</h2>
Fixed headline in component body
5 <p>5 min read</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

All values sit hardcoded inside the function body: the card always displays "Transit Accord Reached" and "5 min read". If the feed renders <ArticleCard /> three times, every card displays identical copy; to show three different stories, a developer must duplicate the function three times. That is why it is called a hardcoded component: the data is fixed directly in code.

React's answer is props: the parent passes attributes on the component tag, and React hands them to the child as an input object.

Props: dynamic attributes configured by parent
1function EditorialFeed() {
2 return (
3 <main className="feed">
4 <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} />
First card
5 <ArticleCard title="Clean Energy Project" readTime={5} />
Card two
6 </main>
7 );
8}

The parent component writes attributes on each <ArticleCard /> tag: title="Rail Strike Ends" and readTime={3}. React collects those attributes into a single object and passes it to ArticleCard as its argument. Inside ArticleCard, the component unpacks { title, readTime } and renders those values. One single component layout now renders hundreds of distinct stories. That is why they are called props: properties passed from parent to child.

Props: unpacking inputs in the parameter list
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
Renders title prop
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
Renders readTime prop
6 </article>
7 );
8}

The child component function shows the other side of the contract: placing { title, readTime } in the parameter list unpacks the incoming properties directly into local variables.

Later, we will see that nested markup passed between a component's opening and closing tags arrives as a special prop named children (Lecture 7).

In this chapter, we learn how props work on our ArticleCard component: how tag attributes compile into a single props object, why we unpack properties in the parameter list with curly braces, why numbers must be passed in curly braces, how default parameter values handle missing data, and why props are strictly read-only. At the end, we compare hardcoded components against props.

In this lesson, props are passed down from a parent with static values. Later lessons build on what we establish today: Lecture 7 passes nested markup with children, Lecture 8 splits components into separate module files, Lecture 10 conditionally renders markup from prop values, Lecture 11 renders lists of items with props, Lecture 12 explores pure rendering guarantees, and Lecture 14 introduces reactive state for values that change over time.

This lesson answers five questions:

  • How do attributes written on a JSX tag reach the child component function?
  • How do we unpack individual values from incoming props without repeating object lookups?
  • Why does passing a number in quotes cause arithmetic bugs on screen?
  • How do default values handle missing properties, null values, and zero?
  • Why does React strictly forbid a component from modifying its own props?

  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy and PascalCase naming): In Lecture 2, we learned that a component is a capitalized function defined at the top level of a file, and React invokes that function declaratively when its custom tag is used.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX Syntax and the single-root rule): In Lecture 3, we learned that JSX compiles tags into element descriptors, requiring a single root element where Fragments (<>...</>) group siblings without adding wrapper elements to the browser DOM.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript Expressions in JSX with curly braces): In Lecture 4, we learned that curly braces ({}) open an evaluation window in content and attributes, quotes pass static string literals, double curlies pass object literals, and null and undefined render as empty slots.

What props are and how React passes them as a single object

In standard JavaScript, functions accept arguments so that a single calculation can run on different inputs. For example, a function double(x) returns x * 2 for any number you provide. React components are JavaScript functions that return user interface markup. If a component could only return hardcoded text, you would need a new component function for every distinct item in your application. React solves this through props, which is short for properties. Props allow a parent component to pass custom data down to child components, letting one single component layout render hundreds of different stories or products.

When you render a custom component tag in JSX, any attributes you write become properties on a single JavaScript object. For instance, writing <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} /> tells React to create an object: { title: "Rail Strike Ends", readTime: 3 } React passes this object as the first and only argument to your ArticleCard component function. In React terminology, the location where you render the tag is called the call site, the attributes are called props, and the component receiving the data is the child component. The attributes on the tag do not reach the browser DOM directly; React hands them exclusively to the component function.

When working with props, modern JavaScript provides a concise syntax called object destructuring. Instead of writing function ArticleCard(props) and repeating props.title and props.readTime throughout your markup, you can write function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) In JavaScript, placing curly braces { } inside the parameter list tells the runtime to automatically unpack specific keys from the incoming object into local variables. This syntax is standard ECMAScript, but it is the universal convention in React because it makes a component's required inputs immediately visible at the top of the function. If a destructured parameter name does not match any attribute on the tag (such as writing { headline } when the tag passed title=), the local variable receives undefined.

Under the hood, the JSX compiler converts every component tag into a function call. As we learned in Lecture 4, writing <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} /> transforms into _jsx(ArticleCard, { title: "Rail Strike Ends", readTime: 3 }) Notice that the second argument to _jsx is a standard JavaScript object literal. React instantiates this object, freezes it shallowly in development mode using Object.freeze(), and provides it to your component when invoking the function. This mechanical reality proves why components receive exactly one object argument rather than a list of separate parameters.

How JavaScript handles prop types, string concatenation, and default values

In JSX, how you wrap an attribute value determines its JavaScript data type. As established in Lecture 4, quotes pass a static string literal (readTime="5"), while curly braces evaluate a live JavaScript expression (readTime={5}). When a child component receives a prop, the runtime respects that exact type. If a component receives "5" as a string and performs addition ({readTime + 1}), JavaScript performs string concatenation via type coercion, converting 1 to "1" and producing "51". By contrast, multiplication ({readTime * 60}) coerces the string to a number and yields 300. This discrepancy can hide bugs during initial testing until an addition operation reveals the error.

When designing components, some props are optional. If a parent component omits an attribute or passes readTime={undefined}, the incoming property is undefined. To prevent blank slots on screen, JavaScript allows you to specify a default parameter value directly inside the destructuring braces: function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 5 }) If the parent does not provide readTime, the local variable automatically takes the fallback value 5. However, default parameter values only trigger when a value is strictly undefined or missing; they do not trigger when a parent passes null or 0.

When working with external API data, database records often contain null for unmeasured fields. If a parent passes readTime={null}, the default parameter readTime = 5 does not engage because null is a defined value. In JSX, {null} renders as an empty string, producing min read. In older JavaScript codebases, developers wrote readTime || 5 using the logical OR operator. However, || treats any falsy value as missing, which replaces a valid 0 (such as a 0-minute quick read) with 5. Modern codebases use the nullish coalescing operator (??): const time = readTime ?? 5; Nullish coalescing checks strictly for null and undefined, preserving valid 0 values while providing a resilient fallback.

The read-only contract, frozen objects, and why mutating inputs corrupts the tree

In React, components must be pure functions with respect to their inputs. A pure function is one that does not alter any objects or variables that existed before it was called, and returns the exact same JSX description given the same inputs. Props represent data owned by the parent component. If a child component were allowed to perform a mutation by directly reassigning props.title = 'Breaking News' it would modify memory owned by the parent. React enforces an immutability contract: props are strictly read-only.

To protect developers from accidental mutations, React shallowly freezes the props object in development mode using Object.freeze(). When code runs inside an ES module, JavaScript automatically executes in strict mode. In strict mode, attempting to assign a property on a frozen object immediately throws a fatal exception: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'title' of object '#<Object>' In older non-strict scripts, the assignment is silently ignored without updating the object.

It is critical to understand that React's development freeze is a diagnostic alarm, not a runtime security sandbox. In production builds, React skips Object.freeze() to maximize rendering performance. Furthermore, Object.freeze() is shallow: if a parent passes an object prop like article={{ title: 'Rail Strike', readTime: 3 }} React freezes only the outer container, leaving nested properties mutable. If a child executes article.title = article.title.toUpperCase() the assignment succeeds in both development and production. This mutation silently corrupts data in the parent and across sibling components showing the same article (such as a sidebar), causing state drift.

Instead of mutating incoming props, a component that needs an altered display format calculates a new local variable during render: const headline = title.toUpperCase(); The component renders {headline} in its JSX while leaving the incoming prop completely untouched. If data must change dynamically over time in response to user events, the component does not modify props; instead, the owner component manages that value using React state (introduced in Lecture 14).

Principles of React: Passing Data with Props

QUESTION 1

Attributes on a tag become the component's one props object

A developer renders three article cards inside an editorial feed container to display morning news dispatches. The developer writes attributes on each JSX tag, providing distinct titles and reading estimates:

Feed Call Sites
1function EditorialFeed() {
Parent container passes attributes
2 return (
3 <main>
4 <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} />
5 <ArticleCard title="Clean Energy Project" readTime={5} />
6 <ArticleCard title="City Park Renovations" readTime={4} />
7 </main>
8 );
9}

However, inside ArticleCard, the component still returns hardcoded text:

ArticleCard Hardcoded Heading
1function ArticleCard() {
2 return <h2>Night Trains Return to Europe</h2>;
Ignores incoming attributes
3}

When the browser renders the page, all three cards display Night Trains Return to Europe The developer checks the browser console, expecting a warning about unused attributes, but the console stays silent.

How do individual cards display their own headlines when rendered from the same component?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React packages attributes into a props object, but the component must read values from that object to display them.

When React evaluates EditorialFeed, it encounters three <ArticleCard /> tags. For each tag, React collects all attributes into a single JavaScript object: { title: "Rail Strike Ends", readTime: 3 } for the first card, and { title: "Clean Energy Project", readTime: 5 } for the second. React then invokes ArticleCard three times, passing that tag's specific object as the sole argument. If you add console.log(props) inside ArticleCard, the console prints three distinct objects in the exact order the tags appear.

Because ArticleCard returned hardcoded text, it completely ignored its incoming argument. React does not automatically project tag attributes into child markup; attributes never reach the browser DOM by themselves. To display the parent's data, the component must accept its props object and interpolate values into returned JSX, such as function ArticleCard({ title }) returning <h2>{title}</h2>

JSX attributes compiling into a single props object argument
JSX Call Site:                               Function Call:
<ArticleCard                         -->     ArticleCard({
  title="Rail Strike Ends"                     title: "Rail Strike Ends",
  readTime={3}                                 readTime: 3
/>                                           })
PRINCIPLE 1

The attributes on a tag become the component's one argument, the props

props a single JavaScript object collecting all attributes passed from parent to child

When you write attributes on a custom component tag in JSX, React collects them into a single props object. React calls your component function with that object as its only argument. Each tag gets its own props object, giving each rendered card its own values. Nothing appears on screen until the component reads from that object.

We should do this:
function ArticleCard({ title }) {
return <h2>{title}</h2>;
reads incoming prop
}
We should not do this:
function ArticleCard() {
return <h2>Night Trains Return</h2>;
ignores tag attributes
}

In our feed test, rendering <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} /> and <ArticleCard title="Clean Energy Project" readTime={5} /> produces two separate calls to ArticleCard. Inside ArticleCard, adding console.log(props) logs {"title":"Rail Strike Ends","readTime":3} and {"title":"Clean Energy Project","readTime":5} in the browser console. When the component returned hardcoded text, both calls returned identical markup. Once the component reads from props, each card displays its own headline and reading time.

QUESTION 2

Unpack the props in the parameter list inside braces

A developer wants to read title and readTime inside ArticleCard. In standard JavaScript functions, passing two pieces of data typically means declaring two parameters. The developer declares both names in the parameter list without braces:

Missing Parameter Braces
1function ArticleCard(title, readTime) {
Binds object to title parameter
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
Crashes attempting to render raw object
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

When the application loads, the browser screen goes blank. The developer opens the browser console and discovers a fatal runtime crash: Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {title, readTime}) Furthermore, when testing with { headline } instead of { title }, the heading renders completely blank without an error message.

How do we extract title and readTime from incoming props without causing runtime errors?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React passes exactly one argument to components, so parameters must be wrapped in curly braces to destructure properties.

In JavaScript, function parameters bind sequentially to incoming arguments. When React renders <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} /> it invokes ArticleCard({ title: "Rail Strike Ends", readTime: 3 }) with exactly one argument. When you declare function ArticleCard(title, readTime) without braces, JavaScript binds the first parameter title to the entire props object, while the second parameter readTime receives undefined.

When React attempts to evaluate <h2>{title}</h2> it encounters a raw JavaScript object inside JSX children. Because objects cannot be converted into DOM text nodes, React halts execution with Objects are not valid as a React child To unpack properties into local variables, wrap the parameter names in curly braces: function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) This triggers object destructuring, creating local variables matching the object keys. If you write { headline } when the tag passed title=, destructuring assigns undefined, leaving an empty slot.

Parameter destructuring unpacking properties versus raw object binding
With Braces:   ({ title, readTime })  --> title = "Rail Strike", readTime = 3
Without:       (title, readTime)      --> title = { title: "...", readTime: 3 }
                                          readTime = undefined
PRINCIPLE 2

Unpack the props in the parameter list, inside braces

destructuring unpacking properties from an object into local variables with braces

React passes only one argument to a component function, the props object. Wrapping parameter names in curly braces uses destructuring to unpack specific properties into local variables. If you omit the braces, the first parameter receives the entire object, causing a runtime crash if rendered directly in JSX.

We should do this:
function ArticleCard({ title }) {
return <h2>{title}</h2>;
unpacks title property
}
We should not do this:
function ArticleCard(title) {
return <h2>{title}</h2>;
crashes: objects are not valid as children
}

When we write function ArticleCard(title, readTime) JavaScript assigns the first argument (the props object) to title, while readTime remains undefined. When React evaluates <h2>{title}</h2> it attempts to render a raw JavaScript object into the DOM and throws: Error: Objects are not valid as a React child (found: object with keys {title, readTime}) Wrapping the parameters in braces ({ title, readTime }) tells JavaScript to extract those exact properties into local variables. If you type { headline } instead of { title }, the variable receives undefined, and the heading renders blank without throwing an error.

QUESTION 3

Pass numbers in curly braces or they arrive as strings

A developer writes an article card that displays reading estimates in multiple formats. The card displays reading time plus an estimated summary time ({readTime + 1} min with the summary), as well as the total seconds ({readTime * 60} seconds). At the JSX call site, the developer writes readTime="5" in quotes:

Quoted Number Attribute
1<ArticleCard
2 title="Rail Strike Ends"
3 readTime="5"
Passes string "5" rather than numerical value
4/>

Inside ArticleCard, the component performs arithmetic on the incoming prop:

Reading Time Calculations
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime }) {
Unpacks parameters
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
5 <p>{readTime + 1} min with the summary</p>
Evaluates "5" + 1
6 <p>{readTime * 60} seconds</p>
Evaluates "5" * 60
7 </article>
8 );
9}

On screen, the seconds calculation displays 300 seconds, which looks correct. However, the first line displays 51 min with the summary instead of 6 min.

Why does passing a number in quotes result in 51 min on screen instead of 6 min?

ANSWER

The code does not do what the reader expected. Quoted attributes pass strings, causing JavaScript addition to perform string concatenation rather than mathematical addition.

In JSX, quotes enclose string literals. Writing readTime="5" passes the string "5" to the component. In JavaScript, the addition operator (+) has dual behavior: it adds numbers together, but when either operand is a string, it converts the other operand to a string and concatenates them via type coercion. Therefore, "5" + 1 becomes "5" + "1", which evaluates to "51".

The bug is deceptive because the multiplication line ({readTime * 60}) displays 300 seconds. In JavaScript, the multiplication operator (*) does not exist for strings; the runtime coerces "5" into the number 5 and performs arithmetic. To pass genuine numbers, wrap them in curly braces: <ArticleCard readTime={5} /> Curly braces evaluate the enclosed expression as JavaScript, delivering a number type where 5 + 1 evaluates to 6.

String concatenation versus numerical addition in JavaScript
Quoted Prop:  readTime="5"  --> "5" + 1 === "51"  (String Concatenation)
Brace Prop:   readTime={5}  -->  5  + 1 === 6     (Numerical Addition)
PRINCIPLE 3

Pass numbers in curly braces, or they arrive as strings

type coercion automatic conversion of a value from one data type to another by JavaScript

An attribute written in quotes always passes a string literal. If your component performs addition on a quoted number, JavaScript uses type coercion to concatenate the values as text, turning "5" + 1 into "51". Pass numbers inside curly braces so they arrive as numbers.

We should do this:
function Card() {
return <ArticleCard readTime={5} />;
passes number 5
}
We should not do this:
function Card() {
return <ArticleCard readTime="5" />;
passes string '5'
}

Testing both call sites reveals why this defect slips past casual checks. In the first card with readTime="5", {readTime * 60} computes 300 because the multiplication operator coerces strings to numbers in JavaScript. However, {readTime + 1} outputs 51 because the plus operator prioritizes string concatenation when either operand is a string. When we change the call site to readTime={5}, {readTime + 1} evaluates to 6, and {readTime * 60} evaluates to 300. Reviewers flag quoted numbers on sight because arithmetic errors surface as soon as a feature adds numbers together.

QUESTION 4

A default fills a missing prop and only a missing one

A developer designs ArticleCard so that readTime is optional. If an article record lacks a reading time estimate, the developer wants the card to display a default estimate of 5 minutes. The developer configures a default parameter in destructuring:

Default Parameter Configuration
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 5 }) {
Sets default parameter
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{title}</h2>
5 <p>{readTime} min read</p>
Renders empty slot for null
6 </article>
7 );
8}

When rendering <ArticleCard title="Park Renovations" /> with no readTime attribute, the card displays 5 min read. When rendering <ArticleCard readTime={0} /> for a brief bulletin, the card displays 0 min read. However, when data arrives from an API where unmeasured articles have readTime: null, the card renders min read with an empty slot.

How do default parameter values behave when an incoming prop is undefined, null, or zero?

ANSWER

The code does not do what the reader wanted. Default parameters only engage when a prop is missing or undefined; they pass null through unchanged.

In JavaScript, default parameter values trigger strictly when an incoming argument is undefined. When a parent omits an attribute or explicitly passes readTime={undefined}, JavaScript substitutes the fallback value 5. However, null is a valid primitive object in JavaScript representing the intentional absence of a value. Because null !== undefined, the default parameter does not engage. In JSX, {null} produces an empty text slot, rendering min read.

To handle null, some developers write readTime || 5. However, the logical OR operator (||) checks for falsiness. Because 0 is falsy in JavaScript, <ArticleCard readTime={0} /> replaces 0 with 5, corrupting valid zero-minute bulletins. The robust solution is the nullish coalescing operator (??): const time = readTime ?? 5; Nullish coalescing replaces only null and undefined, preserving valid 0 values. Furthermore, React 19 does not validate legacy propTypes on function components, so fallback logic must be handled in JavaScript.

Default parameter evaluation across undefined, null, and zero
Input Value:       readTime = 5:      readTime || 5:     readTime ?? 5:
undefined (missing) -> 5 (Default)        -> 5               -> 5
null                -> null (Pass-through)-> 5 (Overridden!) -> 5
0                   -> 0 (Preserved)      -> 5 (Overridden!) -> 0 (Preserved)
PRINCIPLE 4

A default fills a missing prop, and only a missing one

default parameter a fallback value assigned when an incoming argument is undefined

An assignment after = sets a default parameter that fills in when a prop is missing or undefined. A default parameter does not replace null or 0. When data can hold null, compute a fallback with ?? during render, and avoid || because it overwrites valid zero values.

We should do this:
function ArticleCard({ readTime = 5 }) {
return <p>{readTime} min</p>;
fills missing or undefined
}
We should not do this:
function ArticleCard({ readTime }) {
return <p>{readTime || 5} min</p>;
overrides valid 0 with 5
}

We test four cards against readTime = 5: an omitted prop displays 5 min read, readTime={undefined} displays 5 min read, readTime={0} displays 0 min read, and readTime={null} displays min read. Because null passes through default parameters, the label renders blank. When developers attempt to fix this with readTime || 5, passing 0 produces 5 min read, corrupting valid zero-minute reads. Replacing the expression with readTime ?? 5 preserves 0 min read for zero while supplying 5 min read for both null and undefined.

QUESTION 5

Props are read-only so make a new variable instead

A developer wants every article headline to appear in uppercase letters. Because props is a JavaScript object, the developer attempts to mutate the incoming title directly inside the component body before returning markup:

Direct Prop Reassignment
1function ArticleCard(props) {
2 props.title = props.title.toUpperCase();
Attempts in-place mutation
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h2>{props.title}</h2>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

In the local development environment, the browser crashes immediately with TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'title' of object '#<Object>' However, in a production build, the assignment succeeds without an error. Furthermore, when an article object is passed as a prop, mutating article.title succeeds in both builds and turns a sidebar's "Most Read" list into uppercase as well.

Why does reassigning props crash in development, and how should formatted values be calculated?

ANSWER

The code does not do what the reader wanted. Props belong to the parent component and are strictly read-only; components must calculate new variables during render instead of mutating inputs.

In React, components must operate as pure functions. A component should never modify any data that existed prior to its execution. Props represent input data owned and managed by the parent component. To enforce this contract, React shallowly freezes the props object in development using Object.freeze(). Because modern Vite and ES module files execute in JavaScript strict mode, any attempt to assign a property on a frozen object throws a runtime TypeError.

In production builds, React skips Object.freeze() to maximize render speed, meaning mutations fail silently or execute without warning, allowing dangerous bugs to ship. Even worse, Object.freeze() is shallow: if a prop contains a nested object (article={{ title: 'Rail Strike' }}), mutating article.title succeeds in all environments. This mutation modifies shared memory in the parent, causing sibling components that read the same object (such as a sidebar) to unexpectedly display uppercase text. To format data, declare a new local constant during render: const headline = title.toUpperCase()

Direct prop mutation versus pure local derivation during render
Mutation (Corrupts):  props.title = "NEW"  --> Modifies shared parent object
Derivation (Pure):    const headline = ... --> Creates fresh local constant
PRINCIPLE 5

Props are read-only, so make a new variable instead

mutation modifying the properties of an existing object directly in memory

Props belong to the parent component and are strictly read-only. A direct mutation like props.title = ... corrupts data across the component tree. In development, React freezes props so an assignment throws an error. When you need an altered form of a prop, calculate a new variable during render.

We should do this:
function ArticleCard({ title }) {
const headline = title.toUpperCase();
pure local derivation
return <h2>{headline}</h2>;
}
We should not do this:
function ArticleCard(props) {
props.title = props.title.toUpperCase();
crashes: mutating frozen props
}

In our development server, running props.title = props.title.toUpperCase() immediately halts execution with a fatal TypeError because React ran Object.freeze() on the props object. In a production build, Object.isFrozen(props) evaluates to false, allowing the mutation to proceed without error. Furthermore, when article is passed as an object prop, mutating article.title = article.title.toUpperCase() succeeds in both development and production because Object.freeze() is shallow. A sidebar component displaying the same article object suddenly renders uppercase titles as well, causing severe state drift. Calculating const headline = title.toUpperCase() during render protects the parent's data and keeps sibling components completely isolated.

Let's Design a Practical Example

The application consists of three component files: ArticleFeed.jsx acts as the branch container organizing story items, ArticleCard.jsx acts as the reusable leaf component presenting individual articles, and App.jsx acts as the application root coordinating layout.
