Step 1
First, we construct the news feed container
<ArticleFeed.jsx>

We begin by authoring ArticleFeed.jsx. As established in Lecture 5, parent components coordinate child elements and pass data downward. ArticleFeed defines three distinct article items and renders three <ArticleCard /> tags. Notice that ArticleFeed passes title as a quoted string and readTime inside curly braces. For the third card, ArticleFeed omits readTime to test fallback default behavior.

ArticleFeed.jsx
1import ArticleCard from "./ArticleCard.jsx";
2export default function ArticleFeed() {
Feed container
3 return (
4 <main className="feed-container">
5 <ArticleCard title="Rail Strike Ends" readTime={3} />
6 <ArticleCard title="Clean Energy Project" readTime={5} />
7 <ArticleCard title="City Park Renovations" />
8 </main>
9 );
10}

Reviewing ArticleFeed.jsx illustrates how a parent acts as the source of truth for its immediate children. Rather than hardcoding three separate markup layouts, ArticleFeed parameterizes the presentation by supplying distinct attributes at each call site. The feed controls what information appears, while delegating visual structure and formatting to the child card.

Step 2
Next, we build the parameterized article card
<ArticleCard.jsx>

Next, we implement ArticleCard.jsx. The component unpacks title and readTime directly in its parameter list using object destructuring. To ensure cards display a valid reading estimate when parents omit the prop, ArticleCard supplies a default parameter readTime = 5. Furthermore, ArticleCard derives an uppercase summary label pure in render using a local constant rather than mutating incoming props.

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 5 }) {
2 const badgeText = `${readTime} MIN READ`;
Derives badge pure in render
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <span className="badge">{badgeText}</span>
6 <h2>{title}</h2>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Inspecting ArticleCard.jsx highlights two critical architectural patterns. First, parameter destructuring with default values makes the component interface robust: consumers can supply a custom reading time or rely on the 5-minute fallback without writing conditional checks. Second, constructing badgeText as a local string literal during render satisfies React's purity contract. The component receives read-only inputs, derives its presentation values locally, and returns UI markup without altering parent memory.

Step 3
Finally, we assemble the application root
<App.jsx>

Finally, we assemble the application root in App.jsx. App imports ArticleFeed and mounts it inside an application shell wrapper. This completes the three-tier hierarchy: App mounts ArticleFeed, which mounts three parameterized ArticleCard instances.

App.jsx
1import ArticleFeed from "./ArticleFeed.jsx";
2export default function App() {
Root application shell
3 return (
4 <div className="app-shell">
5 <header className="site-header">The Daily Times</header>
6 <ArticleFeed />
7 </div>
8 );
9}

Reviewing App.jsx completes the top-down render pipeline. Data originates in the feed container, flows downward as props into individual card components, and terminates in native HTML elements. At no point does a child component reach upward or horizontally to alter surrounding state.

Component Summary

App

The root application shell coordinates top-level layout. It mounts the publication header banner and the central article feed container. What is its structural role? It provides a stable layout boundary and acts as the entry point for the component tree.

ArticleFeed

This branch container organizes the morning dispatch feed. It defines individual story attributes and mounts three parameterized article cards, demonstrating how parents distribute data downward through props.

ArticleCard

This presentation component frames the headline and reading estimate for an individual story. It unpacks props with destructuring, applies fallback defaults, and derives badge formatting pure in render.

Deconstructing this architecture reveals three core engineering takeaways. First, parameterized components eliminate code duplication: one single ArticleCard function renders three visually identical yet data-distinct cards. Second, parameter destructuring with default values creates resilient component interfaces that gracefully handle optional attributes. Third, calculating formatted labels pure in render preserves the read-only contract, ensuring child components never corrupt shared application data.

Where you will meet this

  1. Content Feeds and Media Portals: Publishing websites parameterize story cards, bylines, and media previews with props, allowing editors to render hundreds of unique articles from a single layout template.
  2. E-Commerce Product Catalogs: E-commerce platforms pass product titles, prices, ratings, and image URLs into reusable product cards, applying fallback defaults when reviews or discounts are absent.
  3. Analytics and Metric Dashboards: SaaS dashboards pass live numbers, trend percentages, and chart identifiers down to modular KPI metric widgets, ensuring numbers arrive in braces for accurate calculation.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you pass data into a component, and why can a component never change its own props?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is testing your grasp of React's component execution model, unidirectional data flow, functional purity, and JavaScript runtime mechanics. A junior candidate says props are "passed like HTML attributes." A senior engineer explains that JSX attributes bundle into a single frozen object passed as the sole argument to the component function, and that props must remain immutable because components must be pure functions with respect to their inputs. Mutating props destroys pure render guarantees, breaks memoization, and causes parent-child state drift across sibling elements.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is assuming that props behave like regular mutable JavaScript function arguments, or attempting to write props.title = props.title.toUpperCase() to clean up display text. Candidates often fail to realize that React freezes props in development, causing fatal TypeError crashes in strict mode. Another frequent trap is forgetting destructuring braces (function Card(title) instead of function Card({ title })), which binds the entire props object to the first parameter and crashes with Objects are not valid as a React child when rendered.

3. What is Actually Going On

Under the hood, the JSX compiler translates component tags into _jsx(Component, propsObject). React instantiates the props object, calls Object.freeze() on it in development, and passes it to the component. Because ES modules execute in JavaScript strict mode, any attempt to assign a property on a frozen object throws a runtime TypeError. In production builds, React skips Object.freeze() to optimize performance, meaning mutations succeed silently in production while failing in development. Furthermore, Object.freeze() is shallow: mutating nested object properties succeeds in all environments, corrupting shared memory in the parent and across sibling components.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Where this gets tricky in production is handling optional props and fallback values. While default parameter syntax ({ readTime = 5 }) cleanly fills in for missing or undefined props, it does not trigger for null or 0. If an API returns null for an uncalculated field, default parameters leave the value as null, rendering an empty slot. Using logical OR (readTime || 5) replaces valid 0 values because 0 is falsy. Senior engineers use nullish coalescing (readTime ?? 5) during render to preserve valid zeros while providing resilient fallbacks. When data must change over time, state management (Lecture 14) is used instead of prop mutation.

Glossary

  • Props: The single read-only JavaScript object containing all attributes passed from a parent component to a child component.
  • Object Destructuring: The JavaScript syntax using curly braces to unpack specific properties from an object into local variables within a parameter list.
  • Type Coercion: The automatic conversion of values from one data type to another by JavaScript, such as concatenating numbers as strings during addition.
  • Default Parameter: A fallback value specified in a function parameter list that assigns automatically when an incoming argument is missing or undefined.
  • Mutation: The direct modification of an existing object's properties in memory, strictly forbidden on props in React.

Beyond the basics

  • Passing props to a component: Master the official guide on passing data, destructuring, and fallback defaults in React (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).
  • Keeping components pure: Understand why React components must never mutate their inputs or external variables during render (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Understanding your UI as a tree: Review how data flows downward through parent-child branches in the render tree (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Passing JSX as children: Explore how components can accept arbitrary nested content through the children prop in Lecture 7 (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#passing-jsx-as-children).
  • State: a component's memory: Discover how components manage data that changes dynamically over time in Lecture 14 (see react.dev/learn/state-a-components-memory).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Prop Passing and Parameter Destructuring

➔ IF passing data to a child component, THEN write attributes on the custom component tag at the JSX call site.

➔ IF unpacking incoming props, THEN wrap parameter names in curly braces matching attribute names to avoid raw object binding crashes.

❒ Prop Types and Fallback Defaults

➔ IF passing numbers, booleans, or JavaScript expressions, THEN wrap values in curly braces to prevent string type coercion bugs.

➔ IF specifying fallback values for optional props, THEN assign default parameters after = in destructuring, using ?? during render if data can contain null.

❒ Immutability Contract and Component Purity

➔ IF formatting or altering incoming prop values for display, THEN calculate a new local variable during render rather than mutating props.

➔ IF data must change dynamically over time in response to user input, THEN manage that data in state rather than modifying props.

DO THIS: Unpack props with destructuring, pass numbers in braces, and calculate derived values pure in render

code.txt
1function ArticleCard({ title, readTime = 5 }) {
2 const badge = `${readTime} MIN READ`;
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <span>{badge}</span>
6 <h2>{title}</h2>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

DO NOT DO THIS: Omit destructuring braces, pass numbers in quotes, or mutate frozen props directly

code.txt
1function ArticleCard(props) {
2 props.title = props.title.toUpperCase();
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h2>{props.title}</h2>
6 <p>{props.readTime + 1}</p>
7 </article>
8 );
9}
NAIVE MUTABLE PROPS
(Direct Assignment & Inlined Clones)		REACT 19 READ-ONLY PROPS
(Destructured Pure Data Flow)
Data DeliveryHardcoded inlined markup or duplicated functionsSingle props object passed as sole argument to child
Parameter AccessUnwrapped parameters binding entire object to one nameCurly brace destructuring extracting clean local variables
Type HandlingQuoted numbers causing string concatenation bugsCurly braces preserving numerical types and expressions
Fallback StrategyLogical OR (`\\`) replacing valid zero valuesDefault parameters and nullish coalescing (??) preserving zeros
Immutability ContractDirect prop reassignment throwing development TypeErrorStrictly read-only; pure local derivations during render
Cross-Tree IntegrityMutations corrupting shared objects across siblingsPure unidirectional flow protecting parent-child boundaries

When it fitsComponents with fixed static copy whose content never varies across the applicationReusable components where the parent supplies distinct data, titles, and numbers

Container Composition with Children &
Prop Spreading

Interview Question   CORE

How do the children prop, spread attributes, and default values work?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built a component that shows a news story with its title and author.
  • 2 One story has no author, but the page still shows the word "By" with nothing after it.
  • 3 How can one component keep the same design for every story and let each story choose its content?

One design, different content for every story

On a news site, every story appears in the same card: the same border, the same spacing, the same layout. Only the content changes. One story has a title and an author, another a title and a photo, another only a title. Every React developer meets this question: how does one card component show different content for each story?

There are two ways to give a card its content.

The first way is props, which you met in Lecture 6. The caller passes values as attributes:

Props: the caller passes values
1<NewsCard title="New Park Opens Today" author="Anna Lyon" />
Values

Inside the card, each value has a fixed place:

Props: inside NewsCard
1<h2>{title}</h2>
2<p>By {author}</p>
Drawn for every story

The card decides what the content looks like: always a title, then a line that starts with "By". The caller only fills in the values. This fits well when every card shows the same pieces in the same order, like a product card that always shows a name and a price. It fits badly when stories differ. A story without an author still gets the line "By" with nothing after it, and a story with a photo has nowhere to put the photo.

The second way is children, which this chapter teaches. Here the caller does not pass values in attributes. It writes the content itself in a place you already know from HTML: between the card's opening tag and its closing tag.

Children: the place for the content
1<CardContainer>
2 The content goes here
This becomes children
3</CardContainer>

Whatever we write in this place, between <CardContainer> and </CardContainer>, React collects automatically and hands to the card inside a prop named children. We never write the word children in the call, and we do not choose the name: React always calls it children.

This is the difference from the first way. With props, the information sits inside the opening tag, in an attribute whose name we choose, such as title. With children, the information sits between the tags, and its name is fixed.

So a story with a photo and no author writes exactly that between the tags, a heading and an image:

Children: the caller writes the content
1<CardContainer>
2 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
3 <img src="/park.jpg" alt="The new park" />
A photo, no author
4</CardContainer>

Both lines, the <h2> and the <img>, arrive in the card as children. Inside the card, one line decides where they appear:

Children: inside CardContainer
1<div className="card">{children}</div>
All of it lands here

The card writes {children} where the content should appear, and it does not need to know what that content is. Now the caller decides the content, and the card gives only the design around it. A story with a photo writes an <img>, and a story without an author simply writes no author line.

Two ways to give a card its content

(1) Give the card its content with props (Lecture 6): the card decides the layout, and the caller passes the values.

(2) Give the card its content with children (this chapter): the caller writes the content, and the card gives the design around it.

Some components need content in more than one place, such as a header and a footer. For those, developers pass JSX in named props or use patterns such as render props, which Lecture 89 covers.

In this chapter, we write one React component that keeps the design the same and lets each story decide its own content. In React, this approach is enabled by a prop named children. We will see what happens when a card forgets to place it, why one prop for every piece breaks when stories differ, and how the card passes on attributes and its class. At the end, we compare the two ways again.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • How does content written between a component's tags reach the component?
  • How do we pass attributes like id and aria-label through a component without listing each one?
  • How do we keep the container's class and add the caller's class, even when the caller passes none?

The questions stand on four earlier lessons:

  • Lecture 3 (JSX): JSX compiles every tag into a _jsx call that returns an object describing the element. Attributes such as aria-label and data-story-id keep their dashes, and class is written className.
  • Lecture 4 (Values in JSX): Curly braces put a JavaScript value into the markup. null, undefined, and false show nothing on the screen, and + joins two strings into one.
  • Lecture 5 (The component tree): Writing one tag inside another builds the tree of components and elements on the page.
  • Lecture 6 (Props): The attributes on a component's tag arrive as one props object, and braces in the parameter list unpack its keys. A default such as author = 'Staff' fills a prop the caller left out.

Content between a component's tags arrives as the children prop

Let's look closely at the second way. CardContainer has one job: to draw the shared design. The story's content goes between its opening and closing tags, the same way you nest an <h2> inside an <article>:

Content between the tags
1<CardContainer>
2 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
This whole line goes to CardContainer
3</CardContainer>

Look at what sits between <CardContainer> and </CardContainer>: the whole line <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2> React does not throw it away. It takes everything written between the opening tag and the closing tag and hands it to CardContainer as a prop. That prop is always called children; you do not choose the name. You can picture it like this: <CardContainer> the children are here </CardContainer>.

So inside CardContainer, the variable children holds the <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2> the caller wrote. If the caller writes three elements between the tags, children holds all three.

The _jsx call from Lecture 3 shows the same thing. The nested element is passed as one more prop, named children:

Compiled call
1_jsx(CardContainer, {
2 children: _jsx("h2", { children: "New Park Opens Today" }),
The nested h2
3});

To show that content, CardContainer unpacks children from its props, as Lecture 6 taught for any prop, and writes {children} in its markup at the place where the content should appear:

Where the container places children
1function CardContainer({ children }) {
2 return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
The h2 lands in the div
3}

Because the content comes from the caller, the same CardContainer works for a different story. Here the caller writes a photo and a headline between the tags:

A photo and a headline as children
1<CardContainer>
2 <img src="/school.jpg" alt="Children walking to school" />
First child
3 <h2>School Starts on Monday</h2>
Second child
4</CardContainer>

Now children holds both elements, and they appear inside the shared design in the order the caller wrote them. Whatever you write between a component's tags reaches that component as its children prop.

A component like CardContainer, which draws a shared design and shows whatever it receives as children, is called a container component. The caller decides the content, and the container decides the design around it. Lecture 10 shows how a container can show nothing at all when it receives no content.

Rest syntax collects the props you did not name

A container often receives more props than it uses itself, such as an id or an aria-label that belong on its outer element. To collect them, we use rest syntax, a plain JavaScript feature. In destructuring, you name the keys you want, and three dots before a last name collect every other key into a new object. Here it is on a simple object:

Rest syntax on a plain object
1const story = { title: 'New Park', id: 'top', date: 'May 3' };
2const { title, ...rest } = story;
Title is 'New Park'
3console.log(rest);
{ id: 'top', date: 'May 3' }

title leaves the object by name, and rest holds the keys that are left. The story object itself does not change.

The props object is an ordinary object, so the same syntax works in a component's parameter list. Say the caller writes <CardContainer id="top" aria-label="Main story">

Rest syntax on props
1function CardContainer({ children, ...rest }) {
2 console.log(rest);
{ id: 'top', 'aria-label': 'Main story' }
3 return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
4}

children takes the nested content by name, and rest collects id and aria-label. Rest syntax takes out the keys you name and gathers all the others into one object.

Spread writes every key of an object as an attribute

Once the remaining props sit together in one object, we need a way to write them onto an element. JSX has a form for this: {...object} inside a tag writes each key of the object as an attribute. To see it, compare two links, one written with spread and one written by hand:

Spread attributes
1const link = { href: '/sport', title: 'Sport news' };
2const first = <a {...link}>Sport</a>;
Link gives href and title
3const second = <a href="/sport" title="Sport news">Sport</a>;
Written by hand

The two links are the same. React reads the object and writes href and title on the <a>, so the browser gets <a href="/sport" title="Sport news">Sport</a> This is called JSX spread attributes.

It works with any object, including keys with dashes:

Spread attributes with dashes
1const ids = { id: 'top', 'data-story-id': '42' };
2const section = <section {...ids}>Top story</section>;
Id and data-story-id

The browser gets <section id="top" data-story-id="42"> Rest syntax gathers keys into an object, and spread writes an object's keys back out as attributes.

Principles of React: Container Composition and Prop Spreading

QUESTION 1

Content placed between tags arrives as the children prop

A developer writes a CardContainer component to give every story on a news site the same design. In the parent component, the developer writes a headline between the container's opening and closing tags:

A headline between the container tags
1function Feed() {
Parent component writes the content
2 return (
3 <CardContainer>
4 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
The content for this story
5 </CardContainer>
6 );
7}

Inside CardContainer, the component returns its <div> but never writes {children}:

A container that forgets children
1function CardContainer() {
Draws the design only
2 return <div className="card" />;
The headline is never placed
3}

When the browser renders the page, DevTools shows an empty <div class="card"></div>. The headline is missing from the screen, and the browser console shows no error.

Why does content written between a component's tags disappear from the screen?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React did hand the headline to CardContainer as children, but the component never put it anywhere.

As the first section showed, everything written between <CardContainer> and </CardContainer> reaches the component as a prop named children. Here that is the whole line <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2> Receiving the prop is only half of the work. The component decides where the content appears by writing {children} in its markup. This CardContainer returns <div className="card" /> and never mentions children, so React draws the empty <div> and the headline goes nowhere. React gives no warning, because a component is free to ignore any prop it receives.

The fix is to unpack children and write it inside the <div>:

The container places children
1function CardContainer({ children }) {
Receives the content
2 return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
The headline goes here
3}
From the caller's tags to the browser
Caller writes:                      Container returns:
<CardContainer>                     <div className="card">
  <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>  -->  {children}
</CardContainer>                    </div>

Browser DOM:
<div class="card">
  <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
</div>
PRINCIPLE 1

Content between the tags arrives as the children prop

children prop the prop that holds everything written between a component's opening and closing tags

Everything you write between a component's opening and closing tags reaches that component as a prop named children. The content appears on the screen only where the component writes {children} in its returned JSX. If the component never writes {children}, React draws the rest of the component and the content is missing, with no warning.

We should do this:
function Card({ children }) {
return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
shows the content
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ children }) {
return <div className="card" />;
content never appears
}

In our runtime test, rendering <CardContainer><h2>New Park Opens Today</h2></CardContainer> with {children} inside the <div> showed the headline inside the card.

QUESTION 2

Let the caller fill the container instead of adding a prop for every piece

The first section showed NewsCard, which receives one prop for each piece of text. A page renders two stories with it, one with an author and one without:

Two stories through NewsCard
1function StoryFeed() {
Renders stories through NewsCard
2 return (
3 <div className="feed">
4 <NewsCard title="New Park Opens Today" author="Anna Lyon" />
5 <NewsCard title="Rain Expected This Weekend" />
No author
6 </div>
7 );
8}

The first story shows "By Anna Lyon". The second story shows the word "By" with nothing after it, because NewsCard draws <p>By {author}</p> for every story, and author is undefined here. Then a third story arrives with a photo, and NewsCard has no place for it.

Do we add a new prop to NewsCard for every piece a story might have?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Every optional piece becomes one more prop, and NewsCard draws each piece for every story, even when the story has none.

To support the photo, NewsCard would need an imageUrl prop, then a check for stories without a photo, then another prop for the next kind of story. Each change edits the same shared file, and the order of the pieces stays fixed inside it: a caller cannot put the author above the title without yet another prop.

CardContainer turns this around. It draws only the shared design and writes {children} where the content goes. Each caller writes the elements its story has, in the order it wants. The story with an author writes the title and the author line. The story without an author writes only the title, so no empty "By" appears. The photo story writes an <img>, and CardContainer does not change at all. A named prop stays only for something every story must show in the same place, such as a title.

One prop per piece versus content from the caller
NewsCard({ title, author }):
+---------------------------------------+
| <h2>Rain Expected This Weekend</h2>   |
| <p>By </p>   (no author!)             |
+---------------------------------------+

CardContainer({ children }):
+---------------------------------------+
| {children}                            |
|   <h2>Rain Expected This Weekend</h2> |
+---------------------------------------+
PRINCIPLE 2

Let the caller fill the container instead of adding a prop for every piece

composition building a component's content from elements the caller writes between its tags

When stories need different content inside the same design, let each caller write its content between the container's tags. This is called composition. Adding a prop for each optional piece makes the component draw that piece for every story, even when the story has none, and every new kind of story changes the shared file. Keep a named prop only for something every story must show in the same place.

It is best practice to do this:
<CardContainer>
<h2>Rain Expected This Weekend</h2>
no author, no empty line
</CardContainer>
Instead of doing this:
<NewsCard
title="Rain Expected This Weekend"
shows "By" with no author
/>

In our test, the story without an author showed "By" with nothing after it through NewsCard. Through CardContainer, the same story showed only its title, and a third story with a photo needed no change to CardContainer.jsx.

QUESTION 3

Spread only the props the container does not use

Callers need to put an id or an aria-label on the card. To pass them all at once, a developer spreads the whole props object onto the container's <div>:

Spreading the whole props object
1function CardContainer(props) {
Receives the full props object
2 return (
3 <div className="card" {...props}>
Every prop lands on the div
4 {props.children}
5 </div>
6 );
7}

A caller renders a story with two props that are meant for the component, not for the browser: <CardContainer isFeatured={true} date="May 3"><h2>New Park Opens Today</h2></CardContainer> When the page loads, the console warns: Warning: React does not recognize the isFeatured prop on a DOM element In DevTools, the element reads <div class="card" date="May 3">

Can we pass the whole props object onto the container element with spread?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Spreading the whole props object writes the component's own props onto the browser element too.

{...props} writes every key of the object as an attribute, and props holds everything the caller passed, including props that only the component should read. React checks the attributes it writes on a browser element such as <div>. For a camelCase name like isFeatured, it warns that the browser does not recognize it. A lowercase name like date passes the check, so React writes date="May 3" straight into the page. If a component reads a title prop for its heading and also spreads everything onto a <div>, the same title becomes a tooltip when the mouse rests on the card.

The fix uses the two tools from the first sections. Rest syntax takes out the props the component reads, { children, isFeatured, ...rest } and leaves only the others in rest, such as id, aria-label, and data-story-id. Then spread writes only {...rest} on the <div>.

Rest syntax keeps the component's props off the div
Props object from the caller:
{ children: <h2>, isFeatured: true, id: "top", aria-label: "Main story" }

Read by CardContainer:          Collected into rest:
children, isFeatured            { id: "top", aria-label: "Main story" }

<div className="card" {...rest}>
Browser DOM: <div class="card" id="top" aria-label="Main story">
PRINCIPLE 3

Spread only the props the container does not use

rest syntax collecting the keys you did not name into a new object with ...rest
JSX spread attributes writing each key of an object as an attribute with {...rest}

When a container passes extra attributes on to a browser element, unpack the props it reads and collect the others with rest syntax: { children, isFeatured, ...rest }. Then write only those others on the element with JSX spread attributes: {...rest}. Spreading the whole props object also writes the component's own props on the element: React warns about camelCase names and writes lowercase ones into the page.

We should do this:
function Card({ isFeatured, children, ...rest }) {
return <div className="card" {...rest}>{children}</div>;
only rest
}
We should not do this:
function Card(props) {
return <div className="card" {...props}>{props.children}</div>;
all props
}

In our runtime test, spreading props with isFeatured={true} and date="May 3" wrote date="May 3" on the <div> and logged a console warning. After the change to { children, isFeatured, ...rest } the console stayed clean, and id and aria-label reached the <div> as intended.

QUESTION 4

Keep the container's class and add the caller's

CardContainer gives every story its design through the class card. To let callers pass other attributes, it writes <div className="card" {...rest}>{children}</div> One caller wants to highlight its story with an extra class:

A caller adds its own class
1function FeaturedStory() {
Highlights one story
2 return (
3 <CardContainer className="featured">
An extra class
4 <h2>New Park Opens Today</h2>
5 </CardContainer>
6 );
7}

The story loses its border and padding. In DevTools, the element reads <div class="featured">. The class card is gone.

How do we keep the container's class and add the caller's class?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. JSX applies attributes from left to right, so the className inside rest replaces the className written before it.

When the same attribute appears twice on one tag, the last one wins. Here className="card" comes first and {...rest} comes after it. Because rest holds className: "featured", that value replaces "card". Moving className="card" after the spread only turns the problem around: then the container's class replaces the caller's. JSX never joins two class names by itself.

So we join them ourselves. A first fix takes className out of the props and adds the two strings with +:

First fix: join the two classes
1function CardContainer({ className, children, ...rest }) {
2 const fullClass = 'card ' + className;
'card featured'
3 return <div className={fullClass} {...rest}>{children}</div>;
4}

The featured story now gets class="card featured". But look at a story that passes no class at all: <CardContainer><h2>Rain Expected This Weekend</h2></CardContainer> Its element reads class="card undefined". The caller left className out, so it is undefined, and + turns undefined into the text "undefined".

An experienced developer adds one more thing: the default from Lecture 6, written in the parameter list. With className = '', a missing class becomes an empty string, and the story gets class="card ", which still matches the .card style. The default fills only a prop that is missing or undefined. A caller who passes null still gets class="card null".

The finished container
1function CardContainer({ className = '', children, ...rest }) {
2 const fullClass = 'card ' + className;
'card ' when none is passed
3 return <div className={fullClass} {...rest}>{children}</div>;
4}
From the lost class to the finished container
Code on the div                          Caller passes    DOM
className="card" {...rest}               "featured"       class="featured"
{...rest} className="card"               "featured"       class="card"
'card ' + className                      "featured"       class="card featured"
'card ' + className                      nothing          class="card undefined"
className = '' and 'card ' + className   nothing          class="card "
PRINCIPLE 4

Around a spread, the last attribute wins; join classes with a default

attribute precedence the left-to-right order in which a later JSX attribute replaces an earlier one
default parameter value a value in the parameter list that fills a prop when it is missing or undefined

JSX applies attributes from left to right, which is called attribute precedence: when the same attribute appears twice on an element, the last one wins. An attribute before {...rest} is a value the caller can replace, and an attribute after it always wins. When both the container and the caller add a class, take className out with a default parameter value, className = '', and join the two strings yourself, so a missing class does not print undefined.

We should do this:
function Card({ className = '', children, ...rest }) {
const fullClass = 'card ' + className;
keeps both classes
return <div className={fullClass} {...rest}>{children}</div>;
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ children, ...rest }) {
return <div className="card" {...rest}>{children}</div>;
card is lost
}

In our test, className="card" before {...rest} gave class="featured", and after it gave class="card". Joining the strings gave class="card featured", and class="card undefined" for a story with no class. With className = '', that story got class="card ".

Let's Design a Practical Example

Now we put the pieces together in a small news page. Three files share the work: CardContainer.jsx draws the shared design for every story, StoryList.jsx writes the content of three different stories, and App.jsx places the page on the screen.

Step 1
First, we write the container component
<CardContainer.jsx>

CardContainer draws the design every story shares. For this, it unpacks children and writes {children} inside its <div>, so each story's content lands in the same place. It also unpacks color and className with defaults, color = 'gray' and className = '', so a caller can leave either one out. Every other prop, such as aria-label, goes into rest and is spread onto the <div>.

CardContainer.jsx
1export default function CardContainer({
2 children, color = 'gray', className = '', ...rest
Reads three props
3}) {
4 const cls = `card card-${color} ${className}`.trim();
5 return (
6 <div className={cls} {...rest}>
Passes on the other props
7 {children}
8 </div>
9 );
10}

The template string builds the class from three parts, and .trim() removes the space left at the end when className is empty. CardContainer never looks inside children. It does not know whether a story has an author, a summary, or only a title.

Step 2
Next, we write three different stories
<StoryList.jsx>

StoryList uses CardContainer three times, and each story writes its own content between the tags. The main story has a headline, a summary, and a date, and it passes color, className, and aria-label. The second story has a headline and an author. The third has only a headline and uses the default color.

StoryList.jsx
1import CardContainer from './CardContainer.jsx';
2

Three stories, one design
4 return (
5 <section className="story-list">
6 <h2 className="section-heading">Today's Stories</h2>
7 <CardContainer
8 color="red" className="featured" aria-label="Main story"
9 >
10 <h3 className="headline">New Park Opens Today</h3>
11 <p className="summary">The park has a lake and a playground.</p>
12 <time className="date">May 3</time>
13 </CardContainer>
14 <CardContainer color="gray">
15 <h3 className="headline">Rain Expected This Weekend</h3>
16 <p className="author">By Clara Foster</p>
17 </CardContainer>
18 <CardContainer>

20 </CardContainer>
21 </section>
22 );
Closes the section
23}

The third story has no author, and no empty "By" appears, because the story simply does not write an author line. Adding a story with a photo would mean writing an <img> between the tags, with no change to CardContainer.jsx.

Step 3
Finally, we place the page inside
<App.jsx>

App is the top of the tree. It renders StoryList inside a <main> element and passes it no props.

App.jsx
1import StoryList from './components/StoryList.jsx';

2

When React renders App, it calls StoryList, which calls CardContainer three times with three different children. The browser shows three stories with the same design and different content.

Component Summary

App

The root component places the news page inside a main element. Notice it passes no props to StoryList. Why? It only decides where the page sits, not what the stories say.

StoryList

The caller component writes the content of each story between CardContainer tags. Notice the three stories have different content, and one passes aria-label and className. Why? Each story decides its own content, while the design stays in one place.

CardContainercolor="..." className="..." aria-label="..."

The container component draws the shared design and places children inside its div. Notice it fills color and className with defaults and spreads the remaining props onto the div. Why? Callers can leave props out or add attributes without changing this file.

Without children, one component would need a prop for every piece a story might have, and it would draw those pieces even for stories that do not have them. With children, CardContainer keeps the design and each caller writes its own content. Because CardContainer unpacks the props it reads and spreads only ...rest, callers can add attributes such as aria-label without the component's own props reaching the page.

Where you will meet this

  1. Dialogs: A dialog component draws the window, the backdrop, and the close button, and each caller writes its own text or form fields between the tags as children.
  2. News and product cards: A card component keeps the same border and spacing for every item, while each item writes its own title, author, date, or photo.
  3. Form fields: A field component draws the label and the error message, and spreads attributes such as id, aria-describedby, and disabled onto the <input> with {...rest}.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do the children prop, spread attributes, and default values work?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand where these values come from. A weak answer treats props as HTML attributes. A strong answer explains that JSX compiles the content between a component's tags into the children prop (_jsx(CardContainer, { children: ... })), that a component which passes attributes on should unpack the props it reads and spread only ...rest, that JSX applies attributes from left to right, and that a default parameter fills a prop the caller left out.

2. The Classic Trap

Assuming children is always an array. With one nested element, children is a single element object. With two or more, it is an array. With plain text, it is a string. Calling children.map() when there is only one child crashes with TypeError: children.map is not a function Another trap is writing <div {...props} /> which writes the component's own props onto the browser element and triggers React warnings.

3. What is Actually Going On

At compile time, the nested JSX becomes the children key of the props object. The container receives element objects that describe the content, not finished HTML. Spread copies the keys of an object as attributes from left to right, and whichever value comes last wins. A default value applies only when a prop is undefined or left out, never when it is null or false.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

If a caller passes a children attribute and also writes content between the tags, <Card children="attr">nested</Card> the content between the tags wins, because the compiler adds it after the attributes. Also, if a container never writes {children}, the components written between its tags never run at all.

Glossary

  • children prop: The prop that holds everything written between a component's opening and closing tags.
  • container component: A component that draws a shared design and shows whatever it receives as children.
  • composition: Building a component's content from elements the caller writes between its tags, instead of adding a prop for every piece.
  • rest syntax: The JavaScript ...rest form in destructuring that collects the keys you did not name into a new object.
  • JSX spread attributes: The {...rest} form in a JSX tag that writes each key of an object as an attribute.
  • default parameter value: A value written in the parameter list, such as className = '', that fills a prop when it is undefined or left out.

Beyond the basics

  • Learn how to pass JSX as children: (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#passing-jsx-as-children).
  • Learn how to forward props with the JSX spread syntax: (see react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#forwarding-props-with-the-jsx-spread-syntax).
  • Understand how React builds the interface as a tree of components: (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree).
  • Read why children can be one element, an array, or text, in the Children API: (see react.dev/reference/react/Children).
  • Read the notes on attributes and children for browser elements: (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).

Summary

Container Composition and Prop Spreading Rules for keeping one design and passing attributes on

❒ Content Through Children

➔ IF stories need different content inside the same design, THEN write {children} in the container and let each caller write its content between the tags, instead of adding a prop for every piece.

➔ IF every card shows the same pieces in the same order, such as a name and a price, THEN props from Lecture 6 are enough.

➔ IF every story must show something in the same place, such as a title, THEN make it a named prop and place {children} next to it.

❒ Passing Attributes On

➔ IF a container passes extra attributes to a browser element, THEN unpack the props it reads and spread only ...rest onto the element.

➔ IF a component receives its own props, such as isFeatured, THEN never spread the whole props object onto a browser element.

❒ Attribute Order and Defaults

➔ IF an attribute should be a default the caller can replace, THEN write it before {...rest}; IF it must always win, THEN write it after {...rest}.

➔ IF a container joins its own class with the caller's class, THEN give className the default '' and join the two strings yourself.

DO THIS: Let callers write the content and join class names yourself

code.txt
1function CardContainer({
2 children,
3 color = "gray",
4 className = "",
5 ...rest
6}) {
7 const cls = `card card-${color} ${className}`.trim();
8 return (
9 <div className={cls} {...rest}>
10 {children}
11 </div>
12 );
13}

DO NOT DO THIS: Spread the whole props object onto the element

code.txt
1function CardContainer(props) {
2 return (
3 <div className="card" {...props}>
4 {props.children}
5 </div>
6 );
7}
ONE PROP PER PIECE
(NewsCard)		CONTENT AS CHILDREN
(CardContainer)
Who decides the contentThe component draws every piece in a fixed orderEach caller writes its own content between the tags
PropsOne more prop for every piece a story might have (author, imageUrl)children plus a few props for the design, such as color
Missing piecesDrawn anyway, such as "By" with no authorNot written, so nothing empty appears
New kind of storyEdit and test the shared component fileNo change to the container; the caller writes the new content
Extra attributesSpreads all props, or copies each attribute by handUnpacks the props it reads and spreads only ...rest
Class namesThe caller's class replaces the base class, or the other way roundJoins both classes, with the default className = ''
When it fitsEvery card shows the same pieces in the same order, such as a name and a priceThe pieces change from story to story, such as an author on one and a photo on another

Splitting Components with ES Module Imports &
Exports

Interview Question   CORE

How do you split components across files, and how do default and named imports differ?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built an article card component and a badge helper inside App.jsx.
  • 2 You move the card to its own file, but the screen is blank and the card is not defined.
  • 3 How do we share components cleanly across files with default and named imports?

Splitting components across files keeps each file easy to scan

Since Lecture 5, every component you write lives in one file, App.jsx. The card and the page that shows it sit side by side, so App uses ArticleCard simply by writing its tag:

App.jsx
1function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
Declared in this file
3}
4export default function App() {
5 return <ArticleCard title="New Park Opens" />;
Used without an import
6}

As the site grows, that one file grows with it. The card, the badge, the header, and the footer all end up in the same long App.jsx, and another page that needs the card cannot reach it without copying its code. So every React developer meets the same question: how does a component written in one file get used in another file?

JavaScript answers it with ES modules, the module system built into the language (ES stands for ECMAScript, the official name of JavaScript). Each file is a module: the names declared in it stay inside that file until the file exports them and another file imports them.

Your project's code lives in a folder named src, and App.jsx sits inside it. When a component moves out, it goes into a folder named components that sits inside src, next to App.jsx:

Project folders: File Explorer
FILE / DIRECTORY
ROLE
ARCHITECTURAL RESPONSIBILITY
src/
Directory
Contains component modules
App.jsx
parent
The starter file, which imports the card by its path
components/
Directory
Contains component modules
ArticleCard.jsx
child
The card component, moved into its own file

You move the card into its own file, ArticleCard.jsx, and export it from there:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
Exported component
3}

And App.jsx imports it by its path:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Imported from file
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard title="New Park Opens" />;
Rendered in page shell
5}

The card is the same function as before; only its place changed. In one file, App could use it directly. Across two files, ArticleCard.jsx must export it and App.jsx must import it, because each module keeps its names private by default.

Later in this track, Lecture 9 shows how main.jsx imports App and hands it to createRoot to attach the React tree to the browser DOM, and Lecture 12 shows why variables declared at the top level of a module must never be mutated during render.

In this chapter, we move components out of App.jsx into their own module files so each component can be reused anywhere in the application. We will see why moving a component without importing it blanks the page, how default and named imports differ in syntax and behavior, and how to choose the right export style for primary components and helper utilities.

This lesson answers three questions:

  • How do you move a component into its own file and make it available to other files?
  • How do default imports and named imports differ in syntax and behavior?
  • When should a component be exported as a default export versus a named export?

The questions stand on six earlier lessons:

  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): A React component is a JavaScript function that starts with a capital letter and returns markup. The export default syntax marks the main function of a file so another file can import and run it.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX): JSX tags compile into element descriptors. Attributes like aria-label keep their dashes, and the HTML class attribute is written as className.
  • Lecture 4 (Values in JSX): Curly braces evaluate JavaScript expressions inside markup. Values like null, undefined, and false render nothing on screen.
  • Lecture 5 (The component tree): Nesting component tags inside JSX builds the tree of elements on the page. A component nested in JSX must be in scope, or JavaScript halts with a ReferenceError.
  • Lecture 6 (Props): Attributes on a component tag arrive as a single props object, and curly braces in the parameter list unpack its keys. Props are read-only inputs.
  • Lecture 7 (Container composition): Content written between opening and closing tags arrives as the children prop. Prop spreading forwards remaining attributes with the rest syntax ...rest.

A module keeps its names private until you export them

We know from Lecture 5 that when two functions are declared in the same file, one function can call the other directly because both exist in the same scope. In modern JavaScript and React, every separate file is an isolated module. Variables, functions, and components declared inside a module are private to that file:

ArticleCard.jsx
1function formatDate(date) {
Private helper function
2 return `Published ${date}`;
3}
4
5export default function ArticleCard({ date }) {
6 return <p>{formatDate(date)}</p>;
Helper called inside file
7}

Notice that formatDate has no export keyword in front of its declaration. That means formatDate is completely private to ArticleCard.jsx. External files cannot read, call, or modify it. Only ArticleCard is marked with export default so only ArticleCard crosses the module boundary.

To import a component from a file in your project, you specify a relative path starting with ./. The ./ tells the build tool to look for the file starting from the folder of the current file:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Relative file path
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard date="Monday" />;
Renders imported card
5}

In contrast, a package import like import { Fragment } from 'react' has no ./ prefix. When a path has no ./ or ../, the build tool looks inside the installed packages in the project's node_modules folder rather than your local source files.

Default exports share one main value, named exports share several

In Lecture 2, we used export default to share the main component from App.jsx. JavaScript provides two primary ways to export values from a module: default exports and named exports. A default export represents the primary component of a file, declared with export default A file can have at most one default export. In contrast, named exports allow a module to share multiple secondary helpers or utilities, declared with export function Name()

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
Primary default export
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}
4
5export function Badge({ text }) {
Secondary named export
6 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
7}

How you export a value dictates how you must import it. A default import is written without curly braces: import ArticleCard from './ArticleCard.jsx' Because a file has only one default export, you can give it any local variable name. A named import is written with curly braces: import { Badge } from './ArticleCard.jsx' The identifier inside the braces must match the exported name character for character:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Combined
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <ArticleCard title="News">
6 <Badge text="LIVE" />
Uses named helper
7 </ArticleCard>
8 );
9}

Notice the curly braces in import { Badge } In JavaScript, these braces look similar to object destructuring, but they are a static module syntax. They tell the JavaScript engine to link directly to the specific named export binding declared in that module. Unlike runtime object destructuring, ES module import bindings are evaluated and linked statically before any component function executes.

Principles of React: Splitting Components with Imports and Exports

QUESTION 1

Moving a component to a new file leaves the screen blank

You have a working article feed where ArticleCard is rendered inside App.jsx. To organize your code, you create a new file named src/components/ArticleCard.jsx move the card function into it, and export it with export default In App.jsx, you keep the card tag in your markup:

App.jsx
1export default function App() {
2 return (
3 <main>
4 <ArticleCard title="Park Opens" />
Card tag in markup
5 </main>
6 );
7}

You refresh the browser. The page is completely blank. When you open the browser development console, you see a red error message: ReferenceError: ArticleCard is not defined

Why does the screen go blank when the component exists in another file in the same project?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Files in a project do not share variables automatically.

In plain HTML scripts, any variable declared in one script tag often lands on the global window object, where other scripts can reach it. In modern JavaScript and React, each file is an isolated module. Variables and component functions declared inside a file stay private to that file. Even though ArticleCard.jsx sits in the same project folder, App.jsx has no access to it by default.

When React attempts to render the App component, JavaScript evaluates the identifier ArticleCard. Because there is no variable, parameter, or import named ArticleCard in App.jsx, JavaScript halts execution and throws a ReferenceError. As Lecture 5 showed, an unhandled error during component execution stops the render, causing React to render nothing and leaving the screen blank.

To fix this error, you add an explicit import statement at the top of App.jsx:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Bridges the module
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <ArticleCard title="Park Opens" />;
In scope and renders
5}
Module boundaries and the import bridge
+-------------------------------+      +-------------------------------+
| src/components/ArticleCard.jsx|      | src/App.jsx                   |
|                               |      |                               |
| export default function       |      | import ArticleCard from       |
|   ArticleCard()               | ===> |   './components/ArticleCard'  |
|                               |      |                               |
| function formatDate()         |      | function App() {              |
|   (private to module)         |      |   return <ArticleCard />      |
+-------------------------------+      +-------------------------------+

Notice what happens to top-level code versus component code. Code written at the top level of a module evaluates once when the file is first imported, regardless of how many other files import it. In contrast, code inside the component function runs on every render for every card instance on screen.

PRINCIPLE 1

Each file is a module, and names cross files only by export and import

module an isolated file with private scope that exposes values only through explicit exports and imports

When React runs an application, each file is an isolated module with its own private scope. Functions, variables, and components declared in a file are not visible to other files by default. A component crosses into another file only when the source file exports it and the destination file imports it. Without an import statement, referencing a component from another file throws a ReferenceError during render, leaving the page blank.

We should do this:
import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
export default function App() {
return <ArticleCard />;
renders imported card
}
We should not do this:
export default function App() {
App.jsx without import statement
return <ArticleCard />;
ReferenceError: not defined
}

In our runtime test with Vite 8.3.4, moving ArticleCard without an import produced a blank page with ReferenceError: ArticleCard is not defined in the browser console. Adding the import statement restored the rendered cards immediately.

QUESTION 2

Importing a named export without braces stops the build

You have extracted ArticleCard.jsx. The file provides two components: ArticleCard as its default export, and Badge as a named export: export function Badge({ text }) In App.jsx, a developer wants to use the badge. They write the import statement without curly braces:

App.jsx
1import Badge from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Wrote default import syntax
2
3export default function App() {
4 return <Badge text="Breaking" />;
Attempts to render badge
5}

When you save the file, the development server stops. The browser displays a build error overlay: The requested module '/src/components/ArticleCard.jsx' does not provide an export named 'default' When you run npm run build, the production bundler halts with [MISSING_EXPORT] "default" is not exported by "src/components/ArticleCard.jsx"

Why does importing the badge without braces fail before any component runs?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A default import requests the module's default export, not a named export.

JavaScript ES modules resolve and verify import bindings statically before any component executes. When you write import Badge from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' without curly braces, you are writing a default import. You are asking the JavaScript engine for the single default export of ArticleCard.jsx, and asking it to bind that value to the local variable name Badge.

However, ArticleCard.jsx exported ArticleCard as its default export, and exported Badge as a named export. The file has no export named default that corresponds to Badge. Because static module verification happens before runtime, Vite detects that the requested default binding does not exist and halts immediately.

The mirror mistake fails the same way. If you write import { ArticleCard } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' with curly braces, the JavaScript engine looks for a named export called ArticleCard. Because ArticleCard was exported as default, the engine reports: The requested module '/src/components/ArticleCard.jsx' does not provide an export named 'ArticleCard'

Matching import syntax to export declaration
EXPORT DECLARATION (ArticleCard.jsx):
  export default function ArticleCard()
  export function Badge()

MATCHING IMPORT STATEMENT (App.jsx):
  import ArticleCard from './ArticleCard.jsx'  (no braces: links to default)
  import { Badge } from './ArticleCard.jsx'    (braces: links to named)

The fix is to match the import syntax to the export declaration. Use a default import without curly braces for ArticleCard, and a named import with curly braces for Badge:

App.jsx
1import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Matched
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <ArticleCard title="News">
6 <Badge text="Breaking" />
Renders correctly
7 </ArticleCard>
8 );
9}
PRINCIPLE 2

Import with the same form the file used to export

default export the primary value of a module, imported without curly braces under any local name
named export a specific value exported by name, imported inside curly braces matching its exact identifier

JavaScript ES modules link imports to exports statically before any component executes. A default export must be imported without curly braces, and the importing file can assign it any local name. A named export must be imported with curly braces, and its name must match the exported identifier character for character. If the import syntax does not match the export declaration, the module fails to link, halting the development server and production build.

We should do this:
import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './Card.jsx';
imports both
<ArticleCard><Badge text="LIVE" /></ArticleCard>;
renders both
We should not do this:
import { ArticleCard } from './Card.jsx';
wrong for default
import Badge from './Card.jsx';
wrong for named export

In our runtime test with Vite 8.3.4, importing a named export without braces halted the dev server with does not provide an export named 'default' while vite build stopped with [MISSING_EXPORT]. Adding curly braces { Badge } resolved both errors.

QUESTION 3

Adding a second default export to a file halts compilation

Inside src/components/ArticleCard.jsx ArticleCard is already exported with export default function ArticleCard Now you want other pages to use Badge as well. You write export default in front of Badge:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
First default export
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}
4
5export default function Badge({ text }) {
Second default export attempt
6 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
7}

When you save the file, the compiler halts immediately with a syntax error: A module cannot have multiple default exports

Why does adding a second default export stop the compiler?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A module can have at most one default export.

In the ECMAScript module specification, the default export is designed to represent the single fallback value of a module. When another file writes import Anything from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' the runtime assigns the default export to the identifier Anything. If a file were allowed to have two default exports, the runtime would have no way to determine which of the two values to provide to the importing file. Therefore, JavaScript forbids multiple default exports at the syntax level.

When a file provides one main component alongside secondary helpers, the idiomatic convention is to export the main component as the default export, and export all secondary helpers as named exports:

ArticleCard.jsx
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
Primary default export
2 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
3}
4
5export function Badge({ text }) {
Secondary named export
6 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
7}
Module export slots: one default, unlimited named
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| Module Export Table (ArticleCard.jsx)                       |
|                                                             |
| [default slot]  ======> ArticleCard                         |
|                         (at most one default per module)    |
|                                                             |
| [named slots]   ======> Badge                               |
|                 ======> formatDate (if exported)           |
|                         (unlimited named exports allowed)   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Always give your component functions explicit names. If you write an anonymous default export like export default () => {} the component has no name. When a runtime error occurs, React's error stack prints The above error occurred in the <default> component: and React DevTools displays <default> instead of a recognizable component name, making debugging difficult.

PRINCIPLE 3

One default export for the main component, named exports for the rest

anonymous component a component function declared without a name identifier in its definition

An ES module allows at most one default export but any number of named exports. When a file provides one primary component, export that component as the default export so callers can import it cleanly. When that same file provides secondary helpers or sub-components that other files also use, export them as named exports. If a file contains two default exports, the compiler stops immediately. Always name your component functions, because an anonymous default export displays as <default> in error callstacks and React DevTools.

We should do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {}
primary component
export function Badge({ text }) {}
secondary named helper
We should not do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {}
first default export
export default function Badge({ text }) {}
duplicate default fails

In our runtime test, attempting to declare two default exports in one module stopped the build with A module cannot have multiple default exports Exporting Badge as a named export allowed both components to compile and render cleanly.

Step 1
First, we extract the primary card component
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We begin by creating a new file on disk: src/components/ArticleCard.jsx Instead of trapping the card inside App.jsx, we declare ArticleCard as a standalone component function. We place a top-level log at the head of the file to observe when the module evaluates. We also create a private helper function, formatDate, that formats publication dates. Because formatDate is only used inside this card, we keep it unexported, ensuring it remains an internal implementation detail:

ArticleCard.jsx
1console.log('ArticleCard loaded');
Runs once on import
2
3function formatDate(date) {
Private helper unexported
4 return `Published ${date}`;
5}
6
7export default function ArticleCard({ title, date, children }) {
8 return (
9 <article className="article-card">
Card container
10 <p className="card-date">{formatDate(date)}</p>

Notice the architecture of this first step. The file opens with a top-level log that executes only once when the module is imported into memory. The formatDate helper function is declared without an export keyword, so it remains completely private to ArticleCard.jsx. External files cannot call or modify it. Finally, ArticleCard is declared as a named function declaration with export default function ArticleCard This ensures that any React runtime error inside this component will clearly display <ArticleCard> in callstacks.

Step 2
Next, we export the status badge as a named export
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We complete ArticleCard.jsx by rendering the card title and nested content, and then adding a secondary component: Badge. Some pages in our application only need to display a status badge without rendering a full article card. When designing a module that contains related sub-components, developers face an architectural crossroad:

  • Option 1 (The Single-Export File Shredding Way): Extract every single two-line helper into its own file (Badge.jsx, DateLabel.jsx), creating dozens of tiny files and cluttered import lists.
  • Option 2 (The Multi-Export Module Way): Keep the primary component as the default export and export closely related sub-components as named exports from the same file.

First, examine Option 1 with excessive file shredding:

Option 1: Over-Shredded Helper Files
1export default function Badge({ text }) {
Two-line component file
2 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
3}

The relative import path ./components/ArticleCard.jsx matches the on-disk file casing exactly, ensuring the project compiles cleanly on both macOS development laptops and Linux CI build servers.

Component Summary

App

The root application shell orchestrates the front-page feed layout. It imports the default article card and named badge helper from their dedicated component module. Notice it contains zero internal helper definitions or card markup of its own. Why? To maintain a clean, declarative container that composes modular components without file bloat.

ArticleCardtitle="..." date="..."

This is the primary article card component. It provides the default export for the module and encapsulates the card's internal layout and private helpers. Notice it exports the main card as a default export while exposing Badge as a secondary named export. When does this matter? To provide callers with a clear primary component while allowing flexible reuse of related sub-components.

In legacy web applications, keeping all components in a single monolithic file resulted in severe maintenance friction, frequent git merge conflicts, and copy-paste duplication. In React, splitting components into standard ES modules establishes clean architectural boundaries. ArticleCard.jsx acts as a dedicated module, exporting its primary component as a default export and secondary utilities as named exports. Because import syntax strictly dictates how values are consumed, developers enjoy build-time verification, clear stack traces, and seamless code reuse across the entire application.

Where you will meet this

  1. Design System Component Libraries: Enterprise UI libraries export primary components (like <Modal />) as default exports, while exposing sub-components (like { ModalHeader, ModalFooter }) as named exports.
  2. File-Based Routing Frameworks: Modern frameworks like Next.js and Remix require each page route file to export a single default React component to represent the page view.
  3. Utility and Icon Packages: Icon libraries package hundreds of SVG icons as individual named exports (import { SearchIcon, CloseIcon }), allowing bundlers to tree-shake unused icons from production bundles.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you split components across files, and how do default and named imports differ?
  • The Hidden Signal: Interviewers ask this question to verify whether you understand the distinction between JavaScript module scope and the global window scope, how bundlers resolve static import bindings before runtime, and why team conventions favor one export pattern over another. Candidates who understand modules can explain that import statements form a static module dependency graph, whereas component execution builds the runtime UI tree.
  • The Classic Trap: The most common mistake is confusing import curly braces with JSX expression braces or runtime object destructuring. Candidates often assume import { ArticleCard } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' destructures a runtime object, unaware that ES module import specifiers are static language bindings checked by the bundler before any code executes. Another frequent trap is exporting anonymous arrow functions as default exports, which strips the component of its identifier and pollutes error stacks with <default>.
  • What is Actually Going On: Each file is an ES module evaluated in its own isolated environment. Build tools like Vite construct a module dependency tree by parsing import and export declarations statically before any component renders. Default exports bind to the module's default key, allowing the importer to assign any local identifier. Named exports bind to explicit named export keys on the module record, enforcing character-for-character identifier matching between exporter and importer.
  • Where It Gets Tricky: A tricky nuance arises with module evaluation timing. Code placed at the top level of a module executes exactly once when the file is first imported, and its exports are cached in memory. In contrast, code placed inside a component function executes on every render. If an engineer places shared mutable state at the top level of a module, that state becomes a global singleton shared across all instances of the component, breaking component isolation and causing severe concurrency bugs.

Glossary

  • module: An isolated JavaScript file with private scope that shares values across file boundaries only through explicit export and import statements.
  • default export: The single primary value or component exported by a module, declared with export default and imported without curly braces under any local name.
  • named export: A specific value or component exported by name using export function imported inside curly braces matching its exact identifier.
  • default import: An import statement written without curly braces that loads the primary default export of a module.
  • named import: An import statement written with curly braces that loads a specific named export from a module.
  • module dependency tree: The hierarchical graph of file relationships formed by import and export statements, used by build tools to bundle application code.

Beyond the basics

  • Importing and exporting components in React: the official guide on organizing components across files and comparing default and named exports (see react.dev/learn/importing-and-exporting-components).
  • The module dependency tree versus the render tree: understanding how bundlers build static file trees while React builds dynamic component trees (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree#the-module-dependency-tree).
  • Keeping components pure and module scope clean: why top-level module code evaluates once on import while component functions must stay side-effect free (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Code splitting and dynamic imports with lazy: loading component modules on demand to reduce initial client bundle size (see react.dev/reference/react/lazy).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways and Module Resolution Rules

❒ Module Organization and Export Choice

➔ ALWAYS give each component that other files use its own module under src/components/, and keep single-use helpers unexported in that file.

➔ NEVER export anonymous component functions like export default () => {} because React prints <default> in error stacks and DevTools.

❒ Import Matching and Casing Discipline

➔ ALWAYS match import syntax to the export style, using default imports without braces for default exports and curly braces for named exports.

➔ IF a file provides one primary component, THEN export that component as the default export.

➔ IF a file provides multiple reusable helpers or sub-components, THEN export them as named exports.

DO THIS: match import syntax to export style and name exported functions

6}

DO NOT DO THIS: mix up default and named syntax or use anonymous components

2import { ArticleCard } from './ArticleCard.jsx';

Mounting the Root Component with createRoot &
Vite Tooling

Interview Question   CORE

How does your root component attach to the browser DOM with createRoot, and how do build tools assemble it?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You built an application component tree in App.jsx, ready to show on screen.
  • 2 You open index.html, but the page shows only an empty div container or halts with script errors.
  • 3 How does your root component attach to the browser DOM with createRoot, and how do build tools assemble it?

The browser starts at index.html and needs an explicit mounting bridge

Every web application begins with an HTML document. When you build a traditional website, you write native HTML tags directly inside HTML files. The browser parses those tags and paints them immediately. In a React application, however, your components return descriptions of markup written in JSX. The browser cannot run JSX syntax on its own. It cannot guess which HTML element your components belong to. To display components on screen, React requires an explicit mounting bridge. This bridge connects your virtual component tree to a real, living HTML element on the page.

When you inspect a new React project, the root index.html file contains almost nothing. You find an HTML shell with an empty <div id="root"></div> tag and a module script. Looking at this empty container, a newcomer wonders how component code ever reaches the screen. A developer might attempt to link App.jsx directly inside index.html using a traditional <script> tag. Or they might double-click index.html to open it as a local file (file://) in Chrome. When they do, the browser fails immediately. The browser encounters raw JSX tags and halts with a fatal syntax error: Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'

The mounting pipeline connects three files. First, index.html provides the host HTML container and loads the entry script. Second, src/main.jsx finds that container and initializes React. Third, src/App.jsx provides the root component that renders the application interface.
