Later in this track, Lecture 14 shows how components update the page by managing state rather than creating new roots. Then Lecture 15 explains how root.render provides the initial trigger for rendering, and Lecture 46 covers how Vite wraps <App /> in <StrictMode> in development.

In this chapter, we master the mounting bridge connecting our component tree to the browser DOM, see why modern tooling is essential, and learn how React 19 handles root creation.

This lesson answers five questions:

  • How does index.html hand a DOM element to React?
  • Why must you serve the project through Vite rather than opening raw files?
  • Why does root.render require an element rather than a bare function?
  • Why did React 19 remove ReactDOM.render?
  • Why does an application use only one root container?

The questions stand on four earlier lessons:

  • Lecture 1 (What React is and the DOM): Plain JavaScript finds an HTML element using document.getElementById('root') which returns the living DOM node or null if no element with that identifier exists on the page.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): A React component is a JavaScript function that starts with a capital letter. Writing <App /> creates a React element that tells React to execute App(), whereas writing App refers to the bare function itself.
  • Lecture 3 (JSX): JSX tags compile into JavaScript function calls (_jsx). Browsers cannot parse raw JSX tags natively without a compiler step.
  • Lecture 8 (Imports and exports): Separate files are isolated modules. An application entry file uses a default import (import App from './App.jsx') to import the root component, and package imports (from 'react-dom/client') load external libraries.

How index.html loads main.jsx through a module script

We know that HTML documents load external scripts using <script> tags. Traditionally, a classic script ran synchronously and treated all code as a single global scope. In modern web development, adding type="module" to a <script> tag tells the browser that the file is an ES module that uses import and export statements.

Modern browser engines automatically defer module scripts. While the browser downloads main.jsx across the network, it continues parsing the rest of the HTML document without pausing. The module script executes only after the entire HTML document has been parsed into memory. Because of this deferred timing, a <script type="module"> tag placed in the <head> of your document can safely find <div id="root"> even though the <div> tag appears further down in the <body>.

index.html
1<head>
2 <title>Item Tracker</title>
3 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Module scripts are deferred until HTML parsing completes
Safe in head
4</head>
5<body>
6 <div id="root">Loading...</div>
Found safely by getElementById
7</body>

If you omit type="module", the browser treats the file as a classic script. The browser cannot run import statements outside a module and stops with Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module

How createRoot and root.render attach components to the page

React separates its core component architecture from browser rendering. The core package, react, manages element descriptions, component logic, and component trees. The browser renderer, react-dom/client, provides the bridge that turns those element descriptions into physical browser DOM nodes. Only the application entry file (main.jsx) imports from react-dom/client; all your component files import purely from react.

Calling createRoot(domNode) creates a React root object for that specific DOM element and gives React exclusive ownership of the HTML inside it. When root.render(<App />) runs for the first time, React wipes whatever placeholder HTML originally lived inside that element (such as "Loading...") and replaces it with the rendered output of <App />. Any HTML written outside that container, such as a static navigation bar or footer in index.html, remains completely untouched.

Calling root.render does not block the browser thread to update the DOM synchronously on the spot. Instead, root.render schedules a render task in React's queue and returns immediately. If you read container.textContent on the line directly following root.render(<App />), the console still prints "Loading..." because React has not painted the DOM yet. The browser paints the updated DOM tree only after the current JavaScript execution frame finishes and yields control back to the browser event loop.

Asynchronous Render Execution
1const container = document.getElementById('root');
2const root = createRoot(container);
Creates concurrent root
3
4root.render(<App />);
Schedules render task asynchronously
5
6console.log(container.textContent);
The next line executes before React paints the DOM:
Still prints: "Loading..."

When you need to tear down a React tree (for example, when a tab panel built in another library removes the container from the page), you can call root.unmount(). Calling root.unmount() empties the container and detaches React. Once unmounted, calling root.render again on that same root throws Cannot update an unmounted root In standard single-page React applications, you rarely need to call root.unmount.

Why Vite transforms JSX and serves modules over HTTP

Web browsers understand ECMAScript, but they do not understand JSX syntax like <App />. If a browser encounters a raw < token inside a JavaScript file, it halts with a syntax error. Furthermore, browsers cannot resolve bare package specifiers like import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' because browsers only know how to load files from explicit paths starting with /, ./, or ../.

To solve these limitations, modern projects use Vite. During development, running npm run dev starts a local HTTP dev server at http://localhost:5173. When the browser requests /src/main.jsx, Vite intercepts the request, transforms the JSX into standard function calls (_jsxDEV), rewrites package imports into browser-accessible URLs, and serves the files over HTTP. When you are ready to deploy, running npm run build compiles your application into static HTML, JavaScript, and CSS bundles inside a dist/ directory.

Terminal
1$ npm run dev
Starts local development server
2
3 VITE v6.0.0 ready in 180 ms
4
5 ➜ Local: http://localhost:5173/
Serves modules over HTTP
6 ➜ Network: use --host to expose

If you double-click index.html from your desktop folder, the browser opens it using the file:// protocol. For security reasons, modern browsers treat the local disk origin as null and block all <script type="module"> tags under cross-origin security rules. To run a modern React application, you must always serve your files over HTTP using the Vite development server.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does double-clicking index.html fail to load React?

When you double-click an HTML file on your desktop, the browser loads it over the local file:// protocol. Modern browsers treat the local filesystem origin as null and block all module scripts (<script type="module">) under strict security policies. The browser console logs: Access to script from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy To run a modern React application, you must always serve your files over an HTTP server. During development, Vite provides an instant HTTP dev server (npm run dev), and for production builds, vite preview serves your compiled dist/ directory locally over HTTP.

Principles of React: Mounting the Root with createRoot

QUESTION 1

An empty div in HTML receives the component tree

The browser loads index.html, which defines <div id="root">Loading...</div> and links the entry script with <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script> In src/main.jsx, a developer attempts to connect the application by searching for an element with the identifier 'app':

Target ID Mismatch
1import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
2import App from './App.jsx';
3
4const container = document.getElementById('app');
Returns null on mismatch
5const root = createRoot(container);
Throws runtime exception
6
7root.render(<App />);

When the browser loads the page, the screen stays completely blank, and the browser console throws: Uncaught Error: Target container is not a DOM element.

Why does the screen stay blank with "Target container is not a DOM element"?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. document.getElementById('app') returns null because no element with that identifier exists in index.html.

The browser executes document.getElementById('app') and scans the loaded HTML document. Because the container in index.html is written as <div id="root">, the lookup finds nothing and returns null. The function createRoot requires a living browser DOM element to manage. Receiving null, createRoot throws an immediate runtime error and halts execution before any component can mount.

The fix is matching the identifier string character for character with the id attribute defined in index.html. When document.getElementById('root') finds the valid <div> element, createRoot takes ownership of that container. Calling root.render(<App />) then replaces the placeholder text "Loading..." with the rendered component output of App.

The mounting bridge from HTML container to component tree
index.html:      <div id="root">Loading...</div>
                       |
                       v
main.jsx:        const container = document.getElementById('root');
                 const root = createRoot(container);
                       |
                       v
DOM tree:        root.render(<App />);  -->  [clears "Loading..."]
                                        -->  <div><App output /></div>
PRINCIPLE 1

index.html loads main.jsx, and main.jsx hands the root element to React

root container the physical HTML element that React takes over to display and manage components

When the browser loads index.html, the module script requests main.jsx. In that file, document.getElementById finds the physical container element, and createRoot hands that container to React. Calling root.render replaces any initial content inside the container with your component tree. If the identifier in getElementById does not match the id attribute in index.html, the method returns null, causing createRoot to throw a fatal error that leaves the page blank.

We should do this:
const element = document.getElementById('root');
const root = createRoot(element);
root.render(<App />);
replaces placeholder content
We should not do this:
const element = document.getElementById('app');
returns null
const root = createRoot(element);
throws on null container
QUESTION 2

Double-clicking index.html blocks the module script

A developer wants to test their project without opening the terminal. They locate index.html in their local desktop folder and double-click the file to open it directly in Chrome:

Browser Address Bar
1file:///Users/developer/project/index.html

The browser displays the initial placeholder text "Loading...", but the React components never paint to the screen. In the developer console, Chrome logs: Access to script at 'file:///Users/developer/project/src/main.jsx' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy: Cross origin requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http, data, chrome, https.

Why does opening index.html directly from disk fail to load the application?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Modern browsers block ES module scripts loaded over the local file:// protocol.

Modern browsers enforce strict security rules around ES modules (<script type="module">). When an HTML file is loaded from your local filesystem using file://, the browser assigns the document an origin of null. The browser blocks any script tag that tries to import external module files from origin null to prevent malicious local script execution. Furthermore, browser engines cannot compile JSX syntax or locate bare package imports like react-dom/client without a development server.

The fix is running the project through Vite by executing npm run dev in your terminal. Vite boots a local HTTP server at http://localhost:5173. When the browser visits this HTTP address, module scripts load under a valid origin without security blocks. Vite compiles JSX on the fly and rewrites package imports so the browser runs them smoothly. For production, npm run build compiles your files into static assets in dist/.

Protocol comparison: file:// vs Vite HTTP server
file:// protocol:
  file:///project/index.html  -->  origin: null  -->  CORS error on module
  browser fails to resolve 'react-dom/client' and cannot parse JSX tags

http:// protocol (Vite dev server):
  http://localhost:5173/      -->  HTTP 200 OK  -->  ES modules load cleanly
  Vite transforms JSX on the fly and maps package names to local file paths
PRINCIPLE 2

Serve the app through Vite, never as raw files

dev server a local HTTP server that transforms JSX and serves modules on demand during development

Web browsers do not understand JSX syntax and cannot resolve package imports like react-dom/client directly from disk. Furthermore, modern browsers treat local disk files loaded over file:// as having a null origin, blocking all module scripts with security errors. Running the Vite development server transforms JSX into standard JavaScript on the fly and serves your application over HTTP. For deployment, Vite bundles your project into static files inside dist.

It is best practice to do this:
<script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Local server URL: http://localhost:5173
HTTP
Instead of doing this:
<script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Double-clicking file:///project/index.html
CORS
QUESTION 3

Passing the bare function App leaves the page empty

In src/main.jsx, a developer imports App and passes the bare component name directly into root.render:

Bare Function Argument
1import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
2import App from './App.jsx';
3
4const container = document.getElementById('root');
5const root = createRoot(container);
6
7root.render(App);
Passing bare function identifier without JSX tags:
Does not mount component

The browser screen remains blank. In the console, React logs: Warning: Functions are not valid as a React child. This may happen if you return a Component instead of <Component /> from render. Or maybe you meant to call this function rather than return it.

Why does root.render require angle brackets around App?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. App is a bare JavaScript function, but root.render expects a React element.

In React, a component is a JavaScript function that returns markup descriptions. When you pass App without angle brackets, you pass the raw function object itself. React cannot display a function object on the screen. Writing <App /> creates a React element: an object descriptor that tells React to execute the App component function and render the resulting JSX tree.

The fix is wrapping App in JSX angle brackets: root.render(<App />). The method root.render accepts React elements, strings, numbers, null, or undefined. If a factory helper function returns a JSX element, call the function so root.render receives the returned element: root.render(createApp()).

Bare function reference vs React element descriptor
root.render(App):
  Value passed: [Function: App]  (raw JavaScript function reference)
  React runtime: Cannot mount bare function -> Error: Functions not valid

root.render(<App />):
  Value passed: { type: App, props: {} }  (React element descriptor)
  React runtime: Calls App(), receives JSX, mounts resulting DOM nodes
PRINCIPLE 3

Pass root.render an element, <App />

React element an object descriptor created with JSX that instructs React what markup to mount

A React component is a JavaScript function, but root.render requires a React element to mount. Writing the bare name App passes a function reference, which React cannot display on the page. Writing <App /> creates an element descriptor that instructs React to call the component function and render its returned markup. When rendering a helper function that returns JSX, call the function first so root.render receives the resulting element.

We should do this:
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(<App />);
passes a React element descriptor
We should not do this:
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(App);
error: Functions are not valid child
QUESTION 4

Older tutorials that call ReactDOM.render fail in React 19

A developer consults an older tutorial and attempts to mount the application using the classic ReactDOM.render syntax:

Legacy Mounting Pattern
1import ReactDOM from 'react-dom';
Legacy package import
2import App from './App.jsx';
3
4const container = document.getElementById('root');
5
6ReactDOM.render(<App />, container);
Legacy mounting method removed in React 19:
Throws runtime TypeError

When the script runs in the browser, JavaScript halts with an uncaught error: TypeError: ReactDOM.render is not a function The screen stays blank.

Why does ReactDOM.render fail in modern React projects?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React 19 completely removed the legacy ReactDOM.render method.

In React 19, legacy mounting functions, including ReactDOM.render, ReactDOM.hydrate, and unmountComponentAtNode, were permanently removed. Applications must import createRoot from the client renderer subpath, 'react-dom/client'. You create the root once with createRoot(container), and call root.render with a single argument: the React element.

If a developer carries over the old two-argument habit and writes root.render(<App />, container) React logs a console warning: Warning: You passed a second argument to root.render(...) but it only accepts one argument. Any root configuration options, such as onUncaughtError, must be passed as the second argument to createRoot(container, options) not to root.render.

Legacy ReactDOM.render vs modern createRoot API
Legacy React (Removed in React 19):
  ReactDOM.render(<App />, container);  -->  TypeError: render is not a function

Modern React 19:
  const root = createRoot(container);   -->  prepares concurrent root container
  root.render(<App />);   -->  schedules mounting with single argument
PRINCIPLE 4

Start the app with createRoot, not with ReactDOM.render

client subpath the react-dom/client import path providing browser-specific root creation functions

React 19 completely removed the legacy ReactDOM.render function. Applications must import createRoot from react-dom/client, initialize the root container once, and call root.render with a single React element argument. The render method accepts only one parameter; passing the DOM container or configuration options as a second argument to root.render triggers a console warning. Pass root options directly to createRoot as its second argument.

We should do this:
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(<App />);
modern client root mounting
We should not do this:
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom';
removed in React 19
ReactDOM.render(<App />, document.getElementById('root'));
QUESTION 5

Calling createRoot twice on the same container triggers a warning

A developer wants to display an application layout and a status card. In src/main.jsx, they find <div id="root"> and call createRoot twice to mount each section:

Duplicate Root Containers
1import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
2import App from './App.jsx';
3import StatusCard from './components/StatusCard.jsx';
4
5const container = document.getElementById('root');
6
7createRoot(container).render(<App />);
First root created
8createRoot(container).render(<StatusCard />);
Duplicate root

The browser renders the list, but the console logs: Warning: You are calling ReactDOMClient.createRoot() on a container that has already been passed to createRoot() before. Instead, call root.render() on the existing root to update it.

Why does calling createRoot multiple times on the same container cause issues?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Initializing multiple roots on the same DOM element creates conflicting root containers.

When you pass a DOM node to createRoot(container), React creates an internal root record and assumes exclusive ownership of the DOM inside that container. Calling createRoot again on that same element creates a second, competing root that attempts to control the same physical DOM nodes. This creates memory leaks, overrides event listeners, and breaks React's update guarantees.

In an application built fully with React, you call createRoot exactly once at startup in main.jsx. All user interface sections should be composed as child components nested inside App. Components update the page using state, not by creating additional roots. If you are embedding React into an existing multi-page website that is only partially built with React, you create one root for each separate physical HTML container on the page.

Single root architecture vs duplicate root warning
Single Root (Correct):
  createRoot(#root)  -->  Root  -->  <App />  -->  <StatusCard />

Duplicate Roots (Broken):
  createRoot(#root)  -->  Root 1  -->  <App />        (competing control)
  createRoot(#root)  -->  Root 2  -->  <StatusCard /> (warning: already passed)
PRINCIPLE 5

Create one root, and nest everything else inside App

single root an application architecture where one root container manages the complete component hierarchy

In an application built fully with React, create a single root container at startup in main.jsx. That root manages the entire DOM tree inside its container. Calling createRoot multiple times on the same DOM element causes conflicting update cycles and logs a warning. Add new interface sections by nesting child components inside App rather than creating additional roots. When embedding React into an existing multi-page website, create one root for each separate physical container element.

It is best practice to do this:
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(<App />);
one root: all components nest inside App
Instead of doing this:
const container = document.getElementById('root');
createRoot(container).render(<App />);
createRoot(container).render(<StatusCard />);
duplicate root

Step 1
First, we inspect the host HTML document
<index.html>

We begin at the root of the project by inspecting index.html. Unlike traditional web pages containing hundreds of lines of static layout markup, our React host document contains a minimal shell. Inside <body>, we define <div id="root"> with a loading placeholder that appears while JavaScript downloads. We link our application entry point using <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script> Because the script tag uses type="module", the browser defers execution until the HTML document is fully parsed, ensuring document.getElementById('root') can always find the container.

index.html
1<!DOCTYPE html>
2<html lang="en">

5 </head>

7 <div id="root"><p>Loading...</p></div>
Host container
8 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Module entry
9 </body>
10</html>

The <div id="root"> element acts as the single boundary that React will control. The <script type="module"> tag tells the browser to treat main.jsx as an ES module and execute it after the document has been parsed.

Step 2
Next, we construct the root application component
<src/App.jsx>

With our host HTML document established, we create src/App.jsx. This component acts as the root of our React component tree. Notice that App.jsx imports purely from 'react' and child component modules; it contains zero imports from 'react-dom' or 'react-dom/client'. By keeping App isolated from the DOM mounting bridge, our component remains pure, testable, and independent of browser-specific mounting code. In this step, App renders the application heading and prepares a container for our child status card.

App.jsx

4 return (
5 <main className="tracker-layout">

8 </main>
9 );
10}

Notice how App acts as the orchestrator. It imports StatusCard as a child component and passes it dynamic props. It never interacts with document.getElementById or touches browser DOM nodes directly.

Then, we declare the child item card component

Following our single root architecture, we grow our application by adding components inside App, rather than creating additional roots. We create src/components/StatusCard.jsx to display active task counts. It receives label and count props, wraps them in a styled container, and renders declarative JSX. Because this component lives in its own module, other views can reuse it without touching App.jsx or the mounting entry file.

Finally, we initialize createRoot and mount the tree
<src/main.jsx>

Finally, we connect our React application to the browser page in src/main.jsx. We import createRoot from 'react-dom/client' and import our top-level App component. We find the container element using document.getElementById('root') We verify that the element exists with if (container) before passing it to createRoot, and call root.render(<App />) with our root JSX tag. When Vite serves this project, React mounts App, clears the loading placeholder, and renders the complete user interface into the browser window.

Notice the clean sequence in main.jsx. We first find the container node. We verify it exists before passing it to createRoot. Once the root is initialized, root.render(<App />) mounts the virtual tree into the physical container.

Component Summary

App

The root application component serves as the top-level container for the entire interface. It composes layout elements and child components like StatusCard. Notice it imports only from React and child modules, remaining completely independent of browser DOM mounting code.

main

The application entry point bridges React to the browser DOM. It imports createRoot from react-dom/client, finds the container element, and mounts <App /> using root.render. When does this execute? It runs once at startup when the browser loads the module script.

StatusCardlabel="..." count=0

The leaf status component displays pending items inside the layout. It receives text data through props and encapsulates card styling. Why does it live inside App? Because all new user interface grows inside the single root component tree rather than creating extra roots.

Where you will meet this

  1. Project Scaffolding and Setup: When you create a new web application using Vite (npm create vite@latest), the generator scaffolds index.html, src/main.jsx, and src/App.jsx using this exact createRoot mounting pattern.
  2. Embedding React into Existing Multi-Page Websites: When adding interactive React widgets to an existing server-rendered website (such as WordPress, Laravel, or Django), you identify specific <div> containers on the page and mount standalone React widgets into them with separate createRoot calls.
  3. Production Diagnostic Audits: During production performance and diagnostic audits, senior engineers inspect main.jsx to verify that root configuration options, error boundaries, and development environment wrappers are correctly initialized.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How does your root component attach to the browser DOM with createRoot, and how do build tools assemble it?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not asking whether you can memorize three lines of boilerplate. They are probing whether you understand the fundamental boundary between the declarative React component model (react) and the imperative browser DOM mounting renderer (react-dom/client). A junior developer treats main.jsx as magic syntax; a senior engineer explains that React needs an explicit mounting bridge to bind virtual element descriptor trees to physical HTML containers, and that build tools transform JSX into browser-compatible modules because native browser engines cannot parse JSX or resolve bare package specifiers.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is assuming that root.render updates the browser DOM synchronously on the spot, or reciting legacy methods from older tutorials. Candidates often claim that ReactDOM.render is still supported, unaware that React 19 completely removed legacy mounting functions. Another fatal trap is writing root.render(App) without JSX angle brackets, passing a raw function reference that causes React to crash with Functions are not valid as a React child

3. What is Actually Going On

The mounting pipeline follows four distinct steps. First, index.html loads main.jsx using a deferred <script type="module"> tag. Second, document.getElementById('root') finds the physical container element in memory. Third, createRoot(container) creates a React root object that takes exclusive ownership of that container. Fourth, root.render(<App />) schedules the mounting of the <App /> element tree into the container. React clears any placeholder content inside the container and paints the component output. In development, Vite intercepts requests, transforms JSX into _jsxDEV calls, and serves native modules over HTTP. For production, vite build bundles everything into static files inside dist/.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if you inspect container.textContent immediately after calling root.render(<App />)? It still contains the old placeholder text because root.render schedules updates asynchronously rather than blocking the JavaScript thread synchronously. What happens if you call createRoot twice on the same container? React logs a warning because duplicate roots create competing ownership of the same DOM tree; you should always create one root per application and nest all UI inside App. What happens if you double-click index.html from your desktop? Modern browsers block module scripts over the file:// protocol with CORS errors, requiring files to be served over HTTP via Vite.

Glossary

  • createRoot: The modern React DOM client method that creates a root container for a physical browser element.
  • root.render: The root method that schedules the rendering of a React element tree into the designated DOM container.
  • root container: The physical HTML element, typically <div id="root">, that React takes over to manage its user interface.
  • module script: An HTML <script type="module"> tag that loads ES modules and automatically defers execution until HTML parsing completes.
  • dev server: A local development HTTP server that compiles JSX on demand and serves native ES modules with instant updates.
  • single root: An application architecture where one root container manages the complete component hierarchy from a single top-level component.

Beyond the basics

  • Official reference documentation for createRoot and its configuration options (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/createRoot).
  • Official guide to building a modern React application from scratch with tools like Vite (see react.dev/learn/build-a-react-app-from-scratch).
  • Official guide to adding React to an existing project or multi-page website (see react.dev/learn/add-react-to-an-existing-project).
  • React 19 upgrade guide detailing the removal of ReactDOM.render and legacy mounting methods (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Root Initialization & Container Ownership

➔ ALWAYS pass an existing DOM element to createRoot and let React take exclusive ownership of that container.

➔ NEVER call createRoot multiple times on the same container; nest all interface sections as child components inside App.

➔ IF you are embedding React into an existing multi-page website with separate widgets, THEN create one root for each separate physical DOM container.

❒ Tooling & Mounting APIs

➔ ALWAYS import createRoot from react-dom/client in your entry file, and pass root.render a React element like <App />.

➔ NEVER open React projects over the file:// protocol; always serve them over HTTP using the Vite development server.

➔ NEVER call the removed ReactDOM.render method or pass a second argument to root.render.

Lecture
10

Conditional Rendering in React

Interview Question   CORE

How do you show, hide, or switch JSX based on a condition?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build an article card that shows an urgent alert and reader comments when enabled.
  • 2 You write {commentCount && <p>Comments</p>}, but a raw number 0 prints on the screen.
  • 3 How do you branch markup cleanly in React without leaving unwanted numbers on the page?

Every web page needs to branch its markup

Every web page needs to adapt its markup to changing data. A shop shows an "Out of Stock" note when an item count reaches zero, an article shows an urgent alert when news breaks, and a discussion section hides comments when they are turned off. In static HTML, all content is permanent and unchanging. In modern applications, data changes constantly based on user actions and server responses. A developer needs a reliable way to show different elements, switch between two options, or render nothing at all.

In plain JavaScript, developers changed visibility by searching the page with document.getElementById and adding a CSS class like hidden, or setting style.display = 'none'. That approach tells the browser what commands to run step by step. In React, a component is a function that returns a description of what the user interface should look like for the current props. You never search the page or toggle classes on DOM nodes yourself. Instead, you write plain JavaScript control flow directly in your component to return the JSX for each case. React compares that description to the page and creates, updates, or removes real DOM nodes to match.

This chapter answers five core questions: How does React show or hide elements without manual DOM queries? How do you protect a component from crashing when data is missing? When should you use a ternary operator instead of logical AND? Why does a count of zero print a stray zero on the screen? How do you organize complex branching without nesting ternaries inside JSX?

Later in this track, Lecture 11 shows how to render lists of items from arrays, using {tags.length > 0 && <ul>{tags.map(...)}</ul>} to guard against empty collections.

  • Lecture 3 (JSX is JavaScript): JSX elements are plain JavaScript object descriptions that React turns into living browser DOM nodes.
  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): Braces inside JSX hold expressions, not statements. Inside braces, booleans, null, and undefined print nothing, while numbers and strings print directly to the screen.
  • Lecture 6 (Passing props): A parent passes values down to children as props. Quoted strings pass text, while curly braces pass numbers, booleans, and variables.

How JavaScript evaluates conditions, operators, and falsy values

In Lecture 4, we learned that curly braces inside JSX open a window where JavaScript evaluates code. However, JavaScript strictly separates statements from expressions. An expression produces a single value that can be passed to a function or assigned to a variable, such as 2 + 2 or user.name. A statement performs an action or controls program flow, such as an if block, a for loop, or a variable declaration. Because JSX tags compile into function calls, you cannot place an if statement directly inside JSX curly braces. For inline branching inside JSX markup, you must use JavaScript expressions.

The ternary operator (? :) is an inline JavaScript expression that takes three operands. First comes a condition, followed by a question mark (?), an expression to evaluate if the condition is truthy, a colon (:), and an expression to evaluate if the condition is falsy. For example, isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate /> checks isLive. If isLive is true, the expression evaluates to <LiveBadge />. If isLive is false, it evaluates to <StaticDate />. Because the whole ternary evaluates to a single value, it fits cleanly inside JSX curly braces.

The logical AND operator (&&) evaluates expressions from left to right using short-circuit evaluation. If the left side is falsy, JavaScript stops immediately and returns that exact left-hand value without evaluating the right side. If the left side is truthy, JavaScript evaluates and returns the right side. For example, in isUrgent && <AlertBadge /> if isUrgent is true, JavaScript evaluates and returns <AlertBadge />. If isUrgent is false, JavaScript stops and returns false.

In JavaScript, values are either truthy or falsy when tested in a boolean condition. There are six primary falsy values: false, null, undefined, 0, NaN, and the empty string "". All other values are truthy, including non-empty strings like "false", objects, and empty arrays []. Because an empty array is truthy, testing tags && <TagList /> evaluates to true even when tags has no items. Testing tags.length > 0 produces an explicit boolean comparison using > that evaluates to false when the list is empty.

JavaScript Expressions
1const alert = isUrgent ? <Alert /> : <Normal />;
Ternary picks one of two
2const badge = isLive && <LiveBadge />;
3const hasTags = tags.length > 0;
Explicit boolean comparison

Why React leaves omitted elements out of the browser DOM

When React runs a component function, the browser DOM has not been updated yet. The component executes in JavaScript memory to produce a tree of React elements. If a component attempts to find its own markup using document.getElementById('comments') the browser method returns null because that element is not in the page yet. Attempting to call .classList.add('hidden') on null throws an unhandled TypeError that halts execution and causes the whole page to go blank.

In plain HTML, setting style={{ display: 'none' }} hides an element visually, but the physical HTML element remains in the browser DOM and accessibility tree, consuming memory and confusing screen readers. In React, conditional rendering uses DOM omission: when a condition is false, the component simply does not include that JSX element in its return value. React compares the returned tree against the real page and removes the corresponding node completely, or never creates it in the first place.

When a component receives data through props, that data may be uninitialized or missing. In JavaScript, reading a property on undefined, such as article.title when article is undefined, throws a fatal TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title') In React, an unhandled error during render unmounts the component tree, blanking the application. An early return checks for missing data at the very top of the function: if (!article) return null; When a component returns null, React renders nothing for that component while leaving the rest of the application intact on screen.

Defensive Early Return
1export default function StoryHeader({ article }) {
2 if (!article) {
3 return null;
Exits early before reading missing data
4 }
5 return <h1>{article.title}</h1>;
Safe property access
6}

Principles of React: Conditional Rendering

QUESTION 1

Calling classList in render throws an error

We want to display an article header and hide reader comments when comments are turned off. A developer coming from vanilla JavaScript searches the document and attempts to toggle a CSS class directly:

Imperative Class Mutation
1export default function ArticleHeader({ commentsEnabled }) {
2 if (!commentsEnabled) {
3 const el = document.getElementById('comments');
4 el.classList.add('hidden');
Query during render
5 }
6 return (
7 <div id="comments">Comments Section</div>
Target node
8 );
9}

When running this code, the browser halts with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'classList') and the whole page goes blank.

Why does calling classList in the component throw an error?

ANSWER

The code does not work. The element does not exist in the document while React runs the component function.

While a component runs, React executes the function in JavaScript memory to calculate a tree of element descriptions. The browser DOM has not been updated yet, so document.getElementById('comments') finds nothing and returns null. Attempting to read .classList on null throws a fatal TypeError that stops rendering and clears the page.

In React, components do not search or mutate DOM nodes directly. Instead, a component branches with plain JavaScript and returns the JSX descriptions for the current case. When the JSX includes an element, React creates the DOM node; when the JSX leaves it out, React creates no node at all.

Imperative DOM query vs declarative JSX branching
Imperative lookup in render:
Component runs -> getElementById finds null -> classList throws -> blank screen

Declarative JSX branching:
commentsEnabled is false -> JSX omits comments -> React creates zero DOM nodes

The fix is to branch directly inside the JSX using logical AND or an early return, returning markup only when comments are enabled.

PRINCIPLE 1

Return the JSX for the case, and let React add or remove the DOM

DOM omission completely leaving an element out of the rendered DOM tree

When a component runs, its elements are not in the browser page yet. Searching the document with getElementById finds null, so calling classList throws an error and blanks the page. In React, a component is a function that returns the JSX for the current case. When the JSX includes an element, React creates the DOM node; when the JSX leaves it out, React performs DOM omission and creates no node at all.

We should do this:
function Card({ showDetails }) {
return <div>{showDetails && <p>Details</p>}</div>;
adds or omits node
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ showDetails }) {
const el = document.getElementById('details');
el.classList.add('hidden');
throws on null
return <div id="details"><p>Details</p></div>;
}
QUESTION 2

Reading properties on missing data blanks the page

An article card component displays story details from an article prop. If the story data has not arrived yet from the server, the component receives undefined as its prop and attempts to read article.title:

Missing Prop Property Access
1export default function StoryCard({ article }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h2>{article.title}</h2>
Article is undefined here
5 </article>
6 );
7}

When this code runs without article data, the console logs TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title') and every element on the screen vanishes.

Why does one missing property access clear the entire page?

ANSWER

The code does not work. Reading a property on undefined throws a fatal JavaScript error that crashes the render pass.

In Lecture 4, we saw that rendering {undefined} directly in JSX produces nothing on the screen without crashing. But reading a property on undefined, such as article.title, is an unhandled JavaScript error. When an error throws during render, React unmounts the entire component tree, leaving the user with a completely blank screen.

The fix is a defensive early return placed at the very top of the component function. Checking if (!article) return null; intercepts the missing data before any property access occurs. When a component returns null, React renders an empty slot for that component, allowing the rest of the application to render safely.

Property read crash vs defensive early return
Unguarded read:
article is undefined -> article.title throws TypeError -> whole page unmounts

Defensive early return:
article is undefined -> if (!article) return null -> rest of page stays visible

When the parent component already knows the data is missing, it can also choose to leave the child component out of its own JSX entirely.

PRINCIPLE 2

Guard missing data with an early return

early return returning from a component function before reaching the main JSX return

When a component needs data from a prop, check that the data exists at the start of the function. Reading a property on undefined throws a TypeError that stops rendering and clears the page. Returning null or placeholder markup before reading any property lets React finish rendering the rest of the application. When the parent component knows the data is missing, it can omit the child in JSX instead.

We should do this:
function Header({ item }) {
if (!item) return null;
guards before reading property
return <h1>{item.title}</h1>;
}
We should not do this:
function Header({ item }) {
return <h1>{item.title}</h1>;
throws TypeError on missing item
}
QUESTION 3

Choosing between a ternary and logical AND

An article header needs to show an urgent alert banner when a story is urgent, and display a live coverage badge or a published date for ongoing coverage. The developer writes:

Ternary and Logical AND
1export default function HeaderBadges({ isUrgent, isLive, date }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="badges">
4 {isUrgent && <Alert />}
Shows badge or nothing
5 {isLive ? <Live /> : <span>{date}</span>}
Picks one of two
6 </div>
7 );
8}

The alert banner appears only for urgent stories, and the header switches cleanly between the live badge and the timestamp.

When should you use a ternary operator instead of logical AND?

ANSWER

The code works. Each operator matches the exact shape of its branch.

The ternary operator evaluates to one of two expressions: condition ? <BranchA /> : <BranchB /> This makes it the right choice when you must choose between two visible outcomes. The logical AND operator evaluates to its right-hand expression when the left side is truthy, and to false when the left side is falsy. Because React suppresses false, logical AND is the right choice when you want to show an element or render nothing at all.

A common mistake is writing two separate && expressions with opposite conditions to simulate a choice: {isLive && <LiveBadge />} and {!isLive && <StaticDate />} This duplicates the condition across two lines. If someone edits one condition and forgets the other, both elements or neither element may appear. When both branches share wrapper markup, branch only the piece that differs, such as className={'card ' + (isUrgent ? 'urgent' : '')}

Branch shape decides the operator
Binary Choice (Branch A or Branch B):
isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate />  -> exactly one element renders

Show-or-Nothing (Branch A or Nothing):
isUrgent && <AlertBadge />  -> badge when true, false suppressed when false
PRINCIPLE 3

A ternary picks one of two, and && shows one or nothing

ternary operator an inline operator that evaluates a condition and chooses between two values
logical AND an operator that evaluates to the right side when the left side is truthy

Use the ternary operator to choose between two different elements, and use logical AND to show one element or nothing. In JSX, a ternary operator evaluates to one of its two branches. The logical AND operator evaluates to its right-hand element when true, and to false when false, which React leaves out of the page. When two branches share common markup, branch only the piece that changes.

We should do this:
{isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate />}
chooses one of two
{isUrgent && <AlertBadge />}
shows badge or nothing
QUESTION 4

An unread counter of 0 prints a raw 0 on screen

An article card component displays an unread comment badge using the logical AND operator:

Unread Counter Short Circuit
1export default function CommentCounter({ count }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="counter-box">
4 {count && <p>{count} Comments</p>}
Count is 0 here
5 </div>
6 );
7}

When a story has 5 comments, the badge displays "5 Comments". But when a story has 0 comments, the screen displays a literal, stray "0" right where the badge should be.

Why does a count of zero print a raw 0 onto the page?

ANSWER

The code does not work. The logical AND operator returns 0, and React renders numbers as visible text.

In JavaScript, && short-circuits and returns its left side whenever that side is falsy. When count is 0, JavaScript evaluates 0 && <Badge /> to 0, not to false. React suppresses booleans (false, true), null, and undefined, but it treats numbers as legitimate user content and renders them as real browser text nodes. Therefore, React creates a DOM text node containing "0" and paints it onto the screen.

The exact same issue occurs with NaN, which prints "NaN" on screen and triggers a console warning. Furthermore, non-empty strings like "false" and empty arrays [] are truthy in JavaScript, so isUrgent="false" and tags && <TagList /> both display their elements.

Short-circuit evaluation of 0 vs comparison
Raw number 0:
count is 0 -> 0 && <Badge /> returns 0 -> React renders text node "0"

Explicit boolean comparison:
count is 0 -> count > 0 is false -> false && <Badge /> returns false (omitted)

The fix is to convert the numeric check into an explicit boolean comparison by writing {count > 0 && <p>{count} Comments</p>} Comparing count > 0 produces false when count is zero, which React suppresses completely.

PRINCIPLE 4

Put a boolean on the left of &&, never a number

stray zero an unwanted 0 displayed on screen when a numeric zero short-circuits in JSX

The logical AND operator returns its left side whenever that side is falsy. In JavaScript, 0 is falsy, so 0 on the left evaluates to the number 0. React leaves booleans, null, and undefined out of the page, but it renders numbers as visible text. A condition with 0 prints a stray zero on the screen. Compare numbers with zero using a comparison operator so the left side is always a real boolean.

We should do this:
function Card({ count }) {
return <div>{count > 0 && <Badge />}</div>;
prints nothing
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ count }) {
return <div>{count && <Badge />}</div>;
0 prints on page
}
QUESTION 5

Branching across multiple states nests ternaries

An article header needs to show an urgent alert badge, a live coverage badge, or nothing at all. The developer chains ternaries inside JSX:

Nested Ternaries in JSX
1export default function StatusHeader({ isUrgent, isLive, title }) {
2 return (
3 <header>
4 {isUrgent ? <Alert /> : isLive ? <Live /> : null}
Nested ternaries
5 <h1>{title}</h1>
6 </header>
7 );
8}

The code runs and displays the correct badge, but code reviewers flag the nested ternaries as difficult to read and maintain.

How do you branch across several conditions without nesting ternaries in JSX?

ANSWER

The code works. The nested ternaries evaluate correctly, but they make the template difficult to read.

Curly braces inside JSX hold only a single expression, so handling three or more branches inline forces you to chain multiple ternary operators. Matching each question mark to its colon requires mental effort, and adding another branch requires editing a fragile expression.

Because JSX elements are plain JavaScript objects in memory, you can move branching above the return statement using standard let variables and if/else statements. You declare a variable such as let badge = null; set it using plain JavaScript statements, and embed {badge} once inside your returned markup.

Nested inline ternaries vs extracted variable above return
Nested inline ternaries:
{isUrgent ? <Alert /> : isLive ? <Live /> : null}  (hard to scan and edit)

Extracted variable above return:
let badge = null;
if (isUrgent) badge = <Alert />;
else if (isLive) badge = <Live />;
return <header>{badge}<h1>{title}</h1></header>;  (clean, readable, flat)

Simple binary choices and short show-or-nothing checks stay inline inside JSX. When branching logic outgrows a single clean expression, extract the logic above the return statement.

PRINCIPLE 5

Move complex branching above the return

local variable a variable declared with let or const inside the component function

Braces inside JSX hold a single expression, so handling several cases inline creates nested ternaries that are hard to read. Move multi-case branching above the return statement using standard if statements and a local variable. Assign the chosen JSX element to that variable, and place the variable inside your markup once. Simple binary choices and short show-or-nothing checks stay inline.

It is best practice to do this:
let badge = null;
if (isUrgent) badge = <AlertBadge />;
else if (isLive) badge = <LiveBadge />;
return <header>{badge}<h1>{title}</h1></header>;
clean placement

Component Summary

App

The root application shell manages layout and feeds data into the component tree. It defines sample article fixtures with varied flags (urgent, live, comment counts) and passes them downward through props.

ArticleHeaderarticle={...}

The conditional header boundary handles all branching logic. It executes an early return for missing data, pre-calculates topic badges before return, and uses ternaries and boolean-guarded logical AND operators inside JSX.

LiveIndicator

The leaf live indicator encapsulates the visual markup and animated dot for live coverage. It is conditionally mounted by ArticleHeader only when the article's isLive flag evaluates to true.

Declarative conditional rendering fundamentally changes how developers build dynamic interfaces. Instead of mutating the DOM after elements are created, React components describe exactly which elements should exist for any given combination of props. By using early returns for missing data, ternaries for binary choices, boolean-guarded logical AND operators for show-or-nothing branches, and variables for complex logic, you build user interfaces that are predictable, resilient to edge cases, and completely free of stray zeroes or layout flickering.

Where you will meet this

  1. Authentication and Navigation Bars: When building site headers, you conditionally render login buttons for guest visitors, user avatars for signed-in members, and administrative links for staff using ternary operators.
  2. Defensive API Data Consumption: When fetching articles, profiles, or product records from a remote server, you protect components against uninitialized data during initial page load using early returns (if (!data) return <p>Loading...</p>;).
  3. Notification Badges and Cart Counters: When displaying notification counters, message alerts, or shopping cart item totals, you guard numeric values with explicit comparisons (unreadCount > 0 && <Badge />) to eliminate the stray zero bug.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you show, hide, or switch JSX based on a condition?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is not asking whether you know the syntax of an if statement or a question mark. They are probing whether you understand how React manages the browser DOM declaratively. A junior candidate talks about toggling CSS classes with document queries. A senior engineer explains that components are pure functions of props and state: React renders what the returned JSX describes, and omits what the JSX leaves out. They immediately highlight the difference between expressions and statements inside JSX braces, explain how React treats falsy values, and address the stray zero trap.

2. The Classic Trap

The most famous trap is writing {count && <Badge />} with a numeric zero. Candidates assume that because 0 is falsy in JavaScript, React will render nothing. But in JavaScript, 0 && <Component /> returns 0. React suppresses booleans, null, and undefined, but it treats numbers as visible user content and renders a literal "0" onto the physical screen. Another classic trap is using two separate inverted && expressions ({isLive && <A />} and {!isLive && <B />}) to simulate an if/else branch, which duplicates the condition and causes visual desynchronization when conditions drift.

3. What is Actually Going On

In React, conditional rendering uses standard JavaScript control flow. Braces inside JSX open an expression window, so an if statement cannot live directly inside markup. For a binary choice between two elements, use a ternary: {isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate />} For a show-or-nothing element, use logical AND: {isUrgent && <AlertBadge />} When a condition evaluates to false, React leaves that element out of the tree entirely; it produces zero DOM nodes, meaning the element is never created in the browser page. When data may be uninitialized, place an early return if (!data) return null; at the top of the component to prevent property read crashes. When logic has three or more cases, move branching above the return statement into standard if statements and a let variable.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if you pass a quoted string like isUrgent="false" to a component? In JavaScript, all non-empty strings are truthy. Writing isUrgent="false" passes the literal string "false", so {isUrgent && <Alert />} evaluates to true and shows the alert. To pass a real boolean, you must use curly braces: isUrgent={false}.

What happens if an uninitialized calculation produces NaN? In JavaScript, NaN is falsy. But like 0, NaN && <Component /> returns NaN. React prints "NaN" directly onto the screen and logs a console warning. Always guard calculations with !Number.isNaN(val) && val > 0

What happens if you check an empty array with tags && <TagList />? In JavaScript, an empty array [] is an object, and all objects are truthy. Even with zero items, tags && <TagList /> evaluates to true, mounting <TagList /> with an empty collection. Always check length: tags.length > 0 && <TagList />

Glossary

  • Conditional Rendering: The technique of displaying, hiding, or alternating user interface markup based on JavaScript conditions and props.
  • Early Return: Exiting a component function early with null or fallback markup before executing the main JSX return.
  • Ternary Operator: A JavaScript inline operator (? :) that evaluates a condition and chooses between two alternative expressions.
  • Short-Circuit Evaluation: The evaluation model where logical AND (&&) stops and returns the left operand immediately if it is falsy.
  • Suppression Whitelist: React's built-in rule that renders zero DOM nodes for booleans (true, false), null, and undefined.
  • Stray Zero: An unwanted 0 displayed on the screen when a numeric zero short-circuits on the left side of logical AND.

Beyond the basics

  • Official conditional rendering guide: patterns for if statements, ternaries, and logical AND (see react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering).
  • Suppression whitelist reference: how React DOM handles empty nodes, booleans, and null in children (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • Preserving and resetting state: how component position in the UI tree controls state lifetime across conditional branches (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).
  • Rendering lists with fallbacks: managing empty array collections with list guards (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Operator Selection & Branch Shape

➔ ALWAYS use logical AND (&&) for show-or-nothing branches, and use the ternary operator (? :) when choosing between two alternate elements.

➔ NEVER use two separate inverted && expressions ({isLive && ...}{!isLive && ...}) to simulate an if/else choice.

❒ Numeric Guarding & Falsy Safety

➔ ALWAYS convert numbers to explicit booleans (count > 0 && ...) before using the && operator to prevent the stray zero bug.

➔ NEVER place a raw numeric counter or unverified calculation on the left side of &&.

❒ Complexity Management & DOM Ownership

➔ IF branching logic exceeds one clean expression THEN move the calculation before the return statement using standard if statements and a variable.

➔ NEVER manipulate CSS classes or styles imperatively using classList on DOM elements managed by React.

Rendering Lists &
Keys in React

Interview Question   CORE

How do you render a list from an array, and why does React demand a key on every item?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build a list of articles from an array of stories.
  • 2 You add a new story at the top, but text typed into the first row stays on the first row.
  • 3 How does React turn an array into a list, and why does each item need a key?

Every web application needs to display collections of items

Every web application displays dynamic collections of items. An online shop displays a grid of products, a social feed shows a list of posts, and a news portal presents breaking articles. In static HTML, each item is hardcoded into the markup one tag at a time. If the collection changes from twenty items to twenty-five, an engineer must edit the template and redeploy the code. In modern applications, collections change constantly: items are added, removed, filtered, and reordered. Modern web frameworks transform raw arrays of data into living user interfaces.

In basic HTML and early templates, developers repeated tags by hand or wrote imperative loops that manually created DOM elements and appended them to the page. In React, a component is a function that returns a description of what the interface should look like. You store your data in standard JavaScript arrays of objects. Instead of repeating JSX tags or writing manual append loops, you project that array of data into an array of JSX elements. React unpacks that array and paints the corresponding DOM nodes in order.

This chapter answers five core questions. How does JavaScript's map method turn an array of data into a list of elements? Where must the key prop be placed when extracting a child component? How do keys give elements persistent identity across re-renders? Why do array indices and random numbers create dangerous keys? Why is props.key undefined inside a child component?

Later in this track, Lecture 12 explores component purity and explains why generating random values during render is forbidden. Lecture 19 demonstrates how to add, remove, and reorder items held in component state. Lecture 61 dives deep into the reconciliation engine to show how keys preserve local component state across complex tree updates.

  • Lecture 3 (JSX is JavaScript): A Fragment groups sibling elements without adding extra wrapper nodes to the browser DOM.
  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): Curly braces in JSX evaluate expressions, and React unpacks an array of elements to render each item in order.
  • Lecture 6 (Passing props): A parent component passes data down to its children by setting attributes on the child element.
  • Lecture 7 (JSX spread attributes): Spread attributes pass all properties of an object to a component as individual props.
  • Lecture 9 (Application mounting): Calling root.render on an existing root updates the DOM with a new element tree.

How JavaScript transforms data arrays with map and arrow functions

In Lecture 4, we saw that curly braces {} inside JSX open an evaluation window for JavaScript expressions. JavaScript represents collections of structured data as arrays of objects, such as const stories = [{ id: 's1', title: 'City Transit Plan' }, { id: 's2', title: 'Clean Energy Accord' }] Each item in the array has properties we can access with dot notation, like story.title. To display every story, we need a way to convert each object in the data array into a corresponding JSX element.

The standard JavaScript array method map() transforms an array into a new array. It takes a callback function as an argument, calls that function once on each item in the original array, and collects the return values into a brand-new array. The original array remains completely untouched. For example, [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2) produces [2, 4, 6]. In React, our callback takes a data object and returns a JSX element, such as stories.map(story => <li>{story.title}</li>) When you place {stories.map(...)} inside a <ul>, React unpacks the resulting array of elements and renders each <li> in order.

In JavaScript, an arrow function can be written with an implicit return or a block body. In an arrow function without curly braces on the right side of the arrow, like story => <li>{story.title}</li> JavaScript uses an implicit return: it automatically returns the single expression following the arrow. However, if you place curly braces after the arrow, like story => { <li>{story.title}</li> } you create a block body. A block body executes code statements line by line, but it returns undefined unless you explicitly write the return keyword. If you omit return, map() returns an array filled with undefined, and React renders zero DOM nodes.

Often, an interface needs to display only a subset of items from an array, such as only featured stories. The standard JavaScript filter() method takes a test predicate function that returns true or false for each item. It produces a new, shorter array containing only the items that returned true. You can chain filter() directly into map(), writing stories.filter(story => story.isFeatured).map(story => <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>) This separates filtering logic from markup projection.

The callback function passed to map() receives three arguments: the current item, the item's numerical array index (starting from 0), and the array itself. Writing stories.map((story, index) => ...) exposes the sequential position of each item. While the index tells you where an item currently sits in the array, that index changes whenever items are prepended, inserted, or reordered.

Transforming Arrays with Map
1const items = [{ id: '1', title: 'First' }, { id: '2', title: 'Second' }];
2const elements = items.map(item => (
3 <li key={item.id}>{item.title}</li>
Implicit return
4));
5const blockList = items.map(item => {
6 return <li key={item.id}>{item.title}</li>;
Explicit return
7});
8const active = items.filter(item => item.id !== '1');

How React reconciles element arrays using persistent keys

In Lecture 3, we learned that JSX tags compile into plain JavaScript objects called React elements. When you write stories.map(story => <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>) the map() method creates an array of these lightweight element descriptors in memory. Inspecting one of these elements in the console reveals a plain object: { type: 'li', key: 's1', props: { children: 'City Transit Plan' } } Notice that key sits on the element object itself, alongside type and props.

When an application updates, React creates a new tree of element descriptions and compares it to the previous tree to determine what needs to change in the real DOM. When comparing lists of child elements, React must figure out which element in the new list corresponds to which element in the old list. Without keys, React falls back to positional matching: it assumes the first new item matches the first old item, the second matches the second, and so on. If an item is added to the top of the array, every subsequent item shifts down one position, causing React to rewrite existing DOM nodes in place and break internal element state.

A key is a special string or number passed to JSX elements in an array that gives each item a permanent element identity. React uses the key to track each item throughout its lifecycle across renders. When a key is present, React does not pair elements by their index position; instead, it matches old and new elements that share the exact same key. If an item moves from the first position to the fifth position, React reuses the existing DOM node and moves it in the page, preserving input values, focus, and scroll position.

Inspecting Keyed Element Objects
1const stories = [{ id: 's1', title: 'Transit Plan' }];
2const elements = stories.map(story => (
3 <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>
Assigns stable key
4));
5console.log(elements[0]);
Logs element object

Principles of React: Rendering Lists and Keys

QUESTION 1

An arrow function with braces renders an empty list

You receive an array of thirty breaking stories from the server. You want to display each headline as a row in a list. Inside your feed component, you call stories.map(). Because you want to add console logging or variable declarations later, you write curly braces around the callback function body:

Feed Without Return Keyword
1function Feed({ stories }) {
2 return (
3 <ul>
4 {stories.map(story => {
5 <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>;
Missing return keyword
6 })}
7 </ul>
8 );
9}

You open the browser. The data array contains thirty stories, but the unordered list renders completely empty. You open the developer console, expecting an error or warning, but the console is clean.

Why does the list render completely blank when the array has thirty stories?

ANSWER

The code does not work. The arrow function callback has a block body but omits the return keyword.

In JavaScript, when an arrow function body begins with a curly brace, it becomes a block body. A block body executes statements sequentially, but it produces no return value unless you write the return keyword. Without return, the function returns undefined.

When stories.map() executes over an array of thirty items, it collects thirty undefined return values into a new array. As Lecture 4 explained, React's suppression whitelist renders zero DOM nodes for undefined. The component returns an array of undefined, so React paints nothing into the browser DOM. The console shows no error because returning undefined is valid JavaScript and valid JSX.

To fix this issue, you must write an explicit return keyword inside the curly braces. Alternatively, remove the curly braces and wrap the JSX tag in parentheses to use an implicit return. When written with a proper return, console.log(storyElements[0]) shows a valid element object with type: 'li', key: 's1', and props: { children: 'City Transit Plan' }

Mapping data objects to React element objects
Data Array              map() Callback          React Elements
----------------------------------------------------------------------
[                       (story) =>              [
  { id: '1', title: 'A' }  <li key="1">A</li>  ->  { type: 'li', ... }
]                                               ]
PRINCIPLE 1

The map method turns an array of data into an array of elements

array transformation converting an array of data objects into a new array of element descriptions using map
explicit return writing the return keyword inside a block body so a function outputs a value

To build a list of elements from an array, call map() on the data. Each call runs the function on one item and collects what it returns into a new array. When the function uses curly braces, write return, or the call returns undefined and the list renders completely empty with no error.

We should do this:
items.map(item => (
<li key={item.id}>{item.title}</li>
returns element
))
We should not do this:
items.map(item => {
<li key={item.id}>{item.title}</li>;
returns undefined

QUESTION 2

The console warns that each child needs a key

To keep your code modular, you extract the markup for each story row into a separate component named StoryItem. You remember that React requires a key on list items, so you place key={story.id} on the root <li> tag inside StoryItem.jsx:

Key Placed Inside Child Component
1function Feed({ stories }) {
2 return (
3 <ul>
4 {stories.map(story => (
5 <StoryItem story={story} />
Missing key on child
6 ))}
7 </ul>
8 );
9}

Inside StoryItem.jsx, you return <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>; The thirty stories appear on screen correctly, but the browser console prints a red warning: "Warning: Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop. Check the render method of Feed."

Why does React print a missing key warning when the list item already has a key?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The key is placed on an inner tag instead of the outermost element returned by map.

React reconciles arrays at the exact level where the array is created. In Feed.jsx, the map() method creates an array of <StoryItem /> elements. React inspects that array to verify that each item in the collection carries a key prop.

When you place key={story.id} on the <li> tag inside StoryItem, that key is attached to an internal element created inside StoryItem's own render pass. React cannot see into StoryItem while it reconciles the child array in Feed. To React, the array contains thirty <StoryItem /> elements, and none of them have a key.

To fix this warning, place key={story.id} directly on the outermost element returned by the map() callback: <StoryItem key={story.id} story={story} /> Keys must be unique among siblings within that specific array; using the same key in a completely different list is valid. If a single item must return multiple adjacent tags without adding a wrapper <div>, use <Fragment key={story.id}> because shorthand <>...</> cannot accept attributes. Furthermore, never put a key inside an object and spread it (<StoryItem {...story} /> where story contains key), because React warns that a key is being spread into JSX.

Key placement at the array boundary
Array Level (Feed)                 Component Internal (StoryItem)
-----------------------------------------------------------------

  <StoryItem                         return (
    key={story.id}  <-- REQUIRED       <li>...</li>  <-- INEFFECTIVE
    story={story}                    );
  />                               }
))

Put the key on the element written inside map

outermost element the top-level JSX element returned directly by the map callback
sibling uniqueness the rule that keys must be distinct within the same array

React checks keys on the elements in the array returned directly by map(). When you map to a component, put the key on that component, not on an HTML element inside it. A key on an inner tag does not identify the item in the array. Keys must be unique among sibling elements in that array.

We should do this:
items.map(item => (
<ItemRow key={item.id} item={item} />
key on mapped item
))

<ItemRow item={item} />
missing key on component
