QUESTION 3

Text typed into a row jumps when a story is added at the top

You want each story row to include an uncontrolled <input> field where editors can type editorial notes. To satisfy the key requirement quickly, you use the array index as the key:

Feed Using Index Keys
1function Feed({ stories }) {
2 const items = stories.map((story, index) => (
3 <li key={index}>
Index key causes state drift
4 {story.title} <input placeholder="Add note..." />
5 </li>
6 ));
7 return <ul>{items}</ul>;
8}

The list renders cleanly, and the console produces zero warnings. An editor clicks the first input box ("City Transit Accord Finalized") and types "verify transit numbers". A breaking headline arrives, and the application prepends an urgent story ("Urgent Alert: Flash Flood") to the top of the array at index 0. The application re-renders with root.render.

Suddenly, the note "verify transit numbers" appears inside the input box for "Urgent Alert: Flash Flood"! Meanwhile, the input box for "City Transit Accord Finalized" is now empty.

Why does typed text jump to the new story when using array indices as keys?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Array index keys force React to match elements by numerical position rather than data identity.

When a component re-renders, React reconciles the new element tree with the previous element tree. To do this efficiently, React pairs elements between renders. When you provide key={index} (or omit keys entirely), React uses positional matching. It pairs the old item at index 0 with the new item at index 0.

Before the update, index 0 was "City Transit Accord Finalized". When the editor typed into the input, the browser stored that text directly in the physical DOM <input> element. When the urgent story was prepended at index 0, the transit story shifted to index 1.

React compares the old tree with the new tree:

  1. At index 0, React sees that the title text changed from "City Transit Accord Finalized" to "Urgent Alert: Flash Flood". It updates the headline text inside the existing DOM node in place.
  2. Because React mutates the existing DOM node at index 0 instead of moving it, the browser's internal input buffer is left untouched. The typed text remains inside the first physical DOM box.
  3. At index 1, React creates a new DOM node or updates an old one, leaving its input empty.

To the user, their typed text appears to jump from the transit story to the urgent headline. The fix is to use a stable ID from the data (key={story.id}). With stable keys, React matches the old s1 element with the new s1 element. It physically moves the existing DOM node down to index 1, carrying the input text, focus, and scroll position with it.

Positional matching vs identity matching on prepend
Index Keys (Positional):             Stable Keys (Identity):
Old Slot 0: Transit [verify]         Old s1: Transit [verify]
New Slot 0: Urgent  [verify] (WRONG) New s9: Urgent  []       (FRESH)
New Slot 1: Transit []               New s1: Transit [verify] (MOVED)

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why do user inputs jump when using index keys? When you use array indices as keys, React tracks elements purely by their numerical order rather than their data identity. When an item is prepended at index 0, every existing item shifts down by one position. React looks at index 0, sees that the title text changed, and mutates the existing DOM node in place. However, the browser's internal input buffer lives directly inside the physical DOM node. Because React reuses the existing node at index 0 instead of moving it, whatever text the user typed stays in that first box. To the user, their typed input appears to jump to the wrong story. To prevent this, you must always provide a permanent database ID (key={story.id}) so React can move the actual DOM node to its new position.
PRINCIPLE 3

The key is how React finds the same row on the next render

element identity a persistent identifier that ties an element to its physical DOM node across renders
positional diffing matching items by index order when keys are missing or based on index

On the next render, React pairs each new element with an old one that shares the same key. When keys match, React keeps the existing browser DOM node, along with whatever the user typed into it. Without keys, or with array indices, React matches items by position. Adding an item at the top forces the new item into the first DOM node, leaving old typed text attached to the wrong content.

We should do this:
items.map(item => (
<li key={item.id}><input /></li>
node moves with id
))
We should not do this:
items.map((item, index) => (
<li key={index}><input /></li>
text jumps to wrong row
))
QUESTION 4

A random key makes every input lose its focus and text

You have an array of stories that do not have an id field. Knowing that array indices cause input text to jump, you decide to generate a unique key on the fly using Math.random():

Feed Using Math.random Keys
1function Feed({ stories }) {
2 const items = stories.map(story => (
3 <li key={Math.random()}>
Random key forces recreation
4 {story.title} <input placeholder="Add note..." />
5 </li>
6 ));
7 return <ul>{items}</ul>;
8}

An editor begins typing a note into the first input box. As soon as the application updates, the input box suddenly loses focus. The editor's cursor vanishes, and all typed text disappears.

Why does generating keys with Math.random clear all inputs and lose focus on every render?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Math.random generates fresh keys on every render pass, destroying and rebuilding all DOM nodes.

A key must remain constant for the same data entity across renders. Because Math.random() executes during render, every item receives a completely new random number each time the component runs.

When React compares the new element tree with the previous tree, it finds that none of the keys match. React assumes that all previous elements were deleted and that completely new elements were created. It destroys every existing DOM node in the list and mounts new nodes from scratch.

This teardown destroys user inputs:

  1. Any active cursor focus is lost because the focused DOM element was removed from the document.
  2. Any uncontrolled input values, text selections, or scroll positions are erased.
  3. Application performance suffers because the browser must recalculate styles and rebuild layout on every update.

A key must come from the data. If the data comes from a database, use its permanent database ID (story.id). If data is created locally in the browser, generate an ID once at creation time using crypto.randomUUID() and store it on the object. The array index is acceptable only when a list is completely static: items are never inserted, deleted, filtered, or reordered, such as lines of a printed poem.

Random key churn vs stable data identity
Render 1: key=0.1824 -> DOM Node A created [focused, text="note"]
Render 2: key=0.7491 -> Keys mismatch! Node A destroyed, Node B created
Result: text lost, focus dropped, full DOM teardown
PRINCIPLE 4

Use a stable ID from the data as the key

stable identifier a permanent ID that remains identical for the same data entity across renders
random key churn generating keys during render, forcing React to destroy and rebuild all DOM nodes

A key must remain the same for the same item across renders. Generating keys with Math.random runs on every render, so no keys ever match and React tears down and rebuilds every DOM node from scratch. Use a permanent ID from the data, such as a database ID or an ID made once with crypto.randomUUID. The array index is safe only for a static list that never inserts, deletes, or changes order.

We should do this:
items.map(item => (
<li key={item.id}><input /></li>
stable database ID
))
We should not do this:
items.map(item => (
<li key={Math.random()}><input /></li>
rebuilds DOM

QUESTION 5

Reading props.key inside a row returns undefined

In your extracted StoryItem component, you want to render an HTML data attribute data-id for analytics tracking. Because you already passed key={story.id} to <StoryItem />, you attempt to read props.key inside the component:

Attempting to Read Key from Props
1function StoryItem(props) {
2 return (
3 <li data-id={props.key}>
Reading props.key yields undefined
4 {props.story.title}
5 </li>
6 );
7}

When you inspect the rendered HTML in developer tools, the data-id attribute is missing. In the console, React prints a warning: "Warning: StoryItem: key is not a prop. Trying to access it will result in undefined being returned. If you need to access the same value within the child component, you should pass it as a different prop."

Why does reading props.key return undefined and print a console warning?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React reserves key for internal reconciliation and strips it from component props.

React treats key (and ref) as special reserved attributes. When JSX compiles into a React element object, React extracts key and stores it directly on the element descriptor (element.key). React intentionally excludes key from the props object.

React does this because key belongs to the parent list reconciler, not to the child component. The child component should not need to know where it sits in a list or what key was assigned to it. As a result, accessing props.key inside StoryItem evaluates to undefined.

If your child component needs the story's ID, you must pass it under a different, explicitly named prop such as storyId={story.id} or id={story.id}. Alternatively, pass the entire story object and read story.id directly from props.story.

React element object property separation
React Element Object
-----------------------------------------------------------
{
  type: StoryItem,
  key: "story-101",        <-- Consumed by React reconciler
  props: {
    story: { ... },        <-- Passed to component function
    storyId: "story-101"   <-- Accessible as props.storyId
  }
}
PRINCIPLE 5

The key is not a prop, so pass the id again

reserved prop a prop like key that React consumes internally and excludes from component props
explicit prop passing passing an identifier under its own prop name so child components can read it

React reserves the key prop for itself and excludes it from the component's props object. Reading props.key inside a component yields undefined and prints a console warning. When a component needs the item's identifier for links, attributes, or handlers, pass that identifier under a different prop name or read it from the data object.

We should do this:
function Item({ item, id }) {
return <li data-id={id}>{item.name}</li>;
reads id prop
}
We should not do this:
function Item(props) {
return <li data-id={props.key}>{props.name}</li>;
undefined
}

Component Summary

App

The root application shell manages the story data collection and maps items into JSX elements. It places the permanent key={story.id} prop on each item component, ensuring React can identify and match items across renders.

StoryItemstory={story}

The list item boundary encapsulates the presentation of a single story. It mounts the category label, displays the headline, and provides an editor input field whose DOM state is preserved by React's key matching.

CategoryLabelcategory={...}

The leaf category label formats and styles the category name into a styled tag. It acts as a pure presentation leaf with zero awareness of list mapping or parent keys.

Where you will meet this

  1. Dynamic Content Feeds and Catalogs: In news portals, social media feeds, and e-commerce catalogs, you map arrays of database records into card components, using permanent entity database IDs as keys to allow smooth insertion and sorting.
  2. Interactive Form Repeaters: In invoice builders, survey creators, or recipe ingredient lists where users can add, remove, and reorder input rows, stable keys ensure that typed text and active focus never jump to the wrong row when an item is deleted.
  3. Tabbed Navigation and Menus: When rendering navigation bars or tab strips from an array of routes, stable keys allow React to track which tab is active without tearing down DOM nodes during navigation.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you render a list from an array, and why does React demand a key on every item?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is probing whether you understand React's reconciliation engine and DOM node preservation, or merely memorized syntax to silence a console warning. A junior developer recites map syntax and claims keys make React faster. A senior engineer explains that keys establish persistent element identity across renders. They contrast positional diffing against key-based matching, explaining that keys allow React to move existing DOM nodes and preserve uncontrolled state during insertions and reordering.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is reaching for the array index as a convenient key (key={index}). Candidates assume index keys are safe because they silence the console warning. But when an item is prepended at index 0, every existing item's index shifts by one. React compares index 0 to index 0, mutating the existing DOM node in place while leaving internal input text, focus, and audio playback attached to the wrong item. Another trap is generating keys on the fly with key={Math.random()}, which forces React to destroy and recreate the entire DOM tree on every single render.

3. What is Actually Going On

In React, you call map() on an array of data. Each call returns a JSX element descriptor, and React unpacks the resulting array in order. If the arrow function has a block body with curly braces, you must write an explicit return, or the list renders empty. React needs a unique, stable key on every element directly returned by map(). React uses that key to pair new elements with old elements on subsequent renders. When keys match, React moves the existing DOM node in place. Without keys, React compares items by array position, overwriting content and scrambling user inputs.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if a list row component tries to read props.key? React reserves key for its own reconciler and strips it from props; props.key evaluates to undefined and triggers a console warning. If the child needs the ID, pass it under a separate prop like id={story.id}. What happens if you need to render multiple sibling tags from a single mapped item without an extra wrapper <div>? You cannot use shorthand <>...</> because shorthand fragments cannot accept attributes; you must import Fragment from 'react' and write <Fragment key={story.id}>. When is the array index safe to use? The index is safe only when the list is completely static: items are never inserted, deleted, filtered, or reordered.

Glossary

  • Array Transformation: Using methods like map to project an array of raw data objects into a new array of JSX element descriptors.
  • Key Prop: A special string or number attribute passed to list elements that React uses to identify items across renders.
  • Positional Diffing: React's fallback reconciliation behavior when keys are absent or based on array index, comparing elements purely by sequential position.
  • Element Identity: The association between a React virtual element and its persistent browser DOM node established by a stable key.
  • Key Churn: An antipattern where keys change on every render (such as from Math.random), forcing React to destroy and recreate all DOM nodes.
  • Reserved Prop: A prop such as key or ref that React consumes internally for reconciliation and does not pass down to the component.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide on rendering data from arrays and keeping list items in order with keys: covers array transformation, filtering, and key rules (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).
  • Official reference documentation explaining why keys are required on list children in createElement: details how React evaluates child collections (see react.dev/reference/react/createElement).
  • Official reference documentation on rendering a list of Fragments with keys: shows how to assign keys to Fragment elements without wrapper DOM nodes (see react.dev/reference/react/Fragment).
  • Official deep dive on preserving and resetting component state using keys across renders: explains how keys control component lifecycles (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Array Transformation & Return Syntax

➔ ALWAYS use array.map() to project data arrays into JSX element arrays inside curly braces.

➔ IF using a block body (=> { ... }) in a map callback THEN write an explicit return statement to prevent rendering an empty list.

❒ Key Placement & Multi-Node Grouping

➔ ALWAYS place the key prop on the outermost element directly returned by the map() callback.

➔ IF an item returns multiple sibling nodes without a wrapper tag THEN use <Fragment key={item.id}> instead of shorthand <>...</>.

❒ Key Source & Reconciliation Safety

➔ ALWAYS use permanent, stable entity IDs from your data (such as database IDs) as list keys.

➔ NEVER use Math.random() to generate keys during render, which causes complete DOM teardown on every update.

➔ IF a list is dynamic THEN avoid array indices as keys to prevent state drift and input bugs.

Lecture
12

Keeping Components Pure

Interview Question   CORE

What does it mean for a component to be pure, and what breaks when it is not?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build an article feed where cards display their position number and reading status.
  • 2 You increment a variable outside the component, but the numbers double on initial page load under StrictMode.
  • 3 What does it mean for a component to be pure, and what breaks when it is not?

Every web application calculates user interfaces from dynamic data

Every web application calculates user interfaces from underlying data. An online store calculates cart summaries, a dashboard computes live metrics, and a content feed transforms arrays of articles into visual cards. In standard JavaScript scripting, developers frequently declare outside variables and write step-by-step instructions that modify those variables or reach into the browser document. In React, a component is a function that calculates what the interface should look like: UI = f(props). To ensure that user interfaces render reliably without visual corruption or race conditions, React assumes that every component function you write is a pure function.

In traditional imperative programming, functions freely read and write global variables, mutate shared lists, or modify the document with document.getElementById(). If a developer numbers list items by incrementing an outside counter variable inside a component, the application quickly breaks. In development mode, the counter increments twice per render, jumping from #1 to #2 and #4. In React, a component treats rendering as a mathematical formula: given the same inputs, it must return the exact same JSX, and it must never change any variable or system that existed before the function ran.

This chapter answers four core questions. What does it mean for a React component to be a pure function? Why does modifying an outside variable double numbers under StrictMode in development? How does local mutation differ from external mutation? Where do side effects and DOM changes belong if they cannot run during render?

Later in this track, Lecture 13 introduces event handlers as the primary home for user-triggered side effects like network requests and notifications. Lecture 14 teaches how state hooks provide components with memory to update the screen over time without breaking render purity. Lecture 46 dives deep into <StrictMode>, exploring how double-invoking updaters and Effects protects applications against concurrency bugs.

  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): Curly braces evaluate JavaScript expressions during render, and StrictMode calls components twice in development.
  • Lecture 5 (The UI tree): Siblings share data through their common parent component, never through shared outside variables.
  • Lecture 6 (Passing props): Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child that must never be mutated.
  • Lecture 9 (Application mounting): Calling root.render on an existing root updates the DOM with a new element tree.

What makes a function pure: identical inputs, identical output, and zero side effects

In Lecture 2 and Lecture 4, we saw that React components are JavaScript functions that accept props and return JSX element descriptions. In computer science and functional programming, a pure function is a function that satisfies two strict rules: first, it minds its own business, meaning it never modifies any variable, object, or system that existed before it was called; second, same inputs always produce the exact same output. A classic example is a math formula such as y = 2x. If x is 2, y is always 4. If x is 3, y is always 6. The answer never changes based on the time of day or what other formulas were calculated earlier.

Pure Calculation
1function PureDouble({ number }) {
Pure: returns exact same JSX for given prop
2 const result = number * 2;
3 return <p>Result: {result}</p>;
Deterministic
4}

React is built directly on this mathematical foundation. React assumes that every component function is a pure calculation. Given the same props, a component must always return the exact same JSX tree. When a component only calculates markup from its inputs without touching outside systems, React can run that component at any time, run sibling components in any order, or run the function multiple times without corrupting application data.

Impure Calculation
1let outsideFactor = 2;
Outside variable
2function ImpureDouble({ number }) {
Impure: output depends on mutable outside variable
3 return <p>Result: {number * outsideFactor}</p>;
4}

How React runs components during render and why StrictMode double-calls in development

In Lecture 4, we learned that development environments wrap the root application in <StrictMode>. To understand why StrictMode behaves the way it does, we must understand the render phase. Rendering refers to the process where React calls your component function to find out what the next screen description should look like. Code written at the top level of your component function body executes during this render phase. Because React may need to recalculate the interface when data changes, React does not promise to call your component exactly once per screen change.

A module-level variable is a variable declared at the top of a file, outside of any component function. While local variables declared inside a component are recreated fresh on every call, a module-level variable lives in module scope and survives for the entire lifetime of the browser tab. If a component modifies a module-level variable during render, that mutation persists across calls.

Module Variable Mutation
1let renderPass = 0;
Module-level variable
2
3export default function CounterCard() {
4 renderPass = renderPass + 1;
Mutates outside variable
5 return <div>Render pass #{renderPass}</div>;
6}

In development, <StrictMode> intentionally calls every component function twice during every render pass. If a component is pure, calling it twice produces identical JSX and causes zero harm. But if a component mutates an outside module variable, that mutation executes twice on page load, immediately exposing the bug.

The difference between local mutation and external mutation

In Lecture 6, we established that props are strictly read-only. In JavaScript, mutation means modifying the contents or properties of an existing object or array in place without creating a new reference. Developers often wonder whether React forbids all JavaScript mutation. The answer is no: React explicitly allows local mutation. Local mutation means changing variables, arrays, or objects that were created inside that exact same render call.

If you create a brand-new array inside a component function body using const items = []; and call items.push(...) inside a loop to assemble list items, that code is completely pure. Because the array was born inside that specific render call, no other component or function in the application can see it. When the component finishes executing, the local array is encapsulated in the returned JSX.

Local Array Mutation
1function ItemList({ count }) {
Safe local mutation: array created in this render
2 const items = [];
Fresh local array
3 for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
4 items.push(<li key={i}>Item {i + 1}</li>);
5 }
6 return <ul>{items}</ul>;
Pure return
7}

However, calling array.push() on an array received as a prop or declared at the module level modifies data that existed before the render. Under StrictMode, that push() runs twice, duplicating items in memory. Furthermore, mutating a local object after passing it into a JSX element modifies the element because both share the same reference.

What belongs in render versus what belongs in event handlers

In Lecture 1, we saw that scripts interact with the DOM using document.getElementById(). In Lecture 10, we saw that reading properties on null throws a TypeError. A side effect is any operation that modifies state outside the current function or interacts with outside systems during execution. Examples include writing to document.getElementById(), modifying document.title, starting a timer with setInterval, making a network request, or logging analytics. Top-level component execution must remain free of side effects because React calls components before their DOM elements exist.

When a component runs for the first time, its HTML tags have not yet been created or mounted in the browser document. Calling document.getElementById('badge').className = 'active' during render fails immediately: document.getElementById() returns null, and assigning a property on null throws an unhandled TypeError that crashes the page. Even on later renders, directly mutating DOM nodes bypasses React's reconciliation engine.

Declarative Ternary Expression
1function StatusIndicator({ isActive }) {
Declarative: evaluates ternary expression during render
2 const statusClass = isActive ? 'online' : 'offline';
3 return <span className={statusClass}>Status</span>;
4}

The pure React approach is declarative: calculate dynamic styles and text directly in the returned JSX using JavaScript expressions like ternary conditional operators (condition ? 'active' : 'inactive'). Changes caused by user actions (like button clicks) belong in event handlers, which run outside of render.

A function is idempotent if running it multiple times with the same inputs always produces the exact same result. Functions like Math.random() and new Date() are non-idempotent: every single invocation returns a different number or timestamp. When a component calls Math.random() in its body, StrictMode runs the function twice and produces two disagreeing numbers. The screen shows the second number, while earlier logs or child components hold the first. To keep components pure, dynamic values and timestamps should be passed downward as props from data that already holds them.

Principles of React: Keeping Components Pure

QUESTION 1

An outside counter variable doubles its numbers on page load

A developer wants three cards in an article list to display sequential numbers. They declare a counter variable at the top of the file outside the component. Inside the card component, they increment that outside variable during render:

Impure Counter Mutation
1let count = 0;
Module-level variable
2
3export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
4 count = count + 1;
Mutates outside variable
5 return <li>#{count}: {title}</li>;
6}

When the page loads, the developer expects to see three cards numbered #1, #2, and #3. Instead, the screen displays #2, #4, and #6. When the root renders again, the numbers jump to #8, #10, and #12.

Why does the counter display doubled numbers on initial page load?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The component mutates an external variable during development double-rendering.

In development mode, React wraps components in <StrictMode>. StrictMode deliberately runs every component function twice during each render pass to detect accidental side effects. Because count is a module-level variable that lives outside the function, the first card increments count to 1 on its first call and to 2 on its second call. The browser displays #2 for the first item on screen.

When the second card renders, it starts from 2. The first call increments count to 3, and the second call increments it to 4. The third card increments count to 5 and 6. If another component reads count, its output depends entirely on which component React decided to call first. On any later render, count never resets; it keeps climbing without bound.

To fix this defect, remove the outside variable completely and pass the item position downward as an explicit prop. Because the card calculates its markup strictly from its props, React can call it once, twice, or ten times, and the output is always #1, #2, and #3.

StrictMode double-invoking an impure counter versus pure props
Impure: let count = 0                Pure: position={index + 1}
Call 1: count = 0 + 1 -> 1           Call 1: reads prop position (1) -> #1
Call 2: count = 1 + 1 -> 2 (shows)   Call 2: position (1) -> #1 (shows)
Next render: count climbs to 8...    Next render: reads prop position (1) -> #1
PRINCIPLE 1

A component must return the same JSX for the same props

pure function a function that produces identical output for identical inputs and causes zero outside side effects
StrictMode double-rendering a development check where React calls component functions twice to catch side effects

React calls a component function to calculate what to show on screen. In development, StrictMode double-rendering calls every component twice to detect unexpected side effects. When a component reads or writes a variable outside itself, each run sees a different value and numbers drift. Treat every component as a pure function: compute output strictly from props and local variables so every run returns identical markup.

We should do this:
function Card({ title, position }) {
return <li>#{position}: {title}</li>;
pure prop calculation
}
We should not do this:
let count = 0;
outside module variable
function Card({ title }) {
count = count + 1;
mutates outside variable
return <li>#{count}: {title}</li>;
}
QUESTION 2

Pushing into an outside array duplicates items across renders

A developer wants to append a promotional banner or featured story to a list before rendering. They call the standard JavaScript push() method directly on an array received as a prop:

External Array Mutation
1export default function StoryTray({ stories, bonusStory }) {
2 stories.push(bonusStory);
Mutates incoming props array
3 return (
4 <ul>
5 {stories.map(story => (
6 <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>
7 ))}
8 </ul>
9 );
10}

When the page loads under <StrictMode>, the list displays two identical copies of the bonus story on the very first render. The browser console prints a warning: Encountered two children with the same key

Can I push an item into an array, or change an object, during render?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Calling push mutates data that existed before the render started.

Data that existed before the component was called (such as an array received as a prop or declared at module level) survives across render passes. Calling stories.push() mutates that preexisting array in place in the caller's memory. Because <StrictMode> calls the component twice during development, stories.push() runs twice on initial load, appending two duplicate items into the array.

Similarly, if you mutate a local object after passing it into a JSX element (such as writing styles.color = 'red' after <Header styles={styles} />), the element displays the modified color because both share the exact same object reference in memory. Once an object is handed to JSX, it must be treated as immutable.

To modify collections safely during render, use local mutation. Create a fresh array inside the component function using array spread syntax ([...stories, bonusStory]) or push into an array created inside that specific render call. Because the new array was born inside that function call, no outside component can see it, and each render pass starts with a clean copy.

External array mutation versus fresh local array creation
External: items.push(bonus)          Local: const list = [...items, bonus]
Call 1: array holds [A, bonus]       Call 1: fresh list holds [A, bonus]
Call 2: array holds [A, bonus, bonus]Call 2: fresh list holds [A, bonus]
Result: duplicated item in memory    Result: identical array on every call
PRINCIPLE 2

Change only what this render created

external mutation changing a variable, array, or object that existed before the current render call
local mutation modifying a fresh variable or array created inside the current render call before passing it to JSX

Never mutate variables, objects, or arrays that existed before the component was called. Calling push() or reassigning properties on shared data changes memory that other components and later renders rely on. To modify data during render, use local mutation: create a brand-new array or object inside the function body and fill it before passing it to JSX.

We should do this:
function Feed({ items, bonus }) {
const list = [...items, bonus];
fresh local array
return <List items={list} />;
}
We should not do this:
function Feed({ items, bonus }) {
items.push(bonus);
mutates incoming props array
return <List items={items} />;
}
QUESTION 3

Modifying the document during render throws an error on initial load

A developer wants to set a dark mode class on a clock widget when it renders at night. Remembering traditional JavaScript DOM manipulation, they query the element directly inside the component body:

Imperative DOM Query
1export default function ClockWidget({ isNight }) {
2 if (isNight) {
3 document.getElementById('clock').className = 'night';
DOM write
4 }
5 return <div id="clock">Current Time</div>;
6}

When the page loads, the screen goes completely white. Opening the browser developer console reveals an unhandled runtime exception: TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'className')

Where do I set document properties, or add a CSS class to an element?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The component queries the browser document before DOM nodes are mounted.

Component functions execute during the render phase, strictly to calculate what the next user interface should look like. During this calculation, React has not yet created or mounted the corresponding browser DOM nodes. When document.getElementById('clock') executes on the initial render, the DOM element does not exist in the document, returning null. Attempting to assign className on null throws an immediate TypeError that halts execution.

Even if the DOM node existed from an earlier render pass, directly modifying DOM nodes by hand bypasses React's declarative reconciliation engine and desynchronizes the user interface. Similarly, writing document.title = title inside the component body alters the browser tab during render, which is a side effect.

The solution is to express visual attributes declaratively directly in the returned JSX. Use a JavaScript ternary conditional operator to calculate the desired class name during render: <div id="clock" className={isNight ? 'night' : 'day'}> React evaluates this expression cleanly and updates the browser DOM node during the commit phase. Side effects that interact with outside systems belong in event handlers, which run in response to user actions outside the render path.

The render phase executes before browser DOM nodes exist
1. Render Phase (Component Body)    2. Commit Phase (DOM Update)
   React calls component function ->   React creates & updates DOM nodes
   document.getElementById returns null -> DOM nodes now exist in page
   TypeError: Cannot set className ->  Event handlers can safely run
PRINCIPLE 3

Keep changes to the outside world out of the render

side effect an operation that changes an outside system or modifies data beyond returning JSX
render phase the synchronous execution where React calls a component function to calculate markup

The component function body runs during the render phase strictly to calculate markup. Never modify DOM nodes, start timers, or trigger network requests directly in the component body. Modifying the DOM during render throws errors because elements do not exist yet. Express visual changes declaratively in JSX, and place outside changes into event handlers.

We should do this:
function Badge({ isUrgent }) {
const cls = isUrgent ? 'urgent' : 'normal';
declarative JSX class
return <span className={cls}>Alert</span>;
}
We should not do this:
function Badge({ isUrgent }) {
const el = document.getElementById('badge');
el.className = 'urgent';
direct DOM mutation crashes
return <span id="badge">Alert</span>;
}
QUESTION 4

Calling Math.random or new Date during render produces disagreeing values

A developer wants each article card in a news feed to pick a random visual badge or display the time it was viewed. They call Math.random() directly inside the component body:

Non-Idempotent Random Pick
1export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
2 const pick = Math.random();
Non-idempotent calculation
3 console.log('Generated pick:', pick);
4 return <h3>Pick {pick}: {title}</h3>;
5}

When the page loads under <StrictMode>, the browser console displays two different numbers for the same card: Generated pick: 0.133 followed by Generated pick: 0.123. The screen displays Pick 0.123.

Can I pick a random highlight, or show the current time, by calling Math.random or new Date inside the component?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Non-idempotent calls produce different results on every invocation.

A pure component must produce idempotent rendering: executing it multiple times with identical inputs must always return the exact same JSX output. Functions like Math.random() and new Date() are non-idempotent because each invocation produces a different number or timestamp. Under <StrictMode>, React deliberately renders the component twice during development. Because Math.random() runs on both passes, the two calls calculate disagreeing values. The browser console displays two different numbers, and the screen shows the result of the second call.

Similarly, calling new Date() in the render body freezes the timestamp at the exact millisecond the component happened to render. The displayed time remains frozen and never advances unless a re-render is triggered.

To preserve component purity, avoid calling non-idempotent functions in the component body. Pass random values or timestamps downward as explicit props from data that already holds them. If a new random value or timestamp must be generated when a user interacts with the page, perform that calculation inside an event handler before passing the result to state.

Non-idempotent call drift under development double-rendering
Call 1 (StrictMode): Math.random() produces 0.133
Call 2 (StrictMode): Math.random() produces 0.123
Screen displays: 0.123 (earlier logs or calculations disagree)
Pure alternative: <Card pick={pick} /> ensures identical values on every run
PRINCIPLE 4

Do not compute what you show from Math.random or new Date during render

non-idempotent call a function call that returns a different value each time it runs with the same arguments
idempotent rendering running a component with identical inputs produces identical output every time

A component must produce idempotent rendering: calling it with the same inputs must always return the exact same JSX. Calling a non-idempotent call like Math.random() or new Date() in the component body produces different values on every call, breaking predictability under StrictMode double-rendering. Pass random values and timestamps downward as props from outside the render.

We should do this:
function Card({ title, pick }) {
return <h3>Pick {pick}: {title}</h3>;
deterministic prop
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ title }) {
const pick = Math.random();
different value on every call
return <h3>Pick {pick}: {title}</h3>;
}

Notice how the CSS class and label text are determined: we use JavaScript ternary conditional operators directly inside the function. We never query the browser DOM or alter class lists imperatively. 1export default function ReadingStatus({ minutes }) {

Component Summary

App

The reading desk shell defines the article collection and calculates item position purely from the array mapping index without outside mutable variables.

ArticleCardposition={1} title="..." minutes={4}

The pure article card receives data through props and renders structured markup with zero DOM queries or external mutations.

ReadingStatusminutes={4}

The pure status badge evaluates ternary operators directly in the JSX return to compute dynamic class names atomically.

Look at how this three-file architecture fulfills the pure rendering contract. In a naive implementation, an engineer might have created a mutable counter in App.jsx, pushed badges into an outside array in ArticleCard.jsx, and queried document.getElementById() in ReadingStatus.jsx. Under StrictMode, that naive setup would display doubled counts (#2, #4), crash with null selector exceptions on initial load, and leak state across renders.

By treating every component as a pure mathematical formula, data flows downward cleanly through props. React can invoke any component in this tree any number of times, and the browser will always render the exact same user interface.

Where you will meet this

  1. Server-Side Rendering and Static Generation: Server frameworks render components on a web server to generate HTML for thousands of concurrent requests; because pure components never touch global variables or shared memory, concurrent visitor requests never contaminate each other's data.
  2. Performance Optimization with Memoization: When a component is pure, React can safely skip re-rendering it if its props have not changed, reusing the previous JSX calculation because a pure formula is guaranteed to return the exact same markup.
  3. Concurrent and Interrupted Rendering: When React prioritizes urgent user inputs over background updates, it can pause or discard a component render in memory and restart it later; pure components guarantee that discarded renders leave zero corrupted traces behind.
  4. Automated Unit Testing: Testing pure components is simple and reliable because you do not need to mock browser DOM globals, reset external counter variables, or clean up leaked side effects between test runs.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What does it mean for a component to be pure, and what breaks when it is not?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is probing whether you understand React's declarative execution loop and the contract of pure rendering, or whether you still write React like traditional imperative jQuery scripts. A junior developer mentions that functions should not change variables. A senior engineer explains that pure components act as mathematical formulas where UI = f(props). They explain that React reserves the right to call components multiple times, in any order, and twice in development under StrictMode. They explain how external mutation causes state drift across renders and how imperative DOM queries during render crash because nodes do not exist yet.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap appears when an interviewer asks why a console.log() inside a component prints twice on page load. Candidates often assume React has an infinite render bug or a double-mount defect, and some admit to deleting <StrictMode> from their root file to silence the logs. In reality, StrictMode deliberately double-invokes components in development as an intentional stress test to expose hidden mutations. Another trap is assuming purity means you cannot use JavaScript arrays or objects; local mutation on fresh data created inside the current render call is 100% pure.

3. What is Actually Going On

In React, component execution is an on-demand calculation. React takes your props and calls your component function to obtain a tree of element descriptors. If your component is pure, calling it once, twice, or ten times produces identical JSX. If your component modifies a module-level variable during render, StrictMode double-rendering executes that mutation twice on the initial page load, causing numbers to double immediately. If a component writes to the DOM during render, the operation fails with a TypeError because React has not created the DOM nodes yet.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if you mutate a local object after passing it into a JSX element, such as styles.color = 'red' after writing <Header styles={styles} />? The element receives the modified value because both share the same reference in memory; values must be treated as immutable once passed to JSX. Why are Math.random() and new Date() forbidden in render output? Both are non-idempotent: they return different values on every call, causing the two StrictMode calls to disagree and freezing timestamps at render time. How do you handle real side effects like network requests or timers? Place them inside event handlers, which execute in response to user actions outside the render path.

Glossary

  • Pure Function: A function that always returns the exact same result given the same inputs and produces zero side effects on outside systems.
  • Side Effect: Any operation that modifies state outside the current function or interacts with outside systems during execution.
  • StrictMode: A React development-only wrapper component that deliberately calls component functions twice to expose unintended side effects.
  • Local Mutation: Modifying variables, arrays, or objects created within the current render execution before they are passed into JSX.
  • Idempotence: The property of a function where running it multiple times with identical inputs produces the exact same outcome without state drift.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide on keeping components pure: explains why React treats components as formulas and how to keep render side-effect free (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Official reference rules on component and hook purity: comprehensive rules on idempotence, local mutation, and render phases (see react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure).
  • Official documentation on StrictMode development checks: covers double-rendering mechanics, log dimming, and side-effect detection (see react.dev/reference/react/StrictMode).
  • Official deep dive on responding to events: explains how event handlers provide a safe home for user interactions and side effects (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events).
  • Official guide on render and commit phases: details the two-step cycle of calculating JSX and applying DOM updates (see react.dev/learn/render-and-commit).

Lecture
13

Responding to Events &
Callback Props

Interview Question   CORE

How do you respond to user events like clicks and typing, and how do callback props communicate back to parents?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build an article feed where each card provides Read and Bookmark buttons.
  • 2 You write onClick={handleSelect()} on a button, but the function executes during page load and does nothing when clicked.
  • 3 How do you respond to user events like clicks and typing, and how do callback props communicate back to parents?

Interactive interfaces respond to user actions through event listeners

Every dynamic web application must respond when users interact with the screen. Readers click buttons to open stories, type search queries into input fields, select items from lists, and save articles for later reading. In traditional scripting and legacy HTML, developers wrote inline string handlers like onclick="handleClick()". In React, components are pure functions, and user interactions are handled declaratively by passing JavaScript function references to event props like onClick and onChange. React listens for browser events, wraps them in synthetic event objects, and executes the designated handler outside of the render cycle.

When developers begin adding interactivity to React components, they often bring imperative habits from classic JavaScript. In JSX, anything placed inside curly braces evaluates immediately while React calculates the component's output. Writing onClick={handleSelect()} with parentheses causes JavaScript to invoke handleSelect() right away during render. The function fires on initial page load before the user ever touches the mouse, and its return value (undefined) is passed to onClick, leaving the button unresponsive when clicked later. Furthermore, when nested components need to update application state, children cannot reassign parent variables directly; they must communicate upward through callback props.

This chapter answers five core questions. Why does calling a function inside JSX braces execute on page load instead of waiting for a click? How do we pass arguments to an event handler without invoking it during render? How does a child component notify its parent about an action without mutating props? Why does clicking a nested button also trigger parent click handlers, and how do stopPropagation and preventDefault differ? Why must interactive controls use native button tags instead of clickable divs?

Later in this track, Lecture 14 introduces state hooks, allowing event handlers to update component memory and trigger interface updates. Lecture 18 explores reading user input via e.target.value inside onChange handlers for complex objects. Lecture 40 explores React 19 <form action={...}>, which handles form submissions automatically without manual calls to e.preventDefault().

  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): A function reference differs from a function call, and React runs component functions to build element trees.
  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): Curly braces evaluate JavaScript expressions immediately during render.
  • Lecture 5 (The UI tree): Data flows downward from parent to child, and siblings communicate through their common parent.
  • Lecture 6 (Passing props): Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child that must never be mutated.
  • Lecture 11 (Rendering lists): Arrow functions and array map() transform collections into lists of element descriptions.
  • Lecture 12 (Keeping components pure): Render functions must remain pure calculations, while user-triggered side effects belong safely in event handlers.

How React connects event props to handler functions

In Lecture 2 and Lecture 4, we saw that JSX curly braces evaluate JavaScript expressions immediately during the render phase. In standard HTML, event attributes like onclick expect a string of code to execute. In React, event listener props are written in camelCase, such as onClick, onChange, onKeyDown, and onSubmit. Instead of a string, React expects an actual JavaScript function value. When the user interacts with the rendered element, React receives the browser event and executes that function.

Function Reference Pattern
1function ActionButton() {
2 function handleClick() {
3 console.log('Button clicked');
Executes on user click
4 }
5 return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click</button>;
6}

The most critical distinction in React event wiring is passing a function reference versus calling a function. When you write onClick={handleClick}, you pass the function itself as an uncalled value; you tell React, "Hold this function reference and call it when the user clicks." If you add parentheses, onClick={handleClick()}, JavaScript executes handleClick right away while constructing the element tree.

Immediate Invocation Mistake
1function BrokenButton() {
2 return <button onClick={handleClick()}>Click</button>;
Fires during render
3}

The return value (typically undefined) is assigned to onClick, leaving the element with no click handler. Event handlers run outside of render, making them the safe and idiomatic home for side effects like logging, network requests, and future state updates.

How callback props pass actions upward without breaking unidirectional data flow

In Lecture 5 and Lecture 6, we established that React strictly enforces unidirectional data flow: data flows downward from parent to child through props, and props are strictly read-only. A child component cannot modify the parent's data or reassign variables in the parent's scope. If a child needs to report a user event to its parent, it cannot reach upward directly.

Callback Prop in Parent
1function Feed() {
2 function handleSelect(id) {
3 console.log('Selected article:', id);
Business logic in parent
4 }
5 return <ArticleCard id="art-1" onSelect={handleSelect} />;
6}

To allow children to communicate upward, React uses callback props. The parent component declares a handler function that knows what action to take (such as selecting a story). The parent passes that function downward to the child as a prop, conventionally prefixed with on (such as onSelect={handleSelect}).

Callback Wiring in Child
1function ArticleCard({ id, onSelect }) {
2 return <button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>Read</button>;
Forwards id
3}

The child component receives the callback prop and attaches it to a native element's event prop, such as a <button onClick={...}>. When the user clicks the button, the child executes the callback, passing relevant data (like the story identifier) upward to the parent. In this way, data still flows down as props, but actions flow upward through function calls. Custom components (like <ArticleCard />) do not possess built-in DOM event listeners; placing onClick on a custom component merely passes a prop named onClick and does nothing unless the child explicitly attaches it to a native HTML element.

How browser events bubble and why stopPropagation differs from preventDefault

When a user interacts with a web page, the browser creates a native event object. React intercepts these native events at the root container and wraps them in a cross-browser SyntheticEvent object, conventionally passed to your handler as e. This event object provides standard properties such as e.target (the specific element that was clicked) and e.currentTarget (the element whose event handler is currently executing).

Event Propagation Control
1function CardActions({ onSave }) {
2 function handleSave(e) {
3 e.stopPropagation();
Stops click from bubbling to parent card
4 onSave();
5 }
6 function handleSubmit(e) {
7 e.preventDefault();
Prevents browser from reloading page
8 }
9 return <button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>;
10}

In the browser DOM, events follow the bubbling mechanism: after an event fires on the innermost clicked element, it propagates upward through all parent elements in the document tree, triggering their event handlers in sequence. If a card contains a bookmark button, clicking the bookmark button fires the button's onClick, bubbles up to the card's onClick, and continues up to the container. To halt this cascade, call e.stopPropagation(). This tells the browser and React not to run event handlers on ancestor elements. In contrast, e.preventDefault() addresses browser default behaviors, such as preventing a <form> submission from reloading the page or preventing an <a> link from navigating. Calling e.stopPropagation() does not cancel default browser actions, and calling e.preventDefault() does not stop event bubbling; each call has a distinct, unrelated responsibility.

Why accessible interaction requires native button controls instead of generic tags

In the browser, interactive elements participate in keyboard navigation. Users navigating with a keyboard or assistive technology press the Tab key to cycle through interactive controls on the page. When an element receives keyboard focus, pressing Enter or Space activates it.

Semantic vs Generic Click Target
1function SafeAction({ onSelect }) {
Accessible: receives Tab focus and responds to Enter/Space
2 return <button type="button" onClick={onSelect}>Select</button>;
3}
4
5function UnsafeAction({ onSelect }) {
Inaccessible: skipped by Tab and ignores Enter/Space
6 return <div className="btn" onClick={onSelect}>Select</div>;
Skips keyboard
7}

React allows you to attach an onClick prop to any JSX tag, including generic tags like <div> or <span>. However, the browser does not treat generic tags as interactive. A <div> with onClick cannot receive keyboard focus via the Tab key, does not respond to Enter or Space key presses, and fails to announce an interactive role to screen readers. In contrast, a native <button> element is built into the browser with full keyboard focus support, standard key activation, and built-in accessibility roles. Developers should always use native <button> elements for clickable actions, using CSS to achieve any desired visual style.

Principles of React: Responding to Events and Callback Props

QUESTION 1

Calling a handler in JSX braces executes on page load

A developer creates a publish button for an editorial workflow. They declare an event handler function inside the component and connect it to a native button element in the returned JSX:

Immediate Invocation Antipattern
1export default function PublishButton() {
2 function handlePublish() {
3 console.log('PUBLISH ran');
Runs during render
4 }
5 return (
6 <button onClick={handlePublish()}>
7 Publish Story
Parentheses invoke immediately
8 </button>
9 );
10}

When the page loads in the browser, the console immediately prints "PUBLISH ran" before the developer ever touches the mouse. When the developer clicks the button afterward, the console remains completely silent, and nothing happens.

Why did adding parentheses after handlePublish cause it to run during render instead of waiting for a user click?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Adding parentheses invokes the function immediately while React calculates the component's output.

In React, JSX curly braces are an evaluation window into JavaScript. Any expression placed inside { ... } runs synchronously during the render phase. When JavaScript encounters handlePublish(), it executes the function right away while constructing the element tree. The function runs on page load, and its return value (undefined) is assigned to the onClick prop. When the user later clicks the button, React finds undefined and takes no action.

To fix this defect, remove the parentheses and pass the bare function name: <button onClick={handlePublish}> By passing the function reference without parentheses, React stores the function in memory and attaches it to the browser button element. The handler executes strictly when the user clicks the button.

Executing during render versus passing an uncalled function reference
Immediate invocation: onClick={handleClick()}
Render: handleClick() executes immediately -> logs "PUBLISH ran"
onClick receives: undefined
User clicks button: nothing happens (handler is undefined)

Function reference: onClick={handleClick}
Render: stores function reference without calling
onClick receives: function handleClick
User clicks button: React invokes handleClick() -> logs "PUBLISH ran"
PRINCIPLE 1

Pass the handler function to an event prop, not its result

function reference passing an uncalled function by name so React can run it later
immediate invocation calling a function during render by adding parentheses in JSX braces

An event prop like onClick takes a function to run later when the user acts. Curly braces evaluate their expression immediately during render. Writing parentheses like onClick={handleClick()} calls the function right away, and onClick receives what it returns, usually undefined. To run code on click, pass the function itself without parentheses: onClick={handleClick}.

We should do this:
<button onClick={handleClick}>
Save
runs on click
</button>
We should not do this:
<button onClick={handleClick()}>
Save
runs in render
</button>
QUESTION 2

Passing an argument directly calls the handler during render

A developer maps over an array of news stories to render a list of cards. Each card needs a Read button that tells the application which specific story was selected:

Argument Invocation in List
1export default function StoryList({ stories, openArticle }) {
2 const items = stories.map(s => (
3 <li key={s.id}>
4 <button onClick={openArticle(s.id)}>Read</button>
In render
5 </li>
6 ));
7 return <ul>{items}</ul>;
8}

When the page loads, the console prints "open a1" and "open a2" immediately during the render pass, without any user interaction. When the developer clicks either button, the console logs nothing.

How do I pass an item identifier to a handler without calling it during render?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Writing openArticle(story.id) invokes the function during render for every item in the list.

Just as with handleClick(), writing openArticle(story.id) inside JSX braces causes JavaScript to execute the call immediately during the mapping loop. Each button's onClick prop receives undefined. When the user clicks the button, the handler is gone.

To pass custom arguments without executing the handler during render, wrap the call inside an inline arrow function: onClick={() => openArticle(story.id)} The arrow function is an anonymous function created during render, but its inner code does not execute until the arrow function itself is called. React stores the arrow function and invokes it when the user clicks the button, which in turn calls openArticle with that card's unique identifier.

Direct invocation in list mapping versus deferred arrow function
Direct call: onClick={openArticle(story.id)}
Mapping item 1: calls openArticle('a1') during render -> returns undefined
Mapping item 2: calls openArticle('a2') during render -> returns undefined
User clicks button 2: button has undefined -> nothing happens

Arrow function: onClick={() => openArticle(story.id)}
Mapping item 1: creates anonymous function () => openArticle('a1')
Mapping item 2: creates anonymous function () => openArticle('a2')
User clicks button 2: React executes arrow function -> calls openArticle('a2')
PRINCIPLE 2

Wrap a handler call that needs arguments in an arrow function

arrow function wrapper an inline function that defers execution until user interaction

When a handler needs arguments from the current item, writing onClick={handleClick(id)} calls the function during render for every item in the list. Wrapping the call in an arrow function creates a function that waits. React stores that function and calls it only when the user clicks, passing the arguments to your handler.

We should do this:
<button onClick={() => select(item.id)}>
Select
runs on click
</button>
We should not do this:
<button onClick={select(item.id)}>
Select
runs in render
</button>
QUESTION 3

Custom components ignore unwired event props

A developer splits their interface into modular components. The parent feed component NewsFeed tracks which story is selected, while an ArticleCard component renders each story's layout. The developer attaches an onClick prop directly to the custom component tag:

Unwired Custom Prop
1function ArticleCard({ title, onClick }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card">
4 <h3>{title}</h3>
5 <button>Read Story</button>
OnClick prop is never attached
6 </article>
7 );
8}

When the user clicks the card or the button, the browser logs nothing. If a junior developer attempts to solve this by having ArticleCard reassign a parent variable directly (selectedId = 'a2'), it changes only a local variable, and the parent still shows "Selected: none".

The Read button is in ArticleCard, but NewsFeed decides what opens. How does the card tell it?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Custom components are JavaScript functions that do not attach DOM event listeners automatically.

Built-in HTML elements (like <button> or <input>) represent real browser DOM elements; React attaches native event listeners to them. In contrast, custom components (like <ArticleCard />) are JavaScript functions. Placing onClick on <ArticleCard /> does not attach an event listener to any DOM node. It merely passes a prop named onClick to ArticleCard. If ArticleCard never forwards that prop to a native element's event prop, the callback is completely ignored.

To communicate user actions from child to parent, use callback props. The parent defines the action logic in a handler function and passes it downward as a prop named after the application action, such as onSelect={handleSelect}. Inside ArticleCard, accept onSelect in props and wire it to a native element's event prop: <button onClick={() => onSelect(article.id)}>Read Story</button> When the user clicks the button, the child executes the callback, passing the article identifier upward to the parent.

Props flowing downward and callback actions firing upward
[NewsFeed] owns handleSelect(id) -> passes onSelect={handleSelect}
      |
      v (Props flow DOWN)
[ArticleCard] receives onSelect -> <button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>
      |
      * (User clicks native button in browser)
      |
      ^ (Callback executes UPWARD)
Calls handleSelect('a2') in NewsFeed
PRINCIPLE 3

Pass a callback prop to let a child report actions to its parent

callback prop a function prop passed from parent to child to report events upward
custom component prop an unhandled prop on a component that does not bind to the DOM

Data in React flows downward through props, so a child cannot change parent variables directly. Putting onClick on a custom component does nothing unless the component attaches it to a real HTML element. To let a child report an action, the parent passes a callback prop such as onSelect. The child calls that function from its button, passing whatever data the parent needs.

We should do this:
function Card({ onSelect, id }) {
return (
<button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>
Open
wires callback prop
</button>
);
}
We should not do this:
function Card({ onClick, id }) {
return (
<div>
<h3>Card {id}</h3>
onClick prop is ignored
</div>
);
}
QUESTION 4

Clicking a nested button triggers parent click handlers

An article card is designed so that clicking anywhere on the card opens the article view. Inside the card, the developer adds a secondary Bookmark button to save the story for later reading:

Nested Event Handlers
1export default function ArticleCard({ story, onOpen, onBookmark }) {
2 return (
3 <article className="card" onClick={() => onOpen(story.id)}>
4 <h3>{story.title}</h3>
5 <button onClick={() => onBookmark(story.id)}>
6 Bookmark
Bubbles to article click
7 </button>
8 </article>
9 );
10}

When the user clicks the Bookmark button, they expect the article to be saved. Instead, the console prints "button: bookmark" and immediately prints "card: open article". The article opens unexpectedly alongside the save action.

Why does clicking Save also open the article, and how do stopPropagation and preventDefault differ?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Browser events bubble upward through the DOM hierarchy, triggering parent click listeners.

In the browser DOM, when an event occurs on a nested element, it executes that element's handler and then bubbles upward through each ancestor element in the tree. Clicking the Bookmark button runs its onClick, bubbles up to the <article> tag, and runs the card's onClick.

To prevent an event from triggering handlers on parent containers, call e.stopPropagation() on the event object inside the child's handler. This tells React and the browser to stop bubbling immediately. In contrast, e.preventDefault() stops default browser behaviors, such as preventing a link navigation or preventing a form submit from reloading the page. Calling e.stopPropagation() does not stop default actions, and calling e.preventDefault() does not stop event bubbling.

Event bubbling upward through ancestors versus stopping propagation
Default bubbling:
[Button] click -> fires button handler -> bubbles UP to [<article>]
Result: both button handler and card handler execute

Propagation stopped:
[Button] click -> calls e.stopPropagation() -> halts event
Result: button handler executes; ancestor card handler is silenced
PRINCIPLE 4

Use stopPropagation for parent handlers and preventDefault for browser actions

event bubbling the browser process where an event travels upward through ancestor elements
stopPropagation prevents an event from triggering handlers on ancestor elements
preventDefault cancels the browser default action without stopping event bubbling

When an element is clicked, the click bubbles upward through every parent element in the tree, running their onClick handlers too. Calling e.stopPropagation() stops the event from reaching parent elements. Browser default actions, like following a link or reloading on form submit, are separate: only e.preventDefault() stops them. Neither call does the other's job.

We should do this:
<button onClick={e => { e.stopPropagation(); onSave(id); }}>
Save
stops parent bubbling
</button>
We should not do this:
<button onClick={() => onSave(id)}>
Save
bubbles up to parent
</button>
QUESTION 5

Using a div for click handling blocks keyboard users

A developer wants a custom visual design for an article selection control. To avoid browser default button styling, they attach an onClick handler to a generic <div> tag:

Clickable Div Antipattern
1export default function SelectControl({ onSelect }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="custom-btn" onClick={onSelect}>
4 Select Story
Inaccessible to keyboard
5 </div>
6 );
7}

The control works when clicked with a mouse. However, when an accessibility auditor navigates the page using the Tab key, the control is skipped completely. When the auditor places focus on an adjacent control and presses Enter or Space, the <div> does nothing.

Can I put onClick on a div and style it as I like?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A div cannot receive keyboard focus or Enter and Space key activation.

React permits attaching an onClick listener to any HTML element, but the browser enforces interactive standards. A generic <div> has no semantic role: the browser does not include it in the Tab focus ring, and pressing Enter or Space while adjacent to it does not fire a click event. Screen readers do not announce it as a button, making it completely invisible to users relying on assistive technology.

To build accessible interfaces, always use a native <button> element for interactive click actions: <button type="button" onClick={handleSelect}>Select Story</button> Native buttons possess built-in keyboard focus support, automatically respond to Enter and Space keystrokes, and communicate an interactive role to screen readers. Developers can easily remove browser default styles using CSS resets while retaining complete accessibility.

Keyboard focus and activation on native button versus generic div
Generic Div: <div onClick={...}>
Tab key navigation: SKIPS element (no focus ring)
Enter / Space key: IGNORED (zero events dispatched)
Screen reader: announces plain static text

Native Button: <button type="button" onClick={...}>
Tab key navigation: RECEIVES focus ring automatically
Enter / Space key: DISPATCHES click event automatically
Screen reader: announces "Select Story, button"
PRINCIPLE 5

Handle user clicks on a button element, not on a div

keyboard focus the browser state indicating which element receives keyboard keystrokes
semantic interactive element a native HTML tag with built-in accessibility and keyboard support

React allows onClick on any element, but the browser gives keyboard focus only to interactive elements. A native <button> receives keyboard focus when pressing the Tab key, and pressing Enter or Space triggers its click handler. A <div> gets neither, so keyboard and screen reader users cannot use it. Always use a <button> for actions and style it with CSS.

We should do this:
<button type="button" onClick={handleSelect}>
Select
accessible via Tab and Enter
</button>
We should not do this:
<div className="btn" onClick={handleSelect}>
Select
inaccessible to keyboard
</div>

Component Summary

App

The application shell owns the article data collection and defines the primary business action handlers (handleSelect, handleSave) passed down as callback props.

ArticleCardstory={story} onSelect={handleSelect} onSave={handleSave}

The interactive card boundary receives article data and callback props, wrapping selection in an arrow function to pass identifiers upward.

ActionButtononAction={() => onSave(story.id)} label="Bookmark"

The accessible action button intercepts clicks, calls e.stopPropagation() to isolate nested actions, and triggers the callback safely.

Look at how this three-file architecture fulfills idiomatic React event design. In a naive implementation, an engineer might have written onClick={handleSelect(story.id)} inside App.jsx, triggering immediate execution on page load. Or they might have placed onClick directly on <ArticleCard />, expecting React to automatically listen for DOM clicks on a custom component tag. Or they might have used a clickable <div> inside ActionButton.jsx, excluding keyboard users and allowing clicks to bubble up and trigger article selection unexpectedly.

By declaring handlers at the owner level, passing uncalled function references through callback props, wrapping argument calls in arrow functions, stopping propagation at the button boundary, and using native <button> elements, our application remains robust, accessible, and completely predictable.

Where you will meet this

  1. Design System Component Libraries: Component libraries build buttons, dialogs, and toggles that accept custom callback props (onPress, onToggle, onDismiss) and wire them internally to native elements while managing propagation.
  2. Data Tables and List Feeds: Rendering collections of items where row selection, deletion, or expansion requires passing row identifiers upward via inline arrow functions without running during render.
  3. Modal Dialogs and Dropdown Menus: Nested popup menus and overlay backdrops require e.stopPropagation() so clicking inside the modal content does not trigger the backdrop's dismissal click handler.
  4. Form Handling and Custom Inputs: Intercepting form submissions with e.preventDefault() to stop full-page browser reloads and handling onChange events across input fields.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you respond to user events like clicks and typing, and how do callback props communicate back to parents?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand React's declarative execution model and unidirectional data flow, or whether you still write React with imperative DOM habits. A junior developer states that you put onClick on elements. A senior engineer explains that event handlers are passed as function references, not invoked in JSX braces. They explain that children cannot mutate parent state, so parent components pass callback props downward, allowing children to invoke those functions with arguments. They clearly separate event bubbling (e.stopPropagation()) from browser default behavior (e.preventDefault()), and they emphasize that interactive controls must use native <button> tags for accessibility.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is writing onClick={handleClick()} instead of onClick={handleClick}. Candidates frequently wonder why a function runs on page load and fails to respond to clicks. Another trap is passing an argument directly: onClick={openItem(id)}, which causes immediate invocation for every item in a list during render. A third trap is putting onClick directly on a custom component tag (like <UserCard onClick={...} />) and expecting React to attach a browser listener, unaware that custom components ignore unhandled props unless explicitly wired to native HTML tags.

3. What is Actually Going On

In React, JSX curly braces evaluate JavaScript synchronously during the render phase. Calling handleClick() inside braces runs the function right away, and its return value (undefined) is passed to onClick. When the user clicks, React finds no function to call. To defer execution, you must pass an uncalled function reference, or wrap calls that require arguments in an arrow function () => handleClick(id) Because props are strictly read-only, child-to-parent communication is achieved through callback props: the parent passes a function down, and the child calls it with arguments. Events bubble up the DOM tree unless stopped by e.stopPropagation(), while e.preventDefault() cancels browser actions like link navigation and form reloads.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if an onClickCapture handler is attached to a parent element? Capture handlers run during the downward capture phase before child handlers execute, so calling e.stopPropagation() inside a child button cannot prevent parent capture handlers from running. Do all React events bubble? No: all events bubble in React except onScroll. What happens if you attach onClick to a <div>? The click works for mouse users, but the <div> cannot receive keyboard focus via the Tab key and ignores Enter and Space key activation, creating an accessibility defect. Always use native <button> elements for actions.

Glossary

  • Event Handler: A JavaScript function passed to a React element's event prop that executes in response to user interaction outside of the render cycle.
  • Callback Prop: A function prop passed from a parent component to a child component allowing the child to report user actions upward.
  • Event Bubbling: The browser process where an event dispatches on an innermost target element and propagates upward through ancestor elements in the DOM tree.
  • stopPropagation: A method on the event object that halts event propagation, preventing ancestor element handlers from executing.
  • preventDefault: A method on the event object that cancels default browser behaviors (such as form submission reloads or link navigation) without affecting event bubbling.
  • Keyboard Focus: The browser state indicating which element currently receives keyboard input and keypress events.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide on responding to events: comprehensive tutorial on event handler props, passing functions, and event propagation (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events).
  • Official reference on common components: reference documentation on supported HTML elements and event handler props in React (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • MDN documentation on event propagation: detailed explanation of the DOM event bubbling and capture lifecycle (see developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/JavaScript/Building_blocks/Events#event_bubbling).
  • MDN guide on button accessibility: best practices for keyboard focus and semantic button controls (see developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/button#accessibility_concerns).
