Component Memory with useState

Interview Question   CORE

Why do ordinary variables forget their values between renders, and how does useState remember?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build a story card with a like counter button, a bookmark save toggle, and a saved preference loader.
  • 2 You add one to a plain local variable on every click and the console counts up, but the screen stays stuck on zero.
  • 3 Why do ordinary variables forget their values between renders, and how does useState remember?

How a component remembers data across renders

In modern web applications, user interfaces respond to reader interactions by remembering choices and displaying updated data. Readers click buttons to like articles, toggle bookmarks, or submit comments. In standard JavaScript programming, developers store changing values in local variables using let. In React, components are pure JavaScript functions that execute to return JSX descriptions of the interface. When an interaction occurs, React calls the component function again from the top. A plain local variable declared inside the function body is re-created on every render, discarding any previous value. To remember data across renders and request screen updates, React components use state declared with the useState Hook.

Beginners often assume that changing a local variable will automatically update the screen, because the variable appears inside the returned JSX. In plain JavaScript, assigning a new value to a variable mutates memory, but it does not tell React to run the component again. Without a render pass, the browser continues displaying the JSX produced during the initial render. Even if another interaction causes the component to re-render, the function executes from its first line, re-initializing the local variable back to its initial value. Furthermore, moving the variable outside the component creates a module-level variable that is shared by every instance on the page, breaking isolation and still failing to trigger updates. To manage interactive data, React provides the useState Hook, which reserves memory outside the component function and returns a setter function that queues a render.

This chapter answers seven core questions. Why does reassigning a local variable fail to update the number on the screen? How does useState pair a value with a setter function to trigger re-renders? Why do ordinary local variables reset back to their initial values when another button re-renders the card? How does React remember state values across renders and differentiate multiple useState calls? Why does each rendered component card keep its own isolated state rather than sharing counts? How do we pass an expensive initial calculation so React runs it only once on mount? Why does calling a state setter directly inside JSX trigger an infinite render loop, and how do we wire handlers correctly?

Later lessons build directly on useState. Lecture 15 explores the trigger, render, and commit phases of the lifecycle. Lecture 16 examines state snapshots, proving why state variables remain constant throughout a single render pass. Lecture 17 introduces updater functions for queued state modifications. Lecture 18 covers updating objects and immutability rules. Lecture 23 explores lifting state up to shared parent components. Lecture 24 covers component identity and state preservation across tree positions. Lecture 37 examines the Rules of Hooks and call order invariants.

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): The screen reflects application data, and React renders components to produce DOM elements.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): Components are JavaScript functions that return JSX, and the browser console logs runtime execution.
  • Lecture 4 (JavaScript in JSX): Curly braces evaluate JavaScript expressions, and ternary operators provide conditional values.
  • Lecture 5 (The UI tree): Components form a hierarchy of parent and child nodes, passing props downward.
  • Lecture 8 (Importing and exporting): Named imports use curly braces to load specific utilities from library modules.
  • Lecture 11 (Rendering lists): Arrow functions provide inline callbacks for array mappings and deferred execution.
  • Lecture 12 (Keeping components pure): Components must remain pure calculations, and module-level variables cause shared mutation bugs.
  • Lecture 13 (Responding to events): Event listeners like onClick expect function references, not immediate function invocations.

Why local variable assignment fails to update the display

In Lecture 1, we learned that user interfaces reflect application data. In Lecture 4, we saw that placing a JavaScript variable inside JSX curly braces like {likes} outputs its value into the rendered HTML. When a component loads, JavaScript initializes local variables declared with let or const and evaluates JSX expressions during that initial execution.

Local Variable Assignment
1function StoryCard() {
2 let likes = 0;
Local variable React does not track
3 function handleLike() {
4 likes = likes + 1;
Mutates local variable in memory
5 console.log('likes:', likes);
Logs 1, 2, 3 in console
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
8}

When a user clicks a button and an event handler executes likes = likes + 1, JavaScript updates the number stored in local memory. However, React has no mechanism to watch plain variable reassignments. React updates the screen only when it executes the component function again to compute a new JSX element tree. Because a plain assignment does not notify React or schedule a render, React never re-runs the component. The DOM continues to display the JSX generated during the very first render pass, leaving the count stuck at 0 on screen while the console logs higher numbers.

Declarative State Introduction
1import { useState } from 'react';
Named import from React
2function StoryCard() {
3 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
State reserved in React
4 function handleLike() {
5 setLikes(likes + 1);
Queues a re-render with next value
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
8}

The state pair and the setter function

In Lecture 8, we learned to import named utilities using curly braces. In JavaScript, array destructuring const [first, second] = array allows unpacking values from an array into distinct variable names.

State Pair Usage
1import { useState } from 'react';
2function StoryCard() {
3 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
Pair: current value and setter
4 function handleLike() {
5 setLikes(likes + 1);
Schedules render with updated value
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
8}

A Hook is a specialized function starting with use that is available only while React renders components. The useState Hook is React's built-in tool for giving a component memory. When called as useState(initialValue), it returns an array with exactly two elements: the current state variable for this render, and a setter function. The state variable is declared with const because its value represents a static snapshot for the current render. To change the value, application code must invoke the setter function: setLikes(likes + 1). Calling the setter writes the new value into React's internal storage and schedules a re-render. Attempting to assign likes = likes + 1 directly throws a TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

Component function re-execution and local variable reset

In Lecture 12, we learned that React components are pure functions. React calls component functions whenever an update is scheduled.

Local Variable Reset Demonstration
1function StoryCard() {
2 let likes = 0;
Runs on every render, resetting to 0
3 const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);
State survives renders
4 function handleLike() {
5 likes = likes + 1;
Changes memory for this render only
6 }
7 return <button onClick={() => setSaved(!saved)}>Save</button>;
8}

A React component is a plain JavaScript function. When a state setter like setSaved executes, React schedules a re-render and calls StoryCard again from the very first line. Every time a function is called in JavaScript, its local scope is created fresh. Any statement such as let likes = 0 executes again, resetting the variable back to zero. The memory from previous calls is wiped clean. If a developer attempts to store a counter in a local let variable alongside a stateful bookmark toggle, clicking Like increases the count in memory, but toggling the bookmark re-executes the function and silently wipes likes back to 0.

How React stores state and matches calls by order

Components frequently manage multiple pieces of interactive data, such as a counter and a boolean toggle.

Multiple State Variables
1function StoryCard() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
Slot 1
3 const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);
Slot 2
4 const nextLikes = () => setLikes(likes + 1);
5 return (
6 <button onClick={nextLikes}>
7 Likes: {likes} {saved ? '(Saved)' : ''}
8 </button>
9 );
10}

If useState(0) executes on every render, why does likes not reset back to 0 like let likes = 0 does? The reason is that state does not live inside the component function; it lives outside the function in React's internal storage node (the fiber). On the initial render, React stores the initial argument 0. On subsequent renders, React ignores the argument 0 and retrieves the value stored in React's memory. When a component calls useState multiple times, React keeps an ordered list of state cells for that component instance. React pairs each useState call to its stored data by its position in the call sequence: call 1 maps to slot 1, and call 2 maps to slot 2.

Component instances and state isolation

In Lecture 5, we learned that a component definition can be rendered multiple times as separate elements in JSX, such as <StoryCard /> rendered twice in App.

Component Instances
1function App() {
2 return (
3 <div>
4 <StoryCard title="Story A" />
Independent state instance 1
5 <StoryCard title="Story B" />
Independent state instance 2
6 </div>
7 );
8}

When a component is rendered multiple times, each rendered element is a distinct component instance. React allocates a separate, isolated state storage record for each instance on the page. Clicking Like on the first StoryCard updates only that card's state; the second card's state remains untouched. If a developer attempts to solve the local variable reset problem by moving let likes = 0 outside the component to module scope, all card instances share that single variable, corrupting isolation and still failing to trigger renders.

Initializer functions for expensive initial state

In JavaScript, expressions passed as function arguments evaluate immediately when the outer function is called.

Expensive Initial State
1function StoryCard({ storyId }) {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(() => readSavedLikes(storyId));
Pass a function to run only on initial mount
3 return <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
4}

When passing an initial value to useState(readSavedLikes(id)), JavaScript executes readSavedLikes(id) on every single render pass, even though React uses the initial value only on the initial mount and discards it thereafter. If the initialization involves reading storage or parsing data, this causes unnecessary performance overhead. To avoid running the calculation on every render, pass an initializer function: useState(() => readSavedLikes(id)) When passed a function, React invokes it only during the initial mount. In development under StrictMode, React calls the initializer twice to check for side-effect purity, but keeps one result.

Wiring setters in event handlers to prevent render loops

In Lecture 13, we learned that event props like onClick must be passed a function reference, not an immediate function invocation.

Event Handler Setter Wiring
1function StoryCard() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 return <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>Like</button>;
Correct: wrapped in an arrow function that waits for a click
4}

When a developer writes <button onClick={setLikes(likes + 1)}> JavaScript executes setLikes(likes + 1) immediately during the render pass because curly braces evaluate expressions. Calling the setter requests a new render before the current render finishes. React immediately begins the next render, which executes setLikes again, creating an infinite loop. React aborts the loop by throwing Too many re-renders. React limits the number of renders to prevent an infinite loop To wire the setter properly, wrap it in an inline arrow function: onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)} or pass a handler reference.

QUESTION 1

Changing a variable does not update the screen

A developer builds a like counter inside StoryCard using a plain local variable:

Stuck Local Counter
1function StoryCard() {
2 let likes = 0;
Local stack variable
3 function handleLike() {
4 likes = likes + 1;
Mutates local variable
5 console.log('likes:', likes);
Prints 1, 2, 3
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
8}

Each click logs an increasing number to the console, but the button label remains unchanged.

I add 1 to likes on every click, and the console counts 1, 2, 3. Why does the screen still say 0 likes?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. In JavaScript, reassigning a local variable modifies memory in the current execution context, but React does not observe plain variable reassignments.

React updates the screen only when it calls the component function again to compute a new JSX description. Because a plain assignment does not request a render, React never re-executes StoryCard. The screen remains frozen on the initial render output.

Local Assignment vs React Runtime
[ User Click ] ---> [ likes = likes + 1 ] ---> Memory: 1, 2, 3
                          |
                          v
                  React NOT Notified
                          |
                          v
               Screen Stays at "0 likes"

To update the screen, the component must store data in React state and request a render using a setter function.

PRINCIPLE 1

Changing a variable does not ask React to update the screen

plain local variable a variable declared with let or const inside a function body that React does not watch
render trigger an explicit request that instructs React to re-execute a component function

In plain JavaScript, assigning a value updates local memory, but React does not track plain variable reassignments. React updates the screen only when it executes the component function again to compute a new JSX description. Because a plain assignment does not request a render, React never re-runs the component, leaving the display frozen on the previous output.

We should do this:
function StoryCard() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
State memory
function handleLike() {
setLikes(likes + 1);
Asks React to re-render
}
return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
}
We should not do this:
function StoryCard() {
let likes = 0;
Local variable React does not track
function handleLike() {
likes = likes + 1;
Mutates memory; no render occurs
}
return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
}

Keeping the value in state and updating with its setter

Constant Assignment Error

The code does not do what we wanted. The useState Hook returns a pair: the current state value and its setter function.

The state variable is declared with const because it represents an immutable snapshot for the current render pass. Directly reassigning likes throws a runtime TypeError. Even if declared with let, direct reassignment only mutates a local identifier without notifying React. To update state, you must call the setter function setLikes(likes + 1).                           v

When React re-runs StoryCard, useState returns the updated count, and the returned JSX renders the new number to the screen.

PRINCIPLE 2

Keep the value in state and change it with its setter

state variable a constant representing the component's state value during the current render
setter function a function provided by useState that updates state and schedules a re-render

The useState Hook provides both the current state snapshot and a dedicated setter function. The state variable is a constant for the current render pass and must never be reassigned directly. Calling the setter stores the next value inside React and requests a re-render where the updated value is returned.

We should do this:

}

Component function re-execution restarts local variables

A developer pairs a stateful bookmark toggle with a local let counter:

Local Variable Reset on Re-render
1function StoryCard() {
2 let likes = 0;

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A React component is a plain JavaScript function. When setSaved triggers a re-render, React calls StoryCard again from the very first line.

Every function call in JavaScript establishes a fresh execution context. The line let likes = 0 runs again, creating a brand new variable initialized to 0. The count accumulated in the previous render pass is discarded.

Local Variable Reset During Re-render
Render 1: StoryCard() ---> let likes = 0 ---> Click Like x2 (likes = 2)

Render 2: StoryCard() ---> let likes = 0 (reset!) ---> Click Like (likes = 1)

Values that must survive across re-renders cannot live in plain local variables. They must be managed by React state.

PRINCIPLE 3

Every render runs the component from the top, so local variables start over

function re-execution React invoking the component function from line 1 on every render pass
local variable reset the re-initialization of function-scoped variables upon every invocation

Every render executes the component function from line 1. Local variables declared with let or const are re-created on each invocation, discarding any data from previous renders. Values that must persist across renders must be placed in state.

We should do this:
function StoryCard() {

Survives render

Re-created and reset on every render

QUESTION 4

React stores state and matches calls by order

A developer inspects a card with multiple useState calls:

Multiple State Calls
1function StoryCard() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
Slot 1
3 const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);
Slot 2
4 const nextLikes = () => setLikes(likes + 1);
5 return (
6 <button onClick={nextLikes}>
7 Likes: {likes} {saved ? '(Saved)' : ''}
8 </button>
9 );
10}

The developer wonders how React avoids resetting likes back to 0 when useState(0) re-runs.

useState(0) runs again on every render. Why does likes not go back to 0 like let likes = 0 does?

ANSWER

The code works as expected. State values do not live inside the component function; they reside outside the function in React's internal storage node for that component instance.

When useState(0) executes during the initial render, React initializes slot 1 with 0. On all subsequent renders, React ignores the argument 0 and hands back the current stored value. React tracks multiple useState calls by their exact order in the execution sequence: call 1 retrieves slot 1, and call 2 retrieves slot 2.

Hook Call Order and Storage Slots
Component Execution:           React Internal Fiber Storage:
1. useState(0)      ------->   Slot 1: [ 2 ] (likes)
2. useState(false)  ------->   Slot 2: [ true ] (saved)

Because call order determines slot mapping, likes preserves its incremented count while saved independently tracks bookmark state.

PRINCIPLE 4

React keeps the state and hands it back on every render, in call order

React internal storage the underlying fiber node structure that retains state across renders
Hook call order the strict sequential index React uses to match hook calls to state cells

State memory lives outside the component function in React internal storage. On re-renders, React ignores the initial state argument and returns the latest stored value, differentiating multiple useState calls strictly by their sequential call order.

We should do this:

Slot 1: like count
const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);
Slot 2: bookmark
return (
<article>
<button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>Like</button>
<button onClick={() => setSaved(!saved)}>Save</button>
</article>
);
}

Render Phase Setter Crash

Call the setter in a handler, never while the component renders

Component Summary

App

The application shell renders independent story cards in a feed, demonstrating instance isolation.

StoryCardstoryId="art-1" title="Urban Transit Reforms"

The state owner manages private state for likes and bookmark status, using an initializer function for stored counts.

LikeButtonlikes={likes} onLike={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}

Look at how this four-file architecture fulfills idiomatic React state architecture. In a naive implementation, an engineer might have stored like counts in a plain local variable, leaving the screen stuck at 0 because plain assignments provide no render trigger. Or they might have moved the variable to module scope, accidentally sharing one count across every card on the page. Or they might have invoked setLikes(likes + 1) directly inside JSX, crashing the application in an infinite render loop.

By declaring state with useState inside the component boundary, passing an initializer function for stored data, isolating instance memory across cards, and passing deferred callback handlers to child buttons, our application remains predictable, resilient, and performant.

Where you will meet this

In production web applications, understanding useState is essential when managing counters, form drafts, accordion panels, and interactive toggles. Teams frequently face bugs where local variables reset unexpectedly because an engineer placed mutable state on the function call stack instead of in React memory.

Another common scenario involves performance bottlenecks caused by eager argument evaluation. Passing expensive storage queries or array decoders directly to useState slows down every subsequent interaction. Converting those calls to initializer functions ensures initial calculations execute only during the initial component mount.

For the interview

The Interview Question: Why do ordinary variables forget their values between renders, and how does useState remember?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to see whether you understand the fundamental execution model of React: that components are pure functions invoked repeatedly over time. Weak candidates view components as persistent class instances or objects with mutable fields. Strong engineers explain that component functions execute from the top on every render, wiping the JavaScript call stack clean. They explain that useState delegates memory retention to React's internal fiber node, which persists data across invocations.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is believing that variable reassignment tells React to update the page. Candidates often assume that assigning likes = likes + 1 automatically syncs the DOM because {likes} sits in JSX. Another trap is attempting to avoid the reset by moving variables to module scope, corrupting instance isolation across the page. A third trap is invoking state setters directly inside JSX, causing infinite render loops.

3. What is Actually Going On

Every render pass calls the component function from line 1, re-initializing all local let and const variables. When useState executes, React pairs the call to a persistent state cell on the component's internal fiber, determined strictly by Hook call index. Calling a setter queues a re-render and updates the stored value. On subsequent renders, React returns the value from its internal fiber, ignoring the initial state argument.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What if a component has multiple state variables? React differentiates them strictly by the order of useState calls, which is why Hooks cannot be placed inside conditions or loops. What about component instances? Each element mounted in the UI tree receives its own isolated fiber record. What about expensive initial values? Passing a function reference defers execution so the computation runs only once during initial mount.

Glossary

  • State Variable: An immutable value returned by useState representing component memory for the current render.
  • Setter Function: A function returned by useState that updates React internal memory and schedules a re-render.
  • Hook: A built-in React function prefixed with use that gives functional components access to state and lifecycle features.
  • Function Re-execution: The process of React calling a component function from line 1 on every render pass.
  • Component Instance: A distinct mounted occurrence of a component in the user interface tree with private state storage.
  • Initializer Function: A function passed to useState that React executes only during initial component mounting.

Beyond the basics

  • Official React documentation on component state: Comprehensive guide to state as component memory (see react.dev/learn/state-a-components-memory).
  • Reference documentation for useState: API documentation covering arguments, returns, and caveats (see react.dev/reference/react/useState).
  • Rules of Hooks documentation: Guide explaining why Hooks must run in deterministic order at the top level (see react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks).
  • React upgrade guide for React 19: Overview of React 19 compiler enhancements and hook behavior (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).

Trigger, Render, &
Commit

Interview Question   CORE

What are the trigger, render, and commit phases of the React lifecycle, and what runs in each?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build a story card with a like counter, a comment input box, and an analytics tracker.
  • 2 You call a state setter and immediately read the text content of the counter paragraph from the DOM to send to a server, but it sends the old count.
  • 3 How do the trigger, render, and commit phases govern screen updates, and what runs in each?

Every screen update follows a three-step lifecycle

In modern web applications, the screen updates in response to user actions. Readers click buttons to like articles, submit feedback, or type comments into text inputs. In traditional browser scripting, developers updated the screen by selecting elements directly with document.querySelector. They changed properties like textContent by hand. In React, application code never mutates DOM nodes directly. Instead, React orchestrates every screen update through a structured three-step lifecycle: triggering a render, rendering components to produce element descriptions, and committing changes to the browser DOM.

When developers transition from classic scripting to React, they often bring imperative DOM habits with them. In plain JavaScript, assigning a new value to element.textContent modifies the page immediately on that exact line. In React, calling a state setter does not touch the DOM right away. It merely requests a future render. React waits until the current event handler finishes before it begins rendering components and committing changes to the document. A developer who attempts to read the DOM immediately after calling a setter finds the old value still sitting on the page. Furthermore, developers frequently worry that re-rendering a component will tear down the entire page. They fear wiping out user input from active form fields, unaware that React preserves identical DOM nodes across renders.

This chapter answers four core questions. How does calling a state setter turn into an updated number on the screen? When state changes, does React run the entire application again or only specific components? If a component re-renders on every interaction, will it wipe out text that the user is actively typing? Why does reading the page immediately after calling a setter return the old count, and where should application side effects read values from?

Later lessons build directly on these three phases. Lecture 16 explores state snapshots, proving why state variables inside the current handler execution retain their initial values. Lecture 24 examines component identity, showing how React uses element position in the tree to preserve or reset DOM nodes. Lecture 46 covers StrictMode, explaining why React invokes component functions twice in development to verify render purity. Lecture 54 explores advanced re-render mechanics, showing how parent renders and context updates cascade through the tree.

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): The screen reflects application data, and React applies minimal updates to DOM nodes rather than rebuilding the page.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): React calls our component functions because JSX names them; our code never calls component functions directly.
  • Lecture 5 (The UI tree): Components form a hierarchy starting at the root, and state updates trigger re-renders down their subtrees.
  • Lecture 9 (Creating a root): Calling createRoot and root.render mounts the application and acts as the initial trigger.
  • Lecture 12 (Keeping components pure): Rendering must remain a pure calculation without mutating external variables or modifying the browser DOM.
  • Lecture 13 (Responding to events): Event handlers execute in response to user actions outside the render cycle and are the safe home for side effects.
  • Lecture 14 (Component memory with useState): Calling a state setter stores the next value and queues a re-render.

How a state change triggers an update that renders and commits

In Lecture 1, we saw that plain JavaScript uses imperative methods like document.getElementById and textContent to modify elements on the page. In standard browser programming, calling document.querySelector('.like-count').textContent = '1' changes the paragraph immediately.

Imperative DOM Mutation
1function BrokenButton() {
2 let likes = 0;
Local variable React does not track
3 function handleClick() {
4 likes = likes + 1;
Mutates variable without triggering render
5 document.querySelector('.count').textContent = likes;
Direct DOM write
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleClick}>Like</button>;
8}

In Lecture 9, we learned that React applications mount by calling createRoot(container).render(<App />) That initial call is the very first trigger in a React application: it tells React to prepare the initial screen. Every interface update in React proceeds through three distinct steps. The first step is the trigger: a request that tells React to calculate a new screen. There are only two triggers: the initial root.render call, and calling a state setter like setLikes.

Declarative State Update
1function LikeButton() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
State memory in React
3 function handleClick() {
4 setLikes(likes + 1);
Triggers a re-render
5 }
6 return <button onClick={handleClick}>Like ({likes})</button>;
7}

The second step is render: React calls your component functions to determine what JSX they return. During rendering, React does not touch the DOM or change any pixels on the screen; it simply collects the new virtual description of the user interface. The third step is commit: React compares the newly returned JSX with the previous render and applies the necessary changes to the real browser DOM. On initial render, React uses appendChild() to insert all created DOM nodes; on re-renders, it modifies only the specific attributes and text nodes that changed. After the commit, the browser performs a browser paint, recalculating geometry and drawing pixels on the physical screen.

How a state update re-renders its component subtree

In Lecture 5, we established that React components organize into a tree structure. A root component like App branches into child components like StoryTitle and LikeCounter, which in turn branch into leaves like LikeLabel.

Subtree Render Hierarchy
1function App() {
2 console.log('App runs');
Runs only on initial render
3 return (
4 <div>
5 <StoryTitle />
Sibling: does not re-render on like
6 <LikeCounter />
Owner: re-renders on state setter
7 </div>
8 );
9}

When a state setter executes, React does not re-render the entire application from the root. Instead, React identifies the specific component that owns the state variable where the setter was called. React re-renders that component, and then recursively re-renders every component returned inside its JSX tree. Parent components higher up the tree do not re-render. Sibling components residing in adjacent branches do not re-render.

Child Component Execution
1function LikeCounter() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 console.log('LikeCounter runs');
Runs on every like
4 return <LikeLabel count={likes} />;
Child runs when parent runs
5}

If App renders StoryTitle and LikeCounter, and LikeCounter renders LikeLabel, calling setLikes inside LikeCounter causes React to call LikeCounter and LikeLabel. Neither App nor StoryTitle is called. Even if LikeLabel returns identical JSX output, React still executes its function to verify its returned elements.

How React preserves DOM nodes and form inputs across renders

A browser web page is constructed from persistent DOM nodes, including element nodes like <p> and <input>, and inner text nodes. When a user types text into an <input> element, the browser stores that typed text inside the input DOM node's internal state. In traditional web development, replacing a container with innerHTML destroys existing DOM nodes and replaces them with new ones, immediately erasing any text the user was typing and resetting keyboard focus.

DOM Node Preservation
1function InteractiveCard() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 return (
4 <div>
5 <p>{likes}</p>
Text node updates in commit
6 <input placeholder="Type comment..." />
Preserved untouched
7 <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>Like</button>
8 </div>
9 );
10}

React does not replace the DOM tree when a component re-renders. During the render phase, React executes your component function and collects the new JSX element tree. In the commit phase, React compares this new JSX tree against the JSX tree from the previous render. React identifies the exact minimal differences. If a <p> element's text changed from "0" to "1", React updates only the specific text node inside that <p>. If an adjacent <input> element was rendered in the same position in the JSX tree with the same props, React leaves its underlying DOM node completely untouched. The input element retains its identity, its typed text, and its active cursor focus. After the commit phase applies these minimal DOM edits, the browser performs a browser paint, drawing the updated pixels onto the screen.

How handler completion governs DOM update timing

In Lecture 12 and Lecture 13, we learned that event handlers run in response to user actions outside the render cycle. Handlers are the designated home for side effects, such as sending analytics pings or making network requests.

Post-Setter DOM Read Defect
1function BrokenTracker() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 function handleLike() {
4 setLikes(likes + 1);
Schedules render for later
5 const text = document.querySelector('.count').textContent;
6 console.log('Sending:', text);
Reads uncommitted DOM value
7 }
8 return <p className="count">{likes}</p>;
9}

When a user clicks a button, the browser dispatches an event, and React invokes your event handler. When your handler executes setLikes(likes + 1), React records the requested state update and schedules a re-render. However, React does not pause your handler or immediately render the component on that line. Your handler continues executing synchronously until it reaches the end of its function block.

Using Computed Variable
1function CorrectTracker() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 function handleLike() {
4 const next = likes + 1;
Compute next value once
5 setLikes(next);
6 console.log('Sending:', next);
Sends fresh computed value
7 }
8 return <p className="count">{likes}</p>;
9}

Only after your handler has fully returned does React begin the render phase, followed by the commit phase. Consequently, if code on the line immediately following a setter call queries the DOM using document.querySelector, the commit phase has not yet occurred. The DOM still holds the old values from the previous render. To send the new value to an external service, you must use the value your code computed directly.

Principles of React: Trigger, Render, and Commit

QUESTION 1

Calling a setter starts an update that reaches the screen in three steps

A developer builds a like counter component. Having worked with plain JavaScript, they try updating the paragraph text directly inside the click handler:

Imperative DOM Mutation Mistake
1export default function LikeCounter() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 function handleLike() {
4 const p = document.querySelector('.like-count');
5 p.textContent = likes + 1;
Mutates DOM directly
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
8}

On the first click, the text inside the button changes to 1. On the second and third clicks, the button still shows 1, and the component never updates past that first click.

I call setLikes(likes + 1). How does the new number get onto the screen?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. In plain JavaScript, assigning textContent modifies the page directly, but React updates the screen through trigger, render, and commit.

When you mutate the DOM by hand, React knows nothing about the change. The state variable likes remains at 0 because no setter was called. Every subsequent click evaluates likes + 1 as 0 + 1, repeatedly writing 1 to the paragraph. In React, application code never touches DOM elements directly. Instead, calling setLikes(likes + 1) initiates a three-step sequence.

First is the trigger: calling setLikes asks React to schedule a render for this component. Second is the render: React calls LikeCounter, which evaluates its JSX and returns the new virtual element tree where likes is 1. During rendering, the page remains unchanged. Third is the commit: React compares the returned JSX with the output from the previous render and updates the text node on the page from 0 to 1.

The Three Steps: Trigger, Render, and Commit
[1. TRIGGER] Click handler calls setLikes(1) -> React queues render
     |
     v
[2. RENDER]  React calls LikeCounter() -> returns JSX with likes = 1
     |       (Page remains completely unchanged during render)
     v
[3. COMMIT]  React updates real DOM text node from "0" to "1"
     |
     v
[4. PAINT]   Browser recalculates layout and draws updated pixels

On initial application mount, root.render(<App />) acts as the very first trigger, and its commit creates and inserts all initial DOM nodes.

PRINCIPLE 1

After a setter call, React runs the component and then changes the page

trigger a request that tells React to calculate an updated user interface
render React calling component functions to compute their latest JSX
commit React updating the browser DOM nodes to match the latest JSX

In plain JavaScript, code updates the screen by mutating DOM nodes directly: p.textContent = 1 changes the page on that line. In React, application code calls a state setter and leaves DOM manipulation to React. Every update proceeds through three steps. First, the setter asks React for an update: this is the trigger. Second, React calls the component function to calculate its latest JSX: this is the render, and the page has not changed yet. Third, React compares the new JSX with the previous output and modifies the DOM where they differ: this is the commit. Changing DOM nodes by hand bypasses these steps and leaves state variables out of sync.

We should do this:
function LikeCounter() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
return (
<button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>
Likes: {likes}
updates via render and commit
</button>
);
}
We should not do this:
function LikeCounter() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
function handleLike() {
const p = document.querySelector('.like-count');
p.textContent = likes + 1;
bypasses render and commit
}
return <button onClick={handleLike}>Like</button>;
}
QUESTION 2

A state change re-renders its own component and the components inside it

A developer organizes an article header where App renders both a static headline and an interactive like counter:

Subtree Component Hierarchy
1export default function App() {
2 console.log('App runs');
Logs on initial render
3 return (
4 <main>
5 <StoryTitle title="Transit Accord" />
6 <LikeCounter />
7 </main>
8 );
9}

The developer adds a console log to each component: App, StoryTitle, LikeCounter, and LikeLabel. When the page loads, all four logs print in sequence. When the developer clicks Like, the console prints only LikeCounter runs and LikeLabel runs.

When I click Like, does React run my whole app again, or only LikeCounter?

ANSWER

The code works as expected. React calls only the component whose state changed and any child components it returns in its JSX.

A state update does not trigger a full re-render of the entire application. When a state setter executes, React targets the specific component that declared the state variable. In our component tree, LikeCounter owns likes, so React calls LikeCounter. React then cascades downward, recursively rendering every child component that LikeCounter returns, calling LikeLabel.

Parent components located above the state owner in the tree do not re-render. Sibling components located in neighboring branches do not re-render. Because App sits above LikeCounter and owns no changing state, React leaves App untouched. Because StoryTitle is a sibling to LikeCounter, React bypasses StoryTitle completely.

Component Re-render Cascade Scope
[App] (Parent Shell) ------------------ Does NOT re-render
  |
  +--- [StoryTitle] (Sibling) --------- Does NOT re-render
  |
  +--- [LikeCounter] (State Owner) ---- RE-RENDERS on setter call
         |
         +--- [LikeLabel] (Child) ----- RE-RENDERS (descendant cascade)

Notice that child components like LikeLabel re-render even if their props have not changed. React executes the child function to verify what JSX elements it produces.

PRINCIPLE 2

A state change runs its own component and the components inside it

state update calling a state setter to request a new render of that component

Components in React form a hierarchical component tree. On initial mount, React renders from the root component downward through every branch. When a state update occurs, React does not re-render the entire application. It calls the specific component that owns the state variable, and then recursively renders the child components returned inside its JSX. Ancestor components above the state owner and sibling components in adjacent branches do not re-render. A child component re-renders even when its props have not changed.

We should do this:
function Feed() {
return (
<main>
<Header />
does not re-render on counter clicks
<Counter />
owns state: re-renders itself and Label
</main>
);
}
QUESTION 3

The commit updates only changed nodes, so typed text stays

A developer adds a comment input field beside the like counter so readers can type feedback while reading:

Interactive Feedback Box
1export default function LikeCounter() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 return <section>
4 <p className="like-count">Likes: {likes}</p>
5 <input type="text" placeholder="Write a comment..." />
6 <button type="button" onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>
7 Like Story
Preserves input text
8 </button>
9 </section>;
10}

The developer types "great post" into the comment box and then clicks Like. The count increments to 1. The typed comment "great post" remains in the input field, and the cursor position does not jump.

If React runs LikeCounter again on every like, will it wipe the comment the reader is typing?

ANSWER

The code works as expected. React compares the new JSX with the previous render and commits changes strictly to the DOM nodes that differ.

A re-render does not recreate the underlying page or reset existing DOM elements. During the render phase, React executes LikeCounter to compute the new JSX element tree. In the commit phase, React compares this new tree against the JSX tree from the previous render to determine minimal differences.

Because the <input> element occupies the exact same position in the JSX tree with identical props, React preserves the existing input DOM node completely untouched. React mutates only the specific text node inside <p className="like-count"> whose content changed from "Likes: 0" to "Likes: 1".

Virtual DOM Reconciliation and Commit Diffing
Previous Render JSX:                  New Render JSX:
<p>Likes: 0</p>                       <p>Likes: 1</p>       <-- DIFF: "0" vs "1"
<input placeholder="Write..." />      <input placeholder="Write..." /> <-- SAME

COMMIT PHASE ACTION:
- Mutate inner text node of <p> from "Likes: 0" to "Likes: 1"
- Leave <input> DOM node completely untouched (preserves typed text and focus)
- Trigger browser paint to draw new characters on screen

The browser preserves the input DOM element's internal state, keeping any typed text intact. Once the commit finishes applying these minimal differences, the browser executes a browser paint to draw the updated text on the screen.

PRINCIPLE 3

The commit changes only what is different, so typed text stays

DOM node an individual HTML element or text object preserved in the browser page
browser paint the browser drawing calculated pixels and layout onto the visual display

Re-rendering a component does not destroy or recreate the underlying page. During the render phase, React calculates the new JSX element tree. In the commit phase, React compares the new tree with the previous one and modifies only the specific DOM node whose text or attributes changed. Elements that remain in the same position in JSX are preserved. An <input> field retains its active focus and any text the user typed. Once the commit completes, the browser performs a browser paint to draw the updated pixels.

We should do this:
function CommentBox() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
return (
<div>
<p>Likes: {likes}</p>
commit updates only this text
<input placeholder="Type..." />
preserved untouched
<button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>Like</button>
</div>
);
}
QUESTION 4

Reading the DOM right after a setter finds the old value

A developer connects an analytics helper to track user engagement. They call the state setter and then read the count from the page to transmit:

Premature DOM Read Inside Handler
1export default function LikeCounter() {
2 const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
3 function handleLike() {
4 setLikes(likes + 1);
Requests re-render
5 const count = document.querySelector('.like-count').textContent;
6 console.log('Sending to server:', count);
7 }
8 return <button onClick={handleLike}>Likes: {likes}</button>;
9}

On the first click, the button updates on screen to show 1. However, the console log prints Sending to server: 0, and the telemetry payload reports 0 instead of 1.

I call setLikes(likes + 1) and then read the number from the page to send it. Why does it send the old number?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The setter asks for a future render, but the DOM does not update until after the current event handler finishes.

A state setter does not mutate the DOM synchronously. Calling setLikes(likes + 1) stores the requested value in React's memory and marks the component as needing a render. Your event handler continues executing synchronously until it reaches the end of its function block.

React waits until all active event handlers have finished before it starts rendering components. The commit phase, where React actually updates the DOM text, occurs only after rendering completes. On the line immediately following setLikes, the commit has not happened yet. The DOM still holds the old text from the previous render.

Handler Execution Timeline and Commit Timing
[HANDLER EXECUTION] handleLike() runs synchronously
  1. setLikes(likes + 1) -> queues next state update for later
  2. querySelector('.like-count').textContent -> finds STALE text "0"!
  3. Handler finishes and returns to the browser
        |
        v
[REACT LIFECYCLE] Begins after handler returns
  4. Render Phase: LikeCounter runs and produces new JSX
  5. Commit Phase: React mutates DOM text node from "0" to "1"
  6. Paint Phase: Browser draws "1" on the screen

To send the correct value to an external service, compute the next value once in a local variable: const next = likes + 1 Pass next to the setter, and pass that same variable directly to your analytics helper.

PRINCIPLE 4

The page changes only after the event handler finishes

event handler the function executing in response to a user action before React renders

Calling a state setter asks React to schedule a future render; it does not update the document on that line of code. Your active event handler runs to completion first. Only after the handler has completely returned does React execute the render phase and commit changes to the page. Reading the DOM immediately after calling a setter reads the stale value from the previous render. When an external service or analytics tracker needs the new value, compute the next value in a local variable and pass that variable to both the setter and the tracking call.

We should do this:
function handleLike() {
const next = likes + 1;
computes next value once
setLikes(next);
sendAnalytics(next);
sends fresh computed value
}
We should not do this:
function handleLike() {
setLikes(likes + 1);
const text = document.querySelector('.count').textContent;
sendAnalytics(text);
sends stale count from uncommitted DOM
}

During the commit phase, React updates only the specific text node inside LikeLabel, leaving the comment input element and all surrounding DOM nodes preserved.

Where you will meet this

In production applications, understanding trigger, render, and commit is vital when integrating analytics trackers, logging user interactions, and handling form inputs. Teams frequently encounter bugs where telemetry payloads send stale counts because an engineer read element.textContent synchronously after calling a state setter. Understanding that handlers run to completion before React renders prevents these synchronization defects.

Another scenario involves complex form layouts. Junior engineers often worry that updating an inline validation message or character counter will re-render the form and wipe out user draft text. Knowing that React's commit phase updates only changed DOM nodes while preserving form elements builds confidence in creating responsive interfaces.

For the interview

The Interview Question: What are the trigger, render, and commit phases of the React lifecycle, and what runs in each?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand React's declarative execution architecture or whether you still think in terms of imperative DOM mutation. Candidates who lack this foundation assume that calling a state setter directly edits the page. Senior engineers explain the three distinct phases: triggering requests an update, rendering invokes pure component functions to produce JSX descriptions, and committing applies minimal differences to the real DOM. They also distinguish React's render phase from the browser's paint phase.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is believing that state setters mutate the DOM synchronously. Candidates often write handlers that call a setter and immediately query the DOM, expecting to see the new value. Another frequent trap is fearing that re-rendering destroys active form inputs, unaware that React reconciliation diffs output and preserves existing DOM nodes. A third trap is confusing React rendering (calling JavaScript functions) with browser painting (drawing pixels on screen).

3. What is Actually Going On

React batches state updates and delays rendering until all active event handlers have returned. During the render phase, React calls component functions from the state owner downward through its returned JSX tree. In the commit phase, React calculates minimal DOM differences and updates only changed text nodes or attributes. Once the commit finishes, the browser performs a paint phase, calculating layout geometry and drawing pixels on the display.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens if a child component returns identical JSX? React still executes the child render function unless wrapped in optimization memoization, but the commit phase makes zero DOM modifications. What about form inputs? React preserves existing DOM nodes if their position in the JSX tree is unchanged, keeping typed text and focus intact. What if you must read the DOM after an update? You must wait for the commit phase to finish, which is why DOM measurements belong in effects or post-commit callbacks.

Glossary

  • Trigger: An event (initial root mounting or a state setter call) that requests React to calculate an updated user interface.
  • Render: The phase where React invokes component functions to calculate their latest JSX element descriptions without modifying the DOM.
  • Commit: The phase where React applies minimal calculated differences to the browser DOM nodes.
  • Browser Paint: The browser engine process of computing layout geometry and drawing pixels onto the visual display following the commit phase.
  • DOM Node: A persistent browser object representing an HTML element or text fragment in the document tree.
  • State Owner: The specific component declaring useState where re-rendering begins following a setter trigger.

Beyond the basics

  • Official React documentation on render and commit: Comprehensive guide to the three-step lifecycle (see react.dev/learn/render-and-commit).
  • Official guide on keeping components pure: Best practices for writing side-effect-free render functions (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Reference documentation for createRoot: Full API reference for initial mount triggers (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/createRoot).
  • Reference documentation for useState: Troubleshooting guide for setter timing and state update queues (see react.dev/reference/react/useState).

❒ Declarative State Triggers

➔ NEVER mutate DOM nodes directly with imperative methods like textContent in React applications.

➔ IF you need to pass updated state to an external service THEN compute the next value in a local variable before updating state.

State as a Snapshot

Interview Question   CORE

Why does state appear frozen inside a render, even right after you set it?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build an interactive feedback card with rating buttons and an analytics tracker.
  • 2 You call setRating(5) and log the rating on the next line, but the console still prints 0.
  • 3 Why does state appear frozen inside a render, even right after you set it?

Every render receives a fixed state snapshot

In modern web applications, user interfaces update dynamically in response to user interactions. When a reader clicks a star rating, submits feedback, or confirms an order, the interface changes to reflect the new data. In plain JavaScript, developers modify memory by reassigning variables directly with =, expecting every subsequent line of code to see the new value immediately. In React, application state behaves differently: it acts as a snapshot. Calling a state setter does not mutate the variable in the running code; instead, it asks React to schedule a future render where useState returns the new value. Understanding that a state variable remains frozen as a constant for the entire duration of a render is essential for coordinating user events, network requests, and delayed callbacks without synchronization bugs.

When developers transition from traditional scripting to React, they often assume that calling a state setter works like variable reassignment. In plain JavaScript, writing rating = 5 changes the variable immediately, so logging rating on the very next line prints 5. In React, calling setRating(5) does not touch the local variable rating in the currently executing function. React keeps state memory outside the component and hands the current render a constant snapshot of that data. The running event handler continues executing using its existing snapshot value. Consequently, reading the state variable on the line immediately following a setter call prints the old value. Furthermore, developers often expect that calling setRating(rating + 1) three times in a row will increment the number by three, unaware that every call in that handler evaluates using the exact same snapshot number.

This chapter answers four core questions. Why does reading a state variable immediately after calling its setter still return the old value? How should an event handler coordinate state updates with external API calls or network dispatches? Why does calling a state setter three times in a row only advance the count by one? If a delayed timer runs after the user selects a new rating, which value does its callback read?

Later lessons build directly on this snapshot mental model. Lecture 17 explores batching and update queues, showing how updater functions r => r + 1 let multiple updates chain together. Lecture 18 covers state objects and immutability, explaining why mutating an existing state object breaks snapshot isolation. Lecture 29 introduces refs, showing how to store mutable values that delayed callbacks can read at their latest version. Lecture 35 covers effect events, showing how effects read reactive values without re-triggering synchronization. Lecture 36 examines effect dependencies, preventing stale closure captures inside background subscriptions.

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): Plain JavaScript modifies memory directly, while React updates the screen by calculating user interface descriptions from data.
  • Lecture 2 (Component anatomy): React calls our component functions because JSX names them; our code never calls component functions directly.
  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): Curly braces open an inline JavaScript window to project variables and evaluate template literals.
  • Lecture 13 (Responding to events): A function is passed to an event prop like onClick, never called during rendering, and handlers execute side effects.
  • Lecture 14 (Component memory with useState): The setter function stores the next state value in React and asks React to render again, while plain local variables reset on every run.
  • Lecture 15 (Trigger, render, and commit): The page updates only after the event handler finishes, so a DOM read immediately after a setter sees the old content.

How React captures state in a render snapshot

In Lecture 14, we learned that calling useState gives a component memory. React preserves state variables outside the component function, and calling a state setter tells React to schedule a re-render. In Lecture 15, we discovered that React runs event handlers to completion before initiating the render and commit phases.

Declarative State Snapshot
1export default function FeedbackSnapshot() {
2 const [rating, setRating] = useState(0);
Rating is constant 0 in this run
3 function handleRate() {
4 setRating(5);
Requests next render with 5
5 console.log(rating);
Still prints 0 in this run
6 }
7 return <button onClick={handleRate}>Rate ({rating})</button>;
8}

When React renders a component, it calls your component function. The useState call retrieves the current state value from React internal storage and returns it to your function. Inside that function execution, the state variable is a standard JavaScript const. It never changes while that function executes. The JSX, local variables, and event handlers are all computed using this fixed value. We call this fixed set of values a snapshot.

Calling a setter function like setRating(5) does not mutate the variable rating in your running code; it only tells React what value to supply in the next render. You can visualize this behavior using the substitution method: if rating is 0 when the component runs, you can mentally substitute 0 for rating everywhere in that render code.

The Substitution Method
1function handleTripleBoost() {
2 setRating(0 + 1);
Substituted: requests 1 for next render
3 setRating(0 + 1);
4 setRating(0 + 1);
Queues 1 again for the screen
5}

Calling setRating(rating + 1) three times in one handler evaluates as setRating(0 + 1) three times. Each call asks React for 1, not 3. The screen moves from 0 to 1, exactly as if you called setRating(1) three times.

How functions capture state across time through closures

In Lecture 13, we saw that event handlers are JavaScript functions passed to JSX elements to handle user events. In standard JavaScript, functions declared inside an outer function have access to the outer function scope.

Delayed Timer Closure
1export default function DelayedConfirmation() {
2 const [rating, setRating] = useState(0);
Snapshot constant for this render
3 function handleSend() {
4 setTimeout(() => {
5 console.log(`Rating: ${rating}`);
Closure reads rating from this render
6 }, 1000);
7 }
8 return <button onClick={handleSend}>Send ({rating})</button>;
9}

Every time React renders a component, it executes the component function from top to bottom, creating fresh event handler functions for that specific render. In JavaScript, an inner function forms a closure: it permanently remembers the variables of the lexical scope where it was created.

When an event handler schedules a delayed callback with setTimeout, that callback closes over the specific snapshot values of the render that created it. The browser native setTimeout method accepts a callback function and a delay in milliseconds, executing the callback after the timer expires. Even if subsequent user clicks trigger new renders that update the screen with fresh state, existing timer callbacks retain the snapshot values from the render where they were scheduled. This behavior prevents timing bugs and race conditions in asynchronous user workflows.

Principles of React: State as a Snapshot

QUESTION 1

Calling a setter leaves the variable unchanged until the next render

A developer builds a reader rating widget for stories. When a reader clicks five stars, the widget must update the screen to show 5 stars. The developer calls setRating(5) and logs rating on the very next line:

StoryFeedback.jsx, first attempt
6 function handleFiveStars() {
7 setRating(5);
Requests next render with 5
8 console.log('rating after setter:', rating);
Still prints 0 here
9 }

The developer opens the browser and clicks the five-star button. The development console prints rating after setter: 0. A body log placed at the top of the component prints render rating = 5 only after the click handler completes, when the button on screen changes to show 5 stars. In a boost button calling setRating(rating + 1) three times, the screen moves from 0 to 1 instead of 3.

I call setRating(5) and log the rating on the next line. Why does it still print 0?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. In plain JavaScript, assigning a variable with = changes it immediately, but React treats state as a snapshot fixed for an entire render.

In plain JavaScript, assigning a variable with rating = 5 overwrites memory in place. In React, const [rating, setRating] = useState(0) provides the running function with a constant value 0 for this specific execution. React stores component state outside the function body. Calling setRating(5) does not mutate the variable in the running code; it stores 5 in React internal storage and queues a future render.

Every line inside the current handler continues reading the constant 0. Furthermore, when calling setRating(rating + 1) three times in one handler, the substitution method shows that each line evaluates 0 + 1 and asks React to replace the value with 1. After the handler returns, React executes the new render, where useState returns 5 (or 1), and the component calculates its new JSX.

State as a Snapshot During Handler Execution
[User Clicks "5 Stars"]
      |
      v
[handleFiveStars Execution: rating is constant 0]
  - setRating(5) queues 5 for next render
  - console.log(rating) reads constant: prints 0
      |
      v
[React Re-renders StoryFeedback with rating = 5]

When code inside the handler needs the new value immediately, compute the next value once in a local variable: const nextRating = 5; setRating(nextRating); console.log('rating =', nextRating);

PRINCIPLE 1

A state variable keeps one value for the whole render

snapshot the fixed set of values React gives to one run of a component

React provides each component run with a fixed snapshot of its state. In that run, a state variable is a standard JavaScript constant. Calling a setter does not change that constant in your running code. The setter only tells React what value to return on the next run. So reading the state variable on the line after the setter still reads the value from the current run. The new value exists only when React calls the component again.

We should do this:
const nextCount = count + 1;
compute the value once
setCount(nextCount);
console.log(nextCount);
logs 1 in this handler
We should not do this:
setCount(count + 1);
console.log(count);
prints the old count, 0
QUESTION 2

Calling an API after a setter sends the old value unless computed once

The developer now connects the rating widget to an analytics helper named sendRating. When a reader clicks five stars, the component must update the screen and notify the analytics server:

StoryFeedback.jsx, sending rating
6 function handleFiveStars() {
7 setRating(5);
Schedules next render with 5
8 sendRating(rating);
Sends stale snapshot value 0!
9 }

The developer clicks the five-star button. The screen updates to show 5 stars. But the analytics server records a rating of 0 stars.

When the reader clicks 5 stars, I set the rating and send it to the server. Which value do I give sendRating?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. The function sendRating executes inside the running handler where rating is still 0.

The developer expects rating to hold 5 because setRating(5) was just called on the preceding line. But rating is a constant 0 for the entire execution of this handler. Passing rating to sendRating(rating) passes 0. The server receives a rating of 0 while the reader sees 5 stars on screen, creating a silent telemetry defect.

To synchronize the server payload with the requested UI state, the handler must compute the next value once in a local variable before calling the setter. Calling const nextRating = 5; setRating(nextRating); sendRating(nextRating); gives 5 to React for the next render and passes 5 to the network helper immediately.

Sending Stale State Versus Computed Next Value
[BROKEN APPROACH]
  setRating(5);
  sendRating(rating);      ---> Sends 0 (stale snapshot)
  Screen updates to 5      ---> Server has 0, UI shows 5 (MISMATCH)

[CORRECT APPROACH]
  const nextRating = 5;    ---> Computed once in local variable
  setRating(nextRating);   ---> Queues 5 for screen
  sendRating(nextRating);  ---> Sends 5 to server (IN SYNC)

By computing the next value once in a variable, both the state setter and the external helper receive the identical value.

PRINCIPLE 2

Compute the next value once and use it after the setter

When an event handler must update state and notify an outside service or API, do not read the state variable right after calling the setter. The state variable still holds the value from the current run. Instead, calculate the new value once in a local variable. Pass that variable to the setter to schedule the screen update, and pass the same variable to the outside function.

We should do this:
const nextCount = 5;
compute next value once
setCount(nextCount);
sendCount(nextCount);
sends 5 to the server
We should not do this:
setCount(5);
sendCount(count);
sends old count 0 to server
QUESTION 3

A delayed timer callback keeps reading the rating from its own render

The developer adds a Send Confirmation button that schedules an alert using setTimeout. When clicked, the widget waits 100 milliseconds and prints a confirmation message:

StoryFeedback.jsx, delayed confirmation
10 function handleSend() {
11 setTimeout(() => {
12 console.log('Thanks for rating ' + rating);
Reads captured snapshot
13 }, 100);
14 }

The user rates 5 stars, clicks Send Confirmation, and quickly clicks 2 stars before the 100-millisecond timer expires. The screen updates to show 2 stars, but the timer callback prints "Thanks for rating 5" in the console.

If the rating changes before the timer fires, which number does the message show?

ANSWER

The code works as expected. The timer callback is a JavaScript closure that retains the state snapshot of the render that created it.

A developer might expect the delayed callback to read the newest rating (2) because it executes after the screen has already re-rendered. In JavaScript, an inner function forms a closure that captures the variables in scope when the function was created. The render where rating was 5 created its own Send handler. Clicking Send created a timer callback that closed over that render constant rating value of 5.

When the user later clicked 2, React re-rendered StoryFeedback with a new constant rating = 2 and generated fresh event handlers for the new screen. That second render does not mutate the variables held by the existing timer callback. When the timer fires, it reads the 5 from its own render snapshot.

Closure Capture Across Component Re-renders
[Render 1: rating = 5]
  |-- "Send" schedules timer (closure captures 5)
  |
  +--> [User clicks 2 Stars -> Render 2: rating = 2]
         |-- Screen updates to 2 Stars
         |
         +--> [Timer expires after 100ms]
                |-- Runs callback from Render 1
                |-- Prints "Thanks for rating 5"

This snapshot behavior is a protective feature. If a user sends a chat message to Alice and immediately switches the active recipient to Bob, a delayed network timeout or confirmation alert still sends the message to Alice, preventing race conditions.

PRINCIPLE 3

An event handler keeps the state of the render that created it

closure a JavaScript function that remembers variables from the scope where it was defined

Every time React runs a component, that run creates its own fresh event handler functions. In JavaScript, an inner function is a closure: it remembers the variables of the function call where it was created. When a timer or delayed callback is scheduled, it closes over the state variables of that specific run. If a later click changes state and causes React to run the component again, the new run gets new state variables and new handlers. The earlier timer callback continues running with the values from the run that created it.

We should do this:
function handleSend() {
setTimeout(() => {
console.log(`Rating: ${count}`);
reads count from this render
}, 3000);
}

StoryFeedback

The state boundary manages rating memory, computes next values, and schedules timer alerts.

RatingControlsonRate={handleRate} onSend={handleSend}

The action controls render rating buttons and dispatch interactions upward through callbacks.

Across our three files, the architectural roles are distinct. App.jsx acts as a static host. StoryFeedback.jsx holds state memory, computes next values once to prevent stale dispatches, and captures render snapshots for timers. RatingControls.jsx provides interactive buttons that dispatch user events upward without owning persistent data.

Where you will meet this

In production applications, understanding state snapshots is vital when sending analytics telemetry, dispatching API requests, and managing delayed notifications. A frequent bug occurs when an engineer calls a state setter and immediately passes the state variable to an analytics helper on the next line, causing telemetry pipelines to record outdated values. Computing the value once in a local variable resolves this issue permanently.

Another universal scenario involves form submissions with delayed confirmation toasts or undo banners. When a user submits an item and quickly navigates or edits another record, delayed timer callbacks rely on closure capture to display the exact data submitted at that moment, rather than whatever record the user is currently editing.

Interviewers frequently probe candidate understanding of state snapshots by asking whether setState is asynchronous or by presenting code snippets that call a setter three times in a single handler. Candidates who explain that state variables are render constants and demonstrate the substitution method immediately distinguish themselves.

For the interview

The Interview Question: Why does state appear frozen inside a render, even right after you set it?

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is probing whether you understand React declarative execution lifecycle and closure mechanics, or whether you still hold an imperative mental model where setters mutate variables in place. Senior engineers explain that React keeps state outside the component and provides each render with an immutable snapshot. They clearly articulate that setters schedule future renders rather than altering variables in currently executing code.

2. The Classic Trap

The classic trap is claiming that "setState is asynchronous, so the variable has not updated yet." This answer confuses the timing of the next render with variable mutability. Even if JavaScript waited, the state variable inside the current function execution is a const primitive; no background process could mutate a local constant in running JavaScript. Another frequent trap is trying to fix the old value by adding a setTimeout(..., 0), unaware that the callback still closes over the same render snapshot.

3. What is Actually Going On

React calls your component function to render the user interface. During that call, useState returns the state value for that specific render. Inside that function execution, the state variable is a constant. Calling a state setter queues a request for React to run the component again with a new value during the next render. The current function continues executing using its existing snapshot values. If code inside the handler needs the new value immediately, it must calculate that value once in a local variable and use it for both the setter and subsequent operations.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

What happens across an await pause in an asynchronous handler? If a handler awaits a network request and reads state after the promise settles, it still reads the snapshot value from the render that created it, even if user clicks in the meantime caused React to re-render. What happens with repeated setter calls? Calling setCount(count + 1) three times queues three requests to replace state with 0 + 1, incrementing the counter by only one. What if code genuinely requires reading the latest mutable value across renders without triggering updates? That requirement calls for a ref (useRef), which React provides specifically for mutable storage outside the render snapshot.

Glossary

  • Snapshot: The immutable set of state values, props, and event handlers provided by React for a single execution of a component function.
  • State Variable: A constant value returned by useState that reflects the component data for the current render.
  • Setter Function: The update function returned by useState that records a requested value in React and schedules a future render.
  • Closure: A JavaScript function that retains access to variables from its defining lexical scope, even when executed at a later time.
  • Substitution Method: The mental debugging technique of replacing state variables with their concrete render values to predict handler behavior.

Beyond the basics

  • Official React documentation on state snapshots: Comprehensive guide explaining how rendering captures snapshots of UI and event handlers (see react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot).
  • Official guide on queueing state updates: In-depth explanation of update queues and updater functions for chaining state transitions (see react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates).
  • Reference documentation for useState: API reference detailing setter caveats, timing, and troubleshooting for old values in logs (see react.dev/reference/react/useState).
  • Rules of React on component purity: Technical rules detailing why props and state must remain immutable during rendering (see react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Declarative State Snapshots

➔ ALWAYS treat state variables as immutable constants for the duration of a single render.

➔ NEVER expect a state setter call to modify the state variable in the currently executing code block.

➔ IF an event handler needs to use an updated value immediately THEN compute the next value once in a local variable before calling the setter.

DO THIS: compute next value once and pass to setter and tracker

code.txt
1function handleRate() {
2 const nextRating = 5;
3 setRating(nextRating);
4 sendAnalytics(nextRating);
5}

DO NOT DO THIS: read state variable immediately after calling setter

code.txt
1function handleRate() {
2 setRating(5);
3 sendAnalytics(rating);
4}
❒ Event Handler Closures & Timing

➔ ALWAYS expect event handlers and timers to capture the state snapshot from the render that created them.

➔ NEVER assume delayed callbacks or code after await will automatically see future state values from subsequent renders.

➔ IF multiple updates must chain together in a single handler THEN use an updater function in Lecture 17.
