Controlled Inputs

Interview Question   CORE

How do you make an input, textarea, or select fully controlled by React state?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You call setText('') after submit, but the old text remains stuck in the textarea.
  • 2 You switch to value={text}, but the field refuses every keystroke while logging a read-only warning.
  • 3 How do you make an input, textarea, or select fully controlled by React state?

The form field keeps its own text, but React state stays out of sync

Today we learn how React form fields bind directly to component memory, why native HTML habits cause fields to freeze or refuse to clear, and how to control text inputs, textareas, selects, and checkboxes cleanly with state.

In modern frontend web applications, user interfaces collect information through interactive forms. Users type search queries, submit feedback comments, choose options from dropdown menus, and toggle confirmation checkboxes. In plain HTML, form fields own their internal text, and scripts inspect the DOM only after submission. In React, this imperative model causes state and the screen to drift out of sync. When an application needs to clear fields after submission, validate text length on the fly, or populate defaults dynamically, the component must become the single source of truth. By binding the field's displayed value to a React state variable through value and updating that state synchronously on every keystroke through onChange, the form control becomes fully controlled. State drives what appears on screen, and clearing state immediately flushes the field.

When engineers transition from vanilla HTML scripting to React, they naturally carry over habits from native form elements. In HTML, a developer writes <textarea>Starting text</textarea> or <input value="Default">, expecting the browser to manage user keystrokes independently while JavaScript reads the field value on submit. In React, passing defaultValue sets the initial text once at mount, after which the DOM node retains its own independent memory. When an event handler later updates a state variable with setText(''), a defaultValue field completely ignores the new state, leaving stale text on screen while counters reset to zero. Conversely, developers who hear that React needs value={text} often supply value without an onChange handler, inadvertently locking the field so it refuses every keystroke while the console logs a read-only warning. Furthermore, checkboxes require checked rather than value, dropdowns require value on the <select> rather than selected on an <option>, and text state must never start as undefined.

This chapter investigates six core questions. Why does calling a state setter fail to clear an input that uses defaultValue? Why does assigning value without an onChange handler freeze the field completely? Why must the onChange handler store exactly what was typed synchronously, rather than modifying or delaying the text? Why does a checkbox require the checked prop and e.target.checked rather than value and e.target.value? Where must the value prop be declared when controlling a select dropdown or textarea? Why does initializing a state variable with useState() trigger an uncontrolled-to-controlled warning on the first keystroke?

Later lessons build directly on these controlled form fundamentals. Lecture 21 explores reacting to input with state, demonstrating how to disable buttons and toggle loading spinners based on form status flags. Lecture 30 introduces DOM refs for imperative operations like focusing an input, while Lecture 39 investigates uncontrolled forms with FormData.

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): State acts as the single source of truth for the user interface, eliminating contradictory component memory.
  • Lecture 4 (JSX expressions): JSX embeds dynamic values in curly braces, and null or undefined evaluate to empty content.
  • Lecture 6 (Component props): Props pass read-only data into components, and nullish coalescing (??) provides safe fallbacks.
  • Lecture 10 (Conditional rendering): JavaScript evaluates truthy and falsy values when determining conditional display logic.
  • Lecture 13 (Event handling): Event handlers receive synthetic event objects (e), call e.preventDefault(), and forms submit via buttons by default.
  • Lecture 14 (Component memory with useState): The useState hook returns a state variable and a setter function that schedules component re-renders.
  • Lecture 15 (Render and commit): React diffs element trees during render and applies only minimal DOM mutations during the commit phase.
  • Lecture 16 (State snapshots): State variables remain fixed constants within a single render, and setTimeout executes callbacks asynchronously.
  • Lecture 18 (Updating objects in state): Form state objects pair input name attributes with state keys using [e.target.name]: e.target.value

Controlled versus uncontrolled form inputs

In Lecture 13, we learned how event handlers capture user interactions, and in Lecture 14, we learned how useState provides a setter that schedules a future render. In Lecture 18, we saw a preview of form inputs where value and onChange were wired to state properties. Today we unpack the exact mechanics of that binding.

In React, form elements operate in one of two distinct modes: uncontrolled or controlled. An uncontrolled field uses defaultValue="initial" (or defaultChecked for checkboxes). React populates the DOM element once when it mounts, after which the browser's internal DOM node manages all subsequent typing and state. If your component updates a state variable later, the uncontrolled DOM node ignores it. In contrast, a controlled field explicitly binds its displayed text to React state via value={text}. On every keystroke, React's synthetic onChange event fires immediately, behaving like the native browser input event rather than the native change event, which only fires after the user leaves the field. The handler calls setText(e.target.value), React re-renders the component, and the commit phase writes the new state value back into the DOM element. Because React drives the field on every render, state is the single source of truth. Clearing state programmatically with setText('') immediately flushes the visible text from the screen.

Uncontrolled Versus Controlled Form Fields
1<textarea defaultValue="Initial note" />
Uncontrolled: browser keeps text; setting state does not clear it
Uncontrolled field
2
3<textarea
Controlled: React state drives field; setting state flushes DOM
4 value={text}
State is single source of truth
5 onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)}
Synchronous state write
6/>

The difference between uncontrolled and controlled form fields centers on three core concepts:

  1. uncontrolled input: a form element whose value is managed internally by the browser DOM node.
  2. defaultValue: a prop that sets the initial field value once at mount without controlling subsequent renders.
  3. controlled input: an input driven by React state via value and updated on every keystroke via onChange.
  4. single source of truth: an architectural invariant where component state dictates exactly what appears on screen.

Synchronous input updates and the text caret

In Lecture 16, we saw that calling a state setter queues a render rather than mutating variables in place, and that setTimeout defers execution until the browser's event loop clears. When managing text inputs, timing and value fidelity become critical to cursor stability.

When a user types into a text input, the browser places the new character at the active cursor position and advances the text caret immediately. In a controlled field, React must synchronize this DOM mutation with component state. If your onChange handler stores an altered string, such as calling e.target.value.toUpperCase(), the text that React renders back into the DOM differs from what the browser natively inserted. When React overwrites the element's value with a modified string, the browser loses track of the user's cursor position and jumps the caret to the very end of the input. If the user was editing text in the middle of a word, their next keystroke lands erroneously at the end of the line. Similarly, if a developer attempts to defer setText inside a setTimeout, React writes the old state back to the DOM before the timer fires, causing fast typing to scramble characters. To preserve seamless caret navigation, onChange must update state synchronously with the exact, unmodified string from e.target.value. Formatting should occur during render display or upon final submission.

Synchronous Event Handling and Caret Stability
1function handleTitleChange(e) {
Correct: stores raw typed text synchronously; cursor position stays stable
2 setTitle(e.target.value);
Caret remains at current edit position
3}
4
5function handleBrokenTitleChange(e) {
Broken: uppercasing during typing forces the caret to jump to the end
6 setTitle(e.target.value.toUpperCase());
Caret jumps to end on keystroke
7}

Managing the text caret during controlled typing introduces three essential concepts:

  1. text caret: the blinking cursor indicating where typed characters appear in an editable field.
  2. synchronous state update: calling the state setter immediately inside the event handler without delay.
  3. caret jump: cursor displacement to the end of a field caused by overwriting DOM text with an altered string.

Checkbox boolean bindings and select value props

In Lecture 4, we learned that JSX expressions evaluate JavaScript variables directly, and in Lecture 6, we learned that passing undefined causes React to fall back to default behavior. When dealing with form elements, undefined carries a specific structural consequence.

Different HTML form elements require specialized prop pairings. A checkbox does not track state through value; in native HTML, an input checkbox has a default value="on". If you write onChange={e => setAgreed(e.target.value)} e.target.value evaluates to the string "on" regardless of whether the box was ticked or unticked. Because "on" is a non-empty string, JavaScript evaluates it as truthy. Passing e.target.value to setAgreed stores "on" on the first click and stores "on" again on the second click. The checkbox remains checked permanently. Checkboxes and radio buttons must pair the checked boolean prop with e.target.checked. Similarly, dropdown menus in React do not set selected on individual <option> elements. Setting <option selected> logs a console error; instead, React declares value={selectedOption} directly on the parent <select> element. Finally, text inputs must never initialize with useState() or undefined. When an input receives value={undefined}, React treats it as an uncontrolled field. When the user types their first letter and state becomes a string, React suddenly switches the input to controlled, logging an error: "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled." Always initialize text fields with an empty string useState('') or provide a fallback value={text ?? ''}.

Form Field Bindings and String Initialization
1<input type="checkbox" checked={on} onChange={e => setOn(e.target.checked)} />
Checkbox: binds checked and reads boolean e.target.checked
2
3<select value={topic} onChange={e => setTopic(e.target.value)}>
Select: declares value on select element
4 <option value="billing">Billing</option>
5</select>
6
7const [title, setTitle] = useState('');
Starts with empty string

Form element specialization requires understanding four foundational concepts:

  1. checked: a boolean prop governing the visual checkmark state of checkboxes and radio buttons.
  2. e.target.checked: the boolean property reporting whether an input element is currently ticked.
  3. select value: the container prop on <select> matching the active option's value.
  4. uncontrolled-to-controlled warning a console error triggered when an input switches from undefined to a string.

Principles of React: Controlled Inputs

QUESTION 1

Calling a state setter fails to clear a textarea with defaultValue

A developer builds a feedback submission component called FeedbackForm. To collect suggestions, the developer declares a textarea initialized with defaultValue="" and updates a local state variable text on each keystroke to display a live character counter:

FeedbackForm.jsx, defaultValue attempt
12 function handleClear() {
13 setText('');
Re-renders character counter to 0/280
14 }
15 return (
16 <form onSubmit={handleClear}>
17 <textarea defaultValue="" onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
18 <span>{text.length}/280 characters</span>
19 </form>
20 );

The user types "Fix the date" into the box. The counter displays "12/280 characters". When the user clicks the submit button, handleClear runs, calling setText(''). The character counter updates to "0/280 characters", but the textarea on screen continues displaying "Fix the date".

After Send, I call setText(''). The counter says 0/280, but the old text stays in the box. Why?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A field with defaultValue sets its text only once at mount, after which the browser DOM manages its text independently of React state.

When you pass defaultValue="" to a form element, React instructs the browser to populate the initial DOM node with that value when the element mounts. After mount, the DOM node maintains its own internal text memory. Each keystroke triggers onChange, which calls setText(e.target.value). That state setter writes the string into React state, allowing the counter to read text.length during rendering.

When the submit handler calls setText(''), React schedules a re-render. During the render pass, the counter evaluates text.length as zero, so the screen renders "0/280 characters". However, because the textarea uses defaultValue, nothing instructs React to synchronize the DOM element with the new state value. React compares the JSX element, notices defaultValue is an initial-mount instruction, and leaves the existing DOM node completely untouched.

Uncontrolled DefaultValue Versus Controlled Value
[setText('')] -> React schedules render
      |
      v
Counter renders 0/280 from state
      |
      v
Textarea uses defaultValue="" (mount only)
      |
      v
[DOM node untouched] -> Screen keeps showing "Fix the date"

To make state drive the textarea after every render, you must replace defaultValue with value={text}. When value is present, React's commit phase writes the state string back into the DOM element on every render, ensuring that calling setText('') empties the box immediately.

PRINCIPLE 1

A controlled field shows what is in state, after every render

defaultValue sets only the initial text when the field mounts; the browser keeps subsequent edits

A field with defaultValue sets its initial text once at mount; after that, the browser keeps the field's own text, so setting state does not change it. A controlled field takes its displayed text directly from React state through value. Each keystroke calls onChange, the handler writes the new text into state, and React writes state back into the field after every render. Because state is the single source of truth, whatever is in state is what the field shows, and clearing state clears the field.

We should do this:
``jsx right
<textarea value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
value drives the textarea from state; setText('') empties it
`
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
<textarea defaultValue="" onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
defaultValue leaves field uncontrolled; setText('') does not clear it
`
QUESTION 2

Assigning value without an onChange handler freezes the input

Having learned that value binds the textarea to state, the developer changes the input to value={text}, but removes the onChange handler, assuming that the browser will let the user type naturally while React reads the value on submit:

FeedbackForm.jsx, missing onChange
10 const [text, setText] = useState('');
11 return (
12 <form>
13 <textarea value={text} />
Missing onChange handler
14 </form>
15 );

The user clicks into the textarea and attempts to type "Hello". No letters appear in the box, the field appears completely frozen, and the browser console logs an error warning that a value prop without onChange renders a read-only field.

I wrote value={text} and the box no longer takes any typing. What broke?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Supplying a value prop makes an input controlled, so without an onChange handler to update state, React overwrites every keystroke with the existing state string.

In React, passing a string to the value prop transforms the input into a controlled component. When the user presses a key on their keyboard, the browser's native engine inserts the typed character into the DOM node for a fraction of a millisecond.

However, because there is no onChange handler to capture the event and call setText, component state remains fixed at its initial value (''). React immediately reconciles the DOM element against the JSX value={text}, notices that the DOM node contains a character while state specifies '', and writes '' back into the DOM element. The typed character vanishes instantly before the user can see it.

Read-Only Reversion on Missing OnChange
User presses key -> Browser DOM receives character
      |
      v
No onChange handler -> Component state remains ''
      |
      v
React reconciles: state ('') !== DOM (char)
      |
      v
[React writes '' back to DOM] -> Character disappears instantly

React detects this contradiction and prints an explicit diagnostic error: "You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler. This will render a read-only field. If the field should be mutable use defaultValue. Otherwise, set either onChange or readOnly." To keep the field editable, you must supply an onChange handler that writes e.target.value into state.

PRINCIPLE 2

Pair every value with an onChange that sets state

readOnly marks a field as intentionally immutable without an onChange handler

Passing a string value makes a form field controlled. Each keystroke changes the field for a moment, but with no onChange handler, nothing stores the new text into state. React writes the existing state value back into the field on render, causing the keystroke to disappear while logging an error advising to set readOnly. If a field should accept user edits, pair its value with an onChange handler that updates state.

We should do this:
``jsx right
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />
onChange updates state on each keystroke, keeping the field editable
`
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
<input value={name} />
value without onChange freezes the field and logs a console error
`
QUESTION 3

Modifying text inside onChange causes the cursor caret to jump

The developer wants headline titles to always appear in uppercase letters. Rather than applying a styling rule, the developer uppercases the text directly inside the onChange event handler:

FeedbackForm.jsx, uppercase in onChange
14 function handleTitleChange(e) {
15 setTitle(e.target.value.toUpperCase());
Stores uppercased text
16 }
17 return <input value={title} onChange={handleTitleChange} />;

The user types "fix the date". Then the user clicks between "fix " and "the" to insert "xy". As soon as the user presses "x", the cursor unexpectedly jumps to the end of the input, and pressing "y" lands at the end of the string, producing "FIX XTHE DATEY".

Headlines are all caps. Can my onChange store e.target.value.toUpperCase()?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Overwriting an input with a modified string causes the browser to lose the user's cursor position, jumping the text caret to the end of the field.

When a user types a letter into an input field, the browser native engine inserts the character at the active cursor position and advances the caret one space forward. When handleTitleChange executes, it receives e.target.value (for example, "fix xthe date"). The handler calls toUpperCase(), storing "FIX XTHE DATE" in React state.

When React re-renders the component and commits the changes, it writes "FIX XTHE DATE" into the input's value property. Because this string does not match what the browser natively placed in the input (lowercase "x" replaced by uppercase "X"), the browser cannot preserve the cursor position within the modified text. The browser defaults to placing the caret at the very end of the input string. When the user types the next character ("y"), that character is inserted at the end of the line.

Caret Jump Displacement on Modified String
User types 'x' in middle: "fix xthe date"
      |
      v
onChange stores uppercased: "FIX XTHE DATE"
      |
      v
React writes modified string -> Browser caret jumps to end
      |
      v
Next letter 'y' typed at end -> "FIX XTHE DATEY"

A similar bug occurs if you wrap state updates in setTimeout. React writes the old state back to the DOM before the timer fires, causing fast typing to drop or scramble characters. You must store e.target.value synchronously and without transformation. If you want uppercase presentation, use CSS text-transform: uppercase, or transform the string upon form submission.

PRINCIPLE 3

Store exactly what was typed, right away

caret the blinking cursor that indicates where the next typed letter lands

When a user types, the browser advances the cursor to the next character position. If onChange stores a transformed string or defers state inside a timer, React writes a value back to the DOM that differs from what the browser received. Overwriting the input resets the cursor position, sending the text caret to the end of the field and scrambling subsequent keystrokes. Always store e.target.value synchronously and unmodified; format text during display or upon submission.

We should do this:
``jsx right
onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}
store raw typed string synchronously; format when displaying or saving
`
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
onChange={e => setName(e.target.value.toUpperCase())}
transforming or delaying the typed value moves the caret to the end
`
QUESTION 4

Reading e.target.value on a checkbox permanently locks it to checked

The developer adds an "urgent" checkbox to flag priority feedback. State variable isUrgent starts as false. The developer binds checked to isUrgent but reads e.target.value in onChange:

FeedbackForm.jsx, checkbox reading value
20 return (
21 <label>
22 <input
23 type="checkbox"
24 checked={isUrgent}
25 onChange={e => setIsUrgent(e.target.value)}
Reads string value
26 />
27 Mark as urgent ({String(isUrgent)})
28 </label>
29 );

The user clicks the checkbox once. The checkbox becomes ticked, and the label displays "Mark as urgent (on)". The user clicks the checkbox a second time to uncheck it, but the checkbox remains stubbornly ticked and the label still displays "Mark as urgent (on)".

For the urgent checkbox, do I write value and e.target.value, like the text fields?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. A checkbox does not report boolean status through value; e.target.value returns the string "on", which is truthy, so the checkbox can never be unchecked.

In native HTML, a checkbox's value attribute specifies the data value submitted with the form when the checkbox is checked. If no value attribute is explicitly assigned, the browser assigns it a default value of "on". Crucially, clicking a checkbox does not change its value property; e.target.value returns "on" on every single click, whether the user is checking or unchecking the box.

Because "on" is a non-empty string, JavaScript evaluates it as truthy. When the user clicks the checkbox the first time, setIsUrgent("on") stores "on" in state, rendering checked={true}. When the user clicks the checkbox a second time, e.target.value is still "on". React receives "on", evaluates it as truthy, and renders checked={true} again. The checkbox becomes permanently locked in the checked state.

Checkbox Target Value Versus Target Checked
[First Click: Tick Box]
e.target.value === "on"      ---> setIsUrgent("on")     ---> checked={true}
      |
      v
[Second Click: Untick Box]
e.target.value === "on"      ---> setIsUrgent("on")     ---> checked={true}
      |
      v
e.target.checked === false   ---> setIsUrgent(false)    ---> checked={false}

To control a checkbox or a radio button, you must bind the checked boolean prop and read the boolean property e.target.checked. The property e.target.checked accurately returns true when the box is checked and false when it is unticked.

PRINCIPLE 4

A checkbox uses checked, and its handler reads e.target.checked

e.target.checked the boolean property indicating whether a checkbox is ticked

A checkbox displays its visual state through the boolean checked prop. In HTML, a checkbox's value attribute defaults to the string "on", so reading e.target.value yields "on" on every click. Because non-empty strings are truthy, storing e.target.value permanently locks the checkbox to checked. Always bind checked to state and read e.target.checked, which provides a clean boolean true or false on every toggle.

We should do this:
``jsx right
<input
checked prop with e.target.checked stores true or false accurately
type="checkbox"
checked={agree}
onChange={e => setAgree(e.target.checked)}
/>
`
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
<input
e.target.value returns "on" every time, so the box never unchecks
type="checkbox"
checked={agree}
onChange={e => setAgree(e.target.value)}
/>
`
QUESTION 5

Setting selected on an option triggers a console warning

The developer adds a category selection dropdown. Relying on standard HTML syntax, the developer marks the default option with the boolean selected attribute:

FeedbackForm.jsx, option selected

23 return (
24 <select onChange={e => setCategory(e.target.value)}>
25 <option value="general">General</option>
26 <option value="support" selected>Support</option>
HTML habit
27 </select>
28 );

When the page loads, the browser console prints an error warning: "Use the defaultValue or value props on <select> instead of setting selected on <option>." Furthermore, when the user clicks a reset button that calls setCategory('general'), the dropdown fails to switch to "General Feedback".

In HTML I mark the default section with selected on its <option>. Do I do the same here?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. React does not support selected on an <option>; dropdown values must be controlled via value on the parent <select> element.

In native HTML, setting <option selected> indicates which item should be initially chosen in a dropdown menu. In React's declarative architecture, form state belongs on the container element that manages user selection, rather than scattered across child option tags.

When React encounters selected on an <option>, it rejects the attribute and prints a console error. Because the <select> tag itself has no value prop, React treats the dropdown as an uncontrolled element. When an event handler calls setCategory('general'), React updates component state, but the <select> DOM element ignores the update and remains stuck on whatever option the user previously picked.

Option Selected Versus Select Value Container
<option selected>           ---> Rejected by React; logs console error
      |
      v
<select> lacks value prop   ---> Dropdown is uncontrolled; ignores state updates
      |
      v
<select value={category}>   ---> React selects matching option automatically

To control a dropdown menu in React, declare value={category} directly on the <select> element, along with an onChange handler that updates state with e.target.value. React inspects the child options and automatically highlights whichever <option> has a value matching the state variable. Similarly, a <textarea> must not place text between opening and closing tags; its content belongs in value.

PRINCIPLE 5

Put value on the field itself, not on an option or between tags

select value selects the matching option declaratively from state

In React, dropdown selection is controlled on the container <select> element, not on individual <option> tags. Setting selected on an <option> logs a console error and breaks state control. Declare value={choice} on the <select> tag, and React automatically selects the matching option. Similarly, write a <textarea> as a self-closing tag with value, never placing child text between <textarea> tags.

We should do this:
``jsx right
<select value={choice} onChange={e => setChoice(e.target.value)}>
select value matches the active option value without touching options
<option value="one">First Option</option>
<option value="two">Second Option</option>
</select>
`
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
<select onChange={e => setChoice(e.target.value)}>
selected on an option logs a console error and breaks state control
<option value="one">First Option</option>
<option value="two" selected>Second Option</option>
</select>
`
QUESTION 6

Starting state with useState() triggers an uncontrolled-to-controlled warning

The developer prepares the form to receive an initial title asynchronously from a remote server. Because the title is not available immediately when the component mounts, the developer initializes state without an argument:

FeedbackForm.jsx, undefined initial state
8 const [title, setTitle] = useState();
Initializes state to undefined
9 return (
10 <input
11 value={title}
12 onChange={e => setTitle(e.target.value)}
13 />
14 );

When the form first renders, the input appears empty. When the user clicks into the field and types the letter "F", the console logs an error warning: "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled. This is likely caused by the value changing from undefined to a defined value, which should not happen."

The headline will come from the server later, so I wrote useState(). Is that fine?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Initializing state with useState() sets the variable to undefined, causing the input to mount uncontrolled before switching to controlled on the first keystroke.

In JavaScript, declaring useState() without an initial value sets the state variable to undefined. When React evaluates <input value={title} /> during initial mount, value={undefined} tells React that no controlled value is being supplied. React concludes that this input is uncontrolled, and lets the browser manage the field.

When the user types the first character, onChange fires and calls setTitle("F"). On the next render, title is now a string. When React reconciles the element, it finds that an input that mounted as uncontrolled now has a defined string value. In React's architecture, an input element must remain either strictly controlled or strictly uncontrolled throughout its entire lifecycle.

Lifecycle Shift from Uncontrolled to Controlled
useState() initializes title = undefined
      |
      v
Initial render: <input value={undefined} /> mounts UNCONTROLLED
      |
      v
User types 'F' -> setTitle("F") schedules render
      |
      v
Next render: <input value="F" /> switches to CONTROLLED (LOGS ERROR)

Switching control mode mid-lifecycle can cause subtle rendering bugs where browser DOM state conflicts with React state. Always initialize text input state with an empty string: useState(''). If the value might arrive asynchronously as null or undefined, provide a safe fallback using nullish coalescing: value={title ?? ''}.

PRINCIPLE 6

Start every value as a string

nullish coalescing ?? falls back to empty string when state is null or undefined

Passing value={undefined} makes React mount the element as an uncontrolled input. When the user types the first letter, state updates to a string, causing the input to switch suddenly from uncontrolled to controlled. React logs a console error because an input must maintain a stable control mode throughout its lifecycle. Always initialize text state with an empty string useState(''), or provide a nullish coalescing fallback with value={text ?? ''}.

We should do this:
``jsx right
const [title, setTitle] = useState('');
initialize with empty string so the field stays controlled from mount
`
or provide a fallback: value={title ?? ''}
We should not do this:
``jsx wrong
const [title, setTitle] = useState();
undefined makes field uncontrolled; subsequent typing triggers warning
`

Component Summary

App

The application shell hosts the feedback manager without owning interactive state, keeping the layout stable.

FeedbackForm

The form boundary owns the four controlled field states and coordinates validation and submission.

FormControlsonClear={handleClear}

The action controls render submission and reset buttons, forwarding user clicks upward.

Where you will meet this

In production frontend applications, controlled form inputs are universal across user authentication screens, search filters, checkout forms, and profile editors. A frequent production bug occurs when an engineer implements a "Clear Form" button that resets component state, only to discover that uncontrolled fields retaining defaultValue stubbornly hold user text on screen. Adopting value paired with onChange guarantees programmatic synchronization.

Another common production bug occurs when teams connect forms to asynchronous APIs where initial user data loads after the component mounts. Initializing state with useState() leaves the field undefined, triggering uncontrolled-to-controlled console warnings that degrade test suites and user experience. Initializing with useState('') or using value={data?.title ?? ''} eliminates this issue permanently.

In technical interviews, candidates are routinely asked how controlled components work under the hood. Interviewers specifically probe whether candidates understand why React's onChange fires on every single keystroke rather than on blur, why checkboxes require e.target.checked instead of e.target.value, and how transforming strings inside onChange disrupts the browser text caret.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you make an input, textarea, or select fully controlled by React state?

A senior response breaks the explanation into four architectural beats:

1. The Single Source of Truth

In React, a controlled component derives its displayed value entirely from state via props: value for text inputs, textareas, and selects, or checked for checkboxes and radio buttons. The component pairs this prop with an onChange handler that captures user interaction and writes the new value into state. State becomes the single source of truth: whatever exists in state is what the DOM renders, and setting state to an empty string programmatically flushes the field.

2. Synchronous Keystroke Updates

React synthetic onChange events fire on every single keystroke, behaving like the native browser input event rather than the native change event, which waits until blur. The onChange handler must store e.target.value synchronously and without transformation. If a handler attempts to uppercase text or delay updates inside setTimeout, React writes a modified string back to the DOM, causing the browser to lose cursor tracking and jump the text caret to the end of the line.

3. Element Specialization: Checkboxes and Selects

Different HTML form elements require specialized property bindings. A checkbox displays its visual state via checked={boolean} and reports changes through e.target.checked; reading e.target.value yields the static string "on", which is truthy and locks the checkbox permanently. Dropdown menus declare value={choice} directly on the parent <select> container rather than setting selected on an <option>, allowing React to match the active option declaratively.

4. Initial Value Guarantees

A controlled text input must maintain a stable control mode throughout its entire lifecycle. Initializing state with useState() sets the variable to undefined, mounting the input as uncontrolled. When the user types their first character, state becomes a string, triggering an uncontrolled-to-controlled console warning. Always initialize text inputs with an empty string useState('') or provide a nullish fallback value={text ?? ''}.

Glossary

  • Controlled Input: A form element whose displayed value is driven by React state and whose changes update that state.
  • Uncontrolled Input: A form element whose value is managed internally by the browser DOM node.
  • Single Source of Truth: The architectural model where one state variable determines what appears on screen.
  • Synthetic onChange: React's cross-browser event firing synchronously on every keystroke like native input.
  • Text Caret: The blinking cursor that indicates where the next typed letter lands in an editable field.
  • defaultValue: A React prop that sets the initial text once at mount without controlling subsequent renders.
  • e.target.checked: The boolean property on a synthetic event reporting whether a checkbox is ticked.

Beyond the basics

  • Official React reference on textarea component: Comprehensive guide to controlled textareas, initial text caveats, and submission behavior (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/textarea).
  • Official React reference on select component: Documentation on controlled dropdown menus, multiple selection arrays, and option values (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/select).
  • Official guide on reacting to input with state: Architectural walkthrough showing how declarative state replaces imperative DOM manipulation (see react.dev/learn/reacting-to-input-with-state).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

➔ ALWAYS pair every value prop with an onChange handler that updates state synchronously.

➔ ALWAYS initialize text input state with an empty string useState('') to prevent uncontrolled warnings.

➔ IF controlling a checkbox or radio button THEN bind checked to boolean state and read e.target.checked.

➔ IF controlling a dropdown selection THEN declare value directly on <select> rather than selected on <option>.

➔ NEVER transform text inside onChange or defer updates in timers; format during display or upon submission.

9 </select>

11 type="checkbox"

13 onChange={e => setIsUrgent(e.target.checked)}
14 />
15 </form>
16);

21

Reacting to Input with State

Interview Question   CORE

How do you design a component that reacts to input with state instead of touching the DOM?

Imagine This Scenario

  • 1 You build a subscription paywall modal where users type a card number and click Subscribe.
  • 2 An imperative handler leaves "Payment failed" and "Welcome, subscriber" on screen together after a retry.
  • 3 How do you design a component that reacts to input with state instead of touching the DOM?

Imperative DOM commands leave conflicting messages on screen

Today we learn how React components react to user actions and network events using declarative state machines, why imperative DOM scripting leaves conflicting UI elements on screen, and how to model form lifecycles cleanly with a single status string.

In modern frontend web applications, user interfaces constantly react to user input and background network events. When a customer subscribes to a service, they type payment details, click a submit button, watch a loading indicator appear while the network request is in flight, and finally see either an error notification or a confirmation banner. In plain JavaScript, developers write imperative commands that modify the DOM element by element: disabling buttons, removing hidden classes, and toggling error styles. Each command changes the page step by step and stays there forever until another explicit command undoes it. If a single branch forgets to reset an element, contradictory elements remain visible simultaneously, displaying an error banner right alongside a welcome message. In React, we solve this synchronization breakdown by declaring visual states first, storing the active state in component memory, and letting JSX describe what each state displays. Event handlers never touch the DOM; they only set the next state.

When developers transition from vanilla JavaScript or jQuery to React, they often bring along imperative scripting habits. When an error occurs, an imperative handler queries the DOM to set errorText.style.display = 'block' When the user retries and the request succeeds, the success handler displays the welcome message, but forgets to hide the error container. The user ends up seeing "Payment failed" and "Welcome, subscriber" at the exact same time. The same defect appears when developers represent the form's lifecycle using three separate boolean state variables: isSubmitting, isSuccess, and isError. Three booleans allow eight distinct combinations, most of which represent impossible real-world states. When a retry succeeds and sets isSuccess to true without resetting isError back to false, the form renders both messages. React replaces both traps with a systematic design process: first, list every visual state; second, identify human and computer triggers; third, store the current state in a single status string.

This chapter investigates three core questions. Why does an imperative handler leave conflicting messages on screen after a retry, and how does JSX driven by status eliminate DOM commands? Where should component design begin: with the click handler, or by listing and mocking visual states before wiring triggers? Why do separate boolean flags create impossible states, and why does a single status string guarantee mutual exclusivity?

Later lessons deepen these state modeling patterns: Lecture 22 investigates choosing the right state structure and removing redundant state variables, while Lecture 26 introduces reducers for managing complex state transitions that depend on previous values.

  • Lecture 1 (What is React): Declarative code describes what the page shows, and React updates the DOM to match without manual element queries.
  • Lecture 5 (The UI Tree): Props flow downward from parent containers to child presentation components.
  • Lecture 6 (Component props): Components accept props with default parameter values to customize their rendering.
  • Lecture 10 (Conditional rendering): Logical AND (&&) operators and early returns render distinct markup based on truthy conditions.
  • Lecture 11 (Rendering lists): Array map() transforms items into JSX element lists with unique key attributes.
  • Lecture 13 (Event handling): Event handlers capture user actions like clicks and submits without executing during render.
  • Lecture 14 (Component memory with useState): The useState hook provides a state variable and a setter function that requests a re-render.
  • Lecture 15 (Render and commit): Calling a setter triggers a render, and React commits the minimal DOM mutations to the screen.
  • Lecture 17 (State updates): Asynchronous event handlers use async and await to coordinate state changes across network operations.
  • Lecture 18 (Updating objects in state): Form fields pair input names with state values using controlled handlers.
  • Lecture 20 (Controlled inputs): Form fields bind value to state and update on every keystroke via onChange, making state the single source of truth.

A component changes its screen across visual states

In Lecture 10, we learned how conditional rendering with early returns and logical AND operators controls what JSX appears on screen, and in Lecture 17, we learned how asynchronous event handlers use async and await to coordinate state changes during network operations. Today we combine those mechanics to model complete visual component states.

A visual state represents the complete visual appearance of a component at a specific moment in its lifecycle. A subscription form typically has four visual states: typing (the card input is editable and the Subscribe button is active), submitting (the input and button are disabled while a loading spinner spins), success (the form is replaced by a welcome message), and error (the button is active again and an error message is visible). The HTML disabled attribute prevents users from clicking buttons or typing into fields. In React, passing a boolean expression like <button disabled={status === 'submitting'}> binds button interactivity directly to state. When coordinating network requests, JavaScript provides try and catch blocks. An async handler runs code inside try, and if a network Promise rejects, execution immediately transfers to the catch block, allowing the component to transition cleanly from submitting to error.

Visual States and Disabled Handling
1async function handleSubmit(e) {
2 e.preventDefault();
3 setStatus('submitting');
Transitions to loading state
4 try {
5 await submitPayment(card);
6 setStatus('success');
Transitions to confirmation
7 } catch {
8 setStatus('error');
Transitions to error state
9 }
10}

The relationship between visual states, form buttons, and network handling involves three core concepts:

  1. visual state: the complete visual appearance of a component for a given state.
  2. disabled attribute: a boolean HTML attribute that prevents user interaction on buttons and inputs.
  3. try...catch: a JavaScript control structure that intercepts errors thrown during asynchronous operations.

Testing visual states with props before wiring triggers

In Lecture 6, we learned that components accept props with default values to configure their output, and in Lecture 11, we saw how array map() renders repeated items into an element list. In this section, we apply those mechanics to inspect every visual state before attaching interactive event handlers.

When developing a complex interactive component, writing event handlers first forces you to test screens by manually triggering every step in the browser. A more disciplined approach is to mock each visual state first. By accepting a status prop with a default value, such as function PaywallModal({ status = 'typing' }) an engineer can change the prop value by hand to verify how submitting, error, or success look without writing any network logic. In fact, rendering an array of statuses side by side with ['typing', 'submitting', 'error', 'success'].map(...) creates a living styleguide showing all four states simultaneously. Once the visual states are verified, you catalogue the triggers that move the component between them. Triggers divide into two categories: human inputs (such as typing into an input field or clicking a button) and computer inputs (such as an incoming network response or a timer firing). Each trigger becomes a single setStatus call in an event handler.

Mocking Visual States with Props
1export default function PaywallModal({ status = 'typing' }) {
2 if (status === 'success') return <p>Welcome, subscriber!</p>;
3 return (
4 <form>
5 <button disabled={status === 'submitting'}>Subscribe</button>
6 {status === 'error' && <p>Payment failed</p>}
Error banner
7 </form>
8 );
9}

The process of mocking visual states and identifying transitions relies on four foundational concepts:

  1. mock: a visual preview rendered with static props to verify UI layout before attaching logic.
  2. living styleguide: rendering multiple visual states simultaneously side by side for visual auditing.
  3. human inputs: user interactions such as keystrokes, button clicks, and form submissions.
  4. computer inputs: system events such as network responses resolving, promises rejecting, and timeouts firing.

One status string prevents impossible states

In Lecture 14, we learned how useState stores component values across renders. Developers often create a boolean state variable for each piece of UI they need to toggle, which works well for independent flags but fails when states are mutually exclusive.

When a component can exist in only one visual mode at a time, representing those modes with separate boolean flags invites critical bugs. For example, using isSubmitting, isSuccess, and isError creates $2^3 = 8$ possible combinations. A state where isError === true and isSuccess === true is an impossible state: a screen cannot logically show a payment failure banner and a subscriber welcome message at the same time. If a retry handler sets setIsSuccess(true) but forgets to call setIsError(false), the component enters this impossible state. Using a single status string state variable with 'typing' | 'submitting' | 'success' | 'error' makes impossible states mathematically impossible, because a string variable can hold exactly one value at any moment. Values that change independently, such as user input (card) or dynamic error messages (error), remain separate state variables alongside status.

Single Status String Versus Multiple Booleans
1const [status, setStatus] = useState('typing');
Single string guarantees mutual exclusivity
One active mode
2const [card, setCard] = useState('');
3
4const [isSubmitting, setIsSubmitting] = useState(false);
Multiple booleans allow contradictory combinations
5const [isSuccess, setIsSuccess] = useState(false);
Can conflict
6const [isError, setIsError] = useState(false);

Representing form states cleanly without combinatorial errors centers on three core concepts:

  1. impossible state: a contradictory combination of state values that causes the UI to render broken or conflicting elements.
  2. single status string: a state variable holding a string enum that guarantees only one visual state is active at a time.
  3. independent state: state variables that change autonomously, such as input field values or error details, kept separate from status.

Principles of React: Reacting to Input with State

QUESTION 1

A successful retry shows the error and welcome messages together

A developer builds a subscription paywall modal where users type a card number and click Subscribe. To handle user interactions, the developer uses imperative DOM scripting, manually finding elements and modifying their styles and properties:

PaywallModal.jsx, imperative attempt
1function handleSubmit(e) {
2 e.preventDefault();
3 document.querySelector('#btn').disabled = true;
Disables button
4 submitPayment(card).then(() => {
5 document.querySelector('#welcome').style.display = 'block';
6 }).catch(() => {
7 document.querySelector('#error').style.display = 'block';
Shows error
8 });
9}

On the first attempt, the payment network request fails. The catch callback runs, and the browser displays "Payment failed". The user corrects their card number and clicks Subscribe a second time. This time the payment succeeds, and the then callback runs. On screen, the modal now displays "Payment failed" and "Welcome, subscriber" simultaneously.

My Subscribe handler disables the button, shows the spinner, and hides the error. Why does the form end up showing "Payment failed" and "Welcome, subscriber" together?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Direct DOM edits stay on the page until another line manually undoes them.

In imperative programming, every command given to the browser changes the DOM directly, and each change remains in place indefinitely. On the first payment attempt, the request failed, so the catch handler executed document.querySelector('#error').style.display = 'block' That line made the error banner visible. On the second attempt, the request succeeded, so the then handler executed document.querySelector('#welcome').style.display = 'block' That line made the welcome message visible. However, because no line in the success path instructed the browser to hide the error banner, the error element remained visible.

React never sees these manual DOM mutations. React does not inspect element styles or query DOM nodes to decide what belongs on screen. When an imperative handler modifies the DOM behind React's back, state and the screen drift out of sync.

To fix this problem, you must remove all direct DOM commands from your event handlers. Instead of telling the browser how to change the page step by step, you describe what the screen displays for each visual state in JSX. You store the current state in a React state variable named status. Your event handlers only call setStatus('submitting'), setStatus('success'), or setStatus('error'). React re-renders the component and updates the DOM to match the JSX for that status. When status transitions to 'success', React unmounts the form and renders only the welcome message, making it physically impossible for the error message to remain visible.

Imperative DOM edits vs declarative status render
Attempt 1 (Fail):
  Imperative: error.style.display = 'block' -> [Payment failed] visible
  Declarative: setStatus('error')           -> renders error JSX

Attempt 2 (Retry Success):
  Imperative: welcome.style.display = 'block' (forgot to hide error!)
              Screen shows: [Payment failed] AND [Welcome, subscriber]
  Declarative: setStatus('success')
              Screen shows: ONLY [Welcome, subscriber]
PRINCIPLE 1

Describe what each status shows, and let handlers only set the status

visual state a distinct screen appearance determined by component data

Imperative commands tell the browser how to change the page step by step, and each change stays until another command undoes it. If a success branch forgets to hide an earlier error, both messages remain on screen together. In React, JSX declares what the screen shows for each visual state, and event handlers only update state. When state changes, React re-renders the component and updates the DOM to match the JSX, so conflicting elements never share the screen.

We should do this:
function Form({ status, setStatus }) {
if (status === 'success') {
return <p>Action complete</p>;
shows only success message
}
return (
<form onSubmit={() => setStatus('loading')}>
<button disabled={status === 'loading'}>Submit</button>
{status === 'error' && <p>Action failed</p>}
</form>
);
}
We should not do this:
function handleSubmit() {
document.querySelector('#status').textContent = 'Loading...';
sendRequest()
.then(() => {
document.querySelector('#success').style.display = 'block';
})
forgot to hide #error, so both messages stay visible
.catch(() => {
document.querySelector('#error').style.display = 'block';
});
}
QUESTION 2

Listing visual states comes before writing event handlers

A developer begins building the subscription modal by immediately writing the submission event handler, attempting to wire button clicks and network requests before establishing what screens the form can display:

PaywallModal.jsx, starting from handlers
1function PaywallModal() {
2 const [card, setCard] = useState('');
Card input state
3 async function handleSubscribe(e) {
4 e.preventDefault();
5 await submitPayment(card);
Network request
6 }
7 return <form onSubmit={handleSubscribe}><button>Subscribe</button></form>;
8}

The developer is unsure how to handle loading spinners, error banners, and success confirmations, and must constantly click the button and trigger mock network errors to test UI layouts.

Where do I start? Do I write the Subscribe handler first?

ANSWER

The code works. However, starting from event handlers makes it hard to see every visual state before writing logic.

When you start building a component from its event handlers outward, you are forced to test your user interface by clicking buttons, filling fields, and triggering real or mocked network failures in the browser. This makes development slow and error-prone because edge-case visual states, such as a network timeout or a validation failure, are difficult to reproduce repeatedly on demand.

Idiomatic React development inverts this workflow by designing from the screen inward across four structured steps:

  1. List the visual states: Write down every distinct visual screen the user can encounter. For a subscription modal, these are typing (the initial editable form), submitting (disabled inputs with an active spinner), success (a confirmation message), and error (the editable form displaying an error banner).
  2. Mock each visual state with props: Implement the JSX for each state inside the component, accepting a status prop with a default value like status = 'typing'. By manually editing the prop or rendering all states side by side with statuses.map(...), you can audit and polish every screen before writing a single line of business logic.
  3. Catalogue human and computer triggers: Identify every event that causes the component to change state. Human triggers include typing in a text field, clicking a submit button, or pressing reset. Computer triggers include a network response arriving, an API call rejecting, or a timer completing.
  4. Connect event handlers: Finally, implement event handlers that call setStatus to transition the component from its current visual state to the next state when a trigger fires.
Visual states and input trigger transitions
[ TYPING ] <----------- [ User types / retries ] ----------+
       |                                                     |
[ Click Subscribe ]                                          |
       v                                                     |
 [ SUBMITTING ] ---> [ Network reject ] ---> [ ERROR ] ------+
       |
[ Network resolve ]
       v
  [ SUCCESS ]
PRINCIPLE 2

List the visual states first, then what moves the form between them

mock a visual demonstration rendered with static props before adding logic

A component that reacts to input is built from the screen inward, not from the handlers outward. First, list every screen the user can see: empty, typing, submitting, success, and error. Second, mock each visual state with a status prop to verify its markup before writing logic. Third, list the human and computer triggers that cause transitions. Finally, wire event handlers that call setStatus to connect those triggers to the visual states.

We should do this:
function Form({ status = 'empty' }) {
if (status === 'success') {
return <p>Success message</p>;
renders success screen
}
return (
<form>
<input disabled={status === 'submitting'} />
<button disabled={status === 'submitting'}>Submit</button>
{status === 'error' && <p>Error message</p>}
</form>
);
}
QUESTION 3

Separate boolean flags allow conflicting states to show together

A developer decides to manage the subscription modal's visual states using three boolean state variables:

PaywallModal.jsx, three booleans attempt
1function handleSubscribe() {
2 setIsSubmitting(true);
3 try {
4 fakePaymentApi();
5 setIsSuccess(true);
Sets success to true
6 } catch {
7 setIsError(true);
Leaves both booleans true after retry
8 }
9}

On the first submission, the request fails, setting isError to true. The user clicks Subscribe again. This time the payment succeeds, and setIsSuccess(true) executes. On screen, the component renders both the "Payment failed" banner and the "Welcome, subscriber" message.

Can I keep isSubmitting, isSuccess, and isError as three booleans instead?

ANSWER

The code does not do what we wanted. Multiple boolean flags allow conflicting states to be active simultaneously.

When you use three independent boolean state variables, JavaScript evaluates $2^3 = 8$ potential combinations. However, out of those eight combinations, only four correspond to real-world visual screens:

  1. isSubmitting: false, isSuccess: false, isError: false -> typing state.
  2. isSubmitting: true, isSuccess: false, isError: false -> submitting state.
  3. isSubmitting: false, isSuccess: true, isError: false -> success state.
  4. isSubmitting: false, isSuccess: false, isError: true -> error state.

The remaining four combinations represent impossible states. A component cannot be simultaneously submitting and successful, nor can it be simultaneously an error and a success. In the code above, when the first payment attempt failed, isError became true. When the second attempt succeeded, the handler set isSuccess to true, but forgot to call setIsError(false). As a result, both isSuccess and isError were true at the same time, causing the JSX conditional checks {isError && <p>Payment failed</p>} and {isSuccess && <p>Welcome, subscriber</p>} to render both messages together.

The solution is to model mutually exclusive visual states with a single status string state variable: const [status, setStatus] = useState('typing') Because a string variable can hold exactly one value at any given instant, impossible states become physically impossible. When the success handler calls setStatus('success'), the old status 'error' is automatically replaced without requiring any manual cleanup.

State variables that change independently, such as user input (card) or dynamic server error text (error), should remain in separate state variables alongside status.

Multiple boolean combinations versus single status string
Three Booleans (2^3 = 8 combinations):
  isSubmitting | isSuccess | isError | Result
  -------------+-----------+---------+-------------------------------
  false        | true      | true    | IMPOSSIBLE: two messages show!
  true         | true      | false   | IMPOSSIBLE: loading & success

Single Status String (1 of 4 mutually exclusive states):
  'typing' | 'submitting' | 'error' | 'success'
  Result: exactly one valid screen rendered at all times
PRINCIPLE 3

Keep states that exclude each other in one status string

impossible state a combination of state values that makes no visual sense

Representing mutually exclusive visual modes with separate boolean variables allows contradictory flags to be active together, creating an impossible state where success and error messages share the screen. A single status string holding named states like 'typing', 'submitting', 'success', or 'error' eliminates impossible combinations because a variable can hold only one string at a time. Keep separate state only for values that change independently, such as typed text.

We should do this:
const [status, setStatus] = useState('typing');
const [text, setText] = useState('');
text changes independently
function handleSuccess() {
setStatus('success');
automatically replaces error or typing
}
We should not do this:
const [isError, setIsError] = useState(false);
const [isSuccess, setIsSuccess] = useState(false);
function handleSuccess() {
setIsSuccess(true);
isError stays true, showing both messages
}

Step 3
Finally, we build the form action controls
<src/components/FormControls.jsx>

In src/components/FormControls.jsx we build the action buttons:

FormControls.jsx
1export default function FormControls({ isSubmitting, onReset }) {
2 return (
3 <div className="form-actions">
4 <button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>Subscribe</button>
5 <button type="button" onClick={onReset} disabled={isSubmitting}>
6 Clear

Where do isSubmitting and onReset come from? They originate in PaywallModal.jsx, where isSubmitting is derived from status === 'submitting' and onReset is passed as a callback handler. Notice that FormControls owns zero local state; it simply holds a communication line to its parent component. When the user clicks the Clear button, the click triggers onReset, executing parent memory to reset status and card. This represents idiomatic inverse data flow.

What would break if we merged FormControls into PaywallModal or gave it local state? Inlining the buttons would bloat the modal container, and giving FormControls local state would trap submission flags inside a presentation leaf where the parent form could not read them. Maintaining FormControls as a pure, stateless leaf enforcing zero useState guarantees that action controls remain completely reusable and easy to test.

Component Summary

App

The application shell hosts the subscription flow without owning form state, maintaining container stability.

PaywallModal

The modal boundary manages the single status string, coordinates network payment submission, and conditionally renders screens.

FormControlsonSubscribe={handleSubmit}, onReset={handleReset}

The action controls render submission and reset buttons, forwarding user clicks upward.

Where you will meet this

In production frontend applications, reacting to input with state is fundamental across authentication modals, payment checkouts, search bars, and multistep wizards. A frequent production bug occurs when teams implement a checkout flow with separate booleans: an intermittent network failure sets isError(true), and when the customer retries successfully, the success handler displays the confirmation receipt while leaving the failure alert visible on screen. Adopting a single status string eliminates this bug completely.

Another common production bug occurs when developers write imperative DOM queries inside React event handlers, such as document.querySelector('#submit-btn').disabled = true If the network request throws an unhandled exception before reaching the catch block, the button remains permanently disabled, locking the user out of the application until they reload the page. Deriving disabled={status === 'submitting'} guarantees that the button restores its interactivity whenever status changes.

In technical interviews, interviewers use this question to evaluate whether a candidate thinks in imperative DOM commands or declarative state machines. Strong candidates immediately recognize that mutually exclusive visual modes must be modeled with a single string enum, explain how to mock states with props before wiring handlers, and describe how React reconciliation guarantees clean UI transitions.

For the interview

The Interview Question: How do you design a component that reacts to input with state instead of touching the DOM?

A senior response deconstructs the problem across four battle-tested architectural beats:

1. The Hidden Signal

The interviewer is probing whether you have transitioned from the imperative DOM manipulation habits of vanilla JavaScript to React's declarative state machine paradigm. Juniors often recite syntax or attempt to fix conflicting UI by querying DOM elements. Seniors demonstrate that React components are state-driven projection functions: you define the visual states first, store the current state in component memory, and let JSX describe what each state displays.

2. The Classic Trap

The primary misconception is managing mutually exclusive visual states with multiple independent boolean flags, such as isSubmitting, isSuccess, and isError. Multiple booleans create $2^N$ possible combinations, allowing impossible states where contradictory flags are true simultaneously. Candidates who rely on booleans frequently write buggy retry handlers that display error alerts and success banners at the same time.

3. What is Actually Going On

Idiomatic React design follows five structured steps:

  1. Identify visual states (typing, submitting, success, error).
  2. Mock each visual state with a status prop to visually audit screens before adding logic.
  3. Catalogue human triggers (typing, clicking) and computer triggers (network responses, timeouts).
  4. Model the active mode using a single status string state variable, keeping independent data like input text in separate state.
  5. Wire event handlers that only call setStatus to transition the component between visual states.

4. Where It Gets Tricky

Edge cases arise during asynchronous network handling and rapid user interaction. An async submission handler must run inside try...catch to catch rejected promises cleanly. Submit buttons must bind disabled={status === 'submitting'} to prevent duplicate submissions during in-flight requests. Finally, user input fields must remain controlled and separate from status so typing remains responsive while the component transitions across states.

Glossary

  • Visual State: A distinct visual presentation of a component determined by its underlying data and lifecycle status.
  • Single Status String: A state variable containing a string enum that guarantees only one mutually exclusive visual mode is active at any time.
  • Impossible State: A contradictory combination of state values that causes the user interface to display invalid or conflicting elements.
  • Human Input: User-driven interactions such as typing into form inputs, clicking buttons, or submitting forms.
  • Computer Input: System-driven interactions such as network responses returning, promises rejecting, or timers completing.
  • Living Styleguide: Rendering all mocked visual states of a component simultaneously to audit and verify layout across all lifecycle phases.

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

➔ ALWAYS list and mock visual states before wiring event handlers or network requests.

➔ ALWAYS represent mutually exclusive visual modes with a single status string state variable.

➔ IF handling asynchronous network transitions THEN wrap requests in try...catch and set status in each branch.

➔ IF disabling form actions during submission THEN derive disabled={status === 'submitting'} directly from state.

➔ NEVER mutate DOM elements or styles directly with document.querySelector inside React handlers.

DO THIS:

code.txt
1function PaywallModal() {
2 const [status, setStatus] = useState('typing');
3 async function handleSubmit(e) {
4 e.preventDefault();
5 setStatus('submitting');
6 try {
7 await submitPayment();
8 setStatus('success');
9 } catch {
10 setStatus('error');
11 }
12 }
13 if (status === 'success') return <p>Welcome, subscriber!</p>;
14 return (
15 <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
16 <button disabled={status === 'submitting'}>Subscribe</button>
17 {status === 'error' && <p>Payment failed</p>}
18 </form>
19 );
20}

DO NOT DO THIS:

code.txt
1function PaywallModal() {
2 function handleSubmit(e) {
3 e.preventDefault();
4 document.querySelector('#btn').disabled = true;
5 submitPayment()
6 .then(() => {
7 document.querySelector('#welcome').style.display = 'block';
8 })
9 .catch(() => {
10 document.querySelector('#error').style.display = 'block';
11 });
12 }
13 return (
14 <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
15 <button id="btn">Subscribe</button>
16 <p id="error" style={{ display: 'none' }}>Payment failed</p>
17 <p id="welcome" style={{ display: 'none' }}>Welcome!</p>
18 </form>
19 );
20}
